knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vector-Valued Radial Continuity and Radial-Directional Derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise extension of radial continuity and radial-directional differentiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n):U\subseteq\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n\). The mapping \(\alpha\) is radial-continuous if every component \(\alpha_i\) is radial-continuous. It is radial-directionally differentiable at \(x^0\in U\) if every \(\alpha_i\) is radial-directionally differentiable there, and its radial-directional derivative is \(\mathrm d\alpha(x^0;r)=(\mathrm d\alpha_1(x^0;r),\ldots,\mathrm d\alpha_n(x^0;r))^\top\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Radial continuity and radial-directional differentiability of a vector-valued mapping are defined componentwise, and the vector derivative is formed from the component derivatives.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm d\alpha(x^0;r)=\bigl(\mathrm d\alpha_1(x^0;r),\ldots,\mathrm d\alpha_n(x^0;r)\bigr)^\top\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent differentiability criteria for a convex function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise equivalence at an interior point of the effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\operatorname{Conv}\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(x\in\operatorname{intdom}f\). The following are equivalent: (i) the directional-derivative mapping \(d\mapsto\lim_{t\downarrow0}[f(x+td)-f(x)]/t\) is linear in \(d\); (ii) there exists a basis with coordinates \((\xi^1,\ldots,\xi^n)\) in which every partial derivative \(\partial f/\partial\xi^i(x)\), \(i=1,\ldots,n\), exists; (iii) \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex function at an interior-domain point, differentiability is equivalent both to linearity of the one-sided directional-derivative map and to the existence of all coordinate partial derivatives in some basis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((i)\iff(ii)\iff(iii)\), where the three conditions are linear directional differentiation, existence of all partial derivatives in some basis, and differentiability at \(x\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex functions are differentiable almost everywhere
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The exceptional set is measured only inside the interior of the effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\operatorname{Conv}\mathbb{R}^n\). Then \(\{x\in\operatorname{intdom}f: f\text{ is not differentiable at }x\}\) has Lebesgue measure zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-dimensional convex function fails to be differentiable only on a Lebesgue-null subset of the interior of its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda^n\bigl(\{x\in\operatorname{intdom}f:f\text{ is not differentiable at }x\}\bigr)=0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interior characterization of epi-Lipschitzian convex sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes pointwise epi-Lipschitz regularity of a convex set by nonemptiness of its ambient interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subset X\) be convex. Then \[\bigl(\forall\bar x\in\Omega,\ \Omega\text{ is epi-Lipschitzian around }\bar x\bigr)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{int}\Omega\neq\varnothing.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex set is epi-Lipschitzian around every one of its points if and only if it has nonempty ambient interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\forall\bar x\in\Omega,\ \Omega\text{ is epi-Lipschitzian around }\bar x)\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{int}\Omega\neq\varnothing.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scalar Radial Continuity and Radial-Directional Derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for a real-valued function on an open Euclidean domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be open, \(x^0\in U\), and \(\alpha:U\to\mathbb R\). For a unit vector \(r\), \(\alpha\) is radial-continuous at \(x^0\) in direction \(r\) if the finite limit \(\alpha_r(x^0):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\alpha(x^0+tr)\) exists; it is radial-continuous at \(x^0\) if this holds for every unit \(r\). It is radial-directionally differentiable at \(x^0\) if there is a positively homogeneous mapping \(\mathrm d\alpha(x^0;\cdot):\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) such that, for every unit \(r\), \(\alpha(x^0+tr)-\alpha_r(x^0)=t\,\mathrm d\alpha(x^0;r)+o_r(t)\) as \(t\downarrow0\), where \(o_r(t)/t\to0\). The mapping \(\mathrm d\alpha(x^0;\cdot)\) is uniquely determined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Radial continuity means that the one-sided limit along each specified ray exists. Radial-directional differentiability means that deviations from those radial limits admit a first-order expansion with a unique positively homogeneous derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha_r(x^0)=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\alpha(x^0+tr)\text{ exists, and when the expansion holds }\mathrm d\alpha(x^0;\cdot)\text{ is the unique radial-directional derivative}\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tangential gradient via the canonical nearest-point extension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the same intrinsic gradient using the canonical extension that is constant along normal fibers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume that \(\Gamma\) is compact and \(\exists h>0\) such that \(b_\Omega\in C^2(S_{2h}(\Gamma))\). For \(f\in C^1(\Gamma)\), define
\[
\nabla_\Gamma f:=\left.\nabla(f\circ p)\right|_\Gamma.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the tubular-neighborhood smoothness assumptions, the tangential gradient of a C1 surface function is the boundary restriction of the ambient gradient of its canonical nearest-point extension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nabla_\Gamma f=\left.\nabla(f\circ p)\right|_\Gamma

children.title: Contingent Tangency
children.top_down_role: Feasible-direction behavior obtained through local sequences.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[T_C(\bar x)=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\liminf_{t\downarrow0}\frac{d(\bar x+t v,C)}{t}=0\right\}.\]

notation.meaning: Euclidean distance from a point to the set C
contingent tangent cone to C at the reference point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional distance characterization of the contingent tangent cone.

source_refs.locator: B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty closed set \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\bar x\in C\), the contingent tangent cone is
\[T_C(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\liminf_{t\downarrow0}\frac{d(\bar x+t v,C)}{t}=0\right\}.\]
Thus a direction is contingent when arbitrarily small positive steps along it can be corrected by an error of order \(o(t)\) to reach \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The contingent cone contains directions along which arbitrarily small positive steps approach the set with error negligible relative to the step size.
knowledge_statements.title: Contingent Tangency

source_witnesses.locator: B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Union-of-branches example showing that contingent tangency can be nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=(\mathbb R\times\{0\})\cup(\{0\}\times\mathbb R)\subset\mathbb R^2\). Then \[T_C(0)=C,\] which is nonconvex: \((1,0),(0,1)\in T_C(0)\), but \((1/2,1/2)\notin T_C(0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the crossing of the coordinate axes, the contingent cone is the nonconvex union of the axes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[T_C(0)=C\text{ is nonconvex}.\]
knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Convexity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Conic Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic finite-dimensional structure of the contingent tangent cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) and \(\bar x\in C\), \(T_C(\bar x)\) is a closed cone containing zero: \[0\in T_C(\bar x),\qquad \lambda T_C(\bar x)\subset T_C(\bar x)\ (\lambda\ge0),\qquad \overline{T_C(\bar x)}=T_C(\bar x).\] It need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The contingent tangent cone is closed and positively homogeneous but need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[0\in T_C(\bar x),\quad \lambda T_C(\bar x)\subset T_C(\bar x)\ (\lambda\ge0),\quad \overline{T_C(\bar x)}=T_C(\bar x).\]

children.title: Bouligand Tangency
children.top_down_role: Bouligand terminology and its associated tangent-cone viewpoint.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[T_C^B(\bar x)=\{v:\exists\,x_k\in C,\ t_k\downarrow0,\ (x_k-\bar x)/t_k\to v\}=T_C(\bar x).\]

notation.meaning: Bouligand tangent cone to C at the reference point
contingent tangent cone defined by the distance characterization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential finite-dimensional definition; Bouligand and contingent tangency coincide here.

source_refs.locator: B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Bouligand tangent cone to \(C\) at \(\bar x\) is
\[T_C^B(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists\,t_k\downarrow0,\ \exists\,x_k\in C,\ \frac{x_k-\bar x}{t_k}\to v\right\}.\]
Equivalently, one may require vectors \(v_k\to v\) with \(\bar x+t_kv_k\in C\). In finite dimensions this cone equals the contingent cone \(T_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Bouligand tangent is the limit of rescaled feasible displacements. In finite dimensions this sequential cone is the contingent tangent cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Bouligand Tangency

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\bar x\in C\), the Bouligand tangent cone \(T_C^B(\bar x)\) is a closed cone. For a general nonconvex set \(C\), it need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Bouligand tangent cone is closed and positively homogeneous, but it may be nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_C^B(\bar x)\) is a closed cone and need not be convex.

children.title: Sequential Tangency Variants
children.top_down_role: Coincidence and distinction among nearby sequential tangent constructions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[T_C(\bar x)=\mathop{\mathrm{Limsup}}_{t\downarrow0}\frac{C-\bar x}{t},\qquad T_C^A(\bar x)=\mathop{\mathrm{Liminf}}_{t\downarrow0}\frac{C-\bar x}{t}.\]

notation.meaning: outer and inner Painleve-Kuratowski set limits

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer- and inner-limit sequential formulations for positive scales.

source_refs.locator: B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The principal sequential variants are
\[T_C(\bar x)=\mathop{\mathrm{Limsup}}_{t\downarrow0}\frac{C-\bar x}{t},\qquad T_C^A(\bar x)=\mathop{\mathrm{Liminf}}_{t\downarrow0}\frac{C-\bar x}{t}.\]
Accordingly, \(v\in T_C(\bar x)\) requires some sequence \(t_k\downarrow0\) and some \(v_k\to v\) with \(\bar x+t_kv_k\in C\). By contrast, \(v\in T_C^A(\bar x)\) requires such correcting vectors \(v_k\to v\) for every prescribed sequence \(t_k\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outer-limit tangency uses some vanishing scale sequence, whereas inner-limit tangency must work along every prescribed vanishing scale sequence.
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Tangency Variants

source_witnesses.locator: B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex-Set Coincidence of Sequential Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coincidence of fixed-base outer- and inner-limit tangency for convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is convex and \(\bar x\in C\), then \[T_C^A(\bar x)=T_C(\bar x)=\overline{\operatorname{cone}(C-\bar x)}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex set, adjacent and contingent tangency coincide with the closure of the cone of feasible displacements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[T_C^A(\bar x)=T_C(\bar x)=\overline{\operatorname{cone}(C-\bar x)}.\]

notation.meaning: conic hull of feasible displacements from the reference point

children.title: Adjacent Tangency
children.top_down_role: Tangential behavior requiring feasibility across prescribed vanishing scales.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[T_C^A(\bar x)=\left\{v:\forall\,t_k\downarrow0\ \exists\,v_k\to v\text{ with }\bar x+t_kv_k\in C\right\}\subset T_C(\bar x).\]

notation.meaning: adjacent tangent cone to C at the reference point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adjacent cone defined by persistence across every positive scale sequence.

source_refs.locator: B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The adjacent tangent cone to \(C\) at \(\bar x\) is
\[T_C^A(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\forall\,t_k\downarrow0\ \exists\,v_k\to v\text{ such that }\bar x+t_kv_k\in C\right\}.\]
Equivalently, \(d(\bar x+t v,C)/t\to0\) as \(t\downarrow0\). Since persistence for every vanishing scale implies existence along some scale, \(T_C^A(\bar x)\subset T_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adjacent tangent remains approximately feasible along every prescribed sequence of positive step sizes, so every adjacent tangent is contingent.
knowledge_statements.title: Adjacent Tangency

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The adjacent tangent cone is closed and positively homogeneous but need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[T_C^A(\bar x)\text{ is a closed cone, not necessarily convex}.\]

children.title: Inner Tangency
children.top_down_role: Tangential behavior stable under nearby base-point perturbations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[T_C^{\mathrm{in}}(\bar x)=\left\{v:\exists\,\varepsilon,\delta>0\ \forall\,t\in(0,\delta),\ \forall\,w\in v+\varepsilon\mathbb B,\ \bar x+t w\in C\right\}.\]

notation.meaning: inner tangent cone under the uniform-neighborhood convention

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: uniform directional-neighborhood definition commonly called the inner or hypertangent cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the uniform-neighborhood convention, also called hypertangency in some texts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the uniform-neighborhood convention, the inner tangent cone is
\[T_C^{\mathrm{in}}(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists\,\varepsilon>0,\ \exists\,\delta>0\ \text{such that }\bar x+t w\in C\ \forall\,t\in(0,\delta),\ \forall\,w\in v+\varepsilon\mathbb B\right\}.\]
Thus feasibility persists simultaneously under all sufficiently small positive steps and all sufficiently small directional perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inner tangent has a whole neighborhood of nearby directions whose sufficiently short rays from the reference point remain feasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Inner Tangency

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uniform directional-neighborhood construction is commonly called a hypertangent or strict feasible-direction construction, while “inner tangent cone” is also used for other objects. An authoritative source with a precise definition is required to establish the convention intended by this leaf.

knowledge_statements.title: Persistence Gap Between Tangency Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A closed sparse subset of the line separates contingent from adjacent tangency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a_k:=2^{-2^k}\), \(C:=\{0\}\cup\{a_k:k\in\mathbb N\}\subset\mathbb R\), and \(\bar x:=0\). For this closed sparse set, \[1\in T_C(0)\setminus T_C^A(0).\] Thus contingent tangency need not persist across every vanishing positive scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the specified supergeometrically sparse closed set, direction 1 is contingent at zero but is not adjacent there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[1\in T_C(0)\setminus T_C^A(0).\]

children.title: Clarke Tangency
children.top_down_role: Robust convexified tangential geometry.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[T_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(\bar x)=\left\{v:\forall\,x_k\to_C\bar x,\ \forall\,t_k\downarrow0\ \exists\,v_k\to v,\ x_k+t_kv_k\in C\right\}.\]

notation.meaning: Clarke tangent cone to C at the reference point
convergence to the reference point through points of C

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Robust sequential definition in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.

source_refs.locator: B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Clarke tangent cone to \(C\) at \(\bar x\) is
\[T_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\forall\,x_k\to_C\bar x,\ \forall\,t_k\downarrow0\ \exists\,v_k\to v\text{ with }x_k+t_kv_k\in C\right\}.\]
It is a closed convex cone and satisfies \(T_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(\bar x)\subset T_C^A(\bar x)\subset T_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Clarke tangent remains approximately feasible under simultaneous perturbations of the base point and step size; the resulting cone is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Clarke Tangency

source_witnesses.locator: B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform Distance Characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent finite-dimensional robust-distance formulation of Clarke tangency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A vector \(v\in\mathbb R^n\) belongs to the Clarke tangent cone exactly when
\[
\lim_{\substack{x\to\bar x,\ x\in C\\t\downarrow0}}\frac{d_C(x+tv)}{t}=0.
\]
Equivalently, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there are a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(\delta>0\) such that
\[
d_C(x+tv)\le\varepsilon t
\quad\text{for all }x\in C\cap U\text{ and }0<t<\delta.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Clarke tangent has uniformly negligible first-order feasibility error for every nearby base point and every sufficiently small positive step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\in T_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(\bar x)\iff \lim_{x\to_C\bar x,\,t\downarrow0}d_C(x+tv)/t=0\).

notation.meaning: Clarke tangent cone to C at the reference point

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Distance Characterization

children.title: Radial Cones
children.top_down_role: Feasible rays generated directly from the reference point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Short-Ray and Conic-Displacement Conventions Differ
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between two radial-cone conventions on a nonconvex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C:=\{0\}\cup\{1/k:k\in\mathbb N\}\subset\mathbb R\) and \(\bar x=0\). Then \[\operatorname{cone}(C-\bar x)=\mathbb R_+,\qquad \{v:\exists\delta>0\ \forall t\in[0,\delta],\ \bar x+tv\in C\}=\{0\}.\] Thus the conic-displacement and whole-short-ray conventions need not agree for a nonconvex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a sequence accumulating at zero, the conic-displacement cone is the nonnegative ray, whereas the whole-short-ray cone is only zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cone}(C-\bar x)=\mathbb R_+\) while the whole-short-ray cone equals \(\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Short-Ray and Conic-Displacement Conventions Differ

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[R_C(\bar x)=\{v:\exists\,\delta>0\ \forall\,t\in[0,\delta],\ \bar x+t v\in C\}.\]

notation.meaning: radial feasible-direction cone to C at the reference point

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard feasible-direction version of the radial cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the short feasible-ray convention for radial directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The radial cone to \(C\) at \(\bar x\) is
\[R_C(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists\,\delta>0\text{ such that }\bar x+t v\in C\ \forall\,t\in[0,\delta]\right\}.\]
Every radial direction is contingent, so \(R_C(\bar x)\subset T_C(\bar x)\). If \(C\) is convex, then \(R_C(\bar x)=\operatorname{cone}(C-\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A radial direction generates a short feasible ray from the reference point. For convex sets, radial directions are precisely conic feasible displacements.
knowledge_statements.title: Radial Cones

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula defines directions whose entire sufficiently short ray is feasible. Many standard references instead define the radial cone as \(\operatorname{cone}(C-\bar x)\), which only requires one feasible positive displacement for a general nonconvex set. A source is needed to confirm the intended convention.

children.top_down_role: First-order constraint surrogates for feasible-direction geometry.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar Multiplier Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual representation of the active-gradient linearized cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the linearized cone of a finite differentiable constraint system at a feasible point \(\bar x\), \[L_C(\bar x)^\circ=\left\{\sum_{i\in I(\bar x)}\lambda_i\nabla g_i(\bar x)+\sum_{j=1}^p\mu_j\nabla h_j(\bar x):\lambda_i\ge0,\ \mu_j\in\mathbb R\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of the linearized cone is generated by nonnegative active-inequality gradients and arbitrary equality-gradient combinations.
assumptions_latex: \(g_i,h_j:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) are differentiable at the feasible point \(\bar x\).
\(L_C(\bar x)\) is the active-gradient linearized cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[L_C(\bar x)^\circ=\left\{\sum_{i\in I(\bar x)}\lambda_i\nabla g_i(\bar x)+\sum_j\mu_j\nabla h_j(\bar x):\lambda_i\ge0,\ \mu_j\in\mathbb R\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.title: Polar Multiplier Representation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedral Structure of the Linearized Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite smooth equality-and-inequality constraint systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite differentiable constraint system at a feasible point \(\bar x\), the active-gradient linearized cone \(L_C(\bar x)\) is a closed convex polyhedral cone determined solely by the equality gradients and active inequality gradients at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The linearized cone is a closed convex polyhedral cone determined by the equality and active-inequality gradients.
assumptions_latex: \(g_i,h_j:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) are differentiable at \(\bar x\).
\(L_C(\bar x)\) is the active-gradient linearized cone of a finite constraint system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_C(\bar x)\) is a closed convex polyhedral cone determined by \(\{\nabla g_i(\bar x):i\in I(\bar x)\}\) and \(\{\nabla h_j(\bar x):1\le j\le p\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Structure of the Linearized Cone

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lineality Space of the Linearized Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural description of the active-gradient cone for a finite differentiable constraint system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the active-gradient linearized cone \(L_C(\bar x)\), \[\operatorname{lin}L_C(\bar x):=L_C(\bar x)\cap(-L_C(\bar x))=\left\{v:\nabla g_i(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}v=0\ \forall i\in I(\bar x),\ \nabla h_j(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}v=0\ \forall j\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The reversible directions of the linearized cone are exactly those orthogonal to every active inequality gradient and every equality gradient.
assumptions_latex: \(g_i,h_j:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) are differentiable at the feasible point \(\bar x\).
\(L_C(\bar x)\) is the active-gradient linearized cone of the finite constraint system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{lin}L_C(\bar x)=\{v:\nabla g_i(\bar x)^\mathsf Tv=0\ (i\in I(\bar x)),\ \nabla h_j(\bar x)^\mathsf Tv=0\ (1\le j\le p)\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Lineality Space of the Linearized Cone

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[L_C(\bar x)=\{v:\nabla g_i(\bar x)^\top v\le0\ (i\in I(\bar x)),\ \nabla h_j(\bar x)^\top v=0\ (j=1,\ldots,p)\}.\]

notation.meaning: active inequality index set at the reference point
linearized cone of the constraint system

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard smooth nonlinear-programming linearized cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional equality-and-inequality constraint system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I(\bar x):=\{i:g_i(\bar x)=0\}\). The linearized cone of the constraint system at \(\bar x\) is
\[L_C(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\nabla g_i(\bar x)^\top v\le0\ \forall\,i\in I(\bar x),\ \nabla h_j(\bar x)^\top v=0\ \forall\,j\right\}.\]
Differentiability of the constraints yields the general inclusion \(T_C(\bar x)\subset L_C(\bar x)\); equality requires additional regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The linearized cone consists of directions satisfying the first-order active inequalities and equality equations. Every contingent tangent satisfies these linearized constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Linearized Cones

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The smooth finite-dimensional linearized cone and the inclusion \(T_C(\bar x)\subset L_C(\bar x)\) are standard and precisely stated, but no inspectable source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Linearization Exactness
children.top_down_role: Regularity regimes where linearized geometry recovers tangential geometry.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedral Linearization Exactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact radial, contingent, and linearized geometry for affine equality-and-inequality systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b,\ Hx=c\},\qquad \bar x\in C,\] and let \(R_C(\bar x)\) denote the feasible-ray cone \(\{v:\exists\delta>0,\ \bar x+t v\in C\ \forall t\in[0,\delta]\}\). With \(I(\bar x)=\{i:A_i\bar x=b_i\}\), \[R_C(\bar x)=T_C(\bar x)=L_C(\bar x)=\{v:A_i v\le0\ (i\in I(\bar x)),\ Hv=0\}.\] No additional constraint qualification is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a polyhedral constraint set, the feasible-ray, contingent, and active-constraint linearized cones coincide without an additional qualification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[R_C(\bar x)=T_C(\bar x)=L_C(\bar x)=\{v:A_i v\le0\ (i\in I(\bar x)),\ Hv=0\}.\]

notation.meaning: feasible-ray radial cone under the convention stated in the record

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Linearization Exactness

knowledge_statements.statement_title: MFCQ Tangent–Linearized Exactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional nonlinear constraints under Mangasarian–Fromovitz regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[C=\{x:g_i(x)\le0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ h_j(x)=0\ (j=1,\ldots,q)\},\] where the constraint functions are continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\in C\). Suppose the equality gradients are linearly independent and there exists \(d\) satisfying \[\nabla h_j(\bar x)^\top d=0\quad\forall j,\qquad \nabla g_i(\bar x)^\top d<0\quad\forall i\in I(\bar x).\] Then \[T_C(\bar x)=L_C(\bar x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mangasarian–Fromovitz regularity makes the active first-order linearization exact for the contingent cone.
assumptions_latex: The constraint functions are continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
The equality gradients at \(\bar x\) are linearly independent.
A direction strictly decreases every active inequality while satisfying the linearized equalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_C(\bar x)=L_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.title: MFCQ Tangent–Linearized Exactness

assumptions_latex: \(g_i\) and \(h_j\) are continuously differentiable near the feasible point \(\bar x\).
The vectors \(\nabla h_j(\bar x)\) are linearly independent.
There exists \(d\) with \(\nabla h_j(\bar x)^\top d=0\) for all \(j\) and \(\nabla g_i(\bar x)^\top d<0\) for every \(i\in I(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[T_C(\bar x)=L_C(\bar x)=\overline{R_C(\bar x)}.\]

notation.meaning: contingent, linearized, and radial cones, respectively

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical MFCQ tangent-cone exactness theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mangasarian-Fromovitz exactness for smooth finite-dimensional constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be the smooth constraint set used in the linearized-cone definition. Suppose the equality gradients at \(\bar x\) are linearly independent and there exists \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfying
\[\nabla h_j(\bar x)^\top d=0\quad\forall j,\qquad \nabla g_i(\bar x)^\top d<0\quad\forall i\in I(\bar x).\]
Then the Mangasarian-Fromovitz constraint qualification holds, and the first-order linearization is exact:
\[T_C(\bar x)=L_C(\bar x)=\overline{R_C(\bar x)}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the Mangasarian-Fromovitz constraint qualification, the contingent cone equals the linearized cone and the closure of the radial cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Linearization Exactness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The MFCQ exactness claim is standard for the stated smooth constraint system, but it lacks an inspectable source. The equality involving \(\overline{R_C(\bar x)}\) also depends on which radial-cone convention is adopted.

children.title: Linearization Gaps
children.top_down_role: Constraint geometries where linearized directions overestimate feasible tangency.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Odd-Power Degeneracy Produces a Strict Linearization Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth scalar inequality with a nonisolated feasible side and vanishing active gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g(x)=x^3\), \(C=\{x:g(x)\le0\}=(-\infty,0]\), and \(\bar x=0\). Since \(g'(0)=0\), \(L_C(0)=\mathbb R\), whereas \[R_C(0)=T_C(0)=(-\infty,0]\subsetneq L_C(0).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For x cubed at most zero, the zero active gradient makes every direction linearly feasible although only nonpositive directions are tangent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_C(0)=T_C(0)=(-\infty,0]\subsetneq L_C(0)=\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.title: Odd-Power Degeneracy Produces a Strict Linearization Gap

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Universal Tangent-to-Linearized Inclusion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional equality-and-inequality systems without a constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[C=\{x:g_i(x)\le0,\ h_j(x)=0\},\] with every constraint differentiable at \(\bar x\in C\), define \[L_C(\bar x)=\{v:\nabla g_i(\bar x)^\top v\le0\ (i\in I(\bar x)),\ \nabla h_j(\bar x)^\top v=0\}.\] Then \[T_C(\bar x)\subseteq L_C(\bar x).\] The inclusion can be strict under a degenerate constraint representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every contingent direction satisfies the active first-order constraints, but degeneracy can introduce spurious linearized directions.
assumptions_latex: All constraint functions are differentiable at the feasible point \(\bar x\).
\(L_C(\bar x)\) is the displayed active-constraint linearized cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_C(\bar x)\subseteq L_C(\bar x)\), with possible strict inclusion.
knowledge_statements.title: Universal Tangent-to-Linearized Inclusion
Linearization Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degenerate smooth inequality showing strict linearized-cone overestimation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be given by \(g(x):=x^2\), let \(C:=\{x\in\mathbb R:g(x)\le 0\}=\{0\}\), and take \(\bar x:=0\). The associated cones satisfy \[T_C(0)=R_C(0)=\{0\}\subsetneq L_C(0)=\mathbb R.\] This is a strict linearization gap for a degenerate active constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the constraint x squared at most zero, the tangent and radial cones at zero contain only zero, whereas the linearized cone is the whole real line.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[T_C(0)=R_C(0)=\{0\}\subsetneq L_C(0)=\mathbb R.\]

children.title: Proximal Normals
children.top_down_role: Normal geometry generated by proximal and nearest-point constructions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[N_C^P(\bar x)=\{\lambda(y-\bar x):\lambda\ge0,\ \bar x\in P_C(y)\}.\]

notation.meaning: proximal normal cone to C at the reference point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nearest-point definition with its equivalent quadratic support inequality.

source_refs.locator: E. Proximal Normals and Polarity p. 212

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The proximal normal cone to \(C\) at \(\bar x\) is
\[N_C^P(\bar x):=\left\{\lambda(y-\bar x):\lambda\ge0,\ \bar x\in P_C(y)\right\}.\]
Equivalently, \(v\in N_C^P(\bar x)\) exactly when there exists \(\sigma\ge0\) such that
\[\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle\le\sigma\lVert x-\bar x\rVert^2\qquad\forall\,x\in C.\]
Thus a proximal normal is generated by a point having \(\bar x\) as a nearest point of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximal normal points from a nearest point of the set toward an external point and equivalently satisfies a quadratic support inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Normals

source_witnesses.locator: E. Proximal Normals and Polarity p. 212

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity and Possible Nonclosedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic algebraic structure and sharp closure boundary for proximal normals to a general closed nonconvex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\bar x\in C\), \(N_C^P(\bar x)\) is a convex cone. For a general closed nonconvex set, this cone need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximal normal cone is convex and positively homogeneous, but it may fail to be closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_C^P(\bar x)\) is a convex cone, but it is not necessarily closed.

notation.meaning: proximal normal cone to C at the reference point

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity and Possible Nonclosedness

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Limiting-Normal Recovery from Proximal Normals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional outer-limit relation connecting projection-generated normals with the limiting normal cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a closed set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) and \(\bar x\in C\),
\[
N_C(\bar x)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{x\to_C\bar x}N_C^P(x).
\]
Equivalently, \(v\in N_C(\bar x)\) exactly when there are \(x_k\in C\) and \(v_k\in N_C^P(x_k)\) such that \(x_k\to\bar x\) and \(v_k\to v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every limiting normal is a limit of proximal normals at nearby set points, and every such limit is limiting normal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_C(\bar x)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{x\to_C\bar x}N_C^P(x)\).

notation.meaning: proximal normal cone to C at x
limiting normal cone to C at the reference point

knowledge_statements.title: Limiting-Normal Recovery from Proximal Normals

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variational characterization of Fréchet epsilon-normals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local-maximization characterization for approximate regular normals to arbitrary sets in Banach spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X$ be a Banach space, $\Omega\subset X$, $\bar x\in\Omega$, $\varepsilon\ge 0$, and $x^*\in X^*$. Then $x^*\in\widehat N_\varepsilon(\bar x;\Omega)$ if and only if, for every $\gamma>0$, the function $\psi_\gamma(x):=\langle x^*,x-\bar x\rangle-(\varepsilon+\gamma)\|x-\bar x\|$ attains a local maximum relative to $\Omega$ at $\bar x$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual vector is an epsilon-Fréchet normal at a point exactly when, for every positive slack gamma, its linear support function minus the norm penalty with coefficient epsilon plus gamma has a relative local maximum there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\in\widehat N_\varepsilon(\bar x;\Omega)\iff \forall\gamma>0,\;\bar x\text{ is a local maximizer of }\psi_\gamma\text{ relative to }\Omega

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between a proximal subgradient and a normalized proximal normal to the epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let x\in\operatorname{dom}f. Then \[\zeta\in\partial_P f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(\zeta,-1)\in N^P_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any point x in the domain of f, a vector ζ is a proximal subgradient of f at x if and only if (ζ,−1) is a proximal normal to the epigraph of f at (x,f(x)).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \zeta\in\partial_P f(x)\iff(\zeta,-1)\in N^P_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x))

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proximal-Normal Formula for the Normal Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential representation of the normal cone of a closed Euclidean set using nearby proximal normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every closed set $S\subset\mathbf E$ and every $x\in S$, $$N_S(x)=\operatorname{conv}\left\{\lim_{r\to\infty}y_r\ \middle|\ y_r\in N_S^p(x_r),\ x_r\in S,\ x_r\to x\right\}.$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a point of a closed set, the normal cone is the convex hull of all limits of proximal normals based at points of the set converging to that point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_S(x)=\operatorname{conv}\left\{\lim_{r\to\infty}y_r\mid y_r\in N_S^p(x_r),\ x_r\in S,\ x_r\to x\right\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normals to Cartesian products
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The identities apply componentwise at every point of the product set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega_i\subset X_i\) and let \(\bar x=(\bar x_1,\bar x_2)\in\Omega_1\times\Omega_2\). Then \(\widehat N(\bar x;\Omega_1\times\Omega_2)=\widehat N(\bar x_1;\Omega_1)\times\widehat N(\bar x_2;\Omega_2)\) and \(N(\bar x;\Omega_1\times\Omega_2)=N(\bar x_1;\Omega_1)\times N(\bar x_2;\Omega_2)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Distance lower bound along a delta-proximal normal
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A local metric consequence of approximate proximal normality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\delta\ge0\), \(x_0\in S\), and \(h\in PN_S^\delta(x_0)\). Then, for every sufficiently small \(t>0\), \[\operatorname{dist}(x_0+th,S)\ge t(1-2\delta)\|h\|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a delta-proximal normal h, sufficiently small positive displacements from x0 along h have distance from S at least t times (1−2 delta) times the norm of h.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dist}(x_0+th,S)\ge t(1-2\delta)\|h\|\quad\text{for all sufficiently small }t>0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proximal and delta-proximal normals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact projection-based normals and their relative-error approximation for a closed set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\subset X\) be closed and \(x_0\in E\). A vector \(h\in X\) is a proximal normal to \(E\) at \(x_0\) if there exists \(\tau>0\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(x_0+\tau h,E)=\tau\lVert h\rVert.\] The set of proximal normals is denoted \(PN_E(x_0)\). For \(\delta\ge0\), \(h\) is a \(\delta\)-proximal normal if \[\operatorname{dist}(h,PN_E(x_0))\le\delta\lVert h\rVert,\] and their set is denoted \(PN_E^\delta(x_0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximal normal is a vector for which some displacement from x0 along that vector has distance to E equal to the displacement length. A delta-proximal normal is within relative error delta of the proximal-normal set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h\in PN_E(x_0)\iff\exists\tau>0:\operatorname{dist}(x_0+\tau h,E)=\tau\lVert h\rVert;\quad h\in PN_E^\delta(x_0)\iff\operatorname{dist}(h,PN_E(x_0))\le\delta\lVert h\rVert

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional sequential definition of the Fréchet normal cone.

source_refs.locator: B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Fréchet normal cone to \(C\) at \(\bar x\) is
\[
\widehat N_C(\bar x):=\left\{v\in X:\limsup_{\substack{x\to\bar x,\ x\in C\\x\ne\bar x}}\frac{\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle}{\|x-\bar x\|}\le 0\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(v\in\widehat N_C(\bar x)\) precisely when
\[
\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle\le o(\|x-\bar x\|)\quad\text{as }x\to\bar x\text{ within }C.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector is Fréchet normal when its pairing with every feasible displacement is nonpositive to first order.
knowledge_statements.title: Fréchet Normal Geometry

source_witnesses.locator: B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Locality of Fréchet Normal Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The cone depends only on the germ of the set at the reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C,D\subset X\) agree in a neighborhood of \(\bar x\), so that \(C\cap U=D\cap U\) for some neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\), then \[\widehat N_C(\bar x)=\widehat N_D(\bar x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing a set away from the reference point does not change its Fréchet normal cone there.
assumptions_latex: \(C\cap U=D\cap U\) for some neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat N_C(\bar x)=\widehat N_D(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Locality of Fréchet Normal Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Convex Conicity and Extreme Local Cases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic algebraic structure and elementary local extremes of the Fréchet normal cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(C\subset X\) and \(\bar x\in C\), \(\widehat N_C(\bar x)\) is a closed convex cone containing \(0\). If \(\bar x\in\operatorname{int}C\), then \(\widehat N_C(\bar x)=\{0\}\); if \(\bar x\) is isolated in \(C\), then \(\widehat N_C(\bar x)=X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fréchet normals form a closed convex cone, equal to zero at interior points and the whole space at isolated points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat N_C(\bar x)\) is a closed convex cone; interior points give \(\{0\}\), and isolated points give \(X\).
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex Conicity and Extreme Local Cases

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fréchet Epsilon-Normal and Tangent-Cone Polar Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polar estimates for Fréchet epsilon-normal and normal cones of an arbitrary subset of a Banach space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let X be a Banach space, let \Omega\subset X with \bar x\in\Omega, and let \varepsilon\ge 0. Then
\[
\widehat N_\varepsilon(\bar x;\Omega)\subset\left\{x^*\in X^*\mid \langle x^*,v\rangle\le\varepsilon\|v\|\text{ for all }v\in T(\bar x;\Omega)\right\}.
\]
This inclusion is an equality if X is finite-dimensional. Moreover,
\[
\widehat N(\bar x;\Omega)\subset\left\{x^*\in X^*\mid \langle x^*,v\rangle\le0\text{ for all }v\in T_W(\bar x;\Omega)\right\},
\]
and the latter inclusion is an equality if X is reflexive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every Fréchet epsilon-normal pairs with every contingent direction by at most epsilon times the direction norm; this characterization is exact in finite dimensions. Every Fréchet normal belongs to the negative polar of the weak contingent cone, with equality in reflexive spaces.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximate Fréchet and limiting normal cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the convention that every normal cone is empty outside the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Banach space and let \(\varnothing\ne\Omega\subset X\). For \(x\in\Omega\) and \(\varepsilon\ge0\), define \(\widehat N_\varepsilon(x;\Omega):=\{x^*\in X^*: \limsup_{u\overset{\Omega}{\to}x}\langle x^*,u-x\rangle/\|u-x\|\le\varepsilon\}\). The cone \(\widehat N(x;\Omega):=\widehat N_0(x;\Omega)\) is the Fréchet normal cone. For \(\bar x\in\Omega\), \(x^*\in N(\bar x;\Omega)\) precisely when there exist \(\varepsilon_k\downarrow0\), \(x_k\overset{\Omega}{\to}\bar x\), and \(x_k^*\overset{w^*}{\to}x^*\) with \(x_k^*\in\widehat N_{\varepsilon_k}(x_k;\Omega)\) for every \(k\). If \(x\notin\Omega\), set \(\widehat N_\varepsilon(x;\Omega)=N(x;\Omega)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An epsilon-normal asymptotically supports the set up to an error proportional to distance. Fréchet normals are the zero-error case, while limiting normals are weak-star limits of approximate Fréchet normals at nearby points with errors tending to zero. All these cones are empty outside the set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N(\bar x;\Omega)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{x\to\bar x,\,\varepsilon\downarrow0}\widehat N_\varepsilon(x;\Omega),\qquad \widehat N(x;\Omega)=\widehat N_0(x;\Omega)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fréchet Normal–Weak Contingent Cone Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Negative-polar duality in reflexive Banach spaces and its finite-dimensional specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let X be reflexive, let \Omega\subset X, and let \bar x\in\Omega. Then
\[
\widehat N(\bar x;\Omega)=T_W(\bar x;\Omega)^*:=\left\{x^*\in X^*\mid \langle x^*,v\rangle\le0\text{ for every }v\in T_W(\bar x;\Omega)\right\}.
\]
If X is finite-dimensional, then
\[
\widehat N(\bar x;\Omega)=T(\bar x;\Omega)^*.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a reflexive Banach space, the Fréchet normal cone is the negative polar of the weak contingent cone. In finite dimensions, it is the negative polar of the ordinary contingent cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat N(\bar x;\Omega)=T_W(\bar x;\Omega)^*,\qquad \dim X<\infty\Rightarrow\widehat N(\bar x;\Omega)=T(\bar x;\Omega)^*.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex-Cone First-Order Optimality Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For a Fréchet differentiable convex functional on a real normed space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a real normed space, let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and Fréchet differentiable, let \(P\subseteq X\) be a convex cone, and let \(x_0\in P\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supporting-function characterizations of Fréchet normals, with stronger global smooth representations under additional Banach-space smoothness hypotheses.

Let $X$ be a Banach space, let $\varnothing
e\Omega\subset X$, and let $ ar x\in\Omega$. (i) If $x^*\in X^*$ and a function $s:U	o\mathbb R$, defined on a neighborhood $U$ of $ ar x$, is Fréchet differentiable at $ ar x$, satisfies $
abla s( ar x)=x^*$, and attains a local maximum relative to $\Omega$ at $ ar x$, then $x^*\in\widehat N( ar x;\Omega)$. Conversely, every $x^*\in\widehat N( ar x;\Omega)$ admits a function $s:X	o\mathbb R$ such that $s(x)\le s( ar x)=0$ for every $x\in\Omega$, $s$ is Fréchet differentiable at $ ar x$, and $

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fréchet Epsilon-Normals to Differentiable Inverse Images
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided inverse-image estimates under differentiability and surjectivity assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let X and Y be Banach spaces, let f:X\to Y, let \Theta\subset Y, and suppose \bar y:=f(\bar x)\in\Theta. If f is Fréchet differentiable at \bar x, then there exists c_1>0 such that, for every \varepsilon\ge0,
\[
\widehat N_\varepsilon(\bar x;f^{-1}(\Theta))\supset \nabla f(\bar x)^*\widehat N_{c_1\varepsilon}(\bar y;\Theta).
\]
If f is strictly differentiable at \bar x and \nabla f(\bar x) is surjective, then there exists c_2>0 such that, for every \varepsilon\ge0,
\[
\widehat N_\varepsilon(\bar x;f^{-1}(\Theta))\subset \nabla f(\bar x)^*\widehat N_{c_2\varepsilon}(\bar y;\Theta)+\varepsilon\mathbb B^*.
\]
If \dim Y<\infty, the second inclusion remains valid when f is continuous around \bar x, Fréchet differentiable at \bar x, and \nabla f(\bar x) is surjective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointwise Fréchet differentiability gives an adjoint pullback of suitably rescaled epsilon-normals into the epsilon-normal cone of the inverse image. Strict differentiability and a surjective derivative give the reverse estimate up to an epsilon dual-ball error. For a finite-dimensional target, local continuity and pointwise Fréchet differentiability with a surjective derivative suffice for that reverse estimate.

f	ext{ Fréchet differentiable at } ar x\Rightarrow\exists c_1>0\  orall\varepsilon\ge0:\ \widehat N_\varepsilon( ar x;f^{-1}(\Theta))\supset
abla f( ar x)^*\widehat N_{c_1\varepsilon}( ar y;\Theta);\quad f	ext{ strictly differentiable at } ar x,\ 
abla f( ar x)	ext{ surjective}\Rightarrow\exists c_2>0\  orall\varepsilon\ge0:\ \widehat N_\varepsilon( ar x;f^{-1}(\Theta))\subset

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The limiting normal cone to \(C\) at \(\bar x\) is the outer sequential limit
\[
N_C(\bar x):=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{x\to_C\bar x}\widehat N_C(x).

\[
v\in N_C(\bar x)\iff \exists x_k\in C,\ v_k\in\widehat N_C(x_k):\ x_k\to\bar x,\ v_k\to v.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict-Subgradient Approximation of Limiting and Horizon Subgradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Here \(x_i\xrightarrow{f}x\) means \(x_i\to x\) and \(f(x_i)\to f(x)\); \(\widehat\partial f\) denotes the strict subdifferential used in the source.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^k\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be lower semicontinuous, let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and let \(\xi\in\mathbb{R}^k\). Then \(\xi\in\partial f(x)\) if and only if there exist \(x_i\xrightarrow{f}x\) and \(\xi_i\to\xi\) such that \(\xi_i\in\widehat\partial f(x_i)\) for every \(i\). Moreover, \(\xi\in\partial^\infty f(x)\) if and only if there exist \(x_i\xrightarrow{f}x\), \(t_i\downarrow0\), and \(\xi_i\to\xi\) such that \(t_i^{-1}\xi_i\in\widehat\partial f(x_i)\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector is a limiting subgradient exactly when it is the limit of strict subgradients at nearby points whose function values converge. It is a horizon subgradient exactly when it is the limit of vectors whose rescalings by factors tending to zero are strict subgradients at such points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \xi\in\partial f(x)\iff\exists\,x_i\xrightarrow{f}x,\ \xi_i\to\xi:\ \xi_i\in\widehat\partial f(x_i)\ \forall i;\qquad \xi\in\partial^\infty f(x)\iff\exists\,x_i\xrightarrow{f}x,\ t_i\downarrow0,\ \xi_i\to\xi:\ t_i^{-1}\xi_i\in\widehat\partial f(x_i)\ \forall i.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regular Normals and the Sequential Representation of Limiting Normals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional regular and limiting normal cones, including their convex-set agreement, possible degeneration of regular normals, and vanishing-error representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) be locally closed around \(\bar x\in\Omega\). For \(x\in\Omega\) near \(\bar x\), define
\[\widehat N(x;\Omega):=\left\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\limsup_{\substack{u\to x,\ u\in\Omega,\ u\ne x}}\frac{\langle v,u-x\rangle}{\|u-x\|}\le 0\right\}.\]
Then \(\widehat N(x;\Omega)\) is closed and convex, and
\[N(\bar x;\Omega)=\left\{v:\exists x_k\xrightarrow{\Omega}\bar x,\ \exists v_k\in\widehat N(x_k;\Omega),\ v_k\to v\right\}.\]
The same representation holds with \(v_k\in\widehat N_{\varepsilon_k}(x_k;\Omega)\) when \(\varepsilon_k\downarrow0\). If \(\Omega\) is convex, the regular and limiting normal cones coincide with the convex-analysis normal cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regular normal cone is closed and convex but can collapse to the zero cone at a boundary point of a nonconvex closed set. The limiting normal cone consists of limits of nearby regular normals, including vanishing-error regular normals. On convex sets, both notions coincide with the convex normal cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N(\bar x;\Omega)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{x\xrightarrow{\Omega}\bar x}\widehat N(x;\Omega),\qquad \Omega\text{ convex}\Longrightarrow \widehat N(\bar x;\Omega)=N(\bar x;\Omega)=N_{\mathrm{conv}}(\bar x;\Omega)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Clarke normal cone to \(C\) at \(\bar x\) is the closed convex hull of the limiting normal cone:
\[
N_C^{\mathrm C}(\bar x):=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}N_C(\bar x).

Consequently, \(N_C^{\mathrm C}(\bar x)\) is a closed convex cone and
\[
\widehat N_C(\bar x)\subset N_C(\bar x)\subset N_C^{\mathrm C}(\bar x).
\]
The second inclusion can be strict for nonconvex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke normal cone is obtained by taking the closed convex hull of all limiting normals.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential Tangent Cone, Polar Cone, and Normal Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential tangent and polar-normal geometry for arbitrary subsets of Euclidean space, including convexity boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \varnothing\ne C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n and x\in C, define \mathcal T(x;C):=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists x^k\in C,\ x^k\to x,\ \tau_k>0,\ \tau_k\to0,\ (x^k-x)/\tau_k\to v\}. For S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n, define S^p:=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:y^Ts\le0\ \forall s\in S\} and \mathcal N(x;C):=\mathcal T(x;C)^p. The tangent cone is closed but need not be convex; if C is closed and convex, then \mathcal T(x;C) is closed and convex. Every S^p, and hence every \mathcal N(x;C), is a closed convex cone. Under the stated convention, S^*=-S^p.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tangent cone consists of limits of feasible secant directions with positive scales tending to zero. The normal cone is the polar of that tangent cone. The tangent cone is closed but can be nonconvex, while it is closed and convex when C is closed and convex. Every polar cone and every normal cone defined this way is closed and convex; with the source's sign convention, the dual cone is the negative of the polar.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal N(x;C)=\mathcal T(x;C)^p,\quad S^p\text{ and }\mathcal N(x;C)\text{ are closed convex cones},\quad S^*=-S^p

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a cone \(K\subset X\), define its negative polar by
\[
K^\circ:=\{v\in X:\langle v,w\rangle\le0\text{ for every }w\in K\}.

\[
\widehat N_C(\bar x)=T_C(\bar x)^\circ.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty cone \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), define \(K^\circ:=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\ \text{for every }x\in K\}\). For any cones \(K_1,K_2\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), \(K_1\subset K_2\) implies \(K_2^\circ\subset K_1^\circ\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be locally closed at \(\bar x\in C\). If \(C\) is both Clarke regular and tangentially regular at \(\bar x\), then its contingent tangent and limiting normal cones determine one another by polarity: \[N_C(\bar x)=T_C(\bar x)^\circ,\qquad T_C(\bar x)=N_C(\bar x)^\circ.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under tangential and Clarke regularity, polarizing the limiting normal cone recovers the contingent tangent cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-to-Tangent Recovery

source_witnesses.locator: F. Tangent-Normal Relations p. 217

children.title: Exactness Boundary
children.top_down_role: Transition from exact polarity to relaxed or convexified recovery.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is locally closed at \(\bar x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_C(\bar x)^\circ\subset T_C(\bar x)^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}T_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates universal polarity from equalities requiring normal and tangential regularity.

source_refs.locator: H.* Irregularity and Convexification p. 225
F. Tangent-Normal Relations p. 217

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every locally closed set \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\bar x\in C\), \[\widehat N_C(\bar x)=T_C(\bar x)^\circ\subset N_C(\bar x)\] and \[N_C(\bar x)^\circ\subset T_C(\bar x)^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}T_C(\bar x).\] Exact equality \(N_C(\bar x)=T_C(\bar x)^\circ\) holds under normal regularity, while exact recovery \(T_C(\bar x)=T_C(\bar x)^{\circ\circ}\) holds when the tangent cone is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without normal and tangential regularity, polarity yields only inclusions and the closed convex hull of the tangent cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Exactness Boundary

children.title: Polar Recovery Failure Regimes

children.title: Tangential Irregularity
children.top_down_role: Failure of compatible local tangent behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is locally closed at \(\bar x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Tangential irregularity is witnessed by \(T_C^C(\bar x)\subsetneq T_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of equality between robust and contingent tangent constructions.

source_refs.locator: H.* Irregularity and Convexification p. 225

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because \(T_C^C(\bar x)\subset T_C(\bar x)\), tangential irregularity at \(\bar x\) is the strict failure \[T_C^C(\bar x)\subsetneq T_C(\bar x).\] It records feasible first-order directions attainable from \(\bar x\) that are not stable under simultaneous perturbation of the base point within \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tangential irregularity occurs when some contingent tangent directions fail the robust Clarke tangent test.
knowledge_statements.title: Tangential Irregularity

source_witnesses.locator: H.* Irregularity and Convexification p. 225

children.title: Normal Irregularity
children.top_down_role: Instability or mismatch among regular, limiting, and convexified normals.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is locally closed at \(\bar x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Normal irregularity is witnessed by \(\widehat N_C(\bar x)\subsetneq N_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of Clarke normal regularity at a locally closed set.

source_refs.locator: B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199
H.* Irregularity and Convexification p. 225

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The universal inclusion is \(\widehat N_C(\bar x)\subset N_C(\bar x)\). The set is normally irregular at \(\bar x\) when this inclusion is strict: \[\widehat N_C(\bar x)\subsetneq N_C(\bar x).\] Equivalently, some limiting normal arises from nearby regular normals but is not itself a regular normal at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normal irregularity means that the limiting normal cone strictly exceeds the regular normal cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal Irregularity

source_witnesses.locator: B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199
H.* Irregularity and Convexification p. 225

children.title: Convexification Gaps
children.top_down_role: Loss of nonconvex directional structure under convexification.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is locally closed at \(\bar x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The tangent convexification gap is \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}T_C(\bar x)\setminus T_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information lost because every polar cone depends only on the closed convex hull.

source_refs.locator: H.* Irregularity and Convexification p. 225

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a locally closed set \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\bar x\in C\), polarity depends only on the closed convex hull of the tangent cone: \[T_C(\bar x)^\circ=\bigl(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}T_C(\bar x)\bigr)^\circ,\qquad T_C(\bar x)^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}T_C(\bar x).\] The convexification gap is \[\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}T_C(\bar x)\setminus T_C(\bar x),\] and it is nonempty precisely when the tangent cone differs from its closed convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polarization loses the distinction between a tangent cone and its closed convex hull; the resulting convexification gap records the unrecoverable tangent directions.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexification Gaps

source_witnesses.locator: H.* Irregularity and Convexification p. 225

children.title: Failed Polar Recovery
children.top_down_role: Regimes where polarity cannot reconstruct the intended primal or dual object.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_C(\bar x)^\circ=\{0\}\neq T_C(\bar x)\) and \(T_C(\bar x)^{\circ\circ}=\mathbb{R}^2\neq T_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate-cross example exhibiting both normal irregularity and failed reverse polarity.

source_refs.locator: H.* Irregularity and Convexification p. 225

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L:=\bigl(\mathbb{R}\times\{0\}\bigr)\cup\bigl(\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}\bigr)\). At the origin, \[T_C(\bar x)=L,\qquad \widehat N_C(\bar x)=L^\circ=\{0\},\qquad N_C(\bar x)=L.\] Therefore \[N_C(\bar x)^\circ=\{0\}\neq T_C(\bar x),\qquad T_C(\bar x)^{\circ\circ}=\mathbb{R}^2\neq T_C(\bar x).\] Thus neither limiting-normal polarity nor bipolarization recovers the nonconvex tangent cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the union of the coordinate axes at the origin, normal polarity collapses the tangent geometry and bipolarization fills the entire plane.
knowledge_statements.title: Failed Polar Recovery

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=\operatorname{epi}f\) and \(\bar z=(\bar x,f(\bar x))\). Then \(T_E(\bar z)\) is a closed cone. Moreover, \[(w,\alpha)\in T_E(\bar z),\ r\geq0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(w,\alpha+r)\in T_E(\bar z),\] and consequently \((0,r)\in T_E(\bar z)\) for every \(r\geq0\). The cone need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The contingent tangent to an epigraph is a closed, upward-stable cone, although it can be nonconvex.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epigraphical representation of the extended generalized directional derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real-valued functions at points where they are finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) and suppose \(f(x)<+\infty\). Then
\[
T_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x))=\operatorname{epi}\bigl(f^\circ(x;\cdot)\bigr),
\]
where
\[
f^\circ(x;v)=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\limsup_{\substack{(y,\alpha)\downarrow_f x\\t\downarrow0}}\inf_{w\in v+\varepsilon B}\frac{f(y+tw)-\alpha}{t},\qquad v\in X.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an extended-real-valued function finite at x, the tangent cone to its epigraph at (x,f(x)) is the epigraph of the extended generalized directional derivative defined by the stated perturbed upper-limit formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x))=\operatorname{epi}\bigl(f^\circ(x;\cdot)\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the lower subderivative by \[df(\bar x)(w):=\liminf_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\w'\to w}}\frac{f(\bar x+t w')-f(\bar x)}{t}.\] Then a pair \((w,\alpha)\) belongs to \(T_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\) exactly when \(\alpha\ge df(\bar x)(w)\). Consequently, \[T_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))=\{(w,\alpha):\alpha\ge df(\bar x)(w)\}=\operatorname{epi}df(\bar x).\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Positively Homogeneous Lower Subderivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural scalar consequences of encoding the lower subderivative by the contingent epigraph tangent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The lower subderivative \(df(\bar x):\mathbb R^n\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) is lower semicontinuous and positively homogeneous: \[df(\bar x)(\lambda w)=\lambda df(\bar x)(w)\qquad(\lambda>0).\] Its epigraph is a closed cone, but it need not be convex; hence \(df(\bar x)\) need not be sublinear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower subderivative is lower semicontinuous and positively homogeneous, but generally need not be convex or sublinear.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(df(\bar x)\) is lower semicontinuous and positively homogeneous, with a possibly nonconvex epigraph.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The limiting subdifferential of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) is encoded by those limiting normals to the epigraph whose vertical component equals \(-1\): \[\partial f(\bar x)=\bigl\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:(v,-1)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\bigr\}.\] Thus normalization of a nonhorizontal epigraph normal recovers a scalar generalized gradient, while normals with zero vertical component belong instead to singular subdifferential geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A limiting subgradient is exactly the horizontal component of an epigraph normal normalized to have vertical component minus one.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The limiting normal cone to the graph is the outer sequential limit of nearby Fréchet normal cones: \[N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y):=\left\{(x^*,y^*):\begin{array}{l}(x_k,y_k)\to(\bar x,\bar y),\ (x_k,y_k)\in\operatorname{gph}F,\\(x_k^*,y_k^*)\to(x^*,y^*),\ (x_k^*,y_k^*)\in\widehat N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(x_k,y_k)\end{array}\right\}.\] This cone is generally nonconvex and supplies the dual geometric carrier for coderivatives.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=\operatorname{gph}F\) and \(\bar z=(\bar x,\bar y)\). The limiting normal cone \(N_G(\bar z)\) is a closed cone and may be nonconvex. Moreover, \[\widehat N_G(\bar z)=T_G(\bar z)^\circ\subset N_G(\bar z).\] If \(G\) is normally regular at \(\bar z\), then \[N_G(\bar z)=\widehat N_G(\bar z)=T_G(\bar z)^\circ.\] Without normal regularity the inclusion can be strict.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized equation and variational-inequality representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized equations with a smooth single-valued term and a closed-graph set-valued term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a continuously Fréchet differentiable mapping \(G:X\to Y\) and a set-valued mapping \(N:X\rightrightarrows Y\) with closed graph, the generalized equation \(\operatorname{GE}(G,N)\) is \[0\in G(x)+N(x).\] If \(F:W\to W^*\) and \(S\subset W\) is closed and convex, then the variational inequality \(\operatorname{VI}(F,S)\) can be represented as the generalized equation \[0\in F(w)+N_S(w),\] where \(N_S\) is the normal-cone mapping of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized equation asks for a point where zero belongs to the sum of a smooth mapping and a closed-graph set-valued mapping. A variational inequality over a closed convex set is the special case obtained by adding the set's normal-cone mapping.
assumptions_latex: G:X\to Y\text{ is continuously Fréchet differentiable}
S\subset W\text{ is closed and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{GE}(G,N):\ 0\in G(x)+N(x),\qquad \operatorname{VI}(F,S)\iff 0\in F(w)+N_S(w)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every direction \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\), define the graphical derivative by \[DF(\bar x\mid\bar y)(u):=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^m:(u,v)\in T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\}.\] Equivalently, its graph is the tangent cone itself: \[\operatorname{gph}DF(\bar x\mid\bar y)=T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y).\] Hence the graphical derivative is the set-valued positively homogeneous mapping that encodes all first-order graph velocities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The graphical derivative maps each input direction to the output directions paired with it in the graph tangent cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each covector \(y^*\in\mathbb{R}^m\), the limiting coderivative of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is \[D^*F(\bar x\mid\bar y)(y^*):=\bigl\{x^*\in\mathbb{R}^n:(x^*,-y^*)\in N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\bigr\}.\] The minus sign on the output covector fixes the standard primal-dual convention. Thus the coderivative is the multifunction obtained by slicing graph normals according to their output component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The coderivative maps an output covector to input covectors whose signed pair is a limiting normal to the graph.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conic Homogeneity of the Limiting Coderivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic homogeneity inherited from the limiting graph-normal cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The graph of the limiting coderivative, \[\operatorname{gph}D^*F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=\{(y^*,x^*):(x^*,-y^*)\in N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\},\] is a closed cone. Consequently, for every \(\lambda>0\), \[D^*F(\bar x\mid\bar y)(\lambda y^*)=\lambda D^*F(\bar x\mid\bar y)(y^*).\] Its graph and values need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The limiting coderivative has a closed conic graph and is positively homogeneous, but it is generally nonconvex.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\) has locally closed graph at \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}D^*F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\) is a closed, possibly nonconvex cone and \(D^*F(\lambda y^*)=\lambda D^*F(y^*)\) for \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Conic Homogeneity of the Limiting Coderivative

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A vector \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is a singular subgradient of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) exactly when it is the horizontal component of a limiting epigraph normal having zero vertical component: \[\partial^\infty f(\bar x)=\bigl\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:(v,0)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\bigr\}.\] These horizontal normals cannot be normalized to vertical component \(-1\), so they record recession-type first-order behavior rather than ordinary limiting subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Horizontal limiting normals to the epigraph, identified by zero vertical component, are exactly the singular subgradients.

children.top_down_role: Dual horizontal structure associated with non-Lipschitz behavior.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\in\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\iff(v,0)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The singular normal geometry of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) is the cone \[\partial^\infty f(\bar x):=\bigl\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:(v,0)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\bigr\}.\] Equivalently, its elements are limits \(v_k\to v\) of scaled regular subgradients \(v_k=\lambda_k u_k\), where \(x_k\to\bar x\), \(f(x_k)\to f(\bar x)\), \(u_k\in\widehat\partial f(x_k)\), and \(\lambda_k\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Singular subgradients are horizontal epigraph normals, equivalently limits of regular subgradients scaled by positive factors tending to zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Singular Normal Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Conic Structure of the Singular Subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic algebraic structure of the singular subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The singular subdifferential \(\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\) is a closed cone containing the origin: \(0\in\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\) and \(\lambda\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\subset\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\) for every \(\lambda\ge0\). It need not be convex for a general lower-semicontinuous nonconvex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The singular subdifferential is a closed cone containing zero but need not be convex.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\) is a closed cone, not necessarily convex.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\ne\{0\}\) rules out local Lipschitz continuity of \(f\) around \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonzero singular subgradients detect failure of local Lipschitz regularity.

source_refs.locator: 2.4.2 Representations of Singular Subgradients and Horizontal Normals to Graphs and Epigraphs p. 223

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is finite and locally Lipschitz on a neighborhood of \(\bar x\), then its singular subdifferential is trivial: \[\partial^\infty f(\bar x)=\{0\}.\] Therefore, the existence of \(v\ne0\) with \((v,0)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\) certifies that \(f\) is not locally Lipschitz around \(\bar x\). The converse need not hold without additional regularity, so trivial singular geometry alone does not universally establish Lipschitz continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every locally Lipschitz function has only the zero singular subgradient; a nonzero one therefore certifies non-Lipschitz behavior.
knowledge_statements.title: Non-Lipschitz Regimes

children.title: Horizontal Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Loss of stable finite-slope behavior through horizontal directions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\cap(\mathbb{R}^n\times\{0\})\ne\{(0,0)\}\) is horizontal degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degeneracy means existence of a nonzero horizontal limiting epigraph normal.

source_refs.locator: 2.4.2 Representations of Singular Subgradients and Horizontal Normals to Graphs and Epigraphs p. 223
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The epigraph is horizontally degenerate at \((\bar x,f(\bar x))\) when \[N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\cap\bigl(\mathbb{R}^n\times\{0\}\bigr)\ne\{(0,0)\}.\] By singular-normal encoding, this condition is equivalent to \(\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\ne\{0\}\). Such a normal has no nonzero vertical component and therefore cannot be rescaled into the form \((v,-1)\) used to encode ordinary limiting subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Horizontal degeneracy occurs exactly when the epigraph has a nonzero limiting normal with zero vertical component.
knowledge_statements.title: Horizontal Degeneracy

source_witnesses.locator: 2.4.2 Representations of Singular Subgradients and Horizontal Normals to Graphs and Epigraphs p. 223

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential Criterion for Horizontal Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent sequence test for the degeneracy condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Horizontal degeneracy at \(\bar x\) is equivalent to the existence of \(x_k\to\bar x\), \(f(x_k)\to f(\bar x)\), \(u_k\in\widehat\partial f(x_k)\), and \(\lambda_k\downarrow0\) such that \(\lambda_k u_k\to v\ne0\). Necessarily \(\|u_k\|\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Horizontal degeneracy is witnessed by a nonzero limit of vanishing rescalings of nearby regular subgradients; those subgradients must be unbounded.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\ne\{0\}\iff\exists x_k,u_k,\lambda_k:\lambda_k u_k\to v\ne0\), with \(\|u_k\|\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Criterion for Horizontal Degeneracy

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epsilon-subgradients of a distance function at projection points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper estimate relating regular epsilon-subgradients at an exterior point to regular epsilon-normals at every exact projection point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subset X\) be nonempty, let \(\bar x\notin\Omega\), and suppose \(\Pi(\bar x;\Omega)\neq\varnothing\). Then, for every \(\varepsilon\in[0,1]\), \[\widehat\partial_\varepsilon d_\Omega(\bar x)\subset\left(\bigcap_{w\in\Pi(\bar x;\Omega)}\widehat N_\varepsilon(w;\Omega)\right)\cap[1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon]S^*.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an exterior point has best approximations in the set, every regular epsilon-subgradient of its distance is a regular epsilon-normal at every projection point and has dual norm between one minus epsilon and one plus epsilon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat\partial_\varepsilon d_\Omega(\bar x)\subset\left(\bigcap_{w\in\Pi(\bar x;\Omega)}\widehat N_\varepsilon(w;\Omega)\right)\cap[1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon]S^*

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial d_C(\bar x)=N_C(\bar x)\cap\mathbb{B}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At every point \(\bar x\in C\), the limiting subdifferential of the distance function is the unit truncation of the limiting normal cone: \[\partial d_C(\bar x)=N_C(\bar x)\cap\mathbb{B}.\] Equivalently, the full normal cone is recovered by positive scaling, \[N_C(\bar x)=\bigcup_{\lambda\ge0}\lambda\,\partial d_C(\bar x).\] Thus distance-function subgradients encode exactly the limiting normal directions whose norm does not exceed one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a point of a closed set, distance subgradients are exactly the limiting normals of norm at most one.
knowledge_statements.title: Distance-Function Subdifferentiation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz and Horizon Properties of the Distance Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global first-order bounds for distance functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The distance function is globally one-Lipschitz: \(|d_C(x)-d_C(y)|\le\|x-y\|\). Consequently, \(\partial d_C(x)\subset\mathbb B\) and \(\partial^\infty d_C(x)=\{0\}\) for every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance to a nonempty closed set is one-Lipschitz, has subgradients of norm at most one, and has trivial horizon subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lip}(d_C)\le1\), \(\partial d_C(x)\subset\mathbb B\), and \(\partial^\infty d_C(x)=\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: horizon subdifferential of the distance function
