knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regular Distance Subgradients on the Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regular counterpart of the seed's limiting formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At every \(\bar x\in C\), \(\widehat\partial d_C(\bar x)=\widehat N_C(\bar x)\cap\mathbb B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a point of the set, regular distance subgradients are exactly regular normals of norm at most one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\partial d_C(\bar x)=\widehat N_C(\bar x)\cap\mathbb B\).
knowledge_statements.title: Regular Distance Subgradients on the Set

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Distance Subgradients Outside the Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exterior representation through nearest points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x\notin C\) and \(v\in\partial d_C(x)\), then \(\|v\|=1\) and there exists \(p\in P_C(x)\) such that \(v=(x-p)/d_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every limiting distance subgradient outside a closed finite-dimensional set is a unit displacement from a nearest point toward the query point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\in\partial d_C(x)\Rightarrow\exists p\in P_C(x):v=(x-p)/d_C(x),\ \|v\|=1\).

notation.meaning: set of nearest points to x in C

knowledge_statements.title: Distance Subgradients Outside the Set

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Convex Distance Subdifferential Formula
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-convex specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\) is closed and convex, then \[\partial d_C(x)=\begin{cases}N_C(x)\cap\mathbb B,&x\in C,\\ \left\{\dfrac{x-P_Cx}{d_C(x)}\right\},&x\notin C.\end{cases}\] Thus \(d_C\) is differentiable off \(C\), with \(\nabla d_C(x)=(x-P_Cx)/d_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex set, the distance subdifferential is the truncated normal cone on the set and the normalized projection residual off the set.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial d_C(x)=N_C(x)\cap\mathbb B\) on \(C\), and \(\partial d_C(x)=\{(x-P_Cx)/d_C(x)\}\) off \(C\).

notation.meaning: unique Euclidean projection of x onto C

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A vector \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is a proximal normal to \(C\) at \(\bar x\) precisely when some point displaced from \(\bar x\) along \(v\) projects back to \(\bar x\): \[v\in N_C^P(\bar x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists r>0\text{ such that }\bar x\in P_C(\bar x+rv).\] Equivalently, for some \(\sigma\ge0\), \[\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle\le\sigma\|x-\bar x\|^2\quad\text{for all }x\in C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximal normal points from a set point toward an exterior point for which that set point is nearest.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-dimensional representations of limiting normals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Requires local closedness and gives both a nearby-Fréchet-normal representation and a metric-projection-residual representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) be locally closed around \(\bar x\in\Omega\). Then
\[
N(\bar x;\Omega)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{x\to\bar x}\widehat N(x;\Omega)
\]
and
\[
N(\bar x;\Omega)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{x\to\bar x}\left[\operatorname{cone}\bigl(x-\Pi(x;\Omega)\bigr)\right].
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a locally closed subset of finite-dimensional space, the limiting normal cone is the outer limit of nearby Fréchet normal cones and also the outer limit of cones generated by nearby metric-projection residuals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N(\bar x;\Omega)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{x\to\bar x}\widehat N(x;\Omega)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{x\to\bar x}\left[\operatorname{cone}\bigl(x-\Pi(x;\Omega)\bigr)\right]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proximinality and Distance Attainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Names the set property whose failure is exhibited by the seed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty set \(C\) in a metric space is proximinal if \(P_C(x):=\{c\in C:d(x,c)=d_C(x)\}\ne\varnothing\) for every \(x\). Distance nonattainment at \(x\) is precisely \(P_C(x)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is proximinal when every query point has a nearest point; nonattainment means the projection set is empty at a query.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty subset of a metric space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ proximinal}\iff P_C(x)\ne\varnothing\ \forall x\); nonattainment at \(x\iff P_C(x)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Proximinality and Distance Attainment

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Convex Hilbert Sets Attain Distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary showing that infinite dimensionality alone does not cause nonattainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every nonempty closed convex subset \(C\) of a Hilbert space has a unique nearest point to each \(x\); equivalently, \(P_C(x)\) is a singleton for every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed convex Hilbert-space sets always have unique nearest points.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|P_C(x)|=1\) for every \(x\in H\).
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex Hilbert Sets Attain Distance

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonunique-Projection Locus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Points at which an attained metric projection has multiple values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty set \(C\) in a metric space, define \[\mathcal M(C):=\{x:|P_C(x)|\ge2\},\qquad P_C(x):=\{c\in C:d(x,c)=d_C(x)\}.\] Thus projection nonuniqueness at \(x\) means \(x\in\mathcal M(C)\); it is distinct from nonattainment, where \(P_C(x)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonunique-projection locus consists of points having at least two nearest points; nonattainment is a different pathology.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty subset of a metric space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\mathcal M(C)\iff |P_C(x)|\ge2\), while nonattainment means \(P_C(x)=\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space \(H\), then \(P_C(x)\) is a singleton for every \(x\in H\). Closedness alone does not ensure uniqueness, as the immutable two-point example demonstrates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed convex subsets of Hilbert space have unique projections, while closed nonconvex sets may have several nearest points.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall x\in H,\ |P_C(x)|=1\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Radial Projection Instability for the Unit Circle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A distinct self-contained example of failure of every continuous local nearest-point selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{u\in\mathbb R^2:\|u\|=1\}\). Then \(P_C(0)=C\), whereas for every \(z\ne0\) with \(\|z\|<1\), \(P_C(z)=\{z/\|z\|\}\). Hence no single-valued selection of \(P_C\) defined on a neighborhood of \(0\) is continuous at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto the unit circle is forced to follow the radial direction away from the center, so no nearest-point selection can be continuous at the center.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_C(0)=C\), \(P_C(z)=\{z/\|z\|\}\) for \(0<\|z\|<1\), and no local single-valued selection is continuous at \(0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-sided directional derivative and Gâteaux differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions of the forward directional derivative and its linear Gâteaux-differentiable specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\), \(\bar x\in C\), and \(d\in\mathbf E\), with \(\bar x+td\in C\) for all sufficiently small \(t>0\). When the limit exists, the one-sided directional derivative is \[f'(\bar x;d)=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(\bar x+td)-f(\bar x)}{t}.\] If these directional derivatives are represented linearly by an element \(a\in\mathbf E\), so that \(f'(\bar x;d)=\langle a,d\rangle\), then \(f\) is Gâteaux differentiable at \(\bar x\), with \(\nabla f(\bar x)=a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The one-sided directional derivative is the forward difference-quotient limit. If its dependence on direction is represented by an inner product with one vector, the function is Gâteaux differentiable and that vector is its derivative.
assumptions_latex: \bar x+td\in C\text{ for all sufficiently small }t>0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f'(\bar x;d)=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(\bar x+td)-f(\bar x)}{t};\qquad f'(\bar x;d)=\langle a,d\rangle\implies\nabla f(\bar x)=a.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower Dini, Clarke, and Michel–Penot directional derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions of three one-sided generalized directional derivatives for a locally Lipschitz real-valued function, together with the Dini sublinearity failure boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be real-valued and locally Lipschitz around \(x\in\mathbf E\). For \(h\in\mathbf E\), define
\[
f^-(x;h)=\liminf_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+th)-f(x)}{t},
\]
\[
f^\circ(x;h)=\limsup_{y\to x,\,t\downarrow0}\frac{f(y+th)-f(y)}{t}
=\inf_{\delta>0}\sup_{\|y-x\|\leq\delta,\,0<t<\delta}\frac{f(y+th)-f(y)}{t},
\]
and
\[
f^\diamond(x;h)=\sup_{u\in\mathbf E}\limsup_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+th+tu)-f(x+tu)}{t}.
\]
In general, \(f^-(x;\cdot)\) need not be sublinear; this failure occurs for \(f(s)=-|s|\) on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower Dini derivative uses a lower limit along a fixed ray, the Clarke derivative permits simultaneous perturbation of the base point, and the Michel–Penot derivative takes a supremum over first-order base-point perturbations. The lower Dini derivative need not be sublinear, as negative absolute value demonstrates.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is real-valued and locally Lipschitz around \(x\in\mathbf E\).
The displayed difference quotients are evaluated where \(f\) is defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed formulas define \(f^-(x;h)\), \(f^\circ(x;h)\), and \(f^\diamond(x;h)\), and \(f^-(x;\cdot)\) is not necessarily sublinear.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-sided directional derivative of a saddle function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition at a finite point of a saddle function, together with the block-direction existence property and the limitation that separate block derivatives do not ensure a simultaneous two-block derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a saddle function on \(\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n\), and suppose \(K(u,v)\) is finite. For \((u',v')\in\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n\), the one-sided directional derivative, when the limit exists, is defined by \[K'(u,v;u',v'):=\lim_{\lambda\downarrow0}\frac{K(u+\lambda u',v+\lambda v')-K(u,v)}{\lambda}.\] The block-direction limits \(K'(u,v;u',0)\) and \(K'(u,v;0,v')\) exist, whereas existence of the simultaneous limit \(K'(u,v;u',v')\) is not guaranteed by the saddle structure alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a finite point of a saddle function, the one-sided directional derivative is the forward difference-quotient limit when it exists. The separate first-block and second-block directional limits exist, but this does not guarantee existence in a direction that changes both blocks simultaneously.
assumptions_latex: K\text{ is a saddle function on }\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K'(u,v;u',v'):=\lim_{\lambda\downarrow0}\frac{K(u+\lambda u',v+\lambda v')-K(u,v)}{\lambda}\text{ when this limit exists};\quad K'(u,v;u',0)\text{ and }K'(u,v;0,v')\text{ exist, but existence of }K'(u,v;u',v')\text{ is not guaranteed in general}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the fixed-direction right-hand directional derivative and records its value for differentiable functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ and $x,d\in\mathbb{R}^n$, the directional derivative of $f$ at $x$ in direction $d$ is, when the limit exists, $f'(x;d)=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+td)-f(x)}{t}$. knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-Sided Directional Derivative and Directional Differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the one-sided directional derivative of scalar maps and its componentwise extension to vector-valued maps on open Euclidean domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, \(x\in\mathcal O\), and \(d\in\mathbb R^n\). For \(f:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R\), its directional derivative at \(x\) along \(d\), when it exists, is \[f'(x;d):=\lim_{\tau\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+\tau d)-f(x)}{\tau}.\] This is the right derivative at \(0\) of \(g(\tau):=f(x+\tau d)\). The function \(f\) is directionally differentiable at \(x\) if this limit exists for every \(d\in\mathbb R^n\). For \(F=(F_1,\ldots,F_m):\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^m\), define \(F'(x;d):=(F_i'(x;d))_{i=1}^m\) when every component derivative exists. The map \(F\) is directionally differentiable at \(x\) if all its component functions are directionally differentiable there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The directional derivative is the one-sided difference-quotient limit along a direction. A scalar function is directionally differentiable at a point if this derivative exists in every direction. For a vector map, the derivative and directional differentiability are defined componentwise.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R\quad\text{or}\quad F:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^m
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f'(x;d)=\lim_{\tau\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+\tau d)-f(x)}{\tau},\qquad F'(x;d)=(F_i'(x;d))_{i=1}^m

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semidirectional and Clarke directional derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions, comparison properties, and a failure boundary for a real-valued function locally Lipschitz near the reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(\bar x\in\mathcal O\), and let \(f:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R\) be Lipschitz continuous near \(\bar x\). For \(v\in\mathbb R^n\), define
\[
\mathrm df(\bar x)(v):=\liminf_{\substack{v'\to v\\ \tau\downarrow0}}\frac{f(\bar x+\tau v')-f(\bar x)}{\tau},
\qquad
f^\circ(\bar x;v):=\limsup_{\substack{x'\to\bar x\\ \tau\downarrow0}}\frac{f(x'+\tau v)-f(x')}{\tau}.
\]
Then
\[
-\infty<\mathrm df(\bar x)(v)
\leq\limsup_{\substack{v'\to v\\ \tau\downarrow0}}\frac{f(\bar x+\tau v')-f(\bar x)}{\tau}
\leq f^\circ(\bar x;v)<\infty.
\]
The functions \(\mathrm df(\bar x)(\cdot)\) and \(f^\circ(\bar x;\cdot)\) are positively homogeneous and Lipschitz continuous; \(f^\circ(\bar x;\cdot)\) is also subadditive and hence convex. The function \(f\) is semidifferentiable at \(\bar x\) if the perturbed-direction limit
\[
\lim_{\substack{v'\to v\\ \tau\downarrow0}}\frac{f(\bar x+\tau v')-f(\bar x)}{\tau}
\]
exists for every \(v\). When it exists, this limit equals the fixed-direction one-sided derivative \(f'(\bar x;v)\). The Clarke derivative may lose local information: for \(f(t)=\min\{t,0\}\), \(f^\circ(0;s)=s\) for every \(s>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a function locally Lipschitz near a reference point, the semidirectional lower derivative is bounded above by the corresponding perturbed-direction upper limit, which is bounded above by the finite Clarke derivative. The lower and Clarke directional functions are positively homogeneous and Lipschitz, while the Clarke derivative is additionally subadditive and convex. Semidifferentiability requires existence of the perturbed-direction limit in every direction; that limit then equals the ordinary one-sided directional derivative. The minimum function example shows that Clarke convexification can lose local information.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R\text{ is Lipschitz continuous near }\bar x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: -\infty<\mathrm df(\bar x)(v)\leq\limsup_{v'\to v,\,\tau\downarrow0}\frac{f(\bar x+\tau v')-f(\bar x)}{\tau}\leq f^\circ(\bar x;v)<\infty,\text{ together with the stated regularity, semidifferentiability, and information-loss properties.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Upper and Lower Convexificators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and general nonconvexity and unboundedness boundaries of convexificators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A closed set \(\partial^*z(x)\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is an upper convexificator of \(z\) at \(x\) if \[D^-z(x;d)\leq\sup_{x^*\in\partial^*z(x)}d^\top x^*\qquad\forall d\in\mathbb{R}^n.\] It is a lower convexificator if \[D^+z(x;d)\geq\inf_{x^*\in\partial^*z(x)}d^\top x^*\qquad\forall d\in\mathbb{R}^n.\] A function admitting both is said to have a convexificator. Convexificators need not in general be convex or bounded. The Clarke, Michel–Penot, and symmetric subdifferentials are examples of convexificators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An upper convexificator bounds the lower Dini derivative from above by its support function, while a lower convexificator bounds the upper Dini derivative from below. Convexificators need not be convex or bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall d\in\mathbb{R}^n:\quad D^-z(x;d)\leq\sup_{x^*\in\partial^*z(x)}d^\top x^*\ \text{for an upper convexificator},\quad D^+z(x;d)\geq\inf_{x^*\in\partial^*z(x)}d^\top x^*\ \text{for a lower convexificator}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed-Direction and Direction-Perturbed Dini Semiderivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines lower and upper forward Dini rates along a fixed direction and while the direction converges to the prescribed direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:V(x)\subset\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R\), where \(V(x)\) is a neighborhood of \(x\), and let \(d\in\mathbb R^N\). Define
\[
\underline D f(x;d)=\liminf_{t\searrow0}\frac{f(x+td)-f(x)}{t},\qquad
\overline D f(x;d)=\limsup_{t\searrow0}\frac{f(x+td)-f(x)}{t},
\]
and
\[
\underline D_{\mathrm{pert}}f(x;d)=\liminf_{\substack{t\searrow0\\w\to d}}\frac{f(x+tw)-f(x)}{t},\qquad
\overline D_{\mathrm{pert}}f(x;d)=\limsup_{\substack{t\searrow0\\w\to d}}\frac{f(x+tw)-f(x)}{t}.
\]
Each liminf or limsup equals the limit, as \(\delta\searrow0\), of the corresponding infimum or supremum over \(0<t<\delta\); in the perturbed case one additionally imposes \(\lVert w-d\rVert<\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower and upper forward Dini semiderivatives are the liminf and limsup of the difference quotient along a fixed direction. Their direction-perturbed variants also allow the direction to converge to the prescribed direction.
assumptions_latex: V(x)\text{ is a neighborhood of }x\in\mathbb R^N
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \underline D f(x;d),\ \overline D f(x;d),\ \underline D_{\mathrm{pert}}f(x;d),\ \overline D_{\mathrm{pert}}f(x;d)\text{ are defined by the displayed one-sided liminf and limsup formulas.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-sided directional derivative and positive homogeneity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the exact forward directional limit, records its weaker status relative to Fréchet differentiability, and establishes positive homogeneity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For F:X\to Y and x,v\in X, the one-sided directional derivative, when it exists, is \[F'(x;v):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{F(x+tv)-F(x)}{t}.\] Such directional derivatives can exist even when F is not Fréchet differentiable at x. If F is Fréchet differentiable at x, then \[F'(x;v)=F'(x)v\quad\text{for all }v\in X.\] If F'(x;v) exists, then for every a>0, F'(x;av) exists and \[F'(x;av)=aF'(x;v).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The forward directional derivative is the limit of the forward difference quotient along a fixed direction. It may exist without full differentiability; Fréchet differentiability makes it the derivative operator applied to the direction. It is positively homogeneous in the direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F'(x;v)=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{F(x+tv)-F(x)}{t};\quad F\text{ Fréchet differentiable at }x\Rightarrow F'(x;v)=F'(x)v;\quad F'(x;av)=aF'(x;v).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Distance to a set and admissible directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance-function definition, closure test, and local characterization of admissible directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a set \(\Omega\), define
\[
\rho_\Omega(y)=\inf_{z\in\Omega}\|z-y\|.
\]
Then \(\rho_\Omega(y)=0\) if and only if \(y\in\operatorname{cl}\Omega\). Furthermore,
\[
g\in\gamma(x,\Omega)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\rho_\Omega(x+\alpha g)=0\quad\text{for every sufficiently small }\alpha>0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The distance to Ω is the infimum of distances to its points and vanishes exactly on its closure. A direction is admissible precisely when every sufficiently short positive step along it has zero distance to Ω.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional differentiability uniform with respect to a parameter
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition together with the two regularity consequences explicitly stated in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X be open, Y compact, and f:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R} be jointly continuous. Fix x\in X and a direction g, and suppose that f'(x,y;g) exists for every y\in Y in the selected Dini or Hadamard sense. Define \omega_{x,g}(\alpha,y)=f(x+\alpha g,y)-f(x,y)-\alpha f'(x,y;g). The function f is directionally differentiable at x in direction g uniformly with respect to y if \forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists\delta(\varepsilon)>0 such that |\omega_{x,g}(\alpha,y)|<\varepsilon\alpha for all y\in Y and 0<\alpha<\delta(\varepsilon). Under these assumptions, uniform differentiability implies continuity of y\mapsto f'(x,y;g). Separately, continuity of the x-derivative on X\times Y is sufficient for differentiability in x uniformly with respect to y.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform directional differentiability requires one step-size threshold that works for every parameter value. It implies continuity of the directional derivative in the parameter. A continuous derivative with respect to x is a sufficient condition for uniform differentiability in x over the compact parameter set.

\forall y\in Y,\ f'(x,y;g)\text{ exists in the selected Dini or Hadamard sense}
\text{For the final sufficient condition: }f\text{ is differentiable in }x\text{ and }\partial f/\partial x\text{ is continuous on }X\times Y

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Upper and Lower Semiregular Convexificators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semiregular convexificators impose support bounds on the stronger corresponding Dini derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\partial^*z(x)\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be a convexificator. It is an upper semiregular convexificator if, for every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[D^+z(x;d)\leq\sup_{x^*\in\partial^*z(x)}d^\top x^*.\] It is a lower semiregular convexificator if, for every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[D^-z(x;d)\geq\inf_{x^*\in\partial^*z(x)}d^\top x^*.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An upper semiregular convexificator bounds the upper Dini derivative from above, while a lower semiregular convexificator bounds the lower Dini derivative from below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall d\in\mathbb{R}^n:\quad D^+z(x;d)\leq\sup_{x^*\in\partial^*z(x)}d^\top x^*\ \text{(upper semiregular)},\quad D^-z(x;d)\geq\inf_{x^*\in\partial^*z(x)}d^\top x^*\ \text{(lower semiregular)}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Time-State Formula for the Lower Dini Derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower Dini differentiation in a forward time-state direction, with a fixed-direction simplification under local Lipschitz continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi:[S,T]\times\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), \((t,x)\in\operatorname{dom}\phi\), and \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Then \[D^{\uparrow}\phi((t,x);(1,v))=\liminf_{h_i\downarrow0,\,v_i\to v}\frac{\phi(t+h_i,x+h_iv_i)-\phi(t,x)}{h_i}.\] If \(\phi\) is Lipschitz continuous on a neighborhood of \((t,x)\), then \[D^{\uparrow}\phi((t,x);(1,v))=\liminf_{h_i\downarrow0}\frac{\phi(t+h_i,x+h_iv)-\phi(t,x)}{h_i}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a forward time-state direction, the lower Dini derivative uses positive time steps and velocities converging to the prescribed velocity. Local Lipschitz continuity permits the velocity to be held fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D^{\uparrow}\phi((t,x);(1,v))=\liminf_{h_i\downarrow0,\,v_i\to v}\frac{\phi(t+h_i,x+h_iv_i)-\phi(t,x)}{h_i},\quad\text{and if \(\phi\) is locally Lipschitz near \((t,x)\), \(v_i\) may be fixed at \(v\)}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Upper and lower weak uniform directional differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise directional definitions and their sign duality; the unrelated extracted footnote is excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X be open, Y compact, f:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}, and (x_0,y_0)\in X\times Y. Suppose f'(x_0,y_0;g) exists. The function f is upper weakly uniformly differentiable at (x_0,y_0) in direction g if \limsup_{\alpha\downarrow0,\,y\to y_0}\frac{f(x_0+\alpha g,y)-f(x_0,y)}{\alpha}\le f'(x_0,y_0;g). It is lower weakly uniformly differentiable there if \liminf_{\alpha\downarrow0,\,y\to y_0}\frac{f(x_0+\alpha g,y)-f(x_0,y)}{\alpha}\ge f'(x_0,y_0;g). Requiring the relevant inequality for every direction g gives the unqualified upper or lower property. Moreover, f is upper weakly uniformly differentiable if and only if -f is lower weakly uniformly differentiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The upper property bounds parameter-perturbed directional difference quotients from above by the reference derivative; the lower property gives the corresponding lower bound. Negating the function interchanges the two properties.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ is open},\quad Y\text{ is compact}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{limsup}_{\alpha\downarrow0,\,y\to y_0}\frac{f(x_0+\alpha g,y)-f(x_0,y)}{\alpha}\le f'(x_0,y_0;g)\quad\text{or}\quad\operatorname*{liminf}_{\alpha\downarrow0,\,y\to y_0}\frac{f(x_0+\alpha g,y)-f(x_0,y)}{\alpha}\ge f'(x_0,y_0;g)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Admissible-direction representation of the upper Dini derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraphical characterization at a finite graph point using the source's admissible-direction cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and set \(y=(x,f(x))\in\operatorname{gr}f\). Then the cone of admissible directions \(\gamma(y,\operatorname{epi}f)\) is upper stable and generates the function \(g\mapsto f_D^{\uparrow}(x;g)\). Thus, with the upper-stable-set generation convention, \[f_D^{\uparrow}(x;g)=\inf\{\mu\in\mathbb R:(g,\mu)\in\gamma(y,\operatorname{epi}f)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a finite graph point, the admissible-direction cone of the epigraph is upward stable, and the thresholds of its vertical fibers generate the upper Dini directional derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \gamma(y,\operatorname{epi}f)\text{ is upper stable and generates }g\mapsto f_D^{\uparrow}(x;g).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extension of a Directional Convexificator by a Normal Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A directional convexificator extends to a convexificator when the continuity-direction set is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be lower semicontinuous, let \(\partial_D^*z(\bar x)\) be a bounded directional convexificator at \(\bar x\), and suppose \(D_z(\bar x)\) is closed and convex. Define \[N_D(0):=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:v^\top d\leq0\ \forall d\in D_z(\bar x)\}.\] Then \[K(\bar x):=\partial_D^*z(\bar x)+N_D(0)\] is a convexificator of \(z\) at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a lower-semicontinuous function with a bounded directional convexificator and a closed convex set of continuity directions, adding the normal cone of that direction set at zero produces a convexificator.
assumptions_latex: \partial_D^*z(\bar x)\text{ is a bounded directional convexificator at }\bar x
D_z(\bar x)\text{ is closed and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K(\bar x):=\partial_D^*z(\bar x)+N_D(0)\text{ is a convexificator of }z\text{ at }\bar x.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dini and Hadamard directional derivatives of a vector-valued mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mappings between finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be open and $H=(h_1,\ldots,h_m):\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$. The Dini directional derivative is $$H'(x;g)=\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{H(x+\alpha g)-H(x)}{\alpha},$$ while the Hadamard directional derivative is $$H'(x;g)=\lim_{\substack{\alpha\downarrow0\\g'\to g}}\frac{H(x+\alpha g')-H(x)}{\alpha}.$$ A derivative of either type exists if and only if every coordinate function has the corresponding derivative, in which case $$H'(x;g)=\bigl(h_1'(x;g),\ldots,h_m'(x;g)\bigr).$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Dini and Hadamard derivatives of a vector-valued mapping are defined through the corresponding vector limits. Existence is equivalent to coordinatewise existence, and the derivative is the vector of coordinate derivatives.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H'(x;g)\text{ exists}\iff \forall i,\ h_i'(x;g)\text{ exists},\qquad H'(x;g)=(h_i'(x;g))_{i=1}^m

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuity Directions and Their Direction Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided directional continuity and the basic failure boundaries of its direction set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\). A vector \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is a continuity direction of \(z\) at \(x\) if \[\lim_{t\downarrow0}z(x+td)=z(x).\] Let \(D_z(x)\) denote the set of all continuity directions at \(x\). Then \(0\in D_z(x)\), but in general \(D_z(x)\) is neither convex nor closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuity direction is a direction along which the function value converges to its value at the base point as positive steps tend to zero. The direction set contains zero but can fail to be convex or closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d\in D_z(x)\iff\lim_{t\downarrow0}z(x+td)=z(x),\qquad 0\in D_z(x),\quad D_z(x)\text{ need not be convex or closed}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Upper Fréchet subgradients and upper Dini directional derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relations among the upper Fréchet subdifferential and the weak and strong upper Dini directional derivatives, including the stated equality regimes and local-Lipschitz formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Banach space, \(\varphi:X\to\mathbb R\), and \(\bar x\in X\). Set \(S_w:=\{x^*\in X^*\mid \langle x^*,z\rangle\ge d_w^+\varphi(\bar x;z)\ \forall z\in X\}\) and \(S:=\{x^*\in X^*\mid \langle x^*,z\rangle\ge d^+\varphi(\bar x;z)\ \forall z\in X\}\). Then \(\widehat\partial^+\varphi(\bar x)\subset S_w\subset S\). If \(X\) is reflexive, then \(\widehat\partial^+\varphi(\bar x)=S_w\); if \(\dim X<\infty\), then \(S_w=S\). Moreover, if \(\varphi\) is locally Lipschitz around \(\bar x\), then for every \(z\in X\), \(d^+\varphi(\bar x;z)=\limsup_{t\downarrow0}\frac{\varphi(\bar x+tz)-\varphi(\bar x)}{t}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The upper Fréchet subdifferential is contained in the dual vectors dominating all weak upper Dini derivatives, which in turn are contained in those dominating all upper Dini derivatives. Reflexivity gives equality in the first inclusion, finite dimensionality gives equality in the second, and local Lipschitz continuity yields the radial upper difference-quotient formula.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ is reflexive for the first equality}
\varphi\text{ is locally Lipschitz around }\bar x\text{ for the difference-quotient formula}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat\partial^+\varphi(\bar x)\subset S_w\subset S;\quad X\text{ reflexive}\Rightarrow\widehat\partial^+\varphi(\bar x)=S_w;\quad \dim X<\infty\Rightarrow S_w=S;\quad \varphi\text{ locally Lipschitz}\Rightarrow d^+\varphi(\bar x;z)=\limsup_{t\downarrow0}\frac{\varphi(\bar x+tz)-\varphi(\bar x)}{t}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gâteaux derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real-valued functions defined near a point in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A vector $v\in\mathbb R^n$ is the Gâteaux derivative of $f$ at $x$ if, for every $g\in\mathbb R^n$, $$f(x+\alpha g)=f(x)+\alpha\langle g,v\rangle+o_g(\alpha),\qquad \frac{o_g(\alpha)}{\alpha}\to0\quad(\alpha\to0).$$ Thus the directional derivative is the linear functional $f'(x;g)=\langle g,v\rangle$; the representing vector is denoted by $\nabla f(x)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Gâteaux derivative at x is the vector representing all fixed-direction derivatives through a linear functional. The remainder may depend on the direction but is negligible relative to the scalar step.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is real-valued and defined on a neighborhood of }x\in\mathbb R^n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall g\in\mathbb R^n,\quad f'(x;g)=\langle g,v\rangle

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proximal Approximation of Dini Subgradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation in base point, function value, and subgradient for lower-semicontinuous extended-real functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}_\infty be lower semicontinuous and let \zeta\in\partial_D f(x). For every \varepsilon>0, there exist z\in x+\varepsilon B and \xi\in\partial_P f(z) such that \[|f(x)-f(z)|<\varepsilon\quad\text{and}\quad|\zeta-\xi|<\varepsilon.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every Dini subgradient of a lower-semicontinuous function can be approximated arbitrarily closely by a proximal subgradient at a nearby point whose function value is also nearby.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists z\in x+\varepsilon B,\ \exists\xi\in\partial_P f(z): |f(x)-f(z)|<\varepsilon\ \land\ |\zeta-\xi|<\varepsilon

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Endpoint Monotonicity from One-Sided Dini Derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Endpoint comparison criteria for continuous scalar functions using lower or upper right Dini derivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $h:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Then
\[
\left(\underline h'_+(\alpha)\ge0\quad\forall\alpha\in(a,b)\right)\Longrightarrow h(b)\ge h(a),
\]
and
\[
\left(\overline h'_+(\alpha)\le0\quad\forall\alpha\in(a,b)\right)\Longrightarrow h(b)\le h(a).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous function has a nondecreasing endpoint comparison when its lower right Dini derivative is nonnegative throughout the interior, and a nonincreasing endpoint comparison when its upper right Dini derivative is nonpositive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[\forall\alpha\in(a,b),\ \underline h'_+(\alpha)\ge0\right]\Rightarrow h(b)\ge h(a),\quad\left[\forall\alpha\in(a,b),\ \overline h'_+(\alpha)\le0\right]\Rightarrow h(b)\le h(a).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smooth-Support Characterization of Dini Subgradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes Dini subgradients by differentiable functions supporting the objective locally from below.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}_\infty and x\in\operatorname{dom}f. Then \zeta\in\partial_D f(x) if and only if there exists a continuous function g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}, differentiable at x with g'(x)=\zeta, such that f-g attains a local minimum at x.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector is a Dini subgradient exactly when it is the derivative at the point of a continuous, pointwise differentiable function that locally supports the objective from below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \zeta\in\partial_D f(x)\iff\exists g\in C(\mathbb{R}^n;\mathbb{R}): g\text{ is differentiable at }x,\ g'(x)=\zeta,\text{ and }f-g\text{ has a local minimum at }x

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dini and Limiting Subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real-valued functions on a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, including the convention at infinite function values and the induced limiting normal cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:\mathbf E\to[-\infty,+\infty]\), \(x\in\mathbf E\) with \(f(x)\in\mathbb R\), and \(v\in\mathbf E\), define
\[
f^-(x;v)=\liminf_{t\downarrow0,\,u\to v}\frac{f(x+tu)-f(x)}{t},\qquad
\partial_-f(x)=\{\phi\in\mathbf E:\langle\phi,v\rangle\le f^-(x;v)\ \forall v\in\mathbf E\}.
\]
If \(f(x)\notin\mathbb R\), set \(\partial_-f(x)=\varnothing\). For \(\delta>0\), let
\[
U(f,x,\delta)=\{z\in\mathbf E:\|z-x\|<\delta,\ |f(z)-f(x)|<\delta\}.
\]
Writing \(\partial_-f(U)=\bigcup_{z\in U}\partial_-f(z)\), define
\[
\partial_af(x)=\bigcap_{\delta>0}\operatorname{cl}\bigl(\partial_-f(U(f,x,\delta))\bigr).
\]
Equivalently, \(\phi\in\partial_af(x)\) iff there exist \(x^r\to x\) and \(\phi^r\to\phi\) such that \(f(x^r)\to f(x)\) and \(\phi^r\in\partial_-f(x^r)\). For \(S\subset\mathbf E\), define \(N_S^a(x)=\partial_a\delta_S(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower Dini derivative is the joint lower limit of forward difference quotients as the step tends to zero and the perturbed direction approaches the specified direction. Dini subgradients are vectors dominated by this derivative in every direction, with an empty Dini subdifferential at an infinite function value. The limiting subdifferential consists of limits of Dini subgradients at nearby points whose function values approach the base value. Applying it to an indicator function defines the limiting normal cone.
assumptions_latex: f(x)\in\mathbb R\text{ for the directional and limiting constructions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial_af(x)=\bigcap_{\delta>0}\operatorname{cl}\!\left(\bigcup_{z\in U(f,x,\delta)}\partial_-f(z)\right),\qquad N_S^a(x)=\partial_a\delta_S(x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex parameterized functions are upper weakly uniformly differentiable
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A global sufficient condition for every point and direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X be an open convex set, Y a compact set, and let f:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R} be continuous. knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A jointly continuous parameterized function whose slices in the decision variable are convex is upper weakly uniformly directionally differentiable at every point, in every feasible infinitesimal direction.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regularized Dini derivative representations in the locally Lipschitz regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The formulas identify regularized upper and lower Dini derivatives with robust two-parameter limsup and liminf quotients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f be locally Lipschitz in a neighborhood of x\in\mathbb{R}^n and let g\in\mathbb{R}^n. Then the regularized upper and lower Dini derivatives are finite and satisfy \bar f_D^{\uparrow}(x;g)=\limsup_{x'\to x,\,\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x'+\alpha g)-f(x')}{\alpha} and \underline f_D^{\downarrow}(x;g)=\liminf_{x'\to x,\,\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x'+\alpha g)-f(x')}{\alpha}. Moreover, whenever the ordinary directional derivative at (x;g) exists, it equals the Hadamard directional derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a locally Lipschitz function, the regularized upper and lower Dini derivatives are finite and are given by robust limsup and liminf difference quotients with both the base point and step varying. An existing directional derivative is consequently Hadamard stable.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is locally Lipschitz in a neighborhood of }x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar f_D^{\uparrow}(x;g)=\limsup_{x'\to x,\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x'+\alpha g)-f(x')}{\alpha},\quad \underline f_D^{\downarrow}(x;g)=\liminf_{x'\to x,\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x'+\alpha g)-f(x')}{\alpha}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional, Gâteaux, Hadamard, and Fréchet Differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical differentiability hierarchy for mappings between Banach spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F:X\to Y map Banach spaces. When it exists, F'(x;v):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}[F(x+tv)-F(x)]/t. The map F is Gâteaux differentiable at x with derivative DF(x)\in\mathcal L(X,Y) if F'(x;v)=DF(x)v for every v\in X. Equivalently, the difference quotients converge pointwise in v, hence uniformly on finite sets. Uniform convergence on compact sets defines Hadamard differentiability, and uniform convergence on bounded sets defines Fréchet differentiability. These requirements become progressively stronger. If X=\mathbb R^n, Hadamard and Fréchet differentiability are equivalent; if F is Lipschitz near x, Gâteaux and Hadamard differentiability are equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a map between Banach spaces, the one-sided directional derivative is the limit of the forward difference quotient. Gâteaux differentiability requires these derivatives in every direction to be represented by one continuous linear operator. Requiring uniform convergence over compact direction sets gives Hadamard differentiability, while uniform convergence over bounded direction sets gives Fréchet differentiability. Hadamard and Fréchet differentiability coincide in finite-dimensional domains, and Gâteaux and Hadamard differentiability coincide for locally Lipschitz maps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Gâteaux}\Leftarrow\text{Hadamard}\Leftarrow\text{Fréchet},\quad X=\mathbb R^n\Rightarrow(\text{Hadamard}\Leftrightarrow\text{Fréchet}),\quad F\text{ locally Lipschitz at }x\Rightarrow(\text{Gâteaux}\Leftrightarrow\text{Hadamard}).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hadamard directional differentiability and Hadamard differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional differentiability stable under simultaneous perturbation of the positive step and direction, including its sequential characterization and linear specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mapping $g:X\to Y$ is Hadamard directionally differentiable at $x$ if $g'(x,h)$ exists for every $h\in X$ and $$g'(x,h)=\lim_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\h'\to h}}\frac{g(x+th')-g(x)}{t}.$$ Equivalently, for every $h_n\to h$ and $t_n\downarrow0$, $$g'(x,h)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{g(x+t_nh_n)-g(x)}{t_n}.$$ If, in addition, $h\mapsto g'(x,h)$ is linear, then $g$ is Hadamard differentiable at $x$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hadamard directional differentiability requires convergence of the directional quotient even when the direction is perturbed as the positive step tends to zero. Equivalently, convergence holds along every such pair of sequences. If the resulting directional derivative is linear in the direction, the mapping is Hadamard differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g'(x,h)=\lim_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\h'\to h}}\frac{g(x+th')-g(x)}{t}\quad\forall h\in X;\qquad g'(x,\cdot)\text{ linear}\Rightarrow g\text{ is Hadamard differentiable at }x.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Upper and lower perturbed directional quantities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional quotients optimized over first-order infinitesimal perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), define
\[
f^*(x,g)=\inf_{\psi\in\Psi_n}\limsup_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+\alpha g+\psi(\alpha))-f(x)}{\alpha},
\qquad
f_*(x,g)=\sup_{\psi\in\Psi_n}\liminf_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+\alpha g+\psi(\alpha))-f(x)}{\alpha},
\]
where \(\Psi_n\) is the set of first-order infinitesimals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a domain point x and direction g, the upper quantity takes the infimum over first-order infinitesimal perturbations of the upper pathwise directional quotient, while the lower quantity takes the corresponding supremum of lower pathwise quotients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^*(x,g)=\inf_{\psi\in\Psi_n}\limsup_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+\alpha g+\psi(\alpha))-f(x)}{\alpha},\quad f_*(x,g)=\sup_{\psi\in\Psi_n}\liminf_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+\alpha g+\psi(\alpha))-f(x)}{\alpha}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hierarchy of Fréchet, weak Hadamard, strong Hadamard, and Gâteaux differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implications among differentiability notions on normed spaces and the stated reflexive-Banach-space equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a normed vector space and let \(f:V(x)\to\mathbb R\) be defined on a neighborhood of \(x\in E\). Fréchet differentiability at \(x\) implies weak Hadamard differentiability, and \(d_H^w f(x;v)=L(x)v\) for every \(v\in E\). Weak Hadamard differentiability implies strong Hadamard differentiability, which implies Gâteaux differentiability. If \(E\) is a reflexive Banach space, weak Hadamard differentiability at \(x\) is equivalent to Fréchet differentiability at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fréchet differentiability implies weak Hadamard differentiability, which implies strong Hadamard differentiability, which implies Gâteaux differentiability. On a reflexive Banach space, weak Hadamard and Fréchet differentiability are equivalent.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong and weak Hadamard semiderivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topology-dependent Hadamard semiderivatives of a function on a normed vector space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a normed vector space, let \(f\) be defined near \(x\in E\), and let \(v\in E\). When the respective limits exist, \[d_H^s f(x;v):=\lim_{\substack{t\searrow0\\w\to v\text{ strongly}}}\frac{f(x+tw)-f(x)}{t},\qquad d_H^w f(x;v):=\lim_{\substack{t\searrow0\\w\rightharpoonup v}}\frac{f(x+tw)-f(x)}{t}.\] Weak Hadamard semidifferentiability implies strong Hadamard semidifferentiability. In finite-dimensional \(E\), the two notions coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The strong version permits norm-convergent perturbations of the direction, while the weak version requires the same limit for weakly convergent perturbations. The weak condition implies the strong condition, and they coincide in finite dimensions.
assumptions_latex: E\text{ is a normed vector space}
f\text{ is defined on a neighborhood of }x\in E
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d_H^w f(x;v)\text{ exists}\Rightarrow d_H^s f(x;v)\text{ exists};\qquad \dim E<\infty\Rightarrow\bigl(d_H^w f(x;v)\text{ exists}\iff d_H^s f(x;v)\text{ exists}\bigr),\text{ and the values are equal.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Upper and lower Hadamard directional derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper and lower Hadamard derivatives defined by perturbed-direction limsup and liminf.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\). The upper and lower Hadamard derivatives of \(f\) at \(x\) in direction \(g\) are \[f_H^{\uparrow}(x,g):=\limsup_{\substack{\alpha\downarrow0\\ g'\to g}}\frac{f(x+\alpha g')-f(x)}{\alpha},\qquad f_H^{\downarrow}(x,g):=\liminf_{\substack{\alpha\downarrow0\\ g'\to g}}\frac{f(x+\alpha g')-f(x)}{\alpha}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an extended-real-valued function on R^n, the upper and lower Hadamard derivatives are the limsup and liminf of the difference quotient as the positive step tends to zero and the perturbed direction approaches the specified direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_H^{\uparrow}(x,g)=\limsup_{\substack{\alpha\downarrow0\\ g'\to g}}\frac{f(x+\alpha g')-f(x)}{\alpha},\quad f_H^{\downarrow}(x,g)=\liminf_{\substack{\alpha\downarrow0\\ g'\to g}}\frac{f(x+\alpha g')-f(x)}{\alpha}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional chain rule with a Hadamard outer function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional scalar compositions through vector-valued inner mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\Omega_1\subset\mathbb R^n$ and $\Omega_2\subset\mathbb R^m$ be open, let $H:\Omega_1\to\Omega_2$ be directionally differentiable at $x\in\Omega_1$, and let $f:\Omega_2\to\mathbb R$ be Hadamard directionally differentiable at $H(x)$. Then $\varphi=f\circ H$ is directionally differentiable at $x$ and $$\varphi'(x;g)=f'(H(x);H'(x;g)).$$ If $H$ is also Hadamard directionally differentiable at $x$, then $\varphi$ is Hadamard directionally differentiable at $x$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hadamard directionally differentiable outer function can be composed with a directionally differentiable inner mapping, yielding the directional chain rule. If the inner mapping is also Hadamard differentiable, the composition is Hadamard differentiable.
assumptions_latex: f:\Omega_2\to\mathbb R\text{ is Hadamard directionally differentiable at }H(x)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (f\circ H)'(x;g)=f'(H(x);H'(x;g));\quad H\text{ Hadamard differentiable at }x\Rightarrow f\circ H\text{ Hadamard differentiable at }x

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is Bouligand differentiable at \(x\) if there exists a continuous positively homogeneous mapping \(F'_B(x;\cdot):X\to Y\) such that \[F(x+u)=F(x)+F'_B(x;u)+r(u),\qquad \lim_{\substack{u\to0\\u\ne0}}\frac{\|r(u)\|}{\|u\|}=0.\] Positive homogeneity means \(F'_B(x;\lambda h)=\lambda F'_B(x;h)\) for every \(h\in X\) and \(\lambda\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bouligand differentiability supplies a continuous positively homogeneous first-order model whose approximation error is smaller than the increment norm.
knowledge_statements.title: Bouligand Directional Differentiability

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.1 Generalized directional derivatives p. 159

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact first-order chain rule for composable Bouligand-differentiable mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F\) is Bouligand differentiable at \(x\) and \(G\) is Bouligand differentiable at \(F(x)\), then \(G\circ F\) is Bouligand differentiable at \(x\), with \[(G\circ F)'_B(x;h)=G'_B\bigl(F(x);F'_B(x;h)\bigr)\qquad(h\in X).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bouligand derivatives obey the ordinary composition rule, with the outer positively homogeneous model applied to the inner model.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bouligand Chain Rule
knowledge_statements.title: Bouligand Chain Rule

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bouligand differentiability is equivalent to a continuous positively homogeneous map giving all perturbed-direction quotient limits, and that map is unique.
review_flags: Finite dimensionality is essential to the stated equivalence from pointwise perturbed-direction limits to the uniform little-o expansion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional equivalence between the uniform Bouligand expansion and a continuous all-direction Hadamard derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is Bouligand differentiable at \(x\) if and only if there exists a continuous positively homogeneous mapping \(A:X\to Y\) such that, for every \(h\in X\), every \(t_k\downarrow0\), and every \(h_k\to h\), \[\frac{F(x+t_kh_k)-F(x)}{t_k}\to A(h).\] In that case \(A\) is unique, \(A(h)=F'_B(x;h)=F'(x;h)\), and \[F(x+u)-F(x)-A(u)=o(\|u\|).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, Bouligand differentiability is equivalent to possessing one continuous positively homogeneous Hadamard derivative model in every direction; that model is unique.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Clarke generalized directional derivative of \(f\) at \(x\) in direction \(h\) is \[f^{\circ}(x;h)=\limsup_{\substack{y\to x\\t\downarrow0}}\frac{f(y+th)-f(y)}{t}.\] The base point may vary with the step, making this derivative robust under nearby perturbations. Local Lipschitz continuity ensures that \(f^{\circ}(x;h)\) is finite for every \(h\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke derivative takes the worst limiting directional growth over positive steps and nearby base points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Moving-Base Strictness for a Concave Corner
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Example separating robust nearby-base growth from fixed-base directional growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(u)=-|u|\), \[f'(0;h)=-|h|,\qquad f^{\circ}(0;h)=|h|.\] Thus the Clarke derivative strictly exceeds the fixed-base derivative whenever \(h\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a concave absolute-value corner, fixed-base growth is negative while robust nearby-base growth is positive.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smooth and Convex Specializations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical coincidence regimes for robust upper directional growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is continuously Fréchet differentiable near \(x\), then \(f^{\circ}(x;h)=\langle\nabla f(x),h\rangle\). If \(f\) is convex and locally Lipschitz near \(x\), then \(f^{\circ}(x;h)=f'(x;h)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke derivative reduces to the gradient pairing for smooth functions and to the ordinary directional derivative for locally Lipschitz convex functions.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is either continuously Fréchet differentiable near \(x\), or convex and locally Lipschitz near \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^{\circ}(x;h)=\langle\nabla f(x),h\rangle\) in the smooth case and \(f^{\circ}(x;h)=f'(x;h)\) in the convex case.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Sublinear Directional Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Core directional structure under local Lipschitz continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is Lipschitz with constant \(L\) near \(x\), then \(h\mapsto f^{\circ}(x;h)\) is positively homogeneous and subadditive, and \[|f^{\circ}(x;h)|\le L\|h\|.\] Hence it is finite, continuous, and sublinear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke derivative is a finite continuous sublinear function bounded by the local Lipschitz constant.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is Lipschitz with constant \(L\) near \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^{\circ}(x;\lambda h)=\lambda f^{\circ}(x;h)\), \(f^{\circ}(x;h+k)\le f^{\circ}(x;h)+f^{\circ}(x;k)\), and \(|f^{\circ}(x;h)|\le L\|h\|\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Full-Measure Representation of the Clarke Upper Derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation using upper Dini derivatives evaluated on an arbitrary inner-full-measure subset of a Lipschitz neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) be defined on an open set \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) and be Lipschitz on a neighborhood \(S\) of \(x\in X\). If \(Q\subset S\) and the inner measure of \(S\setminus Q\) is zero, then, for every \(g\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[f_{\mathrm{Cl}}^{\uparrow}(x,g)=\limsup_{\substack{x'\to x\\x'\in Q}}f_D^{\uparrow}(x',g).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a function Lipschitz near a point, the Clarke upper directional derivative equals the limsup of upper Dini derivatives along any subset whose complement in the neighborhood has inner measure zero.
assumptions_latex: f:X\to\mathbb{R}\text{ is Lipschitz on a neighborhood }S\text{ of }x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_{\mathrm{Cl}}^{\uparrow}(x,g)=\limsup_{\substack{x'\to x\\x'\in Q}}f_D^{\uparrow}(x',g)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic Properties of the Clarke Generalized Directional Derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finiteness, sublinearity, continuity, and sign-reversal properties under a local Lipschitz bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a Banach space and let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be Lipschitz of rank \(K\) near \(x\). Then \(v\mapsto f^{\circ}(x;v)\) is finite, positively homogeneous, and subadditive, and
\[
|f^{\circ}(x;v)|\le K\|v\|\qquad(\forall v\in X).
\]
For every \(v\in X\), \((u,w)\mapsto f^{\circ}(u;w)\) is upper semicontinuous at \((x,v)\), while \(w\mapsto f^{\circ}(x;w)\) is Lipschitz on \(X\) with rank \(K\). Moreover,
\[
f^{\circ}(x;-v)=(-f)^{\circ}(x;v)\qquad(\forall v\in X).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a function locally Lipschitz with rank K, its Clarke directional derivative is a finite sublinear function of the direction, is bounded and Lipschitz with constant K, is jointly upper semicontinuous at each pair (x,v), and transforms under reversal of direction by replacing f with −f.
assumptions_latex: f:X\to\mathbb R\text{ is Lipschitz of rank }K\text{ near }x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{gathered}f^{\circ}(x;\cdot)\text{ is finite, positively homogeneous, and subadditive},\\ |f^{\circ}(x;v)|\le K\|v\|\quad\forall v\in X,\\ (u,w)\mapsto f^{\circ}(u;w)\text{ is upper semicontinuous at }(x,v)\quad\forall v\in X,\\ |f^{\circ}(x;w_1)-f^{\circ}(x;w_2)|\le K\|w_1-w_2\|\quad\forall w_1,w_2\in X,\\ f^{\circ}(x;-v)=(-f)^{\circ}(x;v)\quad\forall v\in X.\end{gathered}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f\) is strictly differentiable at \(x\) if \(\nabla f(x)\) exists and, for every \(g\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[\langle\nabla f(x),g\rangle=\lim_{\substack{x'\to x\\\alpha\downarrow0}}\frac{f(x'+\alpha g)-f(x')}{\alpha}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is strictly differentiable at a point if it has a gradient there and every directional difference quotient converges to the gradient pairing even while the quotient's base point independently approaches that point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall g\in\mathbb{R}^n,\quad \lim_{\substack{x'\to x\\\alpha\downarrow0}}\frac{f(x'+\alpha g)-f(x')}{\alpha}=\langle\nabla f(x),g\rangle

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz Bound on the Clarke Generalized Gradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-norm boundedness inherited from a local Lipschitz rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a Banach space and suppose \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is Lipschitz of rank \(K\) near \(x\). Then
\[
\partial_C f(x)\subseteq B_*(0,K)=\{\zeta\in X^*: \|\zeta\|_{X^*}\le K\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If f is locally Lipschitz near x with rank K, every Clarke generalized gradient at x has dual norm at most K.
assumptions_latex: f:X\to\mathbb R\text{ is Lipschitz of rank }K\text{ near }x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial_C f(x)\subseteq B_*(0,K)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke generalized gradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition as the set of continuous linear functionals dominated by the Clarke generalized directional derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be Lipschitz near \(x\). Its Clarke generalized gradient is \[\partial f(x):=\{\zeta\in X^*: \langle\zeta,v\rangle\le f^\circ(x;v)\ \text{for every }v\in X\}.\] The dual norm is \[\|\zeta\|_*:=\sup\{\langle\zeta,v\rangle:v\in X,\ \|v\|\le1\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke generalized gradient consists of the continuous linear functionals whose value in every direction is bounded above by the Clarke generalized directional derivative. The dual norm is the supremum of the pairing over the primal unit ball.
assumptions_latex: f^\circ(x;\cdot)\text{ is the Clarke generalized directional derivative}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f(x)=\{\zeta\in X^*: \langle\zeta,v\rangle\le f^\circ(x;v)\ \forall v\in X\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sublinearity and Lipschitz bound of the Clarke directional derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finiteness, sublinearity, and the norm bound inherited from local Lipschitz continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be Lipschitz of rank \(K\) near \(x\). Then \(v\mapsto f^\circ(x;v)\) is finite-valued, positively homogeneous, and subadditive on \(X\), and \[|f^\circ(x;v)|\le K\|v\|\qquad\forall v\in X.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If f is K-Lipschitz near x, its Clarke generalized directional derivative is a finite sublinear function of the direction and has absolute value at most K times the direction norm.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is Lipschitz of rank }K\text{ near }x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^\circ(x;\cdot)\text{ is finite-valued, positively homogeneous, and subadditive, and }|f^\circ(x;v)|\le K\|v\|\ \forall v\in X

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke regularity at a point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity defined through agreement of ordinary and Clarke generalized directional derivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is regular at \(x\) if it is Lipschitz near \(x\), admits \(f'(x;v)\) for every \(v\in X\), and \[f^{\circ}(x;v)=f'(x;v)\qquad\forall v\in X.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is regular at x when it is locally Lipschitz, is directionally differentiable in every direction, and each directional derivative equals the corresponding Clarke generalized directional derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is regular at }x\iff\bigl[f\text{ is Lipschitz near }x,\ f'(x;v)\text{ exists and }f^{\circ}(x;v)=f'(x;v)\ \forall v\in X\bigr]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke directional derivative and Clarke regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions and support representation for locally Lipschitz real-valued functions on finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $v:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R$ be locally Lipschitz and let $y^0,r\in\mathbb R^m$. The Clarke directional derivative is \[v^o(y^0;r)=\limsup_{\substack{y\to y^0\\ t\downarrow0}}\frac{v(y+tr)-v(y)}{t}.\] The function is Clarke regular at $y^0$ if $v'(y^0;r)$ exists and equals $v^o(y^0;r)$ for every $r\in\mathbb R^m$. Moreover, \[v^o(y^0;r)=\max_{\zeta\in\partial v(y^0)}\langle\zeta,r\rangle\qquad\forall r\in\mathbb R^m.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke directional derivative is an upper limiting difference quotient in which both the base point and positive step vary. A locally Lipschitz function is Clarke regular at the reference point when every ordinary directional derivative exists and equals its Clarke derivative. The Clarke derivative is the support function of the Clarke generalized gradient.
assumptions_latex: v:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\text{ is locally Lipschitz.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v^o(y^0;r)=\limsup_{\substack{y\to y^0\\ t\downarrow0}}\frac{v(y+tr)-v(y)}{t}=\max_{\zeta\in\partial v(y^0)}\langle\zeta,r\rangle;\quad v\text{ is Clarke regular at }y^0\iff \forall r,\ v'(y^0;r)\text{ exists and equals }v^o(y^0;r).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equality of Lower Dini and Clarke Derivatives under Lower Semicontinuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Locally Lipschitz functions whose lower Dini directional derivative is lower semicontinuous in the base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) be locally Lipschitz on an open set \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^n\). If, for every fixed \(g\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the map \(x\mapsto f_D^{\downarrow}(x,g)\) is lower semicontinuous, then \[f_D^{\downarrow}(x,g)=f_{\mathrm{Cl}}^{\downarrow}(x,g)\qquad\text{for all }x\in X,\ g\in\mathbb{R}^n.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a locally Lipschitz function, if its lower Dini derivative is lower semicontinuous in the base point for every fixed direction, then it equals the Clarke lower derivative at every point and direction.
assumptions_latex: \forall g\in\mathbb{R}^n,\quad x\mapsto f_D^{\downarrow}(x,g)\text{ is lower semicontinuous}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in X\;\forall g\in\mathbb{R}^n,\quad f_D^{\downarrow}(x,g)=f_{\mathrm{Cl}}^{\downarrow}(x,g)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke Generalized Directional Derivative and Subdifferential Characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Robust upper directional growth and its characterization of the Clarke subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g:\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), with \(\Omega\) open, be locally Lipschitz at \(x\in\Omega\). For each \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
g^\circ(x;d):=\limsup_{\substack{y\to x\\t\downarrow0}}\frac{g(y+td)-g(y)}{t}.
\]
This value is finite, and
\[
\partial g(x)=\left\{\xi\in\mathbb{R}^n:\xi^Td\le g^\circ(x;d)\ \text{for every }d\in\mathbb{R}^n\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke generalized directional derivative is the upper limit of nearby forward difference quotients. Local Lipschitz continuity makes it finite, and the Clarke subdifferential comprises exactly the linear forms dominated by it in every direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall d\in\mathbb{R}^n,\quad g^\circ(x;d)=\limsup_{y\to x,\,t\downarrow0}\frac{g(y+td)-g(y)}{t}\in\mathbb{R},\qquad \partial g(x)=\{\xi:\xi^Td\le g^\circ(x;d)\ \forall d\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke Subdifferential by Gradient Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For a locally Lipschitz real-valued function on finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^N\to\mathbb{R}\) be locally Lipschitz and let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^N\). Define \[M_f(x):=\left\{\lim_{j\to\infty}\nabla f(y^j):y^j\to x,\ f\text{ is differentiable at every }y^j\right\}.\] Then \(M_f(x)\) is nonempty, bounded, and closed, and the Clarke subdifferential is \[\partial^C f(x):=\operatorname{conv}M_f(x).\] Its elements are Clarke subgradients, and \(\partial^C f(x)=-\partial^C(-f)(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a locally Lipschitz function, collect all limits of gradients along differentiability points approaching x and take their convex hull. This is the Clarke subdifferential; the gradient-limit set is nonempty, bounded, and closed, and negating the function negates its subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M_f(x)\ne\varnothing,\ M_f(x)\text{ is bounded and closed},\quad \partial^C f(x)=\operatorname{conv}M_f(x),\quad \partial^C f(x)=-\partial^C(-f)(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Consistency of the Clarke Generalized Gradient with Classical Derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction to the Fréchet derivative in the continuously differentiable regime and to the convex subdifferential in the convex lower-semicontinuous regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a Banach space. If \(f\) is continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of \(x\), then
\[
\partial_C f(x)=\{f'(x)\}.
\]
If \(f\) is convex and lower semicontinuous and \(x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), then
\[
\partial_C f(x)=\partial f(x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a point with a continuously differentiable neighborhood, the Clarke generalized gradient is the singleton containing the classical derivative. For a convex lower-semicontinuous function at an interior point of its domain, it equals the convex subdifferential.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is continuously differentiable near }x\quad\text{or}\quad(f\text{ is convex and lsc and }x\in\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[f\in C^1\text{ near }x\Rightarrow\partial_C f(x)=\{f'(x)\}\bigr]\quad\text{and}\quad\bigl[f\text{ convex and lsc},\ x\in\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f\Rightarrow\partial_C f(x)=\partial f(x)\bigr]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak-Star Closed-Graph Property of the Clarke Generalized Gradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer semicontinuity along strongly convergent base points and weak-star cluster points of generalized gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a Banach space and let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be Lipschitz of rank \(K\) near \(x\). Suppose
\[
x_i\to x,\qquad \zeta_i\in\partial_C f(x_i)\quad\forall i.
\]
If \(\zeta\) is a weak-star cluster point of \((\zeta_i)\), then
\[
\zeta\in\partial_C f(x).
\]
In particular, the conclusion holds if \(\zeta_i\to\zeta\) in \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a locally Lipschitz function, generalized gradients at points converging to x cannot have a weak-star cluster point outside the Clarke generalized gradient at x. Norm convergence in the dual is a sufficient special case.
assumptions_latex: f:X\to\mathbb R\text{ is Lipschitz of rank }K\text{ near }x
\zeta\text{ is a weak* cluster point of }(\zeta_i)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \zeta\in\partial_C f(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic sufficient conditions for Clarke regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise regularity properties for locally Lipschitz functions and the resulting Clarke generalized-gradient representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be Lipschitz near \(x\). (a) If \(f\) is strictly differentiable at \(x\), then \(f\) is regular at \(x\). (b) If \(f\) is convex, then \(f\) is regular at \(x\). (c) A finite linear combination with nonnegative coefficients of functions regular at \(x\) is regular at \(x\). (d) If \(f\) is regular at \(x\) and admits a Gâteaux derivative \(Df(x)\), then \(\partial f(x)=\{Df(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict differentiability or convexity implies Clarke regularity at the point, and finite nonnegative linear combinations preserve regularity. If a regular function is Gâteaux differentiable there, its Clarke generalized gradient is the singleton containing that derivative.
assumptions_latex: \text{For (c), the functions are regular at }x\text{ and their coefficients are nonnegative}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Conclusions (a)--(c) give regularity at }x;\quad\text{conclusion (d) gives }\partial f(x)=\{Df(x)\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subderivative criterion for subdifferential regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient characterization by equality of ordinary and regular subderivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is subdifferentially regular at \(\bar x\) if and only if it is finite and locally lower semicontinuous at \(\bar x\) and
\[
df(\bar x)=\widehat d f(\bar x).
\]
Under these conditions, this equality is equivalent to
\[
\operatorname{e-limsup}_{x\to_f\bar x}df(x)=df(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subdifferential regularity at a point is equivalent to finiteness and local lower semicontinuity there together with equality of the ordinary and regular subderivatives. Equivalently, the subderivative equals the epigraphical upper limit of nearby subderivatives under functional convergence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is regular at }\bar x\iff \bigl[f(\bar x)\in\mathbb R,\ f\text{ locally lsc at }\bar x,\ df(\bar x)=\widehat d f(\bar x)\bigr]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structural relations between subderivatives and regular subderivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower semicontinuity, homogeneity, ordering, sublinearity, and epigraphical-limit representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and \(f(\bar x)\in\mathbb R\), both \(df(\bar x)\) and \(\widehat d f(\bar x)\) are lower semicontinuous and positively homogeneous, and
\[
\widehat d f(\bar x)\ge df(\bar x).
\]
If \(f\) is lsc at \(\bar x\), then \(\widehat d f(\bar x)\) is sublinear. If \(f\) is locally lsc at \(\bar x\), then
\[
\widehat d f(\bar x)=\operatorname{e-limsup}_{x\to_f\bar x}df(x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every finite-valued reference point, the ordinary and regular subderivatives are lower semicontinuous and positively homogeneous, with the regular subderivative dominating the ordinary one. Lower semicontinuity at the point makes the regular subderivative sublinear, and local lower semicontinuity represents it as the epigraphical upper limit of nearby subderivatives under functional convergence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: df(\bar x),\widehat d f(\bar x)\text{ are lsc and positively homogeneous},\quad \widehat d f(\bar x)\ge df(\bar x);\quad f\text{ locally lsc at }\bar x\Rightarrow \widehat d f(\bar x)=\operatorname{e-limsup}_{x\to_f\bar x}df(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subderivatives of convex functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided directional derivative, sublinearity, regularity, and domain-interior identities for convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be convex and finite at \(\bar x\). For every \(w\in\mathbb R^n\), the limit
\[
h(w):=\lim_{\tau\searrow0}\frac{f(\bar x+\tau w)-f(\bar x)}{\tau}
\]
exists and defines a sublinear extended-real function satisfying
\[
f(\bar x+\tau w)\ge f(\bar x)+\tau h(w)\qquad(\tau\ge0).
\]
Furthermore,
\[
\widehat d f(\bar x)(w)=df(\bar x)(w)=(\operatorname{cl}h)(w)\quad\text{for all }w.
\]
If
\[
W:=\{w:\exists\tau\ge0,\ \bar x+\tau w\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\},
\]
then \((\operatorname{cl}h)(w)=h(w)\) on \(W\), and
\[
W=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}\widehat d f(\bar x))=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}df(\bar x))=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex extended-real function finite at the reference point, every one-sided directional difference quotient has a limit. The resulting function is sublinear, gives a global raywise lower bound, and its lower-semicontinuous closure equals both the ordinary and regular subderivatives. On the directions reaching the interior of the effective domain, no closure is needed, and this set is the common interior of the domains of all three directional models.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat d f(\bar x)=df(\bar x)=\operatorname{cl}h,\quad h(w)=\lim_{\tau\searrow0}\frac{f(\bar x+\tau w)-f(\bar x)}{\tau}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interior formula for regular subderivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interior, exterior, and boundary evaluation from a robust directional limsup.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be locally lsc at \(\bar x\), with \(f(\bar x)\in\mathbb R\), and define
\[
h(\bar w):=\limsup_{\substack{\tau\searrow0,\ x\to_f\bar x\\ w\to\bar w}}\frac{f(x+\tau w)-f(x)}{\tau},\qquad O:=\{\bar w:h(\bar w)<\infty\}.
\]
Then
\[
\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}\widehat d f(\bar x))=O,
\qquad \widehat d f(\bar x)(\bar w)=h(\bar w)\quad(\bar w\in O).
\]
If \(O\ne\varnothing\), then \(\widehat d f(\bar x)(\bar w)=+\infty\) for \(\bar w\notin\operatorname{cl}O\), while for every \(\bar w\in\operatorname{bdry}O\) and every \(\widehat w\in O\),
\[
\widehat d f(\bar x)(\bar w)=\lim_{\tau\searrow0}h((1-\tau)\bar w+\tau\widehat w).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a locally lower-semicontinuous function finite at the reference point, a robust limsup of nearby directional difference quotients equals the regular subderivative on its finite-valued set, which is exactly the interior of the regular subderivative's domain. When that interior is nonempty, the regular subderivative is infinite outside its closure and its boundary values are limits approached from any interior direction.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is locally lsc at }\bar x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}\widehat d f(\bar x))=O,\quad \widehat d f(\bar x)|_O=h|_O

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regular subderivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraphical definition of the regular first-order directional growth function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and \(\bar x\) with \(f(\bar x)\in\mathbb R\), define \(\Delta_\tau f(x)(w)=[f(x+\tau w)-f(x)]/\tau\). The regular subderivative is
\[
\widehat d f(\bar x):=\operatorname{e-limsup}_{\tau\searrow0,\,x\to_f\bar x}\Delta_\tau f(x),
\]
where \(x\to_f\bar x\) means \(x\to\bar x\) and \(f(x)\to f(\bar x)\). Equivalently,
\[
\widehat d f(\bar x)(\bar w)=\lim_{\delta\searrow0}\limsup_{\substack{x\to_f\bar x\\ \tau\searrow0}}\inf_{w\in B(\bar w,\delta)}\frac{f(x+\tau w)-f(x)}{\tau}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a finite-valued point, the regular subderivative is the epigraphical upper limit of the first-order difference-quotient functions as the step decreases to zero and the base point converges functionally to the reference point. Its value in a direction is equivalently obtained by taking infima over shrinking neighborhoods of that direction before the outer limsup.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat d f(\bar x)=\operatorname{e-limsup}_{\tau\searrow0,\,x\to_f\bar x}\Delta_\tau f(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary Support and Quotient Representation of the Shape Gradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes the support and factorization of a finite-order shape gradient through deformation fields modulo the shape-invariant subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let J be a real-valued shape functional having a shape gradient G(\Omega) for \Omega\subset\mathbb R^N with boundary \Gamma. Then \operatorname{supp}G(\Omega)\subset\Gamma. If \Omega is open or closed and G(\Omega) has order k\ge0, there exists [G(\Omega)]\in(\mathcal D^k/L_\Omega^k)' such that, for every V\in\mathcal D^k(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb R^N), dJ(\Omega;V)=\langle[G(\Omega)],q_LV\rangle_{\mathcal D^k/L_\Omega^k}, where q_L:\mathcal D^k\to\mathcal D^k/L_\Omega^k is the canonical quotient map. Moreover, G(\Omega)=q_L^*[G(\Omega)].
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The shape gradient is supported on the boundary. For an open or closed shape and a finite-order gradient, the derivative depends only on the equivalence class of a deformation field modulo the subspace that produces no first-order shape change; equivalently, the gradient is the transpose pullback of a functional on that quotient.
assumptions_latex: \Omega\text{ is open or closed for the quotient representation}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{supp}G(\Omega)\subset\Gamma,\qquad dJ(\Omega;V)=\langle[G(\Omega)],q_LV\rangle,\qquad G(\Omega)=q_L^*[G(\Omega)].
