knowledge_statements.statement_title: Correspondence of Parameterized, Eulerian, and Hadamard Shape Semiderivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates derivatives of the parameterization map f↦J((I+f)(Ω)) to shape derivatives transported by I+f.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let J be a real-valued shape functional, f,\theta\in\Theta, and I+f\in\mathcal F(\Theta). (i) If J_\Omega has a Gâteaux semiderivative at f in direction \theta, then J has an Eulerian semiderivative at \Omega_f in direction V_\theta^f(t)=\theta\circ[I+f+t\theta]^{-1} for sufficiently small t, and dJ_\Omega(f;\theta)=dJ(\Omega_f;V_\theta^f). (ii) If J has a Hadamard semiderivative at \Omega_f in direction \theta\circ[I+f]^{-1}, then J_\Omega has a Gâteaux semiderivative at f in direction \theta and dJ_\Omega(f;\theta)=d_HJ(\Omega_f;\theta\circ[I+f]^{-1}). Conversely, if J_\Omega has a Gâteaux semiderivative at f in direction \theta\circ[I+f], then J has a Hadamard semiderivative at \Omega_f in direction \theta. If either derivative is linear and continuous for every \theta\in\Theta, then so is the other, with \langle\nabla J_\Omega(f),\theta\rangle_\Theta=\langle G(\Omega_f),\theta\circ[I+f]^{-1}\rangle_\Theta and \langle G(\Omega_f),\theta\rangle_\Theta=\langle\nabla J_\Omega(f),\theta\circ[I+f]\rangle_\Theta.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Gâteaux semiderivative of the parameterized functional yields the corresponding Eulerian shape semiderivative. A Hadamard shape semiderivative pulled back through the deformation yields the Gâteaux semiderivative, with a converse under the stated transformed direction. Linearity and continuity transfer between the two derivative representations, and their gradients are related by composition with the deformation and its inverse.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuous Shape Gradient Implies Fréchet Differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A local differentiability upgrade for a shape functional expressed through deformation parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let J be a real-valued shape functional, \Omega\subset\mathbb R^N, k\ge0, and let \Theta be one of C_0^{k+1}(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb R^N), C^{k+1}(\overline{\mathbb R^N};\mathbb R^N), \mathcal C^{k,1}(\overline{\mathbb R^N}), or \mathcal B^{k+1}(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb R^N). If J_\Omega is Gâteaux differentiable at every f\in B_\varepsilon and f\mapsto\nabla J_\Omega(f):B_\varepsilon\to\Theta' is continuous at f=0, then J_\Omega is Fréchet differentiable at 0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the deformation-parameterized shape functional is Gâteaux differentiable throughout a neighborhood of zero and its gradient is continuous at zero as a dual-space-valued map, then it is Fréchet differentiable at zero.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normal-Trace Representation on a Smooth Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A smooth-boundary consequence of the shape-gradient structure theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the shape-gradient structure theorem holds for an open domain \Omega\subset\mathbb R^N, G(\Omega) has order k\ge0, and \Gamma=\partial\Omega is C^{k+1}. Then each tangent space L_\Omega(x), x\in\Gamma, is an (N-1)-dimensional hyperplane and \Gamma has a unique outward unit normal n\in C^k(\Gamma;\mathbb R^N). The kernel of V\mapsto\gamma_\Gamma(V)\cdot n from \mathcal D^k(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb R^N) to C^k(\Gamma) is L_\Omega^k, and q_L(V)\mapsto\gamma_\Gamma(V)\cdot n is a well-defined isomorphism \mathcal D^k/L_\Omega^k\to C^k(\Gamma). Consequently, there exists g(\Gamma)\in C^k(\Gamma)' supported on \Gamma such that dJ(\Omega;V)=\langle g(\Gamma),\gamma_\Gamma(V)\cdot n\rangle_{C^k(\Gamma)} for every V\in\mathcal D^k. Moreover [G(\Omega)]=p_L^*g(\Gamma) and G(\Omega)=q_L^*[G(\Omega)]. If g(\Gamma)\in L^1(\Gamma), then dJ(\Omega;V)=\int_\Gamma g\,(V\cdot n)\,d\Gamma and G=\gamma_\Gamma^*(gn).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a C^{k+1} boundary, deformation fields modulo tangential fields are identified with their scalar normal traces. Hence every order-k shape derivative is represented by a scalar distribution acting on the normal boundary velocity. If that distribution is integrable, the derivative is the boundary integral of its density times the normal component of the deformation.
assumptions_latex: \text{the assumptions of the shape-gradient structure theorem hold}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: dJ(\Omega;V)=\langle g(\Gamma),\gamma_\Gamma(V)\cdot n\rangle,\qquad g(\Gamma)\in C^k(\Gamma)',\qquad g\in L^1(\Gamma)\Rightarrow dJ(\Omega;V)=\int_\Gamma g(V\cdot n)\,d\Gamma.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Shape Differentiability, Shape Gradient, and Gradient Order
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for real-valued functionals of subsets of Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let J be a real-valued shape functional and \Omega\subset\mathbb R^N. The functional J is shape differentiable at \Omega if it is differentiable at \Omega in every direction \theta\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb R^N). The resulting linear derivative map defines a vector distribution G(\Omega)\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb R^N)' called the shape gradient. For a finite k\ge0, the shape gradient is of order k when G(\Omega) is continuous in the \mathcal D^k(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb R^N)-topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A shape functional is shape differentiable when it is differentiable along every compactly supported smooth deformation field. Its derivative defines a vector-valued distribution called the shape gradient. The gradient has order k when it is continuous for the corresponding D^k topology.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G(\Omega)\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb R^N)',\qquad \operatorname{ord}G(\Omega)=k\iff G(\Omega)\text{ is }\mathcal D^k\text{-continuous}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semiderivative and semidifferentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perturbation-stable directional derivative for an extended-real-valued function at a finite-valued point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}} with f(\bar x) finite. If, for w\in\mathbb{R}^n, the possibly infinite limit \[\mathrm{d}f(\bar x)(w):=\lim_{\substack{\tau\searrow0\\w'\to w}}\frac{f(\bar x+\tau w')-f(\bar x)}{\tau}\] exists, it is the semiderivative of f at \bar x in direction w, and f is semidifferentiable there for w. The function f is semidifferentiable at \bar x if this limit exists for every w\in\mathbb{R}^n.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a point where f is finite, its semiderivative in direction w is the possibly infinite difference-quotient limit as the positive step tends to zero while the perturbed direction tends to w. Semidifferentiability at the point means that this limit exists for every direction.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent characterizations of semidifferentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes semidifferentiability through convergence of first-order difference quotients and a positively homogeneous expansion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}} be finite at \bar x, and write \Delta_\tau f(\bar x)(w)=[f(\bar x+\tau w)-f(\bar x)]/\tau. The following are equivalent: (a) f is semidifferentiable at \bar x; (b) \Delta_\tau f(\bar x) converges continuously to a function h as \tau\searrow0; (c) it converges uniformly on every bounded subset of \mathbb{R}^n to a continuous h; (d) for every \rho>0 there is \mu>0 such that \{\Delta_\tau f(\bar x):0<\tau<\mu\} is equibounded on \rho\mathbb{B} and converges graphically there to a real-valued function h; (e) there is a finite, continuous, positively homogeneous h such that \[f(x)=f(\bar x)+h(x-\bar x)+o(\|x-\bar x\|).\] Each condition implies continuity of f at \bar x, and the semiderivative is finite, continuous and positively homogeneous in w, with h(w)=\mathrm{d}f(\bar x)(w)=f'(\bar x;w).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a function finite at the reference point, semidifferentiability is equivalent to continuous convergence, uniform convergence on bounded sets, or locally equibounded graphical convergence of its first-order difference quotients, and also to a first-order expansion by a finite continuous positively homogeneous function. These conditions imply continuity, and that function is the semiderivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (a)\iff(b)\iff(c)\iff(d)\iff(e),\qquad h(w)=\mathrm{d}f(\bar x)(w)=f'(\bar x;w),\quad f\text{ is continuous at }\bar x.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Contingent epiderivative of an interval-valued mapping at its lower endpoint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and representation for an interval-valued multifunction whose lower endpoint function is convex and continuous at the base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(X,\|\cdot\|_X)$ be a real normed space, let $f,g:X\to\mathbb{R}$, and define $F:X\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}$ by $$F(x):=\{y\in\mathbb{R}\mid f(x)\leq y\leq g(x)\}\quad\text{for every }x\in X.$$ Let $\bar{x}\in X$. knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: DF(\bar{x},f(\bar{x}))\text{ exists and }\forall h\in X,\quad DF(\bar{x},f(\bar{x}))(h)=f'(\bar{x})(h).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Homogeneity, Subadditivity, and Sublinearity of Set-Valued Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supporting terminology used to state structural properties of generalized contingent epiderivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the standing assumptions of Definition 15.10, a set-valued map \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is strictly positively homogeneous if \[F(\alpha x)=\alpha F(x)\quad\text{for every }\alpha>0\text{ and }x\in X.\] It is subadditive relative to \(C\) if \[F(x_1)+F(x_2)\subseteq F(x_1+x_2)+C\quad\text{for every }x_1,x_2\in X.\] It is sublinear if the homogeneity identity holds for every \(\alpha\geq0\) and the subadditivity condition holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-valued map is strictly positively homogeneous when positive scaling commutes with the map. It is subadditive relative to C when the sum of two values is contained in the value at the summed arguments up to C. It is sublinear when homogeneity also includes zero and subadditivity holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}&F\text{ strictly positively homogeneous}\iff (\forall\alpha>0)(\forall x\in X)\ F(\alpha x)=\alpha F(x),\\&F\text{ subadditive}\iff(\forall x_1,x_2\in X)\ F(x_1)+F(x_2)\subseteq F(x_1+x_2)+C,\\&F\text{ sublinear}\iff\text{both conditions hold with homogeneity for all }\alpha\geq0.\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.title: Lower Epiderivative Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower perturbed-direction first-order regime for an extended-real function on a finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional normed space, let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and suppose \(f(\bar x)\in\mathbb R\). For \(t>0\), define \[q_t(h):=\frac{f(\bar x+th)-f(\bar x)}{t}.\] The lower Hadamard epiderivative is \[d^-f(\bar x;h):=\liminf_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\h'\to h}}q_t(h')=\sup_{\varepsilon>0}\inf\{q_t(h'):0<t<\varepsilon,\ \|h'-h\|<\varepsilon\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower Hadamard epiderivative is the liminf of first-order difference quotients under simultaneous vanishing steps and directional perturbations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d^-f(\bar x;h)=\liminf_{t\downarrow0,\,h'\to h}q_t(h')\).

knowledge_statements.title: Epiderivative Coincidence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise coincidence of lower and upper Hadamard epiderivatives in a fixed direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional normed space, let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) satisfy \(f(\bar x)\in\mathbb R\), and fix \(h\in X\). With \[q_t(h'):=\frac{f(\bar x+th')-f(\bar x)}{t},\] one has \[d^-f(\bar x;h)\le d^+f(\bar x;h).\] Moreover, for \(a\in[-\infty,+\infty]\), \[d^-f(\bar x;h)=d^+f(\bar x;h)=a\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\lim_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\h'\to h}}q_t(h')=a\] in the extended real line.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower and upper Hadamard epiderivatives coincide at an extended-real value exactly when the perturbed first-order quotient converges to that value.
assumptions_latex: \(h\in X\), and both epiderivatives use the same perturbed-direction convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d^-f(\bar x;h)=d^+f(\bar x;h)\) if and only if the corresponding perturbed-direction quotient has an extended-real limit.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[q_t(h'):=\frac{f(\bar x+th')-f(\bar x)}{t},\] one always has \(d^-f(\bar x;h)\le d^+f(\bar x;h)\). If both endpoints are finite, define \[G(\bar x;h):=d^+f(\bar x;h)-d^-f(\bar x;h).\] Then \(G(\bar x;h)>0\) if and only if \(q_t(h')\) has no limit as \(t\downarrow0\) and \(h'\to h\). More generally, unequal extended-real endpoints imply the same nonconvergence, but no numerical gap is defined when extended-real subtraction is indeterminate. This conclusion concerns the scalar joint limit and does not by itself assert failure or nonuniqueness of a Painleve-Kuratowski epigraphical limit.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is properly epi-differentiable at \(\bar x\) when \(q_t\) epi-converges to a proper lower-semicontinuous function \(d_e f(\bar x)\).
review_flags: Uses the explicit proper epi-differentiability convention to avoid conflating proper and possibly improper epi-limits.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proper first-order epi-differentiability through Painleve-Kuratowski convergence of difference-quotient epigraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is properly epi-differentiable at \(\bar x\) if there exists a proper lower-semicontinuous function \(d_e f(\bar x):X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) such that \[q_t\xrightarrow{e}d_e f(\bar x)\quad\text{as }t\downarrow0.\] Equivalently, \(\operatorname{epi}q_t\) converges to \(\operatorname{epi}d_e f(\bar x)\) in the Painleve-Kuratowski sense. The limit is unique and is the proper first epi-derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proper epi-differentiability means that the first-order difference quotients epi-converge to one proper lower-semicontinuous function.

Convergence is interpreted sequentially in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_t\xrightarrow{e}g\) exactly when every vanishing-scale convergent-direction sequence satisfies the liminf inequality and every direction has recovery directions along every vanishing scale sequence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential characterization and failure boundary for the first-order quotient family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper lower-semicontinuous \(g\), the convergence \(q_t\xrightarrow{e}g\) as \(t\downarrow0\) is equivalent to both conditions: (i) for every \(t_k\downarrow0\) and \(h_k\to h\), \[\liminf_{k\to\infty}q_{t_k}(h_k)\ge g(h);\] and (ii) for every \(h\) and every \(t_k\downarrow0\), there exist \(h_k\to h\) such that \[\limsup_{k\to\infty}q_{t_k}(h_k)\le g(h).\] Thus proper epi-differentiability fails exactly when no single proper lower-semicontinuous \(g\) satisfies both requirements.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epi-derivative and epi-differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order epigraphical derivative of an extended-real-valued function at a finite-valued point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}} with f(\bar x) finite, and let \Delta_\tau f(\bar x)(w')=[f(\bar x+\tau w')-f(\bar x)]/\tau. If the possibly infinite epi-limit \[\operatorname*{epi-lim}_{\substack{\tau\searrow0\\w'\to w}}\Delta_\tau f(\bar x)(w')\] exists, it is the epi-derivative of f at \bar x for w, and f is epi-differentiable there for w. The function is epi-differentiable at \bar x if this holds for every w, equivalently if \Delta_\tau f(\bar x) epi-converges on \mathbb{R}^n to a function h as \tau\searrow0; it is properly epi-differentiable if h is proper.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epi-derivative is the possibly infinite epi-limit of the first-order difference quotients as the positive step tends to zero and the direction is perturbed toward the specified direction. Epi-differentiability requires this at every direction, and proper epi-differentiability additionally requires the limiting function to be proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is epi-differentiable at }\bar x\iff\Delta_\tau f(\bar x)\xrightarrow[\tau\searrow0]{\mathrm{epi}}h;\qquad f\text{ is properly epi-differentiable}\iff h\text{ is proper}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional normed space and let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\). Suppose that for every \(h\in X\) the directional derivative \[f'(\bar x;h):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(\bar x+th)-f(\bar x)}{t}\] exists. Define the Clarke generalized directional derivative by \[f^{\circ}(\bar x;h):=\limsup_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\t\downarrow0}}\frac{f(x+th)-f(x)}{t}.\] The function \(f\) is directionally regular at \(\bar x\) if \[f'(\bar x;h)=f^{\circ}(\bar x;h)\quad\text{for every }h\in X.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Lipschitz function is directionally regular at a point when each ordinary directional derivative exists and equals the corresponding Clarke generalized directional derivative.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is directionally regular at \(\bar x\) when \(f'(\bar x;h)=f^{\circ}(\bar x;h)\) for every \(h\in X\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp counterexample showing that local Lipschitz continuity and existence of all directional derivatives do not imply directional regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=-|x|\), the ordinary directional derivative exists in every direction and equals \[f'(0;h)=-|h|.\] The Clarke generalized directional derivative is \[f^\circ(0;h)=|h|.\] Thus the two derivatives disagree for every \(h\ne0\), and \(f\) is not directionally regular at zero. Equivalently, the ordinary directional derivative is not sublinear and therefore cannot be a support function. This also shows that negation need not preserve directional regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The locally Lipschitz function minus absolute value has all ordinary directional derivatives, but they equal minus absolute value rather than the Clarke derivative absolute value.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical smooth and convex regimes in which ordinary and Clarke directional constructions coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\), then \[f'(\bar x;h)=f^\circ(\bar x;h)=\langle\nabla f(\bar x),h\rangle.\] If \(f\) is convex and locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\), then \[f'(\bar x;h)=f^\circ(\bar x;h)=\max_{v\in\partial f(\bar x)}\langle v,h\rangle.\] Hence both classes are directionally regular at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuously differentiable functions and locally Lipschitz convex functions are directionally regular, with gradient and subgradient support formulas respectively.

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) and directionally regular at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(\bar x;h)=\sigma_{\partial^C f(\bar x)}(h)=\max_{v\in\partial^C f(\bar x)}\langle v,h\rangle\) for every \(h\), and \(h\mapsto f'(\bar x;h)\) is finite, continuous, and sublinear.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent dual representation and immediate structural consequences of Clarke directional regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite-valued locally Lipschitz function on a finite-dimensional space, \(f^\circ(\bar x;h)=\max_{v\in\partial^C f(\bar x)}\langle v,h\rangle\). Consequently, \(f\) is directionally regular at \(\bar x\) if and only if its ordinary directional derivative exists in every direction and satisfies \[f'(\bar x;h)=\max_{v\in\partial^C f(\bar x)}\langle v,h\rangle\quad\text{for all }h.\] In that case \(h\mapsto f'(\bar x;h)\) is a finite continuous sublinear function. In particular, an existing directional derivative that is not sublinear cannot be directionally regular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a directionally regular point, the ordinary directional derivative is exactly the support function of the Clarke subdifferential and is therefore continuous and sublinear.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary closure calculus for Clarke-directionally regular locally Lipschitz functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m\) be locally Lipschitz and directionally regular at \(\bar x\). For coefficients \(\lambda_i\ge0\), the function \(g=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f_i\) is directionally regular and \[g'(\bar x;h)=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f_i'(\bar x;h).\] The finite maximum \(F=\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i\) is also directionally regular and \[F'(\bar x;h)=\max_{i\in I(\bar x)}f_i'(\bar x;h),\qquad I(\bar x)=\{i:f_i(\bar x)=F(\bar x)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative finite sums and finite maxima preserve directional regularity, with sum and active-index maximum derivative formulas.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional regularity characterized by equality of the ordinary and Clarke generalized directional derivatives, with immediate closure and representation properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g:\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be locally Lipschitz on the open set \(\Omega\). It is Clarke regular at \(x\in\Omega\) if it is directionally differentiable at \(x\) and
\[
g^\circ(x;d)=g'(x;d)\qquad\text{for every }d\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
Convex functions and functions continuously differentiable at \(x\) are Clarke regular there, and nonnegative combinations of functions regular at the same point are regular. Under Clarke regularity at \(x\),
\[
g'(x;d)=\max_{\xi\in\partial g(x)}\xi^Td\qquad\text{for every }d\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Lipschitz function is Clarke regular at a point when it is directionally differentiable there and its ordinary and Clarke directional derivatives agree in every direction. Convex and continuously differentiable functions are regular, nonnegative combinations preserve regularity, and regularity gives a support formula through the Clarke subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g\text{ is Clarke regular at }x\iff g\text{ is directionally differentiable at }x\text{ and }g^\circ(x;d)=g'(x;d)\ \forall d;\quad g'(x;d)=\max_{\xi\in\partial g(x)}\xi^Td\text{ under regularity}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional and Gâteaux derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical differentiability of maps between real linear spaces, with limits taken only through domain-admissible steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X be a real linear space, Y a real topological linear space, \varnothing\ne S\subseteq X, f:S\to Y, and \bar x\in S. For h\in X, the directional derivative is f'(\bar x)(h):=\lim_{\lambda\to0+}[f(\bar x+\lambda h)-f(\bar x)]/\lambda when this limit exists through positive \lambda for which \bar x+\lambda h\in S. The map f is directionally differentiable at \bar x if these limits exist for every h\in X. If the corresponding two-sided, domain-admissible limits exist for every h\in X and h\mapsto f'(\bar x)(h) is a continuous linear map X\to Y, then f'(\bar x) is the Gâteaux derivative of f at \bar x.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directional derivative is a one-sided difference-quotient limit along feasible positive steps. A Gâteaux derivative uses two-sided feasible limits in every direction and must form a continuous linear map.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ is a real linear space}
Y\text{ is a real topological linear space}
\bar x+\lambda h\in S\text{ for the steps used in each limit}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f'(\bar x)(h)=\lim_{\substack{\lambda\to0+\\\bar x+\lambda h\in S}}\frac{f(\bar x+\lambda h)-f(\bar x)}{\lambda};\quad \text{the two-sided family is Gâteaux when }f'(\bar x)\in\mathcal L(X,Y).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semicontinuity ensures exhaustive approximation families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence theorem at a point for a bounded directional derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), where \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) is open, and let \(x\in X\). Suppose \(f\) is directionally differentiable at \(x\) and \(\sup_{\|g\|\le1}f'_x(g)<+\infty\). If \(f'_x\) is upper semicontinuous as a function of \(g\), then \(f\) has an exhaustive family of upper convex approximations at \(x\). If \(f'_x\) is lower semicontinuous as a function of \(g\), then \(f\) has an exhaustive family of lower concave approximations at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a directionally differentiable function whose directional derivative is bounded above on the unit ball, upper semicontinuity of that derivative yields an exhaustive family of upper convex approximations, while lower semicontinuity yields an exhaustive family of lower concave approximations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'_x\text{ u.s.c.}\Rightarrow f\text{ has an exhaustive family of u.c.a.'s at }x;\quad f'_x\text{ l.s.c.}\Rightarrow f\text{ has an exhaustive family of l.c.a.'s at }x.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines pointwise subdifferential regularity and records that directional differentiability alone is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is subdifferentially regular at \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) if it is locally Lipschitz at \(x\) and, for every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the directional derivative \(f'(x;d)\) exists and satisfies \(f'(x;d)=f^\circ(x;d)\). This equality need not follow from directional differentiability alone: for \(f(t)=-|t|\), \(f'(0;1)=-1\) while \(f^\circ(0;1)=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is subdifferentially regular at a point when it is locally Lipschitz there and every classical directional derivative exists and equals the Clarke generalized directional derivative. Directional differentiability alone is insufficient, as shown by minus absolute value at zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is subdifferentially regular at }x\iff f\text{ is locally Lipschitz at }x\text{ and }(\forall d\in\mathbb{R}^n)\;f'(x;d)\text{ exists and equals }f^\circ(x;d).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential Regularity via Directional Derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clarke regularity of a locally Lipschitz function and the stated almost-everywhere consequence when regularity holds globally.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^N\to\mathbb{R}\) be locally Lipschitz. The function \(f\) is subdifferentially regular at \(x\) if, for every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^N\), the ordinary directional derivative \(f'(x;d)\) exists and satisfies \(f'(x;d)=f^{\circ}(x;d)\). If this equality holds at every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^N\) for every direction \(d\), then the Clarke subdifferential \(\partial^C f(x)\) is a singleton for almost every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Lipschitz function is subdifferentially regular at x when all ordinary directional derivatives exist there and equal the Clarke generalized directional derivatives. If this regularity holds everywhere, its Clarke subdifferential is singleton-valued almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is subdifferentially regular at }x\iff\forall d\in\mathbb{R}^N,\ f'(x;d)\text{ exists and }f'(x;d)=f^{\circ}(x;d);\quad [\forall x,d,\ f'(x;d)=f^{\circ}(x;d)]\Rightarrow\partial^C f(x)\text{ is a singleton for a.e. }x

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Smooth Directional Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite continuous selections of smooth functions and their branchwise first-order models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subset\mathbb R^n\) be open. A continuous function \(f:U\to\mathbb R\) is piecewise smooth if there are finitely many functions \(\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_m\in C^1(U)\) such that \[f(x)\in\{\phi_1(x),\ldots,\phi_m(x)\}\quad\text{for every }x\in U.\] Define \[I(x):=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:f(x)=\phi_i(x)\}.\] If \(i\in I(\bar x)\), \(t_k\downarrow0\), \(h_k\to h\), and \(f(\bar x+t_kh_k)=\phi_i(\bar x+t_kh_k)\), then \[\frac{f(\bar x+t_kh_k)-f(\bar x)}{t_k}\to\nabla\phi_i(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}h.\] Thus branchwise first-order limits are drawn from finitely many linear models.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A piecewise-smooth function selects among finitely many smooth pieces; along a sequence that remains on one active piece, its first-order quotient converges to that piece's linearization.
assumptions_latex: \(U\subset\mathbb R^n\) is open and \(f:U\to\mathbb R\) is continuous.
\(\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_m\in C^1(U)\) are finitely many selections satisfying \(f(x)\in\{\phi_1(x),\ldots,\phi_m(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If a sequence approaching \(\bar x\) in direction \(h\) remains on an active branch \(i\), its first-order quotient converges to \(\nabla\phi_i(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}h\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:U\to\mathbb R\) be a continuous selection of finitely many \(C^1\) functions \(\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_m\). Then \(f\) is locally Lipschitz and Bouligand differentiable at every \(\bar x\in U\). Its derivative \(f'_B(\bar x;\cdot)\) is continuous, positively homogeneous, and piecewise linear, and \[f'_B(\bar x;h)\in\{\nabla\phi_i(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}h:i\in I(\bar x)\}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^n).\] Moreover, \[f(\bar x+u)=f(\bar x)+f'_B(\bar x;u)+o(\|u\|).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite continuous piecewise-C1 scalar selection is locally Lipschitz and Bouligand differentiable, with a continuous piecewise-linear derivative selected from active branch linearizations.

knowledge_statements.title: Directional Limit Nonexistence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous one-dimensional counterexample to existence of a one-sided directional derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) by \[f(0)=0,\qquad f(x)=x\sin(\log(1/|x|))\quad(x\ne0).\] The function is continuous at \(0\), while its directional quotient in direction \(1\) satisfies \[\liminf_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(t)-f(0)}{t}=-1<1=\limsup_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(t)-f(0)}{t}.\] Therefore \(f'(0;1)\) does not exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This continuous oscillatory function has directional quotients with lower limit −1 and upper limit 1, so its directional derivative at zero in direction one does not exist.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is defined by \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(x)=x\sin(\log(1/|x|))\) for \(x\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(0;1)\) does not exist.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Persistent bounded oscillation separating lower and upper directional limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) by \[f(0)=0,\qquad f(x)=x\sin(1/x)\quad(x\ne0).\] Its fixed-direction quotient satisfies \[\liminf_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(t)-f(0)}{t}=-1<1=\limsup_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(t)-f(0)}{t}.\] Under the perturbed-direction Hadamard convention, the same endpoint values hold at direction \(1\): \[d^-f(0;1)=-1<1=d^+f(0;1).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For this function the quotient oscillates persistently between −1 and 1; both the fixed-direction and perturbed-direction lower and upper limits remain separated.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is defined by \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(x)=x\sin(1/x)\) for \(x\ne0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Base-Point Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vanishing directional derivatives at one point with unbounded classical derivatives at nearby base points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) by \[f(0)=0,\qquad f(x)=x^2\sin(1/x^2)\quad(x\ne0).\] Then \[f'(0;h)=0\quad\text{for every }h\in\mathbb R,\] whereas for \(x\ne0\), \[f'(x)=2x\sin(1/x^2)-\frac{2}{x}\cos(1/x^2),\] and \(f'\) is unbounded on every neighborhood of \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every directional derivative at zero vanishes, but the classical derivatives at nearby nonzero points are unbounded.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is defined by \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(x)=x^2\sin(1/x^2)\) for \(x\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(0;h)=0\) for every \(h\in\mathbb R\), but \(f'\) is unbounded on every neighborhood of \(0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit moving-base sequence showing that the seed example fails strict semidifferentiability despite having zero directional derivative at the fixed base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(x)=x^2\sin(1/x^2)\) when \(x\ne0\), set \(x_n=(2\pi n)^{-1/2}\) and \(t_n=x_n^5\). Then \(x_n\to0\), \(t_n\downarrow0\), and \[\frac{f(x_n+t_n)-f(x_n)}{t_n}=-\frac{2}{x_n}+o(x_n^{-1})\longrightarrow-\infty.\] In contrast, the fixed-base directional derivative is \(f'(0;1)=0\). Hence the directional model at zero is not stable under simultaneous perturbation of the base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An explicit sequence of nearby base points makes the difference quotients diverge even though the fixed-base directional derivative is zero.

knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Model Breakdown
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hölder growth below order one prevents a finite directional model at linear scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be given by \(f(x)=|x|^{1/2}\). For every \(h\ne0\), \[\frac{f(th)-f(0)}{t}=|h|^{1/2}t^{-1/2}\to+\infty\quad\text{as }t\downarrow0.\] Thus no finite-valued first-order directional model at scale \(t\) represents the nonzero directions at the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the square-root function every nonzero directional quotient diverges to positive infinity at linear scale, so no finite first-order directional model exists there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lim_{t\downarrow0}[f(th)-f(0)]/t=+\infty\) for every \(h\ne0\).

Curved approach sequence along which normalized approximation error persists

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous two-dimensional example separating existence of all fixed-ray directional derivatives from a uniform first-order approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[f(0,0)=0,\qquad f(x,y)=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\,\frac{x^3y}{x^6+y^2}\quad ((x,y)\ne(0,0)).\] The fraction has absolute value at most \(1/2\), so \(f\) is continuous at the origin. For every fixed \(h\in\mathbb R^2\), \(f'(0;h)=0\). Nevertheless, along \(z_s=(s,s^3)\), \[\frac{f(z_s)-f(0)-f'(0;z_s)}{\|z_s\|}=\frac12\] for every \(s\ne0\). Thus the pointwise directional derivative exists in every direction but does not give a uniform first-order approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All fixed-ray directional derivatives at the origin are zero, yet along a curved approach the normalized error remains one half, so the zero directional model is not a uniform first-order model.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise Directional Data Without a Uniform Model

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a proper convex function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), the convex subdifferential is
\[
\partial f(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid f(x)\ge f(\bar x)+\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle\ \text{for all }x\in\mathbb{R}^n\right\}.
\]
Thus \(v\) is a convex subgradient exactly when the affine function with slope \(v\) passing through \((\bar x,f(\bar x))\) globally minorizes \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex subgradient is the slope of an affine function supporting the graph from below at the reference point.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Subdifferential

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex function, zero is a subgradient exactly at its global minimizers.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\in\partial f(x)\iff f(x)+f^*(v)=\langle v,x\rangle\iff x\in\partial f^*(v)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proper closed convex functions in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(v\in\mathbb R^n\), \[v\in\partial f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(x)+f^*(v)=\langle v,x\rangle\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in\partial f^*(v).\] Hence \((\partial f)^{-1}=\partial f^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex subgradient membership is equality in Fenchel-Young, and conjugacy reverses the subdifferential relation.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\Rightarrow\partial f(x)\ne\varnothing\); if \(f\) is finite near \(x\), differentiability at \(x\) is equivalent to \(\partial f(x)\) being a singleton.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise finite-dimensional structure of a proper convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\), \(\partial f(x)\) is closed and convex, and it is nonempty when \(x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\). If \(f\) is finite on a neighborhood of \(x\), then \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\) if and only if \(\partial f(x)\) is a singleton, in which case \(\partial f(x)=\{\nabla f(x)\}\). At boundary points of the domain the subdifferential can be empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex subgradients exist throughout the relative interior, and a singleton subdifferential characterizes differentiability at locally finite points.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every proper closed convex function \(f\), the mapping \(\partial f\) is maximally cyclically monotone. Conversely, \(T:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\) is maximally cyclically monotone if and only if \(T=\partial f\) for some proper closed convex function \(f\); the potential is unique up to an additive constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex subdifferentials are precisely the maximally cyclically monotone mappings.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Wasserstein subdifferentials equal gradients of first variations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For a sufficiently smooth density and finite energy, with a separate quadratic-Wasserstein extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mu=\rho\mathcal L^d\in\mathcal P_p^r(\mathbb R^d)\), where \(\rho\in C^1(\mathbb R^d)\) and \(\mathcal F(\mu)<+\infty\). If \(\mathbf w\in L^q(\mu;\mathbb R^d)\) belongs to the strong subdifferential of \(\mathcal F\) at \(\mu\), then \(\mathbf w=\nabla(\delta\mathcal F/\delta\rho)\) \(\mu\)-a.e. and, for every \(\boldsymbol\xi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^d)\), \[\int \mathbf w\cdot\boldsymbol\xi\,d\mu=-\int \frac{\delta\mathcal F}{\delta\rho}\,\nabla\!\cdot(\rho\boldsymbol\xi)\,dx.\] The same conclusions hold when \(p=2\), \(\rho\in C_c^2(\mathbb R^d)\), and \(\mathbf w\in\partial\mathcal F(\mu)\cap\operatorname{Tan}_\mu\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite-energy probability measure with a C1 density, every strong Wasserstein subdifferential vector field is the gradient of the functional's density first variation and satisfies the corresponding weak integration-by-parts formula. The result also holds in the stated quadratic-Wasserstein tangent-space regime.
assumptions_latex: \mathbf w\in L^q(\mu;\mathbb R^d)\text{ is a strong subdifferential of }\mathcal F\text{ at }\mu
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbf w=\nabla\frac{\delta\mathcal F}{\delta\rho}\quad\mu\text{-a.e.},\qquad \int\mathbf w\cdot\boldsymbol\xi\,d\mu=-\int\frac{\delta\mathcal F}{\delta\rho}\nabla\cdot(\rho\boldsymbol\xi)\,dx\quad\forall\boldsymbol\xi\in C_c^\infty

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity Characterization for Subdifferentially Regular Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes convexity among real-valued functions that are subdifferentially regular everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be subdifferentially regular at every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Then \(f\) is convex if and only if, for all \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[f(y)-f(x)\geq f'(x;y-x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An everywhere subdifferentially regular real-valued function is convex exactly when every increment dominates the directional derivative in the connecting direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex}\iff(\forall x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n)\;f(y)-f(x)\geq f'(x;y-x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential of the Squared 1-Norm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded explicit convex-subdifferential formula, including the zero-vector case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(h:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(h(x)=\|x\|_1^2\), and define \(I_{\ne}(x)=\{i:x_i\ne0\}\) and \(I_0(x)=\{i:x_i=0\}\). For every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
\partial h(x)=2\|x\|_1\left\{z\in\mathbb{R}^n:z_i=\operatorname{sgn}(x_i)\ (i\in I_{\ne}(x)),\ |z_j|\le1\ (j\in I_0(x))\right\}.
\]
In particular, \(\partial h(0)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every vector x, the subdifferential of the square of its l1 norm is twice the l1 norm times the set of l1-norm subgradients: coordinates corresponding to nonzero entries equal their signs, while coordinates corresponding to zero entries lie between −1 and 1. At the origin, the subdifferential is the singleton containing zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial h(x)=2\|x\|_1\{z\in\mathbb{R}^n:z_i=\operatorname{sgn}(x_i)\ \forall i\in I_{\ne}(x),\ |z_j|\le1\ \forall j\in I_0(x)\},\quad \partial h(0)=\{0\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential Continuity at a Differentiability Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collapse of nearby subdifferentials to the derivative and local continuity of the derivative for univariate convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\operatorname{Conv}\mathbb R\), and let \(x_0\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) be a point where \(f\) is differentiable, so that \(Df(x_0)=D_-f(x_0)=D_+f(x_0)\). Then \(\partial f(x)\to Df(x_0)\) as \(x\to x_0\). In particular, if \(f\) is differentiable on a neighborhood of \(x_0\), then \(Df\) is continuous at \(x_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an interior differentiability point of a convex function on the real line, the nearby subdifferential values converge to the derivative. Consequently, if the function is differentiable throughout a neighborhood of that point, its derivative is continuous there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f(x)\to\{Df(x_0)\}\text{ as }x\to x_0;\qquad f\text{ differentiable near }x_0\Rightarrow Df\text{ continuous at }x_0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential of an Affine Infinity Norm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit convex-subdifferential formula for the infinity norm of an affine mapping, including the zero-residual case. This is extraction-grounded evidence without verified item-span alignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} be defined by f(x)=\|Ax+b\|_\infty, where A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, b\in\mathbb{R}^m, and a_i^T is the i-th row of A. Define I_x=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:|a_i^Tx+b_i|=\|Ax+b\|_\infty\}. Then
\[
\partial f(x)=\begin{cases}
A^T B_{\|\cdot\|_1}[0,1],&Ax+b=0,\\
\left\{\displaystyle\sum_{i\in I_x}\lambda_i\operatorname{sgn}(a_i^Tx+b_i)a_i:\lambda_i\geq0,\ \displaystyle\sum_{i\in I_x}\lambda_i=1\right\},&Ax+b\neq0.
\end{cases}
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the infinity norm of an affine mapping, the subdifferential at a nonzero residual is the convex hull of the signed active rows of the matrix. At a zero residual, it is the image under the matrix transpose of the closed unit ball for the l1 norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f(x)=\begin{cases}A^T B_{\|\cdot\|_1}[0,1],&Ax+b=0,\\ \left\{\sum_{i\in I_x}\lambda_i\operatorname{sgn}(a_i^Tx+b_i)a_i:\lambda_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i\in I_x}\lambda_i=1\right\},&Ax+b\neq0.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Top-Eigenvector Subgradient of an Affine Maximum-Eigenvalue Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction of one convex subgradient of the maximum eigenvalue of an affine symmetric-matrix mapping; it is not a complete representation of the subdifferential when the top eigenvalue has multiplicity. This is extraction-grounded evidence without verified item-span alignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let A_0,A_1,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb{S}^n and define \mathcal{A}:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{S}^n by \mathcal{A}(x)=A_0+\sum_{i=1}^m x_iA_i. Let f(x)=\lambda_{\max}(\mathcal{A}(x)). For any x\in\mathbb{R}^m, let \tilde y be a normalized eigenvector of \mathcal{A}(x) corresponding to \lambda_{\max}(\mathcal{A}(x)). Then
\[
(\tilde y^TA_1\tilde y,\tilde y^TA_2\tilde y,\ldots,\tilde y^TA_m\tilde y)^T\in\partial f(x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the maximum eigenvalue of an affine symmetric-matrix mapping, any unit eigenvector associated with the largest eigenvalue yields a subgradient whose coordinates are its quadratic forms with the coefficient matrices. This constructs a subgradient rather than characterizing the entire subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\tilde y^TA_1\tilde y,\tilde y^TA_2\tilde y,\ldots,\tilde y^TA_m\tilde y)^T\in\partial f(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotonicity and One-Sided Limits of the Univariate Convex Subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order, differentiability, and one-sided convergence properties of the subdifferential of a convex function on the real line.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\in\operatorname{Conv}\mathbb R\). Then: (i) if \(x_1<x_2\), \(s_1\in\partial f(x_1)\), and \(s_2\in\partial f(x_2)\), then \(s_1\le s_2\); (ii) the set of points at which \(f\) is not differentiable is at most countable; and (iii) for every \(x_0\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists \(\delta>0\) such that
\[x_0-\delta<x<x_0,\ s\in\partial f(x)\ \Longrightarrow\ D_-f(x_0)-\varepsilon\le s\le D_-f(x_0).\]
Symmetrically, as \(x\downarrow x_0\), the sets \(\partial f(x)\) converge decreasingly to \(D_+f(x_0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential of a convex function on the real line is increasing: every subgradient at an earlier point is no larger than every subgradient at a later point. Such a function is nondifferentiable at at most countably many points. At every interior domain point, nearby subdifferentials converge from the left to the left derivative and from the right to the right derivative, with the corresponding monotone orientation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: s_1\le s_2;\quad \{x:f\text{ is not differentiable at }x\}\text{ is at most countable};\quad \partial f(x)\uparrow D_-f(x_0)\text{ as }x\uparrow x_0,\ \partial f(x)\downarrow D_+f(x_0)\text{ as }x\downarrow x_0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential of the Infinity Norm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded formula preserving the distinct zero and nonzero regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(f(x)=\|x\|_\infty\), and set \(I(x)=\{i:|x_i|=\|x\|_\infty\}\). Then

\end{cases}
\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential of the Coordinatewise Maximum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded specialization of finite-max convex subdifferential calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) by \(f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le n}x_i\), and let \(I(x)=\{i:x_i=f(x)\}\). Then, for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{e_i:i\in I(x)\}
=\left\{\sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_i e_i:\lambda_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_i=1\right\}.
\]
In particular, if \(e=(1,\ldots,1)^T\), then \(\partial f(\alpha e)=\Delta_n\) for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential of the maximum coordinate is the convex hull of the standard basis vectors indexed by coordinates attaining the maximum. Consequently, at any constant vector it is the standard simplex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{e_i:i\in I(x)\}=\left\{\sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_i e_i:\lambda_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_i=1\right\},\qquad \partial f(\alpha e)=\Delta_n\ \forall\alpha\in\mathbb{R}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometric and Analytic Epsilon-Subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions and elementary structural properties for an extended-real-valued function on a Banach space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varphi:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), \(\varepsilon\ge0\), and \(|\varphi(\bar x)|<\infty\). Define \(\widehat\partial_{g\varepsilon}\varphi(\bar x):=\{x^*\in X^*\mid(x^*,-1)\in\widehat N_\varepsilon((\bar x,\varphi(\bar x));\operatorname{epi}\varphi)\}\) and \(\widehat\partial_{a\varepsilon}\varphi(\bar x)=\widehat\partial_\varepsilon\varphi(\bar x):=\{x^*\in X^*\mid\liminf_{x\to\bar x}[\varphi(x)-\varphi(\bar x)-\langle x^*,x-\bar x\rangle]/\|x-\bar x\|\ge-\varepsilon\}\). If \(|\varphi(\bar x)|=\infty\), both sets are defined as empty. For every \(\varepsilon\ge0\), both sets are convex and norm closed; if \(X\) is reflexive, they are weakly closed. They may nevertheless be empty, even for a Lipschitz function and small \(\varepsilon\), as for \(\varphi(x)=-|x|\) at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The geometric epsilon-subdifferential is defined by epsilon-normal vectors to the epigraph with vertical component minus one. The analytic epsilon-subdifferential consists of covectors satisfying the corresponding lower first-order growth inequality. Both are empty at points where the function is not finite, and otherwise are convex and norm closed; in reflexive spaces they are weakly closed. They can still be empty for small epsilon, even for simple Lipschitz functions such as minus absolute value at zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\partial_{g\varepsilon}\varphi(\bar x)\text{ and }\widehat\partial_{a\varepsilon}\varphi(\bar x)\text{ are defined as above, are convex and norm closed, and are empty when }|\varphi(\bar x)|=\infty\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential of Distance to a Closed Convex Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded formula distinguishing points inside and outside the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathbb{E}\) be a Euclidean space and let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{E}\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. For every \(x\in\mathbb{E}\),
\[
\partial d_C(x)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{x-P_C(x)}{d_C(x)},&x\notin C,\\
N_C(x)\cap B[0,1],&x\in C,
\end{cases}
\]
where \(P_C(x)\) is the Euclidean projection onto \(C\), \(N_C(x)\) is the convex normal cone, and \(B[0,1]\) is the closed unit ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty closed convex set in a Euclidean space, the distance function has a unique unit subgradient pointing from the projection to any point outside the set. At a point in the set, its subdifferential is the intersection of the normal cone with the closed unit ball.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial d_C(x)=\begin{cases}(x-P_C(x))/d_C(x),&x\notin C,\\N_C(x)\cap B[0,1],&x\in C.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Convexity Characterized by Strict Subdifferential Monotonicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent strict supporting inequalities and strict subdifferential monotonicity on a convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex. Then \(f\) is strictly convex on \(C\) if and only if, for all distinct \(x_1,x_2\in C\) and all \(s\in\partial f(x_1)\), \[f(x_2)>f(x_1)+\langle s,x_2-x_1\rangle.\] Equivalently, this holds if and only if, for all distinct \(x_1,x_2\in C\) and all \(s_i\in\partial f(x_i)\), \(i=1,2\), \[\langle s_2-s_1,x_2-x_1\rangle>0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex function is strictly convex on a convex set exactly when every subgradient gives a strict supporting inequality between distinct points, equivalently when its subdifferential is strictly monotone there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is strictly convex on }C\iff\forall x_1\neq x_2\in C\ \forall s_i\in\partial f(x_i):\ \langle s_2-s_1,x_2-x_1\rangle>0

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subdifferential existence and compactness at a continuity point, with a conditional local-Lipschitz norm bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-Sided Derivatives of a Univariate Convex Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite one-sided derivatives at interior domain points and their secant-slope representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\in\operatorname{Conv}\mathbb R\) and \(x_0\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\). Then
\[D_-f(x_0)=\lim_{x\uparrow x_0}\frac{f(x)-f(x_0)}{x-x_0}=\sup_{x<x_0}\frac{f(x)-f(x_0)}{x-x_0}\in\mathbb R,\]
\[D_+f(x_0)=\lim_{x\downarrow x_0}\frac{f(x)-f(x_0)}{x-x_0}=\inf_{x>x_0}\frac{f(x)-f(x_0)}{x-x_0}\in\mathbb R,\]
and \(D_-f(x_0)\le D_+f(x_0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every interior point of the domain of a convex function on the real line, both one-sided derivatives exist and are finite. The left derivative is the supremum of the left secant slopes, the right derivative is the infimum of the right secant slopes, and the left derivative does not exceed the right derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D_-f(x_0),D_+f(x_0)\in\mathbb R,\quad D_-f(x_0)=\sup_{x<x_0}\frac{f(x)-f(x_0)}{x-x_0}\le D_+f(x_0)=\inf_{x>x_0}\frac{f(x)-f(x_0)}{x-x_0}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subderivatives and the Subdifferential on the Real Line
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional definition of the convex subdifferential using the left and right derivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\operatorname{Conv}\mathbb R\) and \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). A scalar \(s\in\mathbb R\) is a subderivative of \(f\) at \(x\) when \[D_-f(x)\le s\le D_+f(x).\] The subdifferential is the set of all such subderivatives: \[\partial f(x)=\{s\in\mathbb R:D_-f(x)\le s\le D_+f(x)\}.\] If both one-sided derivatives are finite, then \[\partial f(x)=[D_-f(x),D_+f(x)].\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subderivative is a real number lying between the left and right derivatives. The subdifferential consists of all such numbers and is their closed interval when both derivatives are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f(x)=\{s\in\mathbb R:D_-f(x)\le s\le D_+f(x)\},\qquad D_-f(x),D_+f(x)\in\mathbb R\Rightarrow\partial f(x)=[D_-f(x),D_+f(x)]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimality of the basic subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sequential domination theorem for any presubdifferential satisfying translation, elementary convex compatibility, and an approximate sum rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Banach space. Suppose \(\widehat{\mathcal D}\) is defined for proper lower-semicontinuous \(\varphi:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and satisfies: (M1) translation covariance, \(\widehat{\mathcal D}\phi(u)=\widehat{\mathcal D}\varphi(x+u)\) for \(\phi(u)=\varphi(x+u)\); (M2) for \(\varphi(x)=\langle x^*,x\rangle+\varepsilon\|x\|\), \(\widehat{\mathcal D}\varphi(x)\) is contained in the convex subdifferential; and (M3) whenever \(\varphi_1\) has that form and \(\varphi_1+\varphi_2\) has a local minimum at \(0\), then for every \(\eta>0\) there exist \(x_1,x_2\in\eta\mathbb B\), with \(|\varphi_2(x_2)-\varphi_2(0)|\leq\eta\), such that \(0\in\widehat{\mathcal D}\varphi_1(x_1)+\widehat{\mathcal D}\varphi_2(x_2)+\eta\mathbb B^*\). Then, for every \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}\varphi\), \(\partial\varphi(\bar x)\subset\operatorname*{Limsup}_{x\to\bar x,\,\varphi(x)\to\varphi(\bar x)}\widehat{\mathcal D}\varphi(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every proper lower-semicontinuous function's basic subdifferential is contained in the function-value-attentive sequential outer limit of any presubdifferential satisfying translation covariance, elementary convex compatibility, and the stated approximate sum rule.
assumptions_latex: \varphi:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\text{ is proper and lower semicontinuous}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial\varphi(\bar x)\subset\operatorname*{Limsup}_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\\varphi(x)\to\varphi(\bar x)}}\widehat{\mathcal D}\varphi(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-Sided Derivatives at Domain Endpoints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real secant-slope formulas at finite-valued endpoints of a univariate convex function's domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\in\operatorname{Conv}\mathbb R\) and \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\). If \(x_0\) is the left endpoint of \(\operatorname{dom}f\), then
\[D_+f(x_0)=\lim_{x\downarrow x_0}\frac{f(x)-f(x_0)}{x-x_0}=\inf_{x>x_0}\frac{f(x)-f(x_0)}{x-x_0}\in\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}.\]
If \(x_0\) is the right endpoint, then
\[D_-f(x_0)=\lim_{x\uparrow x_0}\frac{f(x)-f(x_0)}{x-x_0}=\sup_{x<x_0}\frac{f(x)-f(x_0)}{x-x_0}\in\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a left domain endpoint, the right derivative equals the infimum of all right secant slopes and may be minus infinity. At a right endpoint, the left derivative equals the supremum of all left secant slopes and may be plus infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_0=\inf\operatorname{dom}f\Rightarrow D_+f(x_0)=\inf_{x>x_0}\frac{f(x)-f(x_0)}{x-x_0}\in\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\};\quad x_0=\sup\operatorname{dom}f\Rightarrow D_-f(x_0)=\sup_{x<x_0}\frac{f(x)-f(x_0)}{x-x_0}\in\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic and Singular Subdifferentials from Epigraph Normals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraphical definitions and fundamental reductions for a lower-semicontinuous extended-real-valued function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\varphi:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,\infty]\) be finite at \(\bar x\) and lower semicontinuous around \(\bar x\). Define
\[\partial\varphi(\bar x):=\{v:(v,-1)\in N((\bar x,\varphi(\bar x));\operatorname{epi}\varphi)\},\]
\[\partial^\infty\varphi(\bar x):=\{v:(v,0)\in N((\bar x,\varphi(\bar x));\operatorname{epi}\varphi)\}.\]
For the epigraphical multifunction \(E_\varphi(x):=\{\mu:\mu\ge\varphi(x)\}\), these equal \(D^*E_\varphi(\bar x,\varphi(\bar x))(1)\) and \(D^*E_\varphi(\bar x,\varphi(\bar x))(0)\), respectively. The basic subdifferential is \(\{\nabla\varphi(\bar x)\}\) in the smooth case and the convex subdifferential in the convex case. Moreover,
\[\varphi\text{ is locally Lipschitz around }\bar x\iff\partial^\infty\varphi(\bar x)=\{0\}.\]
For a closed set \(\Omega\) and \(\bar x\in\Omega\),
\[\partial\delta_\Omega(\bar x)=\partial^\infty\delta_\Omega(\bar x)=N(\bar x;\Omega).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The basic and singular subdifferentials are vertical slices of the limiting normal cone to the epigraph, equivalently coderivative values of the epigraphical multifunction. The basic subdifferential reduces to the gradient for smooth functions and to the convex subdifferential for convex functions. Vanishing of the singular subdifferential characterizes local Lipschitz continuity, and both subdifferentials of a closed-set indicator equal the limiting normal cone.
assumptions_latex: \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ is closed and }\bar x\in\Omega\text{ for the indicator identity}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial\varphi(\bar x)=\{v:(v,-1)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}\varphi}\},\quad \partial^\infty\varphi(\bar x)=\{v:(v,0)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}\varphi}\},\quad \varphi\text{ locally Lipschitz}\iff\partial^\infty\varphi(\bar x)=\{0\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Convexity Characterized by Strong Subdifferential Monotonicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent first-order growth and strong-monotonicity characterizations on a convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex, let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex, and let \(c>0\). Then \(f\) is strongly convex on \(C\) with modulus \(c\) if and only if, for all \(x_1,x_2\in C\) and all \(s\in\partial f(x_1)\), \[f(x_2)\geq f(x_1)+\langle s,x_2-x_1\rangle+\frac{c}{2}\|x_2-x_1\|^2.\] Equivalently, this holds if and only if, for all \(x_1,x_2\in C\) and all \(s_i\in\partial f(x_i)\), \(i=1,2\), \[\langle s_2-s_1,x_2-x_1\rangle\geq c\|x_2-x_1\|^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex function is strongly convex with modulus c on a convex set exactly when its subgradient inequalities have the corresponding quadratic term, equivalently when its subdifferential is strongly monotone there with modulus c.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is strongly convex on }C\text{ with modulus }c\iff\forall x_1,x_2\in C\ \forall s_i\in\partial f(x_i):\ \langle s_2-s_1,x_2-x_1\rangle\geq c\|x_2-x_1\|^2

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Maximum Rule for Convex Subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded finite-max rule with the stated common-interior qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m\ge1\), let \(f_i:\mathbb{E}\to(-\infty,\infty]\) be proper convex functions for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and define \(f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x)\). If
\[
x\in\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f_i),
\]
then, with \(I(x)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:f_i(x)=f(x)\}\),
\[
\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\left(\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}\partial f_i(x)\right).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a point lying in the interior of every component's domain, the subdifferential of the pointwise maximum of finitely many proper convex functions is the convex hull of the subdifferentials of precisely the active functions.
assumptions_latex: f_i:\mathbb{E}\to(-\infty,\infty]\text{ is proper and convex for }i=1,\ldots,m
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\left(\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}\partial f_i(x)\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex-analytic subgradients and subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition by global affine support, together with its epigraph interpretation and basic set properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a normed space, \(f:X\to\mathbb R_\infty\), and \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). A functional \(\zeta\in X^*\) is a convex-analytic subgradient of \(f\) at \(x\) if \[f(y)-f(x)\geq\langle\zeta,y-x\rangle\qquad\forall y\in X.\] Equivalently, \(y\mapsto f(x)+\langle\zeta,y-x\rangle\) supports \(f\) at \(x\), and the corresponding hyperplane supports \(\operatorname{epi}f\) at \((x,f(x))\). The subdifferential is \[\partial f(x):=\{\zeta\in X^*:f(y)-f(x)\geq\langle\zeta,y-x\rangle\ \forall y\in X\}.\] It is convex and weak-star closed, and \(x\mapsto\partial f(x)\) is a set-valued map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex-analytic subgradient is a continuous linear functional whose affine function globally supports the given function at the point. All such functionals form a convex, weak-star closed subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f(x)=\{\zeta\in X^*:f(y)-f(x)\geq\langle\zeta,y-x\rangle\ \forall y\in X\}\text{ is convex and weak-star closed}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) finite at \(\bar x\), the proximal subdifferential is
\[
\partial_P f(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid \exists r>0,\ \exists\delta>0:\ f(x)\ge f(\bar x)+\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle-\frac r2\|x-\bar x\|^2\ \text{whenever }\|x-\bar x\|<\delta\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(v\in\partial_P f(\bar x)\) when \(\bar x\) is a local minimizer of \(x\mapsto f(x)-\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle+(r/2)\|x-\bar x\|^2\) for some \(r>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximal subgradient supplies a local affine lower support after allowing a negative quadratic error.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proximal subgradient and proximal subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local quadratic-support definition in the dual space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An element \(\zeta\in X^*\) is a proximal subgradient of \(f\) at \(x\) if there exist \(\sigma\geq 0\) and a neighborhood \(V\) of \(x\) such that \[f(y)-f(x)+\sigma\lVert y-x\rVert^2\geq\langle\zeta,y-x\rangle\qquad\forall y\in V.\] The proximal subdifferential \(\partial_Pf(x)\) is the set of all such \(\zeta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximal subgradient at x is a dual vector giving local affine lower support up to a nonnegative quadratic error. The proximal subdifferential is the set of all such vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \zeta\in\partial_Pf(x)\iff\exists\sigma\geq0\;\exists V\ni x\;\forall y\in V:\ f(y)-f(x)+\sigma\lVert y-x\rVert^2\geq\langle\zeta,y-x\rangle.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional characterization of strict continuity and subdifferential regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes functions that are both strictly continuous and regular throughout an open set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f be finite on an open set O\subset\mathbb{R}^n. Then f is strictly continuous and regular on O if and only if, for every x\in O and w\in\mathbb{R}^n, the finite limit h(x,w)=\lim_{\tau\searrow0}\frac{f(x+\tau w)-f(x)}{\tau} exists and x\mapsto h(x,w) is upper semicontinuous for each fixed w. Under these equivalent conditions, h is jointly upper semicontinuous in (x,w), f is semidifferentiable on O, and for all x\in O and w\in\mathbb{R}^n,\quad h(x,w)=\lim_{\substack{\tau\searrow0\\w'\to w}}\frac{f(x+\tau w')-f(x)}{\tau}=\limsup_{\substack{\tau\searrow0\\x'\to x\\w'\to w}}\frac{f(x'+\tau w')-f(x')}{\tau}=d f(x)(w)=\widehat d f(x)(w)=\max_{v\in\partial f(x)}\langle v,w\rangle. Moreover, \partial f:O\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n is nonempty convex-valued, outer semicontinuous, and locally bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite function on an open set is strictly continuous and regular there exactly when every one-sided directional derivative exists finitely and is upper semicontinuous in the base point for each fixed direction. The derivative is then jointly upper semicontinuous, stable under perturbation of direction and base point, equals both variational directional derivatives and the support function of the limiting subdifferential, while the subdifferential mapping is nonempty convex-valued, outer semicontinuous, and locally bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is strictly continuous and regular on }O\iff \forall x\in O,\forall w\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ h(x,w)\in\mathbb{R}\text{ exists and is usc in }x;\text{ the stated derivative identities and properties of }\partial f\text{ follow}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Separated multiplier criterion for linear suboptimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An equivalence between multiobjective linear suboptimality and a scalarized subdifferential-normal multiplier system under three alternative regularity regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to Z\) be Lipschitz near \(\bar x\), let \(\dim X<\infty\), and let \(\Omega\subset X\) and \(\Theta\subset Z\) be locally closed near \(\bar x\) and \(\bar z:=f(\bar x)\in\Theta\), respectively. Assume one of: (a) \(\dim Z<\infty\) and either \(\Omega=X\) or \(f\) is strictly differentiable at \(\bar x\); (b) \(Z\) is Asplund, \(\Omega=X\), \(\Theta\) is normally regular and SNC at \(\bar z\), and \(f\) is strictly Lipschitzian at \(\bar x\); or (c) \(Z\) is Asplund, \(\Omega\) is normally regular at \(\bar x\), \(\Theta\) is normally regular and SNC at \(\bar z\), and \(f\) is \(N\)-regular at \(\bar x\). Then \(\bar x\) is linearly suboptimal with respect to \((f,\Omega,\Theta)\) if and only if there exists \(0\ne z^*\in Z^*\) such that \(0\in\partial\langle z^*,f\rangle(\bar x)+N(\bar x;\Omega)\) and \(z^*\in N(\bar z;\Theta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite-dimensional decision space and a locally Lipschitz vector objective, each of three alternative finite-dimensional or Asplund regularity regimes makes linear suboptimality equivalent to the existence of a nonzero objective-space multiplier that is normal to the target set and satisfies the scalarized subdifferential-plus-feasible-normal stationarity condition.
assumptions_latex: f:X\to Z\text{ is Lipschitz around }\bar x,\quad \dim X<\infty.
\Omega\subset X\text{ and }\Theta\subset Z\text{ are locally closed around }\bar x\text{ and }\bar z=f(\bar x)\in\Theta.
\text{At least one of regimes (a), (b), or (c) stated in the theorem holds.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar x\text{ is linearly suboptimal}\iff\exists\,0\ne z^*\in Z^*:\ 0\in\partial\langle z^*,f\rangle(\bar x)+N(\bar x;\Omega),\quad z^*\in N(\bar z;\Theta).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke chain rule with equality-recovery regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized-gradient calculus for a finite-dimensional inner mapping h=(h_1,\ldots,h_n) and outer scalar function g.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the locally Lipschitz composition setting f=g\circ h, where h=(h_1,\ldots,h_n), one has \partial f(x)\subseteq\overline{\operatorname{co}}^{w^*}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i\zeta_i:\ \zeta_i\in\partial h_i(x),\ \alpha\in\partial g(h(x))\right\}. Equality holds if any of the following applies: (i) g is regular at h(x), every h_i is regular at x, and every \alpha\in\partial g(h(x)) has nonnegative components; then f is regular at x. (ii) g is strictly differentiable at h(x) and n=1; then the weak-star closed convex hull is unnecessary. (iii) g is regular at h(x) and h is strictly differentiable at x; then f is regular at x and the convex-hull operation is unnecessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a locally Lipschitz composition, the Clarke generalized gradient is contained in the weak-star closed convex hull of sums formed from outer generalized-gradient coefficients and inner generalized gradients. Equality is recovered under regularity plus nonnegative outer coefficients, for a scalar inner function with strictly differentiable outer function, or for a regular outer function with strictly differentiable inner mapping; the theorem also states the corresponding regularity and convexification simplifications.
assumptions_latex: g\text{ and }h_i\text{ satisfy the local Lipschitz hypotheses of the composition setting}
\text{For equality, one of conditions (i), (ii), or (iii) holds}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f(x)\subseteq\overline{\operatorname{co}}^{w^*}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i\zeta_i:\zeta_i\in\partial h_i(x),\alpha\in\partial g(h(x))\right\},\quad\text{with equality and the stated simplifications under (i)--(iii).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regular points and first variations of probability functionals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines regularity through finiteness on mixtures with compactly supported bounded-density probabilities, then defines the first variation at such a point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F:\mathcal P(\Omega)\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}. A measure \rho\in\mathcal P(\Omega) is regular for F if F((1-\varepsilon)\rho+\varepsilon\widetilde\rho)<+\infty for every \varepsilon\in[0,1] and every \widetilde\rho\in\mathcal P(\Omega)\cap L_c^\infty(\Omega). If \rho is regular, a first variation \frac{\delta F}{\delta\rho}(\rho), when it exists, is any measurable function g such that \left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}F(\rho+\varepsilon\chi)\right|_{\varepsilon=0}=\int_\Omega g\,d\chi for every \chi=\widetilde\rho-\rho with \widetilde\rho\in\mathcal P(\Omega)\cap L_c^\infty(\Omega).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an extended-real functional on probability measures, rho is regular when every mixture of rho with any compactly supported probability having a bounded density remains in the finite domain of the functional. At a regular rho, a first variation, if it exists, is any measurable function whose integral against every admissible perturbation equals the derivative of the functional in that perturbation direction at zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho\text{ is regular}\iff (\forall\varepsilon\in[0,1])(\forall\widetilde\rho\in\mathcal P(\Omega)\cap L_c^\infty(\Omega))\;F((1-\varepsilon)\rho+\varepsilon\widetilde\rho)<+\infty;\quad \frac{\delta F}{\delta\rho}(\rho)=g\Rightarrow \left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}F(\rho+\varepsilon\chi)\right|_{\varepsilon=0}=\int_\Omega g\,d\chi.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-Sided Regularity Relationships
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The converse implications require local Lipschitz continuity, and the converse to strict differentiability additionally requires finite-dimensionality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varphi:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be continuous around \(\bar x\). Let (a) mean that \(\varphi\) is graphically regular at \(\bar x\), (b) that it is simultaneously lower and upper regular there, and (c) that it is strictly differentiable there. Then \((c)\Rightarrow(a)\Rightarrow(b)\). If \(\varphi\) is locally Lipschitz around \(\bar x\), then \((b)\Rightarrow(a)\). If, additionally, \(\dim X<\infty\), then \((a)\Rightarrow(c)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict differentiability implies graphical regularity, which implies simultaneous lower and upper regularity. Under local Lipschitz continuity, lower and upper regularity imply graphical regularity; in finite dimensions, graphical regularity then also implies strict differentiability.
assumptions_latex: \varphi\text{ is locally Lipschitz around }\bar x\text{ for the converse }(b)\Rightarrow(a)
\varphi\text{ is locally Lipschitz around }\bar x\text{ and }\dim X<\infty\text{ for }(a)\Rightarrow(c)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (c)\Rightarrow(a)\Rightarrow(b),\qquad (b)\Rightarrow(a)\text{ under local Lipschitz continuity},\qquad (a)\Rightarrow(c)\text{ under local Lipschitz continuity and }\dim X<\infty

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normal-Cone Intersection Rule under Transversality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limiting-normal and tangent-cone calculus for two closed sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in S_1\cap S_2\), where \(S_1,S_2\subset\mathbb R^n\) are closed and transversal at \(x\), meaning \(-N^L_{S_1}(x)\cap N^L_{S_2}(x)=\{0\}\). Then \(N^L_{S_1\cap S_2}(x)\subset N^L_{S_1}(x)+N^L_{S_2}(x)\). If both sets are regular at \(x\), the inclusion is an equality, \(S_1\cap S_2\) is regular at \(x\), and \(T_{S_1\cap S_2}(x)=T_{S_1}(x)\cap T_{S_2}(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transversality gives an upper normal-cone intersection rule. If both sets are regular, the rule is exact, their intersection remains regular, and its tangent cone is the intersection of the individual tangent cones.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the equality and tangent conclusions, }S_1\text{ and }S_2\text{ are regular at }x.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N^L_{S_1\cap S_2}(x)\subset N^L_{S_1}(x)+N^L_{S_2}(x);\quad S_1,S_2\text{ regular at }x\Rightarrow\begin{cases}N^L_{S_1\cap S_2}(x)=N^L_{S_1}(x)+N^L_{S_2}(x),\\S_1\cap S_2\text{ is regular at }x,\\T_{S_1\cap S_2}(x)=T_{S_1}(x)\cap T_{S_2}(x).\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Upper Semicontinuity of the Convexified Envelope at Zero Scale
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary upper semicontinuity of the convexified scale envelope associated with a continuous subdifferential approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Cf(x,\varepsilon)\) be a continuous approximation of \(\partial f\) on a compact set \(X\), continuous with respect to \((x,\varepsilon)\) for \(x\in X\) and \(\varepsilon>0\). Assume that \(\operatorname{conv}C_Lf(x)=C_0f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\). For the mapping
\[
Q(x,\varepsilon):=\operatorname{conv}\!\bigcup\{Cf(x,t):0\le t\le\varepsilon\},
\]

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under compactness, positive-scale continuity, and the compatibility condition between the limiting and zero-scale sets, the convexified scale envelope is upper semicontinuous at every zero-scale point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regular, Limiting, and Singular Subdifferential Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential construction of limiting and singular subgradients from regular or vanishing-error regular subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\operatorname{dom}\varphi\), define
\[\widehat\partial\varphi(x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\liminf_{\substack{u\to x,\ u\ne x}}\frac{\varphi(u)-\varphi(x)-\langle v,u-x\rangle}{\|u-x\|}\ge0\right\}.\]
Writing \(x_k\xrightarrow{\varphi}\bar x\) when \(x_k\to\bar x\) and \(\varphi(x_k)\to\varphi(\bar x)\),
\[\partial\varphi(\bar x)=\left\{v:\exists x_k\xrightarrow{\varphi}\bar x,\ \exists v_k\in\widehat\partial\varphi(x_k),\ v_k\to v\right\},\]
\[\partial^\infty\varphi(\bar x)=\left\{v:\exists x_k\xrightarrow{\varphi}\bar x,\ \exists\lambda_k\downarrow0,\ \exists v_k\to v,\ v_k\in\lambda_k\widehat\partial\varphi(x_k)\right\}.\]
Both representations remain valid when the regular subdifferentials are replaced by their \(\varepsilon_k\)-enlargements, defined by replacing the lower bound \(0\) by \(-\varepsilon_k\), provided \(\varepsilon_k\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regular subdifferential is defined by a first-order lower-support inequality. Limiting subgradients are limits of regular subgradients along points converging both in argument and function value. Singular subgradients are limits of vanishing positive scalings of such regular subgradients. Vanishing-error regular subgradients give the same representations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial\varphi(\bar x)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{x\xrightarrow{\varphi}\bar x}\widehat\partial\varphi(x),\qquad \partial^\infty\varphi(\bar x)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{\substack{x\xrightarrow{\varphi}\bar x\\ \lambda\downarrow0}}\lambda\widehat\partial\varphi(x)
