knowledge_statements.statement_title: Partial basic and singular subgradient inclusions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relations between subgradients of a fixed-variable slice and coordinate projections of full subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\varphi:X\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be lower semicontinuous around \((\bar x,\bar y)\) and SNEC there. Suppose \((0,y^*)\in\partial^\infty\varphi(\bar x,\bar y)\Rightarrow y^*=0\). Then
\[\partial_x\varphi(\bar x,\bar y)\subset\{x^*\in X^*: \exists y^*\in Y^*,\ (x^*,y^*)\in\partial\varphi(\bar x,\bar y)\},\]
\[\partial_x^\infty\varphi(\bar x,\bar y)\subset\{x^*\in X^*: \exists y^*\in Y^*,\ (x^*,y^*)\in\partial^\infty\varphi(\bar x,\bar y)\}.\]
If \(\varphi\) is lower regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\), then \(\varphi(\cdot,\bar y)\) is lower regular at \(\bar x\) and the first inclusion is equality. If \(\varphi\) is also epigraphically regular there, the second inclusion is equality and the slice is epigraphically regular at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a singular-coordinate qualification, partial basic and singular subgradients lie in the coordinate projections of the full subdifferentials. Lower or epigraphical regularity yields the corresponding equalities and regularity of the slice.
assumptions_latex: \varphi:X\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\text{ is l.s.c. around and SNEC at }(\bar x,\bar y)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial_x\varphi(\bar x,\bar y)\subset\operatorname{proj}_{X^*}\partial\varphi(\bar x,\bar y),\quad \partial_x^\infty\varphi(\bar x,\bar y)\subset\operatorname{proj}_{X^*}\partial^\infty\varphi(\bar x,\bar y),\text{ with the stated regularity-based equalities}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) finite at \(\bar x\), its Fréchet subdifferential is
\[
\widehat\partial_F f(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid \liminf_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\x\ne\bar x}}\frac{f(x)-f(\bar x)-\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle}{\|x-\bar x\|}\ge0\right\}.
\]
The quotient is interpreted in the extended-real sense. Equivalently, \(v\in\widehat\partial_F f(\bar x)\) if and only if \(f(x)\ge f(\bar x)+\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle+o(\|x-\bar x\|)\) as \(x\to\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Fréchet subgradient gives a first-order local lower approximation whose error is negligible relative to displacement.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bornological subdifferentials and derivative comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the bornological subdifferential and derivative and records the stated equivalences, differentiability implication, and failure boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\beta\) be a bornology on \(X\): a family of bounded, centrally symmetric subsets, closed under positive scalar multiplication and finite unions, with \(\bigcup_{B\in\beta}B=X\). Define \(x^*\in\partial^\beta f(x)\) when
\[
\forall B\in\beta\ \forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists\delta>0\ \forall t\in(0,\delta)\ \forall h\in B:\quad
\langle x^*,h\rangle\le \frac{f(x+th)-f(x)}{t}+\varepsilon.
\]
The point, norm-compact, weakly compact, and bounded bornologies give respectively the Gâteaux \((G)\), Hadamard \((H)\), weak-Hadamard \((WH)\), and Fréchet \((F)\) notions. If \(f\) is locally Lipschitz, then \(\partial^Hf(x)=\partial^Gf(x)\); if \(X\) is reflexive, then \(\partial^Ff(x)=\partial^{WH}f(x)\). When
\[
\partial^\beta f(x)\cap-\partial^\beta(-f)(x)=\{x^*\},
\]
define \(\nabla^\beta f(x)=x^*\); for concave \(f\), the source states \(\{\nabla^\beta f(x)\}=\partial^\beta f(x)\). If \(f\) is convex and weak-Hadamard differentiable at \(x\), and \(\ell_1(\mathbb N)\not\subset X\), then \(f\) is Fréchet differentiable at \(x\). Conversely, on every smooth nonreflexive Banach space there exists a distance function that is weak-Hadamard differentiable everywhere but fails to be Fréchet differentiable at some point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bornology determines a uniform directional subdifferential. Point, compact, weakly compact, and bounded bornologies yield the Gâteaux, Hadamard, weak-Hadamard, and Fréchet variants. Hadamard and Gâteaux subdifferentials coincide for locally Lipschitz functions, while Fréchet and weak-Hadamard variants coincide on reflexive spaces. The bornological derivative is the singleton common to the subdifferentials of f and -f. For convex functions, weak-Hadamard differentiability implies Fréchet differentiability when X contains no copy of l1; this implication fails for general distance functions on smooth nonreflexive Banach spaces.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is convex and weak-Hadamard differentiable at }x\text{ and }\ell_1(\mathbb N)\not\subset X\text{ for the Fréchet-differentiability implication}
X\text{ is smooth and nonreflexive for the distance-function counterexample}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial^Hf(x)=\partial^Gf(x)\ \text{under local Lipschitzness};\quad \partial^Ff(x)=\partial^{WH}f(x)\ \text{when }X\text{ is reflexive};\quad \nabla^\beta f(x)\text{ is defined by }\{\nabla^\beta f(x)\}=\partial^\beta f(x)\cap-\partial^\beta(-f)(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local-Lipschitz Equivalence of Fréchet and Gâteaux Differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: At a fixed point in finite-dimensional Euclidean space, using one-sided directional derivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^N\to\mathbb{R}\) be locally Lipschitz and let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^N\). Then \(f\) is Fréchet differentiable at \(x\) if and only if, for every \(v\in\mathbb{R}^N\), the limit \(df(x;v)=\lim_{t\searrow0}[f(x+tv)-f(x)]/t\) exists and the map \(v\mapsto df(x;v)\) is linear and continuous. In that case \(df(x;v)=\nabla f(x)\cdot v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Lipschitz real-valued function on finite-dimensional Euclidean space is Fréchet differentiable at a point exactly when all one-sided directional derivatives there exist and together form a linear continuous function of the direction; this function is the gradient pairing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is Fréchet differentiable at }x\iff\bigl[\forall v\in\mathbb{R}^N,\ df(x;v)\text{ exists and }v\mapsto df(x;v)\text{ is linear and continuous}\bigr].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variational inequality and lambda-monotonicity of Wasserstein subgradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization under the regularity hypothesis (10.1.1a) and geodesic \(\lambda\)-convexity (10.1.6).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(\phi\) satisfies (10.1.1a) and is \(\lambda\)-convex along geodesics. For \(\mu\in D(|\partial\phi|)\) and \(\xi\in L^2(\mu;X)\), \(\xi\in\partial\phi(\mu)\) if and only if, for every \(
u\in D(\phi)\), \[\phi(
u)-\phi(\mu)\ge\int_X\langle\xi(x),\mathbf t_\mu^
u(x)-xangle\,d\mu(x)+ rac{\lambda}{2}W_2^2(\mu,
u).\] In particular, if \(\xi_i\in\partial\phi(\mu_i)\) for \(i=1,2\) and \(\mathbf t=\mathbf t_{\mu_1}^{\mu_2}\), then \[\int_X\langle\xi_2(\mathbf t(x))-xi_1(x),\mathbf t(x)-xangle\,d\mu_1(x)\ge\lambda W_2^2(\mu_1,\mu_2).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a geodesically lambda-convex functional, Wasserstein Fréchet subgradient membership is equivalent to a global lambda-corrected support inequality. Subgradients at two measures consequently satisfy a lambda-monotonicity inequality along the optimal transport map.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi\) satisfies (10.1.1a): it is proper and lower semicontinuous and \(D(|\partial\phi|)\subset\mathcal P_2^r(X)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\xi\in\partial\phi(\mu)\) exactly when the global \(\lambda\)-variational inequality holds for every \(\nu\in D(\phi)\); pairs of subgradients satisfy the stated \(\lambda\)-monotonicity inequality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fréchet Subdifferentiability Characterizations of Asplund Spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent density, existence, and approximate-subgradient properties for all proper lower-semicontinuous functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $X$ be a Banach space and let $\mathcal A$ be the class of all proper lower-semicontinuous functions $\varphi:X	o\overline{\mathbb R}$. The following are equivalent: (a) $X$ is Asplund; (b) for every $\varphi\in\mathcal A$, the points $(x,\varphi(x))$ with $\widehat\partial\varphi(x)
eq\varnothing$ are dense in $\operatorname{gph}\varphi$; (c) every $\varphi\in\mathcal A$ has some $x\in\operatorname{dom}\varphi$ with $\widehat\partial\varphi(x)
eq\varnothing$; (d) for every $\varphi\in\mathcal A$ and $\varepsilon>0$, some $x\in\operatorname{dom}\varphi$ satisfies $\widehat\partial_{g\varepsilon}\varphi(x)
eq\varnothing$; and (e) for every $\varphi\in\mathcal A$ and $\varepsilon>0$, some $x\in\operatorname{dom}\varphi$ satisfies $\widehat\partial_{a\varepsilon}\varphi(x)
eq\varnothing$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Banach space is Asplund exactly when every proper lower-semicontinuous function is Fréchet subdifferentiable somewhere. Equivalently, such points are dense in the function's graph, or the stated geometric and analytic epsilon-Fréchet subdifferentials are nonempty somewhere for every positive epsilon.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal A=\{\varphi:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}:\varphi\text{ is proper and l.s.c.}\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X\text{ is Asplund}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \forall\varphi\in\mathcal A,\ \{(x,\varphi(x)):\widehat\partial\varphi(x)\neq\varnothing\}\text{ is dense in }\operatorname{gph}\varphi\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \text{conditions (c)--(e).}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential, boundedness, and differentiability characterizations of finite dimensionality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence theorem for continuous convex functions and dual sequences on a normed space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a normed linear space. The following are equivalent: (i) \(X\) is finite-dimensional; (ii) weak-star convergence and norm convergence agree for sequences in \(X^*\); (iii) every continuous convex \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is bounded on bounded subsets of \(X\); (iv) for every continuous convex \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), \(\partial f\) is bounded on bounded sets, meaning \(\bigcup_{x\in B}\partial f(x)\) is bounded for every bounded \(B\subset X\); and (v) for every continuous convex \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), each point of Gâteaux differentiability is a point of Fréchet differentiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normed space is finite-dimensional exactly when weak-star and norm convergence agree for dual sequences, continuous convex functions and their subdifferentials are bounded on bounded sets, and Gâteaux differentiability of such functions always upgrades to Fréchet differentiability.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ is a normed linear space.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Conditions (i)--(v) above are equivalent.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fréchet Differentiability via Lower and Upper Fréchet Subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint nonemptiness characterizes Fréchet differentiability; a one-sided singleton condition does not suffice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\varphi:X	o\overline{\mathbb R}\) satisfy \(|\varphi( ar x)|<\infty\). Then \(\widehat\partial\varphi( ar x)
eq\varnothing\) and \(\widehat\partial^{+}\varphi( ar x)
eq\varnothing\) if and only if \(\varphi\) is Fréchet differentiable at \( ar x\). In that case, \(\widehat\partial\varphi( ar x)=\widehat\partial^{+}\varphi( ar x)=\{
abla\varphi( ar x)\}\). Hence, if either subdifferential is not a singleton, the other is empty. A singleton in only one construction is insufficient: for \(\varphi(x)=\max\{0,x\sin(1/x)\}\) when \(x
eq0\) and \(\varphi(0)=0\), \(\widehat\partial\varphi(0)=\{0\}\) while \(\widehat\partial^{+}\varphi(0)=\varnothing\), and \(\varphi\) is not Fréchet differentiable at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-valued function is Fréchet differentiable at a point exactly when both its lower and upper Fréchet subdifferentials are nonempty; both then equal the singleton containing the gradient. A singleton in only one of the two subdifferentials does not imply differentiability, as the stated oscillatory example demonstrates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(\widehat\partial\varphi( ar x)
eq\varnothing\ \land\ \widehat\partial^{+}\varphi( ar x)
eq\varnothing\iff\varphi	ext{ is Fréchet differentiable at } ar x\), and then \(\widehat\partial\varphi( ar x)=\widehat\partial^{+}\varphi( ar x)=\{
abla\varphi( ar x)\}\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Gradient Continuity Criterion for Fréchet Differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex functions that are Gâteaux differentiable on a neighborhood in a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\) be Gâteaux differentiable on a neighborhood \(D\) of \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). Then (i) \(\nabla f\) is strong-to-weak continuous on \(D\); and (ii) \(f\) is Fréchet differentiable at \(x\) if and only if \(\nabla f\) is norm-continuous at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function is Gâteaux differentiable on a neighborhood of a domain point, its gradient is norm-to-weak continuous throughout that neighborhood, and the function is Fréchet differentiable at the point exactly when its gradient is norm-continuous there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nabla f\text{ is strong-to-weak continuous on }D\quad\text{and}\quad[f\text{ is Fréchet differentiable at }x\iff\nabla f\text{ is norm-continuous at }x]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regular Functional via Strong–Weak Subdifferential Closedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for the functional and subdifferential in the ambient setting under consideration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A functional $\phi$ is regular if, for every sequence such that
\[
\xi_n\in\partial\phi(v_n),\qquad \varphi_n=\phi(v_n),\qquad v_n\to v,
\qquad \xi_n\rightharpoonup\xi,
\qquad \varphi_n\to\varphi,
\]
it follows that
\[
\xi\in\partial\phi(v)\qquad\text{and}\qquad \varphi=\phi(v).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A functional is regular when its value-augmented subdifferential graph is sequentially closed for strong convergence of points, weak convergence of subgradients, and convergence of function values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \xi\in\partial\phi(v)\quad\text{and}\quad\varphi=\phi(v).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniqueness of the Fréchet derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness of the classical Fréchet derivative between real normed spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X,Y be real normed spaces, let \varnothing\ne S\subseteq X be open, let f:S\to Y, and let \bar x\in S. If f is Fréchet differentiable at \bar x, then its Fréchet derivative at \bar x is uniquely determined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Fréchet-differentiable map has exactly one Fréchet derivative at the given point.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is Fréchet differentiable at }\bar x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A,B\in\mathcal L(X,Y)\text{ both satisfy the Fréchet approximation at }\bar x\Rightarrow A=B.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Singleton Subdifferential Characterization of Differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise finite-dimensional characterization for proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\dim\mathcal H<\infty\). Let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\) and \(x,u\in\mathcal H\). Then \(\partial f(x)=\{u\}\) if and only if \(f\) is Fréchet differentiable at \(x\) and \(u=\nabla f(x)\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f(x)=\{u\}\iff\bigl(f\text{ is Fréchet differentiable at }x\text{ and }u=\nabla f(x)\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fréchet and strong subgradients in quadratic Wasserstein space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition under the regular-measure hypothesis that supplies unique optimal maps from the base measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\phi:\mathcal P_2(X)	o(-\infty,+\infty]\) satisfy (10.1.1a), let \(\mu\in D(|\partial\phi|)\), and let \(\xi\in L^2(\mu;X)\). Then \(\xi\in\partial\phi(\mu)\) when \[\liminf_{
u	o\mu} rac{\phi(
u)-\phi(\mu)-\int_X\langle\xi(x),\mathbf t_\mu^
u(x)-xangle\,d\mu(x)}{W_2(\mu,
u)}\ge0.\] Equivalently, \[\phi(
u)-\phi(\mu)\ge\int_X\langle\xi(x),\mathbf t_\mu^
u(x)-xangle\,d\mu(x)+o(W_2(\mu,nu)).\] Such a \(\xi\) is a strong subgradient when it also satisfies \[\phi(\mathbf t_\#\mu)-\phi(\mu)\ge\int_X\langle\xi(x),\mathbf t(x)-xangle\,d\mu(x)+o(\|\mathbf t-\mathbf i\|_{L^2(\mu;X)}).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Wasserstein Fréchet subgradient provides first-order lower support along optimal-transport displacements, with an error negligible relative to Wasserstein distance. It is strong when the corresponding expansion also holds for map-induced pushforwards near the identity.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi\) satisfies (10.1.1a): it is proper and lower semicontinuous and \(D(|\partial\phi|)\subset\mathcal P_2^r(X)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The liminf inequality defines \(\xi\in\partial\phi(\mu)\); the additional pushforward inequality defines a strong subgradient.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fréchet subdifferential difference rule and necessary condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A difference rule for two arbitrary extended-real-valued functions finite at the reference point, together with its local-minimum consequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\varphi_1,\varphi_2:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be finite at \(\bar x\), and suppose \(\widehat\partial\varphi_2(\bar x)\ne\varnothing\). Then
\[\widehat\partial(\varphi_1-\varphi_2)(\bar x)\subseteq\bigcap_{v\in\widehat\partial\varphi_2(\bar x)}\left(\widehat\partial\varphi_1(\bar x)-v\right)\subseteq\widehat\partial\varphi_1(\bar x)-\widehat\partial\varphi_2(\bar x).\]
In particular, if \(\bar x\) is a local minimizer of \(\varphi_1-\varphi_2\), then \(\widehat\partial\varphi_2(\bar x)\subseteq\widehat\partial\varphi_1(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Fréchet subdifferential of a difference lies in every translate of the first function's Fréchet subdifferential by a Fréchet subgradient of the second. Consequently, local minimality forces every Fréchet subgradient of the second function to belong to that of the first.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat\partial(\varphi_1-\varphi_2)(\bar x)\subseteq\bigcap_{v\in\widehat\partial\varphi_2(\bar x)}\left(\widehat\partial\varphi_1(\bar x)-v\right)\subseteq\widehat\partial\varphi_1(\bar x)-\widehat\partial\varphi_2(\bar x),\quad \bar x\in\operatorname{locmin}(\varphi_1-\varphi_2)\Rightarrow\widehat\partial\varphi_2(\bar x)\subseteq\widehat\partial\varphi_1(\bar x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Upper-subdifferential necessary condition for a linearly subminimal solution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A Fritz John-type multiplier condition for linear subminimality in a Banach-space constrained problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\bar x\in\Delta\) be linearly subminimal for \((\varphi_0,\Delta)\), and suppose \(\Omega\) is locally closed around \(\bar x\). Assume either that \(X\) admits a Lipschitzian \(C^1\) bump function, or that \(X\) is Asplund and \(\varphi_i(\bar x)<0\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Then, for every choice \(x_i^*\in\widehat\partial^{+}\varphi_i(\bar x)\), \(i=0,\ldots,m\), there exists \(0\ne(\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_m)\in\mathbb R^{m+1}\) such that \(\lambda_i\ge0\) for \(i=0,\ldots,m\), \(\lambda_i\varphi_i(\bar x)=0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and \(-\sum_{i=0}^{m}\lambda_i x_i^*\in N(\bar x;\Omega)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a feasible point is linearly subminimal, the base set is locally closed there, and the stated bump-function or Asplund-space hypothesis holds, then every selection of Fréchet upper subgradients admits a nonzero vector of nonnegative multipliers satisfying complementarity for the inequality functions and a normal-cone stationarity inclusion.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ admits a Lipschitzian }C^1\text{ bump function}\quad\text{or}\quad\bigl(X\text{ is Asplund and }\varphi_i(\bar x)<0\ \forall i=1,\ldots,m\bigr)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\,0\ne\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^{m+1}:\quad \lambda_i\varphi_i(\bar x)=0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad-\sum_{i=0}^{m}\lambda_i x_i^*\in N(\bar x;\Omega).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smooth local lower-support representation of a Fréchet subgradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents each Fréchet subgradient by the gradient of a differentiable local minorant touching the function at the reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varphi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be finite at \(\bar x\), and let \(v\in\widehat\partial\varphi(\bar x)\). Then there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and a function \(\psi:U\to\mathbb{R}\) such that \(\psi(\bar x)=\varphi(\bar x)\), \(\psi\) is Fréchet differentiable at \(\bar x\), \(\nabla\psi(\bar x)=v\), and \(\psi-\varphi\) attains a local maximum at \(\bar x\) on \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every Fréchet subgradient of a function finite at the reference point is the gradient there of a differentiable local lower support touching the function at that point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists U\ni\bar x,\ \exists\psi:U\to\mathbb R:\ \psi(\bar x)=\varphi(\bar x),\ \psi\text{ is Fréchet differentiable at }\bar x,\ \nabla\psi(\bar x)=v,\ \text{and }\bar x\text{ locally maximizes }\psi-\varphi\text{ on }U.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epsilon-Stationary Point Near a Smooth Approximate Minimizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient estimate obtained near a prescribed approximate minimizer under local Fréchet differentiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X$ be a Banach space and let $\varphi:X\to\mathbb R$ be proper, lower semicontinuous, and bounded below. Suppose $\varepsilon,\lambda>0$, $\varphi(x_0)\leq\inf_X\varphi+\varepsilon$, and $\varphi$ is Fréchet differentiable on a neighborhood $U$ of $x_0$ containing $B_\lambda(x_0)$. Then there exists $\bar x\in X$ such that $\|\bar x-x_0\|\leq\lambda$, $\varphi(\bar x)\leq\varphi(x_0)$, and $\|\nabla\varphi(\bar x)\|\leq\varepsilon/\lambda$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Fréchet-differentiable approximate minimizer can be replaced by a no-worse point within distance lambda whose gradient norm is at most epsilon divided by lambda.
assumptions_latex: \varphi:X\to\mathbb R\text{ is proper, l.s.c., and bounded below}
\varphi\text{ is Fréchet differentiable on a neighborhood }U\supseteq B_\lambda(x_0)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\bar x\in X:\ \|\bar x-x_0\|\leq\lambda,\quad \varphi(\bar x)\leq\varphi(x_0),\quad \|\nabla\varphi(\bar x)\|\leq\varepsilon/\lambda.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fréchet Subdifferential and Its Proper Domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for proper lower-semicontinuous extended-real-valued functionals on a Hilbert space. The extracted equivalent small-o formula is omitted because its limit expression is truncated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $X$ be a Hilbert space and let $\phi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and lower semicontinuous. The Fréchet subdifferential is defined by
\[
\xi\in\partial\phi(v)\iff v\in D(\phi)\ \text{and}\ \liminf_{w\to v}\frac{\phi(w)-\phi(v)-\langle\xi,w-v\rangle}{\lVert w-v\rVert}\ge 0.
\]
Its proper domain is
\[
D(\partial\phi):=\{v\in X:\partial\phi(v)\neq\varnothing\}\subseteq D(\phi).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector is a Fréchet subgradient at a finite-valued point when the normalized first-order linearization error has nonnegative lower limit. The proper domain of the subdifferential consists of points possessing at least one such subgradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \xi\in\partial\phi(v)\iff v\in D(\phi)\ \text{and}\ \liminf_{w\to v}\frac{\phi(w)-\phi(v)-\langle\xi,w-v\rangle}{\lVert w-v\rVert}\ge0,\qquad D(\partial\phi)=\{v\in X:\partial\phi(v)\neq\varnothing\}\subseteq D(\phi).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variational descriptions of Fréchet subgradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable-minorant, smooth-support, and global bump-function representations of Fréchet subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\varphi:X	o\overline{\mathbb R}\) be proper and finite at \( ar x\). If \(s\) is defined near \( ar x\), is Fréchet differentiable at \( ar x\), satisfies \(
abla s( ar x)=x^*\), and \(\varphi-s\) has a local minimum at \( ar x\), then \(x^*\in\widehat\partial\varphi( ar x)\). Conversely, every \(x^*\in\widehat\partial\varphi( ar x)\) is the derivative at \( ar x\) of a function \(s:X	o\mathbb R\) satisfying \(s( ar x)=\varphi( ar x)\) and \(s\leq\varphi\). If \(X\) admits an \(\mathcal S\)-smooth bump function, \(\mathcal S\in\{\mathcal F,\mathcal{LF},\mathcal{LC}^1\}\), then there is an \(\mathcal S\)-smooth local function \(s\) with \(
abla s( ar x)=x^*\) and \(\varphi(x)-s(x)-\|x- ar x\|^2\geq\varphi( ar x)-s( ar x)\) locally. If \(X\) admits a Fréchet-smooth renorm, this \(s\) can be concave, and if additionally \(\varphi\) is bounded below it can be defined with the inequality on all of \(X\). If \(\varphi\) is bounded below and \(X\) admits the stated smooth bump function, there is a bump function \(b\) with \(
abla b( ar x)=x^*\) such that \(\varphi-b\) has a global minimum at \( ar x\); moreover, suitable global \(\mathcal S\)-smooth \(s\) and \(	heta\) satisfy \(
abla s( ar x)=x^*\), \(	heta(x)=0\iff x=0\), \(	heta(x)\leq\|x\|^2\) for \(\|x\|\leq1\), and \(\varphi(x)-s(x)-	heta(x- ar x)\geq\varphi( ar x)-s( ar x)\) for all \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differentiable local support produces a Fréchet subgradient, and every Fréchet subgradient is represented by a differentiable global minorant. Smooth bump-function and boundedness assumptions yield the stronger local and global support representations stated above.
assumptions_latex: \(\varphi:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is proper and finite at \(\bar x\).
The smooth-support conclusions assume that \(X\) admits an \(\mathcal S\)-smooth bump function for \(\mathcal S\in\{\mathcal F,\mathcal{LF},\mathcal{LC}^1\}\).
Concavity assumes a Fréchet-smooth renorm; the global conclusions additionally assume that \(\varphi\) is bounded below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fréchet subgradients admit the stated differentiable-minorant and, under the additional hypotheses, smooth local or global support representations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rademacher theorem for locally Lipschitz mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional vector-valued form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and let \(F:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R^m\) be locally Lipschitz. If \(\Omega:=\{x\in\mathcal D:F\text{ is Fréchet differentiable at }x\}\), then \(\mathcal D\setminus\Omega\) is Lebesgue negligible. Consequently, \(\Omega\) is dense in \(\mathcal D\) and \(\mathcal D\subseteq\operatorname{cl}\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Lipschitz mapping on an open finite-dimensional domain is Fréchet differentiable almost everywhere; its differentiability points are therefore dense in the domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal D\setminus\Omega\) is Lebesgue negligible, hence \(\Omega\) is dense in \(\mathcal D\) and \(\mathcal D\subseteq\operatorname{cl}\Omega\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) finite at \(\bar x\), the regular subdifferential is
\[
\widehat\partial f(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid f(x)\ge f(\bar x)+\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle+o(\|x-\bar x\|)\ \text{as }x\to\bar x\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, membership means that for every \(\eta>0\), some \(\delta>0\) satisfies \(f(x)\ge f(\bar x)+\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle-\eta\|x-\bar x\|\) whenever \(\|x-\bar x\|<\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regular subdifferential collects slopes supporting the function locally up to a first-order negligible error.

knowledge_statements.title: Fréchet–Regular Coincidence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminological coincidence under the standard finite-dimensional lower-subdifferential convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be finite at \(\bar x\). When the Fréchet and regular lower subdifferentials are both defined by the first-order condition
\[
\liminf_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\x\ne\bar x}}\frac{f(x)-f(\bar x)-\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle}{\|x-\bar x\|}\ge 0,
\]
they coincide:
\[
\widehat\partial_F f(\bar x)=\widehat\partial f(\bar x).
\]
Thus “Fréchet” and “regular” name the same lower subdifferential under this convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite-dimensional variational analysis, the Fréchet and regular lower subdifferentials are the same object when both use the standard first-order lower-approximation convention.
assumptions_latex: Both symbols use the lower first-order quotient convention in Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\partial_F f(\bar x)=\widehat\partial f(\bar x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\) with \(f(\bar x)\in\mathbb{R}\), and let \(\widehat N\) denote the Fréchet regular normal cone. Then
\[
v\in\widehat\partial f(\bar x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (v,-1)\in\widehat N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x)).
\]
Consequently, regular subgradients are exactly the horizontal components of regular epigraph normals whose vertical component is normalized to \(-1\). This identifies first-order lower support of \(f\) with regular normal geometry of its epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector is a regular subgradient exactly when adjoining vertical component minus one produces a regular normal to the epigraph.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional Characterization of Regular Subgradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional lower-Hadamard directional characterization and resulting convex geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be finite at \(\bar x\), and define
\[
df(\bar x)(w):=\liminf_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\w'\to w}}\frac{f(\bar x+t w')-f(\bar x)}{t}.
\]
Then
\[
\widehat\partial f(\bar x)=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle v,w\rangle\le df(\bar x)(w)\ \text{for every }w\in\mathbb{R}^n\right\}.
\]
Consequently, \(\widehat\partial f(\bar x)\) is closed and convex, possibly empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regular subgradients are exactly the linear functionals dominated in every direction by the lower Hadamard directional derivative; consequently the regular subdifferential is closed and convex, though it may be empty.
assumptions_latex: \(df(\bar x)\) denotes the lower Hadamard directional derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\partial f(\bar x)=\{v:\langle v,w\rangle\le df(\bar x)(w)\ \forall w\}\), and this set is closed and convex.

notation.meaning: lower Hadamard directional derivative of f at the reference point in direction w

knowledge_statements.title: Directional Characterization of Regular Subgradients

children.top_down_role: Approximate regular subgradients used in sequential representations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\partial_\varepsilon f(\bar x)\) permits a first-order lower error of at most \(\varepsilon\|x-\bar x\|\).

source_refs.locator: 1.3.2 Frechet-Like \( \varepsilon \)-Subgradients and Limiting Representations p. 87

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \(f(\bar x)\in\mathbb{R}\), and \(\varepsilon\ge0\), define
\[
\widehat\partial_\varepsilon f(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid \liminf_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\x\ne\bar x}}\frac{f(x)-f(\bar x)-\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle}{\|x-\bar x\|}\ge-\varepsilon\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(v\in\widehat\partial_\varepsilon f(\bar x)\) when \(f(x)\ge f(\bar x)+\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle-(\varepsilon+o(1))\|x-\bar x\|\) as \(x\to\bar x\). For \(\varepsilon=0\), this reduces to the Fréchet subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An epsilon-subgradient is a Fréchet subgradient whose local first-order support inequality may lose epsilon times the displacement.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Tolerance Is Not a Minkowski Enlargement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Downward cusp showing that positive tolerance can create approximate regular subgradients even when the exact regular subdifferential is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(x)=-|x|\) at \(0\),
\[
\widehat\partial_\varepsilon f(0)=
\begin{cases}
\varnothing,&0\le\varepsilon<1,\\
[1-\varepsilon,\,\varepsilon-1],&\varepsilon\ge1.
\end{cases}
\]
In particular, \(\widehat\partial f(0)=\varnothing\), whereas \(\widehat\partial_1f(0)=\{0\}\). Hence, in general,
\[
\widehat\partial_\varepsilon f(\bar x)\ne\widehat\partial f(\bar x)+\varepsilon\mathbb B.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the downward cusp the exact regular subdifferential is empty, but sufficiently large tolerance produces epsilon-subgradients. Thus the epsilon-subdifferential is not generally an epsilon-ball enlargement of the exact regular subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\partial_\varepsilon f(0)=\varnothing\) for \(\varepsilon<1\) and \([1-\varepsilon,\varepsilon-1]\) for \(\varepsilon\ge1\); hence the Minkowski-enlargement formula fails in general.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive Tolerance Is Not a Minkowski Enlargement

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometry and Monotonicity of Fréchet Epsilon-Subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional structural properties of the tolerance-indexed family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be finite at \(\bar x\). For every \(\varepsilon\ge0\),
\[
\widehat\partial_\varepsilon f(\bar x)=\left\{v:\langle v,w\rangle\le df(\bar x)(w)+\varepsilon\|w\|\ \text{for all }w\in\mathbb{R}^n\right\},
\]
where \(df\) is the lower Hadamard directional derivative. Thus every \(\widehat\partial_\varepsilon f(\bar x)\) is closed and convex, and
\[
0\le\varepsilon_1\le\varepsilon_2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\widehat\partial_{\varepsilon_1}f(\bar x)\subseteq\widehat\partial_{\varepsilon_2}f(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epsilon-subdifferential consists of linear functionals dominated by the lower directional derivative up to epsilon times direction length. Its values are closed, convex, and nested as epsilon increases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each \(\widehat\partial_\varepsilon f(\bar x)\) is closed and convex, and \(\widehat\partial_{\varepsilon_1}f(\bar x)\subseteq\widehat\partial_{\varepsilon_2}f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Geometry and Monotonicity of Fréchet Epsilon-Subdifferentials

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Limiting representations of basic subgradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer-limit formulas using geometric and analytic Fréchet epsilon-subdifferentials, with a finite-dimensional simplification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\varphi:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and \(|\varphi(\bar x)|<\infty\), then \[\partial\varphi(\bar x)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{\substack{x\xrightarrow{\varphi}\bar x\\ \varepsilon\downarrow0}}\widehat\partial_{g\varepsilon}\varphi(x)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{\substack{x\xrightarrow{\varphi}\bar x\\ \varepsilon\downarrow0}}\widehat\partial_{a\varepsilon}\varphi(x),\] where \(x\xrightarrow{\varphi}\bar x\) means \(x\to\bar x\) and \(\varphi(x)\to\varphi(\bar x)\). If additionally \(\varphi\) is lower semicontinuous around \(\bar x\) and \(\dim X<\infty\), then \[\partial\varphi(\bar x)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{x\xrightarrow{\varphi}\bar x}\widehat\partial\varphi(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a finite-valued point, the basic subdifferential is the sequential outer limit of either geometric or analytic Fréchet epsilon-subdifferentials along points whose locations and function values converge. For a locally lower-semicontinuous function on a finite-dimensional space, ordinary Fréchet subdifferentials suffice.
assumptions_latex: For the representation without epsilon-subgradients, \(\varphi\) is lower semicontinuous around \(\bar x\) and \(\dim X<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial\varphi(\bar x)\) equals the stated sequential outer limits of approximate, and under the additional assumptions exact, Fréchet subdifferentials.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) finite at \(\bar x\), define the limiting subdifferential by
\[
\partial_L f(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid \exists x_k\to\bar x,\ f(x_k)\to f(\bar x),\ \exists v_k\to v:\ v_k\in\widehat\partial f(x_k)\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, with \(x\to_f\bar x\) denoting simultaneous point and function-value convergence,
\[
\partial_L f(\bar x)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{x\to_f\bar x}\widehat\partial f(x).
\]
No convexification is performed in this outer limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The limiting subdifferential consists of limits of regular subgradients at nearby points with convergent function values.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) finite at \(\bar x\), the Mordukhovich, or basic, subdifferential is
\[
\partial_M f(\bar x):=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\f(x)\to f(\bar x)}}\widehat\partial f(x).
\]
Thus \(v\in\partial_M f(\bar x)\) precisely when sequences \(x_k\to\bar x\) and \(v_k\to v\) exist such that \(f(x_k)\to f(\bar x)\) and \(v_k\in\widehat\partial f(x_k)\) for all \(k\). The construction retains nonconvex first-order information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Mordukhovich subdifferential is the unconvexified outer limit of nearby regular subdifferentials under function-value convergence.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be finite at \(\bar x\). Under the standard finite-dimensional definitions, the limiting subdifferential and the Mordukhovich basic subdifferential coincide:
\[
\partial_L f(\bar x)=\partial_M f(\bar x)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\f(x)\to f(\bar x)}}\widehat\partial f(x).
\]
Both sides therefore consist of exactly the strong limits \(v_k\to v\) of regular subgradients \(v_k\in\widehat\partial f(x_k)\) along sequences satisfying \(x_k\to\bar x\) and \(f(x_k)\to f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, “limiting” and “Mordukhovich basic” denote the same unconvexified sequential subdifferential.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Subgradient Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete one-dimensional illustration of unconvexified limiting structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) finite at \(\bar x\), the regular and Mordukhovich subdifferentials satisfy
\[
\widehat\partial f(\bar x)\subseteq\partial_M f(\bar x).
\]
The inclusion can be strict, and the Mordukhovich subdifferential need not be convex. For the locally Lipschitz function \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) defined by \(f(x)=-|x|\),
\[
\widehat\partial f(0)=\varnothing,\qquad \partial_M f(0)=\{-1,1\}.
\]
This example displays the unconvexified structure of the basic limiting construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regular subdifferential is contained in the limiting one, but the inclusion can be strict and the limiting set can be nonconvex; for minus absolute value at zero it is the two-point set consisting of minus one and one.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(f(\bar x)\in\mathbb{R}\) for the general inclusion.
For the example, \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) is defined by \(f(x)=-|x|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\partial f(\bar x)\subseteq\partial_M f(\bar x)\), and for \(f(x)=-|x|\), \(\widehat\partial f(0)=\varnothing\) while \(\partial_M f(0)=\{-1,1\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Clarke Subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional locally Lipschitz definition and limiting-subgradient representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Clarke subdifferential of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) is
\[
\partial^C f(\bar x):=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle v,d\rangle\leq f^\circ(\bar x;d)\ \text{for every }d\in\mathbb{R}^n\},
\]
where
\[
f^\circ(\bar x;d):=\limsup_{x\to\bar x,\,t\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+td)-f(x)}{t}.
\]
For locally Lipschitz \(f\), the set \(\partial^C f(\bar x)\) is nonempty, compact, and convex, and
\[
\partial^C f(\bar x)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}\partial f(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke subdifferential consists of the vectors dominated by the Clarke generalized directional derivative. For a locally Lipschitz function, it is a nonempty compact convex set equal to the closed convex hull of the limiting subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^C f(\bar x)\) is a nonempty compact convex set and equals \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}\partial f(\bar x)\).

source_refs.locator: 4.3 Subdifferentials and Regularity p. 170

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support-Function Characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual equivalence between the Clarke generalized directional derivative and Clarke subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(d\in\mathbb R^n\),
\[
f^\circ(\bar x;d)=\max_{v\in\partial^C f(\bar x)}\langle v,d\rangle
=\sigma_{\partial^C f(\bar x)}(d).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke generalized directional derivative is the support function of the Clarke subdifferential.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^\circ(\bar x;d)=\sigma_{\partial^C f(\bar x)}(d)\) for every \(d\).
knowledge_statements.title: Support-Function Characterization

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Upper Semicontinuity and Local Boundedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stability of the finite-dimensional Clarke-subdifferential mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There are a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(L<\infty\) such that
\[
\partial^C f(x)\subseteq L\mathbb B\quad(x\in U).
\]
If \(x_k\to x\in U\), \(v_k\to v\), and \(v_k\in\partial^C f(x_k)\), then \(v\in\partial^C f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a locally Lipschitz point, Clarke subgradients are uniformly bounded and the Clarke-subdifferential mapping is upper semicontinuous.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz on a neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mapping \(x\mapsto\partial^C f(x)\) is locally bounded and upper semicontinuous near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.title: Upper Semicontinuity and Local Boundedness

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reachable-Gradient Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional representation through gradients at nearby differentiability points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D_f\) be the differentiability set of \(f\) and
\[
G_f(\bar x):=\left\{\lim_{k\to\infty}\nabla f(x_k):x_k\to\bar x,\ x_k\in D_f\right\}.
\]
Then
\[
\partial^C f(\bar x)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}G_f(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke subdifferential is the closed convex hull of limits of gradients at nearby differentiability points.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^C f(\bar x)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}G_f(\bar x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke Subdifferential via the Generalized Directional Derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for a locally Lipschitz real-valued function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be locally Lipschitz at \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Its Clarke subdifferential at \(x\) is
\[
\partial f(x):=\left\{\xi\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid f^{\circ}(x;d)\ge \xi^{\mathsf T}d\ \text{for every }d\in\mathbb{R}^n\right\}.
\]
Each \(\xi\in\partial f(x)\) is called a subgradient of \(f\) at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke subdifferential consists of the vectors whose linear forms are dominated in every direction by the Clarke generalized directional derivative; its elements are called subgradients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f(x)=\{\xi\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid f^{\circ}(x;d)\ge \xi^{\mathsf T}d\ \forall d\in\mathbb{R}^n\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Differentiability and Singleton Clarke Subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise characterization of strict differentiability for locally Lipschitz functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is strictly differentiable at \(x\), then \(f\) is Lipschitz near \(x\) and \(\partial_C f(x)=\{D_s f(x)\}\). Conversely, if \(f\) is Lipschitz near \(x\) and \(\partial_C f(x)=\{\zeta\}\), then \(f\) is strictly differentiable at \(x\) and \(D_s f(x)=\zeta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict differentiability at x implies local Lipschitz continuity and a singleton Clarke subdifferential containing the strict derivative. Conversely, a locally Lipschitz function whose Clarke subdifferential at x is a singleton is strictly differentiable there, with derivative equal to that singleton element.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is strictly differentiable at }x\quad\text{for the forward implication}
f\text{ is Lipschitz near }x\text{ and }\partial_C f(x)=\{\zeta\}\quad\text{for the converse}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial_C f(x)=\{D_s f(x)\}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f\text{ is strictly differentiable at }x\ \text{under the stated local Lipschitz conditions}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X be compact. For every \delta>0 and \mu>0, there exists \varepsilon>0 such that x\mapsto\partial_\varepsilon f(x) is a continuous (\delta,\mu)-approximation of x\mapsto\partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}f(x) on X.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a compact set, any prescribed positive displacement and enlargement tolerances can be attained by a suitable continuous epsilon-subdifferential approximation of the Clarke subdifferential mapping.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\varepsilon>0\text{ such that }x\mapsto\partial_\varepsilon f(x)\text{ is a continuous }(\delta,\mu)\text{-approximation of }\partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}f\text{ on }X

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke-subdifferential chain rule for a strictly differentiable inner mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-valued outer function between Banach spaces; the regularity condition is interpreted at F(x), where the outer function is evaluated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f=g\circ F, where F:X\to Y is strictly differentiable at x and g:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty] is finite and directionally Lipschitz at F(x). If \operatorname{range}D_sF(x)\cap\operatorname{int}\{v\in Y:g^\circ(F(x);v)<+\infty\}\neq\varnothing, then \partial f(x)\subset D_sF(x)^*\bigl(\partial g(F(x))\bigr). If g is regular at F(x), equality holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the inner mapping is strictly differentiable and the extended-valued outer function is finite and directionally Lipschitz at the image point, the stated range–interior qualification gives a Clarke-subdifferential chain-rule inclusion. Regularity of the outer function at the image point makes the inclusion an equality.
assumptions_latex: F:X\to Y\text{ is strictly differentiable at }x
g\text{ is finite and directionally Lipschitz at }F(x)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial(g\circ F)(x)\subset D_sF(x)^*\bigl(\partial g(F(x))\bigr),\quad\text{with equality if }g\text{ is regular at }F(x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex consistency of the Clarke subdifferential and generalized directional derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies Clarke's generalized derivatives with their convex-analysis counterparts when the function is convex and locally Lipschitz at the point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in U\subseteq X\), and suppose that \(f\) is convex on \(U\) and Lipschitz near \(x\). Then \(\partial_C f(x)=\partial_{\mathrm{cvx}}f(x)\), and, for every \(v\in X\), \(f^{\circ}(x;v)=f'(x;v)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If f is convex on U and Lipschitz near x, then its Clarke subdifferential at x equals its convex-analysis subdifferential, and its Clarke generalized directional derivative equals its directional derivative in every direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial_C f(x)=\partial_{\mathrm{cvx}}f(x)\quad\text{and}\quad (\forall v\in X)\;f^{\circ}(x;v)=f'(x;v)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(f:\mathbf E\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz around \(x\in\mathbf E\), and \(S\subset\mathbf E\) has measure zero. Then

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Clarke Chain Rule under Local Openness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The outer subdifferential is evaluated at \(y=H(x)\), resolving the dimensionally inconsistent repeated base-point symbol in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable on a neighborhood \(B_\delta(x)\), set \(y=H(x)\), and suppose the image under \(H\) of every neighborhood of \(x\) contains a neighborhood of \(y\). Let \(f\) be Lipschitz on an open set \(Y\ni y\), with \(H(B_\delta(x))\subseteq Y\), and define \(\varphi(x')=f(H(x'))\). Then \(\varphi\) is Lipschitz near \(x\) and \[\partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}\varphi(x)=H'(x)^*\partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}f(y)=\{H'(x)^*\ell':\ell'\in\partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}f(y)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a continuously differentiable inner mapping is locally open at the base point and the outer function is Lipschitz, then the composition is locally Lipschitz and its Clarke subdifferential is exactly the adjoint derivative image of the outer Clarke subdifferential.
assumptions_latex: \forall U\ni x,\ H(U)\text{ contains a neighborhood of }y
f\text{ is Lipschitz on an open }Y\ni y
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varphi\text{ is locally Lipschitz near }x\quad\text{and}\quad\partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}\varphi(x)=H'(x)^*\partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}f(y)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximation of the Clarke Subdifferential Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform outer approximation by Clarke subgradients from a fixed neighborhood, up to a fixed additive error ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set-valued mapping b:X\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n is an approximation of x\mapsto\partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}f(x) if there exist \delta>0 and \mu>0 such that, for every x\in X,\quad \partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}f(x)\subset b(x)\subset \partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}f(x+\mathcal B_\delta)+\mathcal B_\mu.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-valued mapping b approximates the Clarke subdifferential mapping when it contains the Clarke subdifferential at every point and is contained in the Clarke subgradients obtained from a fixed delta-neighborhood, enlarged by a fixed mu-ball.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in X,\quad \partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}f(x)\subset b(x)\subset \partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}f(x+\mathcal B_\delta)+\mathcal B_\mu

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity characterized by monotonicity of the Clarke subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes convexity of a locally Lipschitz function on an open convex set by monotonicity of its Clarke subdifferential mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq X\) be open and convex, and let \(f\) be Lipschitz near every point of \(U\). Then \(f\) is convex on \(U\) if and only if \(\partial_C f\) is monotone on \(U\); equivalently, for all \(x,x'\in U\), \(\zeta\in\partial_C f(x)\), and \(\zeta'\in\partial_C f(x')\), one has \(\langle x-x',\zeta-\zeta'\rangle\geq 0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function that is Lipschitz near every point of an open convex set U is convex on U exactly when its Clarke subdifferential is monotone there.
assumptions_latex: U\subseteq X\text{ is open and convex}
f\text{ is Lipschitz near every point of }U
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex on }U\iff (\forall x,x'\in U)(\forall\zeta\in\partial_C f(x))(\forall\zeta'\in\partial_C f(x'))\;\langle x-x',\zeta-\zeta'\rangle\geq 0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke Subdifferential Sum Inclusion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The general sum rule for locally Lipschitz summands; equality is not asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) are locally Lipschitz near \(x\) and \(f=f_1+f_2\), then \[\partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}f(x)\subseteq \partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}f_1(x)+\partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}f_2(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke subdifferential of a sum is contained in the Minkowski sum of the Clarke subdifferentials of its summands.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}f(x)\subseteq\partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}f_1(x)+\partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}f_2(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite linear-combination rule for Clarke subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite scalar combinations of functions locally Lipschitz at a common point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb N\), let each \(f_i:X\to\mathbb R\) be Lipschitz near \(x\), and let \(\lambda_i\in\mathbb R\). Then \(f:=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i f_i\) is Lipschitz near \(x\) and \[\partial_C\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i f_i\right)(x)\subseteq\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i\partial_C f_i(x).\] Equality holds if every \(f_i\) is regular at \(x\) and every \(\lambda_i\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite scalar combination of functions Lipschitz near x remains Lipschitz there, and its Clarke subdifferential is contained in the corresponding Minkowski combination. Equality holds when every function is regular at x and all coefficients are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f:=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i f_i\text{ is Lipschitz near }x,\quad \partial_C f(x)\subseteq\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i\partial_C f_i(x),\quad \bigl[\forall i,\ f_i\text{ regular at }x,\ \lambda_i\geq0\bigr]\Longrightarrow\partial_C f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i\partial_C f_i(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Sum Rule for Clarke Subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the general inclusion for arbitrary real coefficients and the equality and regularity conclusions under nonnegative coefficients and regular summands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be locally Lipschitz at \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(\lambda_i\in\mathbb{R}\), and define \(f=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f_i\). Then \(f\) is locally Lipschitz at \(x\) and \[\partial f(x)\subseteq\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\partial f_i(x).\] If additionally every \(f_i\) is subdifferentially regular at \(x\) and every \(\lambda_i\geq0\), then \(f\) is subdifferentially regular at \(x\) and equality holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite real linear combination of locally Lipschitz functions remains locally Lipschitz, and its Clarke subdifferential is contained in the corresponding Minkowski sum. For nonnegative coefficients and regular summands, the sum is regular and equality holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is locally Lipschitz at }x,\quad\partial f(x)\subseteq\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\partial f_i(x);\quad[(\forall i)\;f_i\text{ is subdifferentially regular at }x,\ \lambda_i\geq0]\Rightarrow[f\text{ is subdifferentially regular at }x,\ \partial f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\partial f_i(x)].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke Subdifferential and Generalized Gradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the Clarke subdifferential through the upper and lower Clarke directional derivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Clarke subdifferential \(\partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}f(x)\) is the convex compact set that is the subdifferential of \(g\mapsto f_{\mathrm{Cl}}^{\uparrow}(x,g)\) and the superdifferential of \(g\mapsto f_{\mathrm{Cl}}^{\downarrow}(x,g)\). Equivalently, for every \(g\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[f_{\mathrm{Cl}}^{\uparrow}(x,g)=\max_{\ell\in\partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}f(x)}\langle\ell,g\rangle,\qquad f_{\mathrm{Cl}}^{\downarrow}(x,g)=\min_{\ell\in\partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}f(x)}\langle\ell,g\rangle.\] Each \(\ell\in\partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}f(x)\) is called a generalized gradient of \(f\) at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke subdifferential is the convex compact set whose maximum and minimum linear evaluations represent the Clarke upper and lower directional derivatives. Its elements are generalized gradients.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(x\) lie in the regime where the Clarke upper and lower directional derivatives and the associated convex compact set are defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_{\mathrm{Cl}}^{\uparrow}(x,g)=\max_{\ell\in\partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}f(x)}\langle\ell,g\rangle,\quad f_{\mathrm{Cl}}^{\downarrow}(x,g)=\min_{\ell\in\partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}f(x)}\langle\ell,g\rangle.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke mean value theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mean-value representation along a nondegenerate line segment for a locally Lipschitz function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x,y\in X\) with \(x\ne y\), and suppose \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is Lipschitz on a neighborhood of \([x,y]\). Then there exist \(z\in(x,y)\) and \(\xi\in\partial_C f(z)\) such that \[f(y)-f(x)=\langle\xi,y-x\rangle.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If f is Lipschitz on a neighborhood of the segment joining distinct points x and y, then at some interior point z there is a Clarke subgradient whose pairing with y minus x equals f(y) minus f(x).
assumptions_latex: f:X\to\mathbb R\text{ is Lipschitz on a neighborhood of }[x,y]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists z\in(x,y)\ \exists\xi\in\partial_C f(z):\ f(y)-f(x)=\langle\xi,y-x\rangle

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates the Clarke subdifferential of a function in the stated class to its quasidifferential components.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sign symmetry of the convexified limiting subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-semicontinuous functions that are locally Lipschitz at the reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gradient-Limit Representation of the Clarke Subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation by limiting gradients on an almost-everywhere differentiability set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be Lipschitz on a neighborhood \(S\) of \(x\). Let \(Q\subset S\) satisfy \(\mu_*(S\setminus Q)=0\), and suppose \(f\) is differentiable on \(Q\). Define \[A=\left\{\ell:\exists x_i\in Q,\ x_i\to x,\ \nabla f(x_i)\to\ell\right\},\qquad D=\operatorname{co}A.\] Then \(A\) and \(D\) are compact and \[\partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}f(x)=D=\operatorname{co}A.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a Lipschitz function differentiable on a set whose complement has inner measure zero, its Clarke subdifferential is the convex hull of all gradient limits along that set approaching the point; the gradient-limit set and its convex hull are compact.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is Lipschitz on a neighborhood }S\text{ of }x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}f(x)=\operatorname{co}\left\{\ell:\exists x_i\in Q,\ x_i\to x,\ \nabla f(x_i)\to\ell\right\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke subdifferential chain rule with a smooth inner mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition of a locally Lipschitz scalar function with a continuously differentiable mapping between Banach spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be Banach spaces, let \(F:X\to Y\) be continuously differentiable near \(x\), and let \(g:Y\to\mathbb R\) be Lipschitz near \(F(x)\). Then \(f:=g\circ F\) is Lipschitz near \(x\) and \[\partial_C f(x)\subseteq F'(x)^*\partial_C g(F(x)).\] If \(F'(x):X\to Y\) is onto, then equality holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The composition of a locally Lipschitz scalar function with a continuously differentiable mapping is locally Lipschitz. Its Clarke subdifferential is contained in the adjoint derivative image of the outer function's Clarke subdifferential, with equality when the inner mapping's derivative is onto.
assumptions_latex: F:X\to Y\text{ is continuously differentiable near }x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f:=g\circ F\text{ is Lipschitz near }x,\quad\partial_C f(x)\subseteq F'(x)^*\partial_C g(F(x)),\quad F'(x)\text{ onto}\Longrightarrow\partial_C f(x)=F'(x)^*\partial_C g(F(x))

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke Tangent and Normal Estimates for a Lipschitz Sublevel Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preserves the general inclusion directions and the strengthened equalities and set-regularity conclusion under function regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be locally Lipschitz, let \(S=\{u\in X:f(u)\le0\}\), and suppose \(x\in S\) and \(0\notin\partial_C f(x)\). Then
\[T_S^C(x)\supseteq\{v\in X:f^\circ(x;v)\le0\},\qquad N_S^C(x)\subseteq\{\lambda\zeta:\lambda\ge0,\ \zeta\in\partial_C f(x)\}.\]
If, in addition, \(f\) is regular at \(x\), both inclusions are equalities, \(S\) is regular at \(x\), and \(T_S^C(x)=T_S(x)\) and \(N_S^C(x)=N_S(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a locally Lipschitz sublevel set at a point where zero is excluded from the Clarke subdifferential, the Clarke tangent cone contains every direction having nonpositive Clarke directional derivative, and the Clarke normal cone is contained in the nonnegative cone generated by the Clarke subdifferential. If the function is regular at the point, both inclusions become equalities and the sublevel set is regular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_S^C(x)\supseteq\{v\in X:f^\circ(x;v)\le0\},\quad N_S^C(x)\subseteq\{\lambda\zeta:\lambda\ge0,\ \zeta\in\partial_C f(x)\};\quad f\text{ regular at }x\Rightarrow\text{ both inclusions are equalities, }S\text{ is regular at }x,\ T_S^C(x)=T_S(x),\ N_S^C(x)=N_S(x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unique Clarke Subgradient Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes singleton Clarke subdifferentials by strict differentiability and records the resulting regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbf E\to\mathbb R\) be locally Lipschitz around \(x\in\mathbf E\), and let \(\phi\in\mathbf E\). Then \(\partial_C f(x)=\{\phi\}\) if and only if \(\phi\) is the strict derivative of \(f\) at \(x\). When these equivalent conditions hold, \(f\) is regular at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a real function locally Lipschitz near x, the Clarke subdifferential is the singleton {phi} exactly when phi is the strict derivative at x. In that case the function is regular at x.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial_C f(x)=\{\phi\}\iff \phi\text{ is the strict derivative of }f\text{ at }x,\qquad\text{and these conditions imply that }f\text{ is regular at }x

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonsmooth Fermat Necessary Conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary generalized-subgradient conditions for unconstrained local minima and maxima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varphi:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be finite at \(\bar x\). If \(\bar x\) is a local minimum of \(\varphi\), then \[0\in\widehat\partial\varphi(\bar x)\subseteq\partial\varphi(\bar x).\] If \(\bar x\) is a local maximum, then \[0\in\widehat\partial^{+}\varphi(\bar x)\subseteq\partial^{+}\varphi(\bar x).\] Consequently, at either kind of local extremum, \[0\in\widehat\partial\varphi(\bar x)\cup\widehat\partial^{+}\varphi(\bar x)\subseteq\partial^{0}\varphi(\bar x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a finite local minimum, zero is a regular and hence limiting subgradient. At a finite local maximum, zero is an upper regular and hence upper limiting subgradient. Thus zero belongs to the symmetric subdifferential at either local extremum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar x\text{ local minimum}\Rightarrow0\in\widehat\partial\varphi(\bar x)\subseteq\partial\varphi(\bar x);\quad \bar x\text{ local maximum}\Rightarrow0\in\widehat\partial^+\varphi(\bar x)\subseteq\partial^+\varphi(\bar x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Outer state-constraint subdifferential and conditional multiplier support
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definition for a state-constrained differential-inclusion problem, together with a complementary-slackness consequence conditional on inclusion (10.1), whose full statement is not present in the extract.

knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferential Inclusions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional locally Lipschitz hierarchy at a finite-valued reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a proper lower-semicontinuous function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) that is finite at \(\bar x\),
\[
\widehat\partial f(\bar x)\subseteq\partial f(\bar x).
\]
If \(f\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\), then
\[
\widehat\partial f(\bar x)\subseteq\partial f(\bar x)\subseteq\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}\partial f(\bar x)=\partial^C f(\bar x).
\]
For nonregular nonconvex functions, either successive inclusion can be strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regular subgradients are limiting subgradients. If the function is locally Lipschitz near the reference point, limiting subgradients lie in the Clarke subdifferential; either successive inclusion can be strict for a nonregular nonconvex function.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is proper and lower semicontinuous with \(f(\bar x)<+\infty\).
For the inclusion involving \(\partial^C f(\bar x)\), \(f\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\partial f(\bar x)\subseteq\partial f(\bar x)\), and under local Lipschitz continuity, \(\widehat\partial f(\bar x)\subseteq\partial f(\bar x)\subseteq\partial^C f(\bar x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Subdifferential regularity of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) entails
\[
\widehat\partial f(\bar x)=\partial f(\bar x).
\]
If, additionally, \(f\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) and \(\partial f(\bar x)\) is closed and convex, then Clarke convexification introduces no enlargement and
\[
\widehat\partial f(\bar x)=\partial f(\bar x)=\partial^C f(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a subdifferentially regular point, regular and limiting subdifferentials coincide. Local Lipschitz continuity and convexity of that set also yield Clarke coincidence.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict-Differentiability Coincidence Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Singleton coincidence under strict differentiability in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f\) is strictly differentiable at \(\bar x\), then
\[
\widehat\partial f(\bar x)=\partial f(\bar x)=\partial^C f(\bar x)=\{\nabla f(\bar x)\}.
\]
In particular, the conclusion holds when \(f\) is continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict differentiability collapses the regular, limiting, and Clarke subdifferentials to the classical gradient singleton; local continuous differentiability is a standard sufficient condition.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is strictly differentiable at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\partial f(\bar x)=\partial f(\bar x)=\partial^C f(\bar x)=\{\nabla f(\bar x)\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sufficient Conditions for Subdifferential Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lists smoothness, convexity, and closure under finite positive linear combinations as sufficient regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Then \(f\) is subdifferentially regular at \(x\) if any one of the following holds: (i) \(f\) is continuously differentiable at \(x\); (ii) \(f\) is convex; or (iii) \(f=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f_i\), where \(\lambda_i>0\) and every \(f_i\) is subdifferentially regular at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuous differentiability at the point, convexity, or representation as a finite positive linear combination of functions regular at the point is sufficient for subdifferential regularity.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is continuously differentiable at }x\;\lor\;f\text{ is convex}\;\lor\;\bigl(f=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f_i,\ \lambda_i>0,\ f_i\text{ is subdifferentially regular at }x\bigr)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is subdifferentially regular at }x.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

\[
\widehat\partial f(\bar x)=\partial f(\bar x)=\partial_{\mathrm{cvx}}f(\bar x)

knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferential Separation Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical one-dimensional strict-separation example.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) defined by \(f(x)=-|x|\),
\[
\widehat\partial f(0)=\varnothing\subsetneq\partial f(0)=\{-1,1\}\subsetneq\partial^C f(0)=[-1,1].
\]
Thus both successive inclusions in the regular–limiting–Clarke hierarchy are strict at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the downward cusp given by minus the absolute value, the regular subdifferential at zero is empty, the limiting subdifferential consists of minus one and one, and the Clarke subdifferential is the interval between them. Both successive inclusions are strict.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At \(0\), \(\widehat\partial f(0)=\varnothing\), \(\partial f(0)=\{-1,1\}\), and \(\partial^C f(0)=[-1,1]\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is locally Lipschitz around \(\bar x\) if there exist an open neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and a constant \(L\geq0\) such that
\[
|f(x)-f(y)|\leq L\|x-y\|\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in U.
\]
In particular, \(f\) is finite and continuous throughout a possibly smaller neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is locally Lipschitz around a point when one uniform Lipschitz bound holds for every pair of points in a neighborhood.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke subdifferential and its basic geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition through the convex subdifferential of the generalized directional derivative, including the stated compactness and norm bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^k\to\mathbb{R}\) be Lipschitz continuous on a neighborhood of \(x\), with local Lipschitz constant \(K\). Its Clarke subdifferential at \(x\) is \[\bar\partial f(x):=\{\xi\in\mathbb{R}^k:f^0(x,v)\geq \xi\cdot v\ \text{for every }v\in\mathbb{R}^k\}.\] Equivalently, it is the convex subdifferential of \(v\mapsto f^0(x,v)\) at \(v=0\). The set \(\bar\partial f(x)\) is nonempty, compact, and convex, and every \(\xi\in\bar\partial f(x)\) satisfies \(\|\xi\|\leq K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke subdifferential consists of vectors whose linear forms are dominated by the generalized directional derivative in every direction. It is the convex subdifferential of that direction map at zero and is nonempty, compact, convex, and bounded by the local Lipschitz constant.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is Lipschitz continuous on a neighborhood of }x\text{ with constant }K
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar\partial f(x)=\{\xi:f^0(x,v)\geq\xi\cdot v\ \forall v\in\mathbb{R}^k\},\quad \bar\partial f(x)\neq\varnothing,\quad \bar\partial f(x)\text{ is compact and convex},\quad \|\xi\|\leq K\ \forall\xi\in\bar\partial f(x).

knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz-to-Vanishing Passage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential mechanism behind Lipschitz-to-horizon vanishing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on a neighborhood of \(\bar x\), then every regular subgradient \(v\in\widehat\partial f(x)\) at a sufficiently nearby point \(x\) satisfies \(\|v\|\leq L\). Consequently, whenever \(x_k\to\bar x\), \(f(x_k)\to f(\bar x)\), \(v_k\in\widehat\partial f(x_k)\), and \(\lambda_k\downarrow0\),
\[
\lambda_kv_k\longrightarrow0.
\]
Thus every limit admitted by the sequential horizon construction is zero, and
\[
\partial^\infty f(\bar x)=\{0\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a locally Lipschitz function, nearby regular subgradients are uniformly bounded by the Lipschitz modulus. Scaling any such sequence by positive scalars tending to zero gives only the zero horizon limit.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on a neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_kv_k\to0\) for every such sequence, and hence \(\partial^\infty f(\bar x)=\{0\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Sum Singular Qualification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional no-abnormal-cancellation condition and its role in limiting-subdifferential sum calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\). The singular qualification at \(\bar x\) is
\[
\left[v_i\in\partial^\infty f_i(\bar x),\ \sum_{i=1}^m v_i=0\right]\Longrightarrow v_1=\cdots=v_m=0.
\]
If each \(f_i\) is lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\) and finite there, this qualification yields the finite-dimensional limiting sum-rule inclusion
\[
\partial F(\bar x)\subseteq\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The qualification excludes cancellation among nonzero horizon subgradients. For finitely many lower-semicontinuous summands in finite dimensions, it validates the limiting-subdifferential sum inclusion.
assumptions_latex: \(f_i:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), are lower semicontinuous on a neighborhood of \(\bar x\) and finite at \(\bar x\).
Whenever \(v_i\in\partial^\infty f_i(\bar x)\) and \(\sum_i v_i=0\), every \(v_i\) is zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(\sum_{i=1}^m f_i)(\bar x)\subseteq\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(\bar x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A standard singular qualification for the finite sum \(F:=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\) is
\[
\left[v_i\in\partial^\infty f_i(\bar x),\ \sum_{i=1}^m v_i=0\right]\Longrightarrow\left[v_1=\cdots=v_m=0\right].
\]
It rules out cancellation among nonzero abnormal multipliers. Under the accompanying hypotheses of the limiting sum rule, this condition yields
\[
\partial F(\bar x)\subseteq\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular qualification forbids nonzero horizon subgradients from canceling. Under the sum-rule hypotheses, this validates decomposition of each limiting subgradient into summand subgradients.

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise Linear–Quadratic Subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex finite-maximum piecewise linear–quadratic functions with a common quadratic term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be symmetric positive semidefinite, define
\[
q_i(x):=\tfrac12\langle x,Qx\rangle+\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i\quad (i=1,\ldots,m),
\]
and set
\[
f(x):=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}q_i(x),\qquad I(x):=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:q_i(x)=f(x)\}.
\]
Then \(f\) is a convex piecewise linear–quadratic function and
\[
\partial f(x)=\operatorname{co}\{Qx+a_i:i\in I(x)\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a maximum of finitely many convex quadratics sharing the same quadratic term, the function is convex piecewise linear–quadratic, and its subdifferential is the convex hull of the gradients of its active pieces.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is symmetric positive semidefinite, and \(q_i(x)=\tfrac12\langle x,Qx\rangle+\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is convex piecewise linear–quadratic and \(\partial f(x)=\operatorname{co}\{Qx+a_i:i\in I(x)\}\).

notation.meaning: subdifferential, common to convex and limiting constructions here

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is convex piecewise linear-quadratic when its domain has a finite polyhedral cover on whose members \(f\) agrees with quadratic functions.

notation.meaning: Polyhedral pieces covering the effective domain

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic finite-dimensional definition allowing extended-real polyhedral domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proper lower-semicontinuous convex function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is piecewise linear-quadratic if \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is covered by finitely many polyhedral sets \(C_j\) and, for each \(j\), \[f(x)=\tfrac12\langle x,Q_jx\rangle+\langle a_j,x\rangle+b_j\qquad(x\in C_j).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex PLQ function is a proper closed convex extended-real function represented by finitely many quadratic formulas on polyhedral pieces.
