knowledge_statements.title: Convex Piecewise Linear-Quadratic Functions

assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, closed, convex, and piecewise linear-quadratic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*\) is proper closed convex PLQ and \((\partial f)^{-1}=\partial f^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel conjugacy within the proper closed convex PLQ class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, convex, and piecewise linear-quadratic, then its Fenchel conjugate \[f^*(v)=\sup_x\{\langle v,x\rangle-f(x)\}\] is also proper, closed, convex, and piecewise linear-quadratic, and \[(\partial f)^{-1}=\partial f^*.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fenchel conjugacy preserves the convex PLQ class and interchanges its subdifferential with the inverse mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugacy Closure of Convex PLQ Functions
knowledge_statements.title: Conjugacy Closure of Convex PLQ Functions

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is PLQ if and only if \(\operatorname{gph}\partial f\) is a finite union of convex polyhedral sets.

notation.meaning: Graph of the convex subdifferential mapping

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional structural characterization of proper closed convex PLQ functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proper lower-semicontinuous convex function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is piecewise linear-quadratic if and only if its convex subdifferential is piecewise polyhedral, equivalently, \[\operatorname{gph}\partial f\] is a finite union of convex polyhedral sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed convex PLQ functions are exactly the convex functions with piecewise-polyhedral subdifferential mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Piecewise-Polyhedral Subdifferential Characterization
knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Polyhedral Subdifferential Characterization

children.title: Lower-Curvature Subdifferential Classes
children.top_down_role: Lower-curvature-controlled nonconvex subgradient regimes.

children.title: Weakly Convex Subdifferentials
children.top_down_role: Subgradient geometry under weak convexity.

assumptions_latex: For some \(\rho\ge 0\), the function \(x\mapsto f(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}\|x\|^2\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)=\partial\!\left(f+\frac{\rho}{2}\|\cdot\|^2\right)(x)-\rho x\), with the displayed global quadratic support inequality.

notation.meaning: Limiting subdifferential of f at x; it agrees here with the shifted convex subdifferential.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional global weak convexity with the limiting subdifferential.

source_refs.locator: 4.4.3 Weakly convex functions p. 214

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), set \(g=f+\frac{\rho}{2}\|\cdot\|^2\). Then \[\partial f(x)=\partial g(x)-\rho x.\] Equivalently, \(v\in\partial f(x)\) if and only if \[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle v,y-x\rangle-\frac{\rho}{2}\|y-x\|^2\qquad\text{for every }y\in\mathbb{R}^n.\] Thus the subdifferential of a weakly convex function consists exactly of its global quadratic-support slopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weakly convex function has subgradients exactly when it admits global affine supports with a quadratic downward correction.
knowledge_statements.title: Weakly Convex Subdifferentials

source_witnesses.locator: 4.4.3 Weakly convex functions p. 214

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is \(1\)-weakly convex and \(0\in\partial f(0)\), but \(0\) is a strict local maximum and is not a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of convex-style optimality for a positive weak-convexity modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\cos x\), the function \(f+\frac12|\cdot|^2\) is convex, so \(f\) is \(1\)-weakly convex. Moreover, \(0\in\partial f(0)=\{0\}\), although \(0\) is a strict local maximum and is not a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero subgradient of a weakly convex function certifies stationarity, not minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weakly Convex Stationarity Need Not Certify a Minimum
knowledge_statements.title: Weakly Convex Stationarity Need Not Certify a Minimum

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f+\rho I\) is maximally monotone and \(\langle v-w,x-y\rangle\ge-\rho\|x-y\|^2\) for all graph pairs.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional operator structure inherited from the convex quadratic shift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is \(\rho\)-weakly convex, then \(\partial f+\rho I=\partial(f+\frac\rho2\|\cdot\|^2)\) is maximally monotone. Consequently, for every \((x,v),(y,w)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\), \[\langle v-w,x-y\rangle\ge-\rho\|x-y\|^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The limiting subdifferential of a rho-weakly convex function is rho-hypomonotone, and its rho-shift is maximally monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hypomonotonicity of the Weakly Convex Subdifferential
knowledge_statements.title: Hypomonotonicity of the Weakly Convex Subdifferential

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial_Pf(x)=\widehat\partial f(x)=\partial f(x)=\partial_c(f+\frac\rho2\|\cdot\|^2)(x)-\rho x\), a closed convex set that may be empty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise subdifferential structure inherited from the convex quadratic shift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), \[\partial_Pf(x)=\widehat\partial f(x)=\partial f(x)=\partial_c\!\left(f+\tfrac\rho2\|\cdot\|^2\right)(x)-\rho x.\] This set is closed and convex, although it can be empty at boundary points of \(\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a weakly convex function, proximal, regular, and limiting subdifferentials coincide with a translated convex subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coincidence and Convexity of Weakly Convex Subgradients
knowledge_statements.title: Coincidence and Convexity of Weakly Convex Subgradients

children.title: Prox-Regular Subdifferentials
children.top_down_role: Subgradient geometry under prox-regularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Prox-Regular Subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subgradient-attentive finite-dimensional prox-regularity at a specified graph pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is prox-regular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\) if there exist \(r\ge 0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \[f(x')\ge f(x)+\langle v,x'-x\rangle-\frac r2\|x'-x\|^2\] whenever \(\|x-\bar x\|<\varepsilon\), \(\|x'-\bar x\|<\varepsilon\), \(|f(x)-f(\bar x)|<\varepsilon\), and \(v\in\partial f(x)\) satisfies \(\|v-\bar v\|<\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prox-regularity requires a uniform local quadratic lower support for nearby subgradients whose base points, function values, and slopes approach the reference graph pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated localized quadratic-support inequality defines prox-regularity of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\).

source_refs.locator: 4.3 Subdifferentials and Regularity p. 170

source_witnesses.locator: 4.3 Subdifferentials and Regularity p. 170

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Localized Hypomonotonicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hypomonotonicity on the subgradient-attentive localization used in prox-regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For graph pairs \((x_i,v_i)\), \(i=1,2\), in a sufficiently small subgradient-attentive localization of \((\bar x,\bar v)\), prox-regularity with parameter \(r\) implies \(\langle v_1-v_2,x_1-x_2\rangle\ge-r\|x_1-x_2\|^2\). Equivalently, the localized mapping \(x\mapsto\partial f(x)+rx\) is monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A prox-regular subdifferential is locally hypomonotone around the designated graph pair.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is prox-regular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\) with parameter \(r\).
Both graph pairs lie in the defining attentive localization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \langle v_1-v_2,x_1-x_2\rangle\ge-r\|x_1-x_2\|^2.
knowledge_statements.title: Localized Hypomonotonicity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Localized Proximal Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local, not global, proximal stability around a prox-regular graph pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is additionally prox-bounded and subdifferentially continuous at \((\bar x,\bar v)\), then for sufficiently small \(\lambda>0\) with \(\lambda r<1\), an attentive localization of \((I+\lambda\partial f)^{-1}\) around \((\bar x+\lambda\bar v,\bar x)\) is single-valued and Lipschitz. The associated localized Moreau envelope is \(C^1\) and satisfies \(\nabla e_\lambda f(z)=\lambda^{-1}(z-P_\lambda f(z))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With prox-boundedness and subdifferential continuity, prox-regularity yields a locally single-valued proximal map and smooth local Moreau envelope.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, prox-bounded, prox-regular, and subdifferentially continuous at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_\lambda f=(I+\lambda\partial f)^{-1}\text{ has a single-valued Lipschitz localization, and }\nabla e_\lambda f=\lambda^{-1}(I-P_\lambda f).
knowledge_statements.title: Localized Proximal Stability

children.title: Lower-Curvature Overlap
children.top_down_role: Shared subgradient behavior across weakly convex and prox-regular regimes.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\rho\)-weakly convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is prox-regular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\), with quadratic parameter \(r=\rho\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global weak convexity implies prox-regularity at every limiting-subgradient pair.

source_refs.locator: 4.4.3 Weakly convex functions p. 214
4.3 Subdifferentials and Regularity p. 170

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x,x'\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and every \(v\in\partial f(x)\), weak convexity yields \[f(x')\ge f(x)+\langle v,x'-x\rangle-\frac{\rho}{2}\|x'-x\|^2.\] Consequently, for every \((\bar x,\bar v)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\), the defining prox-regularity inequality holds with \(r=\rho\), without further localization beyond the subgradient-attentive conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every globally weakly convex function is prox-regular at each limiting-subgradient pair, using its weak-convexity modulus.
knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Curvature Overlap

source_witnesses.locator: 4.4.3 Weakly convex functions p. 214
4.3 Subdifferentials and Regularity p. 170

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strictness of the Lower-Curvature Inclusion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the converse from prox-regularity to global weak convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The \(C^2\) function \(f(x)=-x^4\) is prox-regular at every graph pair \((\bar x,f'(\bar x))\), because its curvature is bounded below locally. However, \(f''(x)=-12x^2\) is unbounded below, so \(f+(\rho/2)|\cdot|^2\) is nonconvex for every finite \(\rho\). Hence prox-regularity does not imply global weak convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prox-regularity is local and does not imply global weak convexity; minus x to the fourth separates the classes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is prox-regular at every }(\bar x,f'(\bar x))\text{ but is not globally weakly convex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Strictness of the Lower-Curvature Inclusion

children.title: Prox-Regularity Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Lower-curvature geometries where proximal stability breaks down.

knowledge_statements.title: Prox-Regularity Failure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A downward cusp violates every finite local quadratic-support modulus at either limiting subgradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=-|x|\), the limiting subdifferential at the origin is \(\partial f(0)=\{-1,1\}\). The function \(f\) is not prox-regular at \(0\) for either \(v=1\) or \(v=-1\): no finite quadratic parameter gives the required local lower-support inequality at either graph pair \((0,1)\) or \((0,-1)\). Thus local Lipschitz continuity and lower semicontinuity do not by themselves imply prox-regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The downward cusp minus absolute value is locally Lipschitz and lower semicontinuous but fails prox-regularity at the origin for either limiting slope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(\partial f(0)=\{-1,1\}\), the function is not prox-regular at \(0\) for either limiting subgradient.

children.title: Difference-of-Convex Subdifferentials
children.top_down_role: Subgradient structures associated with convex differences.

assumptions_latex: \(g,h:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper convex functions and are finite near \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The decomposition generates \(\partial g(x)-\partial h(x)\); if \(h\) is differentiable at \(x\), then \(\partial f(x)=\partial g(x)-\nabla h(x)\).

notation.meaning: Minkowski difference of the two convex subdifferential sets.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decomposition-dependent DC subgradient structure and its exact smooth-concave-part specialization.

source_refs.locator: 4.4.4 Difference-of-convex functions p. 224

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The chosen DC decomposition associates with \(f\) the set \[\partial g(x)-\partial h(x)=\{u-w:u\in\partial g(x),\ w\in\partial h(x)\}.\] This set depends on the decomposition and is used in the DC criticality condition \(0\in\partial g(x)-\partial h(x)\). If \(h\) is differentiable at \(x\), the limiting-subdifferential smooth-perturbation rule gives the intrinsic identity \[\partial f(x)=\partial g(x)-\nabla h(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A DC decomposition yields differences of convex subgradients; this equals the intrinsic limiting subdifferential when the subtracted convex term is differentiable.
knowledge_statements.title: Difference-of-Convex Subdifferentials

source_witnesses.locator: 4.4.4 Difference-of-convex functions p. 224

knowledge_statements.statement_title: DC Directional Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary directional stationarity for a finite-valued DC decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\bar x\) locally minimizes \(g-h\), then \(g'(\bar x;d)\ge h'(\bar x;d)\) for every \(d\). For finite convex components this is equivalent to \(\partial h(\bar x)\subseteq\partial g(\bar x)\), which is generally stronger than DC criticality \(\partial g(\bar x)\cap\partial h(\bar x)\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local minimizer of a finite DC function must contain the subtracted component's subdifferential in that of the first component.
assumptions_latex: The functions \(g,h\) are convex and finite near \(\bar x\).
\(f=g-h\), and \(\bar x\) is a local minimizer of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g'(\bar x;d)\ge h'(\bar x;d)\ \forall d\iff\partial h(\bar x)\subseteq\partial g(\bar x).
knowledge_statements.title: DC Directional Stationarity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: DC Criticality Is Not Sufficient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of decomposition-dependent DC criticality as an optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(g(x)=0\), \(h(x)=|x|\), and \(f=g-h=-|x|\), one has \(0\in\partial g(0)-\partial h(0)\). Thus \(0\) is DC-critical, although it is a strict local maximum of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DC criticality can hold at a strict local maximum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\in\partial g(0)-\partial h(0),\quad 0\text{ is not a local minimizer of }f.
knowledge_statements.title: DC Criticality Is Not Sufficient

children.title: Active-Piece Subdifferential Family
children.top_down_role: Active-piece subgradient geometry for extremum and selection constructions.

children.title: Maximum-Type Subdifferentials
children.top_down_role: Active-piece subgradient geometry for pointwise maxima.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)=\partial_C f(x)=\operatorname{co}\{\nabla f_i(x):i\in I(x)\}\).

notation.meaning: Indices attaining the maximum at x.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite maximum of continuously differentiable real-valued pieces.

source_refs.locator: 4.3 Subdifferentials and Regularity p. 170

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I(x)=\{i:f_i(x)=f(x)\}\). The finite maximum is subdifferentially regular at \(x\), and its limiting and Clarke subdifferentials coincide: \[\partial f(x)=\partial_C f(x)=\operatorname{co}\{\nabla f_i(x):i\in I(x)\}.\] Only gradients of active pieces enter the convex-hull representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential of a finite smooth maximum is the convex hull of gradients of the pieces active at the point.
knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Type Subdifferentials

source_witnesses.locator: 4.3 Subdifferentials and Regularity p. 170

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Active-Gradient Stationarity Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order stationarity for a finite smooth maximum and its convex sufficiency boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The condition \(0\in\partial f(\bar x)\) is equivalent to the existence of \(\lambda_i\ge0\), \(i\in I(\bar x)\), with \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\) and \(\sum_i\lambda_i\nabla f_i(\bar x)=0\). It is necessary at a local minimizer and sufficient for global minimality when all pieces are convex. Without convexity it is not sufficient; for example, \(\max\{-x^2,-2x^2\}=-x^2\) is stationary at its strict local maximum \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stationarity of a smooth finite maximum is a convex balance of active gradients; it is sufficient under convexity but not generally.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) is continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\in\partial f(\bar x)\iff\exists\lambda\in\Delta_{I(\bar x)}:\sum_{i\in I(\bar x)}\lambda_i\nabla f_i(\bar x)=0.

notation.meaning: Simplex of weights supported on the active indices.

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Gradient Stationarity Certificate

children.title: Minimum-Type Subdifferentials
children.top_down_role: Active-piece subgradient geometry for pointwise minima.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)\subseteq\{\nabla f_i(x):i\in I(x)\}\), with equality under active-piece attainability.

notation.meaning: Indices attaining the minimum at x.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite minimum of smooth pieces, using the limiting rather than Clarke subdifferential.

source_refs.locator: 4.3 Subdifferentials and Regularity p. 170

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I(x)=\{i:f_i(x)=f(x)\}\). Then every limiting subgradient is an active gradient: \[\partial f(x)\subseteq\{\nabla f_i(x):i\in I(x)\}.\] If, for every \(i\in I(x)\), there are points \(x_k\to x\) at which \(i\) is the unique minimizing index, then \[\partial f(x)=\{\nabla f_i(x):i\in I(x)\}.\] Unlike the maximum rule, no convex hull is generally valid for the limiting subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Limiting subgradients of a smooth finite minimum are active gradients; all active gradients occur when each piece is uniquely active arbitrarily nearby.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Type Subdifferentials

source_witnesses.locator: 4.3 Subdifferentials and Regularity p. 170

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regular Subdifferential of a Smooth Minimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regular-subdifferential boundary for a finite minimum of smooth functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f=\min_i f_i\), the regular subdifferential at \(\bar x\) is nonempty exactly when all active gradients coincide. In that case it is the singleton containing their common value; otherwise it is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth finite minimum has a regular subgradient at a tie exactly when all active gradients agree.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) is continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reachable-Gradient Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite smooth minimum; reachable gradients are limits at nearby differentiability points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G(\bar x)\) be the set of limits of classical gradients \(\nabla f(x_k)\) at differentiability points \(x_k\to\bar x\). Then \(G(\bar x)\subseteq\{\nabla f_i(\bar x):i\in I(\bar x)\}\), \(\partial f(\bar x)=G(\bar x)\), and \(\partial_Cf(\bar x)=\operatorname{co}G(\bar x)\). Thus merely value-matching but locally unrealized pieces need not contribute.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The limiting subdifferential of a smooth finite minimum consists of reachable active gradients, and its Clarke subdifferential is their convex hull.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) is continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f(\bar x)=G(\bar x),\qquad \partial_Cf(\bar x)=\operatorname{co}G(\bar x).

notation.meaning: Limits of gradients at nearby differentiability points.

knowledge_statements.title: Reachable-Gradient Representation

children.title: Selection-Type Subdifferentials
children.top_down_role: Subgradient behavior for functions assembled through local selections.

assumptions_latex: The locally Lipschitz function \(f\) is a continuous selection: \(f(z)\in\{f_1(z),\ldots,f_m(z)\}\) near \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial_C f(x)\subseteq\operatorname{co}\{\nabla f_i(x):i\in I(x)\}\).

notation.meaning: Pieces whose value agrees with the selection at x.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clarke subdifferential containment for a locally Lipschitz continuous finite selection.

source_refs.locator: 4.3 Subdifferentials and Regularity p. 170

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(I(x)=\{i:f_i(x)=f(x)\}\). At every differentiability point \(z\) of \(f\) sufficiently near \(x\), its gradient equals the gradient of a locally selected active piece. Consequently, \[\partial_C f(x)\subseteq\operatorname{co}\{\nabla f_i(x):i\in I(x)\}.\] Equality need not hold because some value-matching pieces may never be selected on a nearby region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke subdifferential of a smooth-piece selection lies in the convex hull of gradients of value-matching pieces, possibly strictly.
knowledge_statements.title: Selection-Type Subdifferentials

source_witnesses.locator: 4.3 Subdifferentials and Regularity p. 170

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Realized-Gradient Clarke Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Locally Lipschitz continuous finite selection of smooth pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G(\bar x)\) be the set of limits of \(\nabla f(x_k)\) at differentiability points \(x_k\to\bar x\). Then \(G(\bar x)\) consists of gradients of locally realized, value-matching pieces and \(\partial_Cf(\bar x)=\operatorname{co}G(\bar x)\). The limiting subdifferential satisfies only \(\partial f(\bar x)\subseteq\operatorname{co}G(\bar x)\) in this general selection class; equality with \(G(\bar x)\) can fail, as the selection \(f(x)=\max\{x,-x\}=|x|\) has \(G(0)=\{-1,1\}\) but \(\partial f(0)=[-1,1]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke subdifferential is the convex hull of gradients realized nearby; general selections need not have limiting subdifferential equal to the unconvexified realized-gradient set.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) is continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
The locally Lipschitz function \(f\) is a continuous local selection from \(\{f_1,\ldots,f_m\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial_Cf(\bar x)=\operatorname{co}G(\bar x),\qquad \partial f(\bar x)\subseteq\operatorname{co}G(\bar x).

notation.meaning: Limits of classical gradients at nearby differentiability points.

knowledge_statements.title: Realized-Gradient Clarke Representation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rejected Unconvexified Limiting Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Builder claim rejected for the general finite-selection class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The proposed identity \(\partial f(\bar x)=G(\bar x)\) under an unspecified “standard finite piecewise-\(C^1\) realization condition” is not valid for the stated class: finite maxima are continuous smooth-piece selections, and \(|x|=\max\{x,-x\}\) has \(G(0)=\{-1,1\}\) while \(\partial |\cdot|(0)=[-1,1]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The limiting subdifferential of a general smooth-piece selection need not equal its set of reachable classical gradients.
assumptions_latex: The class includes arbitrary locally Lipschitz continuous selections of finitely many smooth pieces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f(\bar x)=G(\bar x)\text{ is false in general}.
knowledge_statements.title: Rejected Unconvexified Limiting Representation

intermediate_metadata.reason: The local inventory is the seed containment and the exact Clarke convex hull of realized gradients, together with the sharp failure of an unconvexified limiting formula. Maximum- and minimum-specific identities, transition geometry, and vector generalized Jacobians are excluded as adjacent scopes. The builder's claimed general identity \(\partial f=G\) is deferred as false.

children.title: Active-Piece Transitions

assumptions_latex: For either \(f=\max_i f_i\) or \(f=\min_i f_i\), let \(I(x)=\{i:f_i(x)=f(x)\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x_k\to x\), \(i_k\in I(x_k)\), and a fixed index \(i\) occurs along a subsequence, then continuity gives \(f_i(x)=f(x)\), hence \(i\in I(x)\). Thus \(I\) is outer semicontinuous. Moreover, if \(i\notin I(x)\), then \(i\notin I(z)\) throughout some neighborhood of \(x\). New active pieces may nevertheless appear at a transition point, so active-gradient subdifferential formulas can enlarge discontinuously there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Active indices cannot persist into a limit unless active there, although additional pieces may become active exactly at a transition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Differentiability at an Active Tie
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order differentiability criterion for finite differentiable maxima and minima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f=\max_i f_i\) or \(f=\min_i f_i\), the directional derivative at \(\bar x\) is respectively the maximum or minimum of \(\langle\nabla f_i(\bar x),d\rangle\) over \(i\in I(\bar x)\). Consequently, \(f\) is differentiable at \(\bar x\) if and only if all active gradients coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite differentiable maximum or minimum is differentiable at a tie exactly when all active gradients agree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is differentiable at }\bar x\iff \nabla f_i(\bar x)=\nabla f_j(\bar x)\quad\forall i,j\in I(\bar x).

notation.meaning: Active indices at the reference point.

knowledge_statements.title: Differentiability at an Active Tie

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Active-Piece Transition Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local transition notion for a finite active-index mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \(\bar x\) is an active-piece transition point when every neighborhood of \(\bar x\) contains some \(x\) with \(I(x)\ne I(\bar x)\); equivalently, \(I\) is not locally constant at \(\bar x\). A persistent tie need not be a transition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An active-piece transition is a point where the active-index set is not locally constant.
assumptions_latex: The finite active-index mapping \(I\) is defined near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\) is a transition point if and only if \(I\) is not locally constant there.
knowledge_statements.title: Active-Piece Transition Point

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unique-Activity Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite continuous maximum or minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Finiteness and continuity imply that indices inactive at \(\bar x\) remain inactive on some neighborhood, so \(I(x)\subseteq I(\bar x)\) locally. In particular, if \(I(\bar x)=\{i\}\), then \(I(x)=\{i\}\) throughout a sufficiently small neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: No inactive piece becomes active sufficiently near the reference point, and unique activity is locally stable.
assumptions_latex: The family \(\{f_i\}_{i=1}^m\) is finite and continuous near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists U\ni\bar x\ \forall x\in U:\ I(x)\subseteq I(\bar x);\quad I(\bar x)=\{i\}\Rightarrow I(x)=\{i\}\text{ on a smaller }U.
knowledge_statements.title: Unique-Activity Stability

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional derivative of a local Lipschitz inverse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inverse directional calculus under local bi-Lipschitz invertibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$ be a Lipschitz homeomorphism near $x_0$, with neighborhoods $\mathcal O$ and $\mathcal N$, and let $g=(f|_{\mathcal O})^{-1}$. If $f$ is directionally differentiable at $x\in\mathcal O$, then $g$ is directionally differentiable at $f(x)$. For every $h\in\mathbb{R}^n$, $g'(f(x);h)=v$, where $v$ is the unique vector satisfying $h=f'(x;v)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The local inverse is directionally differentiable at the image of any point where the original locally bi-Lipschitz map is directionally differentiable. Its derivative in direction h is the unique v satisfying f prime at x in direction v equals h.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is a Lipschitz homeomorphism near }x_0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall h\in\mathbb{R}^n,\quad g'(f(x);h)=v,\quad\text{where }v\text{ is uniquely determined by }f'(x;v)=h.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict differentiability of a vector-valued mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines strict differentiability by a uniform two-point linear approximation near the reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mapping F:D\to\mathbb{R}^m is strictly differentiable at \bar x with derivative A if A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m is linear and F(x')=F(x)+A(x'-x)+o(|x'-x|) as x,x'\to\bar x with x'\ne x; equivalently, \frac{F(x')-F(x)-A(x'-x)}{|x'-x|}\to0 as x,x'\to\bar x,\ x'\ne x, with x,x'\in D.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector-valued mapping is strictly differentiable at a reference point when one linear map approximates every nearby two-point increment, with an error that is little-o of the distance between the two points.
assumptions_latex: x,x'\in D,\quad x,x'\to\bar x,\quad x'\ne x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lim_{\substack{x,x'\to\bar x\\x'\ne x}}\frac{F(x')-F(x)-A(x'-x)}{|x'-x|}=0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz homeomorphism near a point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local bi-Lipschitz invertibility for a Euclidean self-map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A map $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$ is a Lipschitz homeomorphism near $x_0$ if there exist open neighborhoods $\mathcal O$ of $x_0$ and $\mathcal N$ of $f(x_0)$ such that $f|_{\mathcal O}:\mathcal O\to\mathcal N$ is bijective and both $f|_{\mathcal O}$ and $(f|_{\mathcal O})^{-1}:\mathcal N\to\mathcal O$ are Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A map is a Lipschitz homeomorphism near a point if it bijectively maps a neighborhood of that point onto a neighborhood of its image and both the restricted map and its inverse are Lipschitz.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional approximations of a set-valued mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-induced admissible, tangent, feasible, and intermediate directional mappings at a graph point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $a:X\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m$ have nonempty values on an open set $X\subset\mathbb R^n$, and let $(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}a$. For $g\in\mathbb R^n$, define
\[\gamma(x,y;g)=\{w:\exists\alpha_0>0,\ y+\alpha w\in a(x+\alpha g)\ \forall\alpha\in(0,\alpha_0)\},\]
\[K(x,y;g)=\{w:\exists\psi_1\in\Psi_m,\psi_2\in\Psi_n,\ y+\alpha w+\psi_1(\alpha)\in a(x+\alpha g+\psi_2(\alpha))\ \forall\alpha>0\},\]
\[\Gamma(x,y;g)=\{w:\exists g_k\to g,\ w_k\to w,\ \alpha_k\downarrow0,\ y+\alpha_kw_k\in a(x+\alpha_kg_k)\},\]
and
\[\widetilde K(x,y;g)=\{w:\exists\psi\in\Psi_m,\ y+\alpha w+\psi(\alpha)\in a(x+\alpha g)\ \forall\alpha>0\}.\]
Here $\Psi_d$ is the class of first-order infinitesimals with values in $\mathbb R^d$. The mappings $\gamma(x,y;\cdot)$, $K(x,y;\cdot)$, and $\Gamma(x,y;\cdot)$ are positively homogeneous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a graph point of a set-valued mapping, four directional approximations are defined using exact rays, first-order perturbations, or convergent graph sequences. The source explicitly states positive homogeneity for the admissible, tangent, and feasible mappings.
assumptions_latex: \Psi_d\text{ is the class of first-order infinitesimals into }\mathbb R^d
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \gamma,\ K,\ \Gamma,\ \widetilde K\text{ are defined as above, and }w\in F(g)\Rightarrow\lambda w\in F(\lambda g)\text{ for }F\in\{\gamma,K,\Gamma\},\ \lambda>0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Distance characterization of the intermediate directional mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Membership in the intermediate approximation characterized by convergence toward scaled displaced images.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}a$ and $g\in\mathbb R^n$. With $\rho(w,\xi)=\inf_{z\in\xi}\|w-z\|$,
\[\widetilde K(x,y;g)=\left\{w:\rho\!\left(w,\frac{a(x+\alpha g)-y}{\alpha}\right)\longrightarrow0\ \text{as }\alpha\downarrow0\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector belongs to the intermediate directional approximation exactly when its distance from the scaled displaced image tends to zero as the scale decreases to zero.
assumptions_latex: \widetilde K\text{ is the intermediate directional mapping defined in the preceding context}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widetilde K(x,y;g)=\left\{w:\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}\rho\!\left(w,\alpha^{-1}(a(x+\alpha g)-y)\right)=0\right\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Derivative and lower-limit representations of the intermediate approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent representations and closedness properties of graph-based directional approximations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For $(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}a$ and $g\in\mathbb R^n$,
\[\widetilde K(x,y;g)=\{w:\rho'_a([x,y],[g,w])=0\}=\liminf_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{a(x+\alpha g)-y}{\alpha}.\]
Consequently, $\widetilde K(x,y;g)$ is closed. Moreover, $\Gamma(x,y;g)$ and $K(x,y;g)$ are closed for every $g$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The intermediate directional approximation is the zero set of the indicated directional distance derivative and the lower set-limit of scaled displaced images. It is closed, and the feasible and tangent directional sets are also closed for every direction.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conic and convex characterizations of positively homogeneous mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization and linearity boundary for set-valued positively homogeneous mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For H:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m, H is positively homogeneous if and only if \operatorname{gph}H is a cone; then H(0) and \operatorname{dom}H are cones. If H is positively homogeneous, it is graph-convex if and only if
H(w_1+w_2)\supset H(w_1)+H(w_2)\quad\forall w_1,w_2\in\mathbb{R}^n.
Moreover, if H is graph-convex, H(0)=\{0\}, and \operatorname{dom}H=\mathbb{R}^n, then there exists A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} such that H(w)=Aw for every w\in\mathbb{R}^n.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive homogeneity is equivalent to the graph being a cone, and it forces both the domain and the value at zero to be cones. Within this class, graph convexity is equivalent to superadditivity of the images. A graph-convex mapping with zero value {0} and full domain must be an ordinary linear mapping.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H\text{ positively homogeneous}\iff\operatorname{gph}H\text{ is a cone};\quad H\text{ graph-convex}\iff \forall w_1,w_2,\ H(w_1+w_2)\supset H(w_1)+H(w_2),\quad [H(0)=\{0\},\operatorname{dom}H=\mathbb{R}^n]\Rightarrow \exists A,\ H(w)=Aw.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positively homogeneous set-valued mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for a general set-valued mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A mapping H:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m is positively homogeneous if
0\in H(0)\quad\text{and}\quad H(\lambda w)=\lambda H(w)\quad\text{for every }w\in\mathbb{R}^n\text{ and }\lambda>0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-valued mapping is positively homogeneous when its value at zero contains zero and scaling an argument by any positive scalar scales the entire image by the same scalar.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\in H(0)\ \text{and}\ \forall w\in\mathbb{R}^n\ \forall\lambda>0,\ H(\lambda w)=\lambda H(w).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sublinear set-valued mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition, geometric characterization, and stated horizon-mapping example.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Graphical derivatives, coderivatives, and regular variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for a set-valued mapping at a graph point, including the single-valued notation convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let S:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m, \bar x\in\operatorname{dom}S, and \bar u\in S(\bar x). For w\in\mathbb{R}^n and y\in\mathbb{R}^m, define
z\in DS(\bar x\mid\bar u)(w)\iff (w,z)\in T_{\operatorname{gph}S}(\bar x,\bar u),
\quad v\in D^*S(\bar x\mid\bar u)(y)\iff (v,-y)\in N_{\operatorname{gph}S}(\bar x,\bar u),
and
z\in\widehat DS(\bar x\mid\bar u)(w)\iff (w,z)\in\widehat T_{\operatorname{gph}S}(\bar x,\bar u),
\quad v\in\widehat D^*S(\bar x\mid\bar u)(y)\iff (v,-y)\in\widehat N_{\operatorname{gph}S}(\bar x,\bar u).
If S(\bar x)=\{\bar u\}, the conditioning \mid\bar u may be suppressed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a graph point (x̄,ū), the graphical derivative and regular graphical derivative are determined by the tangent and regular tangent cones to the graph, while the coderivative and regular coderivative are determined by the corresponding normal cones with the dual direction sign reversed. If S is single-valued at x̄, the value ū may be omitted from the notation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: DS,\widehat DS,D^*S,\widehat D^*S\text{ are defined by the stated tangent- and normal-cone equivalences.}

knowledge_statements.title: Graphical Derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional contingent graphical derivative at a fixed graph point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(h\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the graphical derivative of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is \[DF(\bar x\mid\bar y)(h):=\{k\in\mathbb{R}^m:(h,k)\in T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\}.\] Equivalently, \(k\in DF(\bar x\mid\bar y)(h)\) exactly when there exist \(t_j\downarrow0\) and \((h_j,k_j)\to(h,k)\) such that \(\bar y+t_jk_j\in F(\bar x+t_jh_j)\) for every \(j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The graphical derivative maps an input direction to the output directions that jointly belong to the contingent cone of the mapping's graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(DF(\bar x\mid\bar y)(h)=\{k\in\mathbb{R}^m:(h,k)\in T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Homogeneity Does Not Imply Linearity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute-value mapping at its cusp.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\), \(F(x)=|x|\),
\[
DF(0)(h)=\{|h|\}\qquad(h\in\mathbb R).
\]
Thus \(DF(0)\) is single-valued and positively homogeneous but is not additive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The graphical derivative of absolute value at zero sends a direction to its absolute value and therefore is not linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(DF(0)(h)=\{|h|\}\), and \(DF(0)\) is not additive.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive Homogeneity Does Not Imply Linearity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Conic Graph and Positive Homogeneity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional contingent graphical derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every graph point \((\bar x,\bar y)\),
\[
\operatorname{gph}DF(\bar x\mid\bar y)=T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)
\]
is a closed cone. Consequently, for every \(\lambda>0\),
\[
DF(\bar x\mid\bar y)(\lambda h)=\lambda DF(\bar x\mid\bar y)(h).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graphical derivative has a closed conic graph and is positively homogeneous, although it need not be linear or single-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}DF(\bar x\mid\bar y)\) is a closed cone and \(DF(\bar x\mid\bar y)(\lambda h)=\lambda DF(\bar x\mid\bar y)(h)\) for \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Conic Graph and Positive Homogeneity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Graph and contingent derivative of a set-valued mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the graph and contingent graph-based derivative of a multifunction between real normed spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be real normed spaces and let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\). Then \(\operatorname{graph}(F):=\{(x,y)\in X\times Y\mid y\in F(x)\}\). For \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{graph}(F)\), the set-valued map \(D_cF(\bar x,\bar y):X\rightrightarrows Y\) whose graph satisfies \(\operatorname{graph}(D_cF(\bar x,\bar y))=T(\operatorname{graph}(F),(\bar x,\bar y))\) is called the contingent derivative of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The graph of a multifunction contains exactly the pairs whose second component belongs to the image of the first. Its contingent derivative at a graph point is the multifunction whose graph equals the contingent tangent cone to the original graph at that point.

knowledge_statements.title: Paratingent Graphical Derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional paratingent derivative defined through moving graph base points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Z\) be a finite-dimensional normed space, let \(C\subseteq Z\), and let \(z\in C\). Define
\[
T_C^P(z):=\left\{w\in Z:\exists z_k\to z,\ z_k\in C,\ t_k\downarrow0,\ w_k\to w,\ z_k+t_kw_k\in C\right\}.
\]
For \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\), the paratingent graphical derivative is
\[
D^PF(\bar x\mid\bar y)(h):=\left\{k\in Y:(h,k)\in T^P_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\right\},\qquad h\in X.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{gph}D^{P}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=T^{P}_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The paratingent graphical derivative consists of graph velocities obtained while the scale tends to zero and the graph base point approaches the reference graph point.
assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has locally closed graph near \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}D^{P}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=T^{P}_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\).

T_C^P(z)=-T_C^P(z),\qquad \lambda T_C^P(z)=T_C^P(z)\quad(\lambda>0).

Consequently,
\[
D^PF(\bar x\mid\bar y)(-h)=-D^PF(\bar x\mid\bar y)(h),
\qquad
D^PF(\bar x\mid\bar y)(\lambda h)=\lambda D^PF(\bar x\mid\bar y)(h).
\]

knowledge_statements.title: Tangential-Limit Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison under the standard inner, contingent, and paratingent tangent-cone conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=\operatorname{gph}F\) and \(z=(\bar x,\bar y)\). With
\[
T_C^i(z):=\liminf_{t\downarrow0}\frac{C-z}{t},\qquad T_C(z):=\limsup_{t\downarrow0}\frac{C-z}{t},
\]
and with \(T_C^P(z)\) formed by additionally allowing the base point in \(C\) to approach \(z\), one has
\[
T_C^i(z)\subseteq T_C(z)\subseteq T_C^P(z).
\]
Consequently,
\[
D^iF(\bar x\mid\bar y)(h)\subseteq DF(\bar x\mid\bar y)(h)\subseteq D^PF(\bar x\mid\bar y)(h)
\]
for every \(h\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every inner graph velocity is a contingent graph velocity, and every contingent graph velocity is a paratingent graph velocity.
assumptions_latex: All three graphical derivatives use the same finite-dimensional product-space topology.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}D^{i}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\subseteq\operatorname{gph}DF(\bar x\mid\bar y)\subseteq\operatorname{gph}D^{P}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\).

notation.meaning: Inner, contingent, and paratingent graphical derivatives, respectively.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[
C:=\{0\}\cup\{2^{-n}:n\in\mathbb N\},
\]
every \(v>0\) belongs to \(T_C(0)\): take \(x_n=2^{-n}\) and \(t_n=x_n/v\). Hence \(T_C(0)=[0,\infty)\). In contrast, no \(v>0\) belongs to
\[
T_C^i(0):=\liminf_{t\downarrow0}\frac{C}{t},

\[
T_C^i(0)=\{0\}\subsetneq[0,\infty)=T_C(0).
\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fréchet derivative in normed spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines differentiability by a bounded linear first-order approximation and records its basic consequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X,Y be normed spaces and F:X\to Y. A derivative of F at x is an operator F'(x)\in L_C(X,Y) such that \[\lim_{u\to x,\,u\ne x}\frac{\|F(u)-F(x)-F'(x)(u-x)\|_Y}{\|u-x\|_X}=0.\] If it exists, it is unique; differentiability is invariant under replacing the norms by equivalent norms and implies continuity of F at x.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Fréchet derivative at x is the unique continuous linear operator whose approximation error is little-o of the displacement. Its existence is invariant under equivalent norms and implies continuity at x.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(u)=F(x)+F'(x)(u-x)+o(\|u-x\|_X);\quad F'(x)\text{ is unique, and differentiability at }x\Rightarrow F\text{ is continuous at }x.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First-order approximation of a set-valued mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines sequential first-order approximation in a fixed direction and records the equivalent asymptotic expansion; proof material is omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m be closed, let X\subseteq\operatorname{dom}a be open, and fix x\in X, y\in a(x), a direction g, and a set A_g(y)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m. The mapping a allows a first-order approximation at (x,y) in direction g with respect to A_g(y) if, for every sequence \alpha_k\downarrow0 and every y_k\in a(x+\alpha_k g) with y_k\to y, \rho\!\left((y_k-y)/\alpha_k,A_g(y)\right)\to0. Equivalently, for every such pair of sequences there exist v_k\in A_g(y) such that y_k=y+\alpha_kv_k+o(\alpha_k), with o(\alpha_k)/\alpha_k\to0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed set-valued mapping admits the approximation set A_g(y) at (x,y) in direction g when every scaled value increment along that direction approaches A_g(y). Equivalently, each such increment has a first-order coefficient in A_g(y) and a remainder negligible relative to the step size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall\{\alpha_k\},\{y_k\},\quad \rho\!\left(\frac{y_k-y}{\alpha_k},A_g(y)\right)\to0\iff\exists v_k\in A_g(y):\ y_k=y+\alpha_kv_k+o(\alpha_k),\ \frac{o(\alpha_k)}{\alpha_k}\to0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proto-Derivative Identification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional identification under Painlevé–Kuratowski graphical convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F\) is proto-differentiable at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar y\), then \[\operatorname{gph}F'_{\bar x,\bar y}=T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)=\operatorname{gph}DF(\bar x\mid\bar y).\] Hence the proto-derivative has a closed conic graph and is positively homogeneous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convergent family of graphical difference quotients has the contingent graphical derivative as its common limit.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is proto-differentiable at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) exactly when \(\operatorname{gph}\Delta_tF\) converges as \(t\downarrow0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional graphical-convergence definition for a set-valued mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(t>0\), define the difference-quotient mapping by
\[
\Delta_tF(h):=\frac{F(\bar x+th)-\bar y}{t}.
\]
The mapping \(F\) is proto-differentiable at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar y\) when the graphs \(\operatorname{gph}\Delta_tF\) have a Painleve-Kuratowski limit as \(t\downarrow0\), equivalently when their inner and outer graphical limits coincide. The mapping whose graph is this common limit is the proto-derivative:
\[
\operatorname{gph}F'_{\bar x,\bar y}:=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\operatorname{gph}\Delta_tF.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proto-differentiability means that the graphs of first-order difference-quotient mappings converge to one well-defined limiting graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Proto-Differentiability

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semiderivative and Semidifferentiability of a Set-Valued Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional full limits of set-valued difference quotients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $S:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m$, $\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}S$, and $\bar u\in S(\bar x)$. For $\bar w\in\mathbb{R}^n$, if the graphical set limit $\displaystyle\lim_{\substack{\tau\searrow0\\w\to\bar w}}\frac{S(\bar x+\tau w)-\bar u}{\tau}$ exists, it is the semiderivative of $S$ at $\bar x$ for $\bar u$ and $\bar w$. If this limit exists for every $\bar w\in\mathbb{R}^n$, then $S$ is semidifferentiable at $\bar x$ for $\bar u$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The semiderivative in a direction is the full set limit of the mapping's directional difference quotients as the positive scale tends to zero and the direction approaches the given direction. The mapping is semidifferentiable at the graph point when this limit exists in every direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{semi}DS(\bar x\mid\bar u)(\bar w):=\lim_{\substack{\tau\searrow0\\w\to\bar w}}\frac{S(\bar x+\tau w)-\bar u}{\tau}\quad\text{when the limit exists};\qquad S\text{ is semidifferentiable iff it exists for every }\bar w\in\mathbb{R}^n.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometric Characterization and Inverse Stability of Proto-Differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence with geometric derivability, a sufficient graphical-regularity condition, and invariance under inversion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For $S:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m$ and $\bar u\in S(\bar x)$, $S$ is proto-differentiable at $\bar x$ for $\bar u$ if and only if $\operatorname{gph}S$ is geometrically derivable at $(\bar x,\bar u)$. In particular, graphical regularity of $S$ at $\bar x$ for $\bar u$ implies proto-differentiability there. Whenever $S$ is proto-differentiable at $\bar x$ for $\bar u$, $S^{-1}$ is proto-differentiable at $\bar u$ for $\bar x$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proto-differentiability at a graph point is equivalent to geometric derivability of the graph there. Graphical regularity is sufficient for proto-differentiability, and proto-differentiability is preserved when the mapping is inverted.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(f\) is semidifferentiable at \(\bar x\) if, for every \(h\in X\), there exists \(f'(\bar x;h)\in Y\) such that
\[
\lim_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\h'\to h}}\frac{f(\bar x+th')-f(\bar x)}{t}=f'(\bar x;h).
\]
The perturbation \(h'\to h\) is part of the requirement. The resulting mapping \(h\mapsto f'(\bar x;h)\) is positively homogeneous, although it need not be additive or linear.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semidifferentiability equivalences for a maximal monotone mapping and its resolvent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between semidifferentiability of a maximal monotone mapping, its graphical derivative, and its resolvent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $T:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n$ be maximal monotone, let $\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}T$, $\bar v\in T(\bar x)$, and for $\lambda>0$ set $R_\lambda=(I+\lambda T)^{-1}$ and $\bar z_\lambda=\bar x+\lambda\bar v$. The following are equivalent: (a) $T$ is semidifferentiable at $\bar x$ for $\bar v$; (b) $DT(\bar x\mid\bar v)$ is single-valued; (c) $R_\lambda$ is semidifferentiable at $\bar z_\lambda$ and $DR_\lambda(\bar z_\lambda)$ is bijective. These properties imply that $T$ is continuous at $\bar x$, $T(\bar x)=\{\bar v\}$, $DT(\bar x\mid\bar v)=DT(\bar x)$ is maximal monotone and everywhere continuous, and
\[T(x)\subset T(\bar x)+DT(\bar x)(x-\bar x)+o(\lVert x-\bar x\rVert)\mathbb B.\]
Moreover, the following are equivalent: $T$ is differentiable at $\bar x$; $DT(\bar x\mid\bar v)$ is linear; and $R_\lambda$ is differentiable at $\bar z_\lambda$ with nonsingular Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a maximal monotone mapping, semidifferentiability at a graph point is equivalent both to single-valuedness of its graphical derivative and to semidifferentiability of its resolvent with bijective derivative. The analogous differentiable, linear-derivative, and nonsingular-resolvent conditions are also equivalent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (a)\Longleftrightarrow(b)\Longleftrightarrow(c),\qquad (a')\Longleftrightarrow(b')\Longleftrightarrow(c').

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semidifferentiability from Proto-Differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions connecting proto-differentiability, Lipschitz-like regularity, and semidifferentiability of multifunctions and single-valued mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let S:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m and \bar u\in S(\bar x). If S is proto-differentiable at \bar x for \bar u and has the Aubin property there, then S is semidifferentiable there. In particular, strict continuity together with graphical regularity implies semidifferentiability. If F:D\to\mathbb{R}^m is single-valued, \bar x\in\operatorname{int}D, and F is strictly continuous at \bar x, then F is semidifferentiable at \bar x if and only if it is proto-differentiable there. Calmness at \bar x suffices for this equivalence when DF(\bar x) is single-valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proto-differentiable multifunction with the Aubin property is semidifferentiable; strict continuity and graphical regularity are sufficient. For a single-valued mapping at an interior point, strict continuity makes proto-differentiability equivalent to semidifferentiability, and calmness suffices when the graphical derivative is single-valued.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak and strict-weak bornological differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines scalarized weak differentiability for mappings between Banach spaces and records derivative-existence boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to Y\) map Banach spaces and let \(\beta\) be a bornology on \(X\). It is strictly-weakly \(\beta\)-differentiable at \(\bar x\) if \(\langle y^*,f\rangle\) is strictly \(\beta\)-differentiable there for every \(y^*\in Y^*\). It admits an \(sw\beta\)-derivative \(A\in\mathcal L(X,Y)\) when \(\lim_{x\to\bar x,\,t\downarrow0}\langle y^*,[f(x+tv)-f(x)]/t-Av\rangle=0\) for all \(v\in X\) and \(y^*\in Y^*\), uniformly for \(v\) in each member of \(\beta\). Weak \(\beta\)-differentiability is defined analogously without strictness; its derivative satisfies the same limit with \(x=\bar x\). Such derivatives are unique when they exist, but scalarized differentiability alone need not yield an operator derivative. The gap is absent if \(Y\) is reflexive and \(f\) is Lipschitz at \(\bar x\), or if \(f\) is weakly directionally differentiable there. Weak and norm-based notions agree when \(\dim Y<\infty\), but may differ in infinite dimensions, even for Lipschitz mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak bornological differentiability requires every dual scalarization of the mapping to be bornologically differentiable. A weak derivative is a bounded linear operator realizing the corresponding difference quotients in the weak topology, uniformly over each bornologically bounded direction set; strict-weak differentiability uses nearby base points. Derivatives are unique but need not exist merely from scalarized differentiability. Existence is assured in the stated reflexive-Lipschitz or weakly directionally differentiable cases. Weak and norm notions coincide for finite-dimensional ranges but can differ in infinite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The weak and strict-weak }\beta\text{-differentiability notions and their operator derivatives are as stated, with the specified uniqueness, existence conditions, and finite-dimensional boundary.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz consequences of weak bornological differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes pointwise radial Lipschitz control from full local Lipschitz continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to Y\) map Banach spaces, let \(\bar x\in X\), and let \(\beta\geq\mathcal H\). If \(f\) is \(w\beta\)-differentiable at \(\bar x\), then there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(\ell>0\) such that \(\|f(x)-f(\bar x)\|\leq \ell\|x-\bar x\|\) for every \(x\in U\). If \(f\) is strictly \(w\beta\)-differentiable at \(\bar x\), then \(f\) is Lipschitz continuous on a neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bornology at least as strong as the Hadamard bornology, weak bornological differentiability gives a local Lipschitz estimate relative to the reference value. Strict weak bornological differentiability gives full Lipschitz continuity around the point.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is graphically regular at \(\bar x\) when its graph is normally regular at \((\bar x,F(\bar x))\), namely when
\[
\widehat N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,F(\bar x))=N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,F(\bar x)).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Graphical regularity and weak differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates mixed and normal graphical regularity to weak Fréchet and strict weak Hadamard differentiability, preserving the sequential and Lipschitz conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to Y\), where \(X\) is Asplund and \(Y\) is Banach. If \(f\) is both \(w\mathcal F\)-differentiable and strictly \(w\mathcal H\)-differentiable at \(\bar x\), then \(f\) is \(M\)-regular there. If the sequential convergence condition of Definition 3.25(ii) also holds, then \(f\) is \(N\)-regular there. Conversely, if \(f\) is Lipschitz continuous around \(\bar x\), then \(M\)-regularity—and, in particular, \(N\)-regularity—implies both \(w\mathcal F\)-differentiability and strict \(w\mathcal H\)-differentiability at \(\bar x\).

Under local Lipschitz continuity, mixed regularity, and in particular normal regularity, implies both differentiability properties.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(f\) is strictly differentiable at \(\bar x\) with strict derivative \(A\) if
\[
\lim_{\substack{x,u\to\bar x\\x\ne u}}\frac{\|f(x)-f(u)-A(x-u)\|}{\|x-u\|}=0.
\]
Equivalently, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that
\[
\|f(x)-f(u)-A(x-u)\|\leq\varepsilon\|x-u\|
\]
for all distinct \(x,u\in U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict differentiability uniformly approximates every nearby two-point increment by the same linear map, not merely increments based at the reference point.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}} be finite on an open set O. knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) and
\[
\widehat N_{\operatorname{gph}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))=N_{\operatorname{gph}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x)).

Then there exists a linear mapping \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) such that

\lim_{\substack{x,u\to\bar x\\x\ne u}}\frac{\|f(x)-f(u)-A(x-u)\|}{\|x-u\|}=0.

children.title: Strictness Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Graphically regular regimes that do not yield strict differentiability.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is defined by \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(x)=x^2\sin(1/x)\) for \(x\ne0\).
Differentiability and strict differentiability are considered at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(0)=0\), but \(f\) is not strictly differentiable at \(0\).

notation.meaning: Ordinary derivative of \(f\) at the origin.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordinary differentiability does not imply strict differentiability, even under local Lipschitz continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
f(x):=\begin{cases}x^2\sin(1/x),&x\ne0,\\0,&x=0.\end{cases}
\]
Then \(f\) is locally Lipschitz and differentiable at \(0\), with \(f'(0)=0\), because \(f(x)/x\to0\). For \(x\ne0\),
\[
f'(x)=2x\sin(1/x)-\cos(1/x),
\]
which does not converge to \(0\) as \(x\to0\). Suitable nearby pairs therefore have difference quotients bounded away from \(0\), so
\[
\lim_{\substack{x,u\to0\\x\ne u}}\frac{|f(x)-f(u)|}{|x-u|}\ne0.
\]
Hence differentiability at the point does not ensure strict differentiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Lipschitz function may have a derivative at the reference point while nearby secant slopes continue to oscillate, preventing strict differentiability.
knowledge_statements.title: Strictness Failure Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example correctly targets the failure of strict differentiability and the failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but it has no citation and includes proof text. A sourced, proof-free candidate is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional Generalized-Jacobian Chain Rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional-image chain rule for a composition of locally Lipschitz vector mappings, with equality for a continuously differentiable outer mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m be Lipschitz near x and let G:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^k be Lipschitz near F(x). Then, for every v\in\mathbb{R}^n,
\[
\partial(G\circ F)(x)v\subset\operatorname{co}\{BAv:B\in\partial G(F(x)),\ A\in\partial F(x)\}.
\]
If G is continuously differentiable near F(x), then equality holds and convexification is unnecessary:
\[
\partial(G\circ F)(x)v=JG(F(x))\,\partial F(x)v.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In every direction, the generalized-Jacobian image of a composition is contained in the convex hull of products of outer and inner generalized Jacobians. A continuously differentiable outer mapping gives equality without convexification.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is continuously differentiable near }F(x)\quad\text{for the equality case}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial(G\circ F)(x)v\subset\operatorname{co}\{BAv:B\in\partial G(F(x)),\ A\in\partial F(x)\};\qquad G\in C^1\text{ near }F(x)\Rightarrow\partial(G\circ F)(x)v=JG(F(x))\partial F(x)v

children.title: Differentiability-Point Foundations
children.top_down_role: Almost-everywhere differentiability and limiting-Jacobian foundations for matrix-valued generalized derivatives.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is locally Lipschitz on an open set \(U\).
\(D_f\subset U\) denotes the set of classical differentiability points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U\setminus D_f\) has Lebesgue measure zero, so limiting-Jacobian constructions may use sequences from \(D_f\).

notation.meaning: Set of points where \(f\) is classically differentiable.
Classical Jacobian at a differentiability point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Rademacher foundation for limiting matrix derivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
By Rademacher's theorem, a locally Lipschitz mapping \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is classically differentiable at almost every point of \(U\); equivalently,
\[
\mathcal L^n(U\setminus D_f)=0.
\]
In particular, every nonempty open neighborhood contained in \(U\) meets \(D_f\). Since local Lipschitz continuity also bounds \(\|Jf(x)\|\) at almost every differentiability point by a local Lipschitz modulus, sequences of Jacobians along differentiability points approaching a reference point admit convergent subsequences whenever their base points remain in a compact neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local Lipschitz continuity gives differentiability almost everywhere and locally bounded classical Jacobians, supplying the sequences used by limiting generalized Jacobians.
knowledge_statements.title: Differentiability-Point Foundations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Rademacher claim and its local Jacobian-boundedness consequence are standard and the theorem kind fits, but no source or locator is supplied for either nontrivial assertion.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical example showing that a Bouligand Jacobian need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=|x|\), the ordinary derivative equals \(-1\) for \(x<0\) and \(1\) for \(x>0\). Therefore \[\partial_B f(0)=\{-1,1\},\] so a Bouligand Jacobian need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the kink of the absolute-value function, the Bouligand Jacobian consists of the two one-sided derivatives and is nonconvex.

Unlike the Clarke generalized Jacobian, this definition does not take a convex hull.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
\(D_f\) is the set of classical differentiability points of \(f\).

notation.meaning: Bouligand, or limiting, Jacobian of \(f\) at \(\bar x\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional limiting-Jacobian definition for locally Lipschitz mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D_f\) be the set where \(f\) is classically differentiable. The Bouligand Jacobian of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) is
\[
\partial_Bf(\bar x):=\left\{A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}:\exists x_k\in D_f,\ x_k\to\bar x,\ Jf(x_k)\to A\right\}.
\]
Thus only actual Jacobian matrices at nearby differentiability points are selected, and no convexification is performed. Local Lipschitz continuity and almost-everywhere differentiability ensure that this set is nonempty and compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Bouligand Jacobian collects every matrix limit of ordinary Jacobians evaluated at differentiability points approaching the reference point.
knowledge_statements.title: Bouligand Jacobian

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The limiting-Jacobian definition and compactness claim are standard in finite dimensions, but no source confirms the notation, convention, or stated nonemptiness and compactness.

children.title: Clarke Generalized Jacobian
children.top_down_role: Convexified matrix derivative for locally Lipschitz mappings.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Boundedness and Outer Semicontinuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional locally Lipschitz mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\), then \(\partial_CF\) is locally bounded and outer semicontinuous at \(\bar x\): if \(x_k\to\bar x\), \(A_k\in\partial_CF(x_k)\), and \(A_k\to A\), then \(A\in\partial_CF(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nearby Clarke generalized Jacobians are uniformly bounded, and limits of their matrices remain in the generalized Jacobian at the limiting point.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is locally Lipschitz on a neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Limsup}_{x\to\bar x}\partial_CF(x)\subseteq\partial_CF(\bar x)\), and \(\partial_CF\) is locally bounded near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.title: Local Boundedness and Outer Semicontinuity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Singleton Characterization of Strict Differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical-consistency characterization for finite-dimensional locally Lipschitz mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A locally Lipschitz mapping \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is strictly differentiable at \(\bar x\) with strict derivative \(A\) if and only if
\[
\partial_CF(\bar x)=\{A\}.
\]
In particular, if \(F\) is \(C^1\) near \(\bar x\), then \(\partial_CF(\bar x)=\{JF(\bar x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke generalized Jacobian is a singleton exactly in the strictly differentiable regime; continuously differentiable mappings reduce to their ordinary Jacobian.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is strictly differentiable at }\bar x\text{ with derivative }A\iff\partial_CF(\bar x)=\{A\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Singleton Characterization of Strict Differentiability

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke Generalized Mean-Value Inclusion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional vector-valued mean-value theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \([x,y]\) lies in an open set on which \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is locally Lipschitz, then
\[
F(y)-F(x)\in\operatorname{co}\{A(y-x):z\in[x,y],\ A\in\partial_CF(z)\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Lipschitz increment is a convex combination of generalized-Jacobian actions encountered along the joining segment.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is locally Lipschitz on an open neighborhood of \([x,y]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(y)-F(x)\in\operatorname{co}\{A(y-x):z\in[x,y],\ A\in\partial_CF(z)\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Clarke Generalized Mean-Value Inclusion

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke Jacobian Chain Inclusion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition of finite-dimensional locally Lipschitz mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) and \(G:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^m\) is locally Lipschitz near \(F(\bar x)\), then
\[
\partial_C(G\circ F)(\bar x)\subseteq
\operatorname{co}\{BA:A\in\partial_CF(\bar x),\ B\in\partial_CG(F(\bar x))\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clarke Jacobians of a Lipschitz composition lie in the convex hull of compatible products of outer and inner Clarke matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial_C(G\circ F)(\bar x)\subseteq\operatorname{co}\{BA:A\in\partial_CF(\bar x),\ B\in\partial_CG(F(\bar x))\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Clarke Jacobian Chain Inclusion

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial_Cf(\bar x)=\operatorname{co}\partial_Bf(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Clarke generalized Jacobian of \(f\) at \(\bar x\).
Convex hull in the finite-dimensional matrix space.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Clarke convexification of limiting classical Jacobians.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Clarke generalized Jacobian of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) is the convex hull of its Bouligand Jacobian:
\[
\partial_Cf(\bar x):=\operatorname{co}\partial_Bf(\bar x)
=\operatorname{co}\left\{\lim_{k\to\infty}Jf(x_k):x_k\in D_f,\ x_k\to\bar x\right\}.
\]
Because \(f\) is locally Lipschitz and the matrix space is finite-dimensional, \(\partial_Cf(\bar x)\) is a nonempty compact convex subset of \(\mathbb R^{m\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke generalized Jacobian is the compact convex hull of all limiting ordinary Jacobians obtained near the reference point.
knowledge_statements.title: Clarke Generalized Jacobian

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The convexified limiting-Jacobian definition is standard and definition is the correct kind, but no authoritative source confirms the convention or the accompanying nonempty compact convex conclusion.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke generalized Jacobian and its basic properties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and basic finite-dimensional properties for locally Lipschitz mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be locally Lipschitz, let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^m\), let \(E_F\) be the set where \(F\) is not differentiable, and let \(E\subset\mathbb{R}^m\) be any measure-zero set. Then
\[
\partial F(x)=\operatorname{co}\left\{\lim_{i\to\infty}DF(x_i):x_i\to x,\ x_i\notin E\cup E_F\right\}.
\]
The set \(\partial F(x)\) is nonempty and convex and, as a subset of \(\mathbb{R}^{nm}\), compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a locally Lipschitz mapping from R^m to R^n, the Clarke generalized Jacobian at x is the convex hull of limiting Jacobian matrices obtained at differentiability points approaching x, after excluding any measure-zero set. It is nonempty, convex, and compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial F(x)=\operatorname{co}\left\{\lim_{i\to\infty}DF(x_i):x_i\to x,\ x_i\notin E\cup E_F\right\}\text{ is nonempty, convex, and compact in }\mathbb{R}^{nm}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized-Jacobian Mean Value Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-increment inclusion for a Lipschitz vector mapping on an open convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let U\subset\mathbb{R}^n be open and convex, let F:U\to\mathbb{R}^m be Lipschitz on U, and let x,y\in U. Then
\[
F(y)-F(x)\in\operatorname{co}\bigl(\partial F([x,y])\bigr)(y-x),
\]
where \partial F([x,y])=\bigcup_{z\in[x,y]}\partial F(z).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a Lipschitz vector mapping on an open convex set, its increment belongs to the image of the displacement under the convex hull of generalized Jacobians encountered along the connecting segment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(y)-F(x)\in\operatorname{co}\bigl(\partial F([x,y])\bigr)(y-x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke inverse function theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local two-sided Lipschitz invertibility under generalized-Jacobian nonsingularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be open, let \(F:X\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be locally Lipschitz, and let \(x_0\in X\). Suppose every operator in \(\partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}F(x_0)\) is invertible, and set \(y_0=F(x_0)\). Then there exist \(\eta,\delta>0\) and a Lipschitz mapping \(F^{-1}:\operatorname{int}\mathcal B_\eta(y_0)\to\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \(F(F^{-1}(y))=y\) for every \(y\in\operatorname{int}\mathcal B_\eta(y_0)\), and \(F^{-1}(F(x))=x\) for every \(x\in\operatorname{int}\mathcal B_\delta(x_0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a locally Lipschitz map from an open subset of Rⁿ to Rⁿ has only invertible operators in its Clarke generalized Jacobian at x₀, then it has a Lipschitz local inverse near F(x₀), and the two maps are mutual inverses on suitable neighborhoods.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\eta,\delta>0\ \exists F^{-1}\text{ Lipschitz on }\operatorname{int}\mathcal B_\eta(y_0):\quad F(F^{-1}(y))=y\ \forall y\in\operatorname{int}\mathcal B_\eta(y_0),\quad F^{-1}(F(x))=x\ \forall x\in\operatorname{int}\mathcal B_\delta(x_0).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform separation induced by a nonsingular Clarke generalized Jacobian
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A local uniform-separation property used in the nonsmooth inverse-function theory for locally Lipschitz mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be open and let \(F:X\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be locally Lipschitz. If \(x_0\in X\) and every operator in \(\partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}F(x_0)\) is invertible, then there exist \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(\delta>0\) such that, for every \(g\in\mathbb{R}^n\), there is a unit vector \(\ell\) satisfying \(\langle\ell,v\rangle\geq\varepsilon\lVert g\rVert\) whenever \(x\in\mathcal B_\delta(x_0)\) and \(v\in a_{\partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}F(x)}(g)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a locally Lipschitz map whose Clarke generalized Jacobian at x₀ consists entirely of invertible operators, there are positive uniform constants ε and δ such that every vector g admits a unit direction ℓ having inner product at least ε times the norm of g with every admissible v in a_{∂Cl F(x)}(g), uniformly for x in the δ-ball about x₀.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\varepsilon,\delta>0\;\forall g\in\mathbb{R}^n\;\exists\ell\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ \lVert\ell\rVert=1:\ \forall x\in\mathcal B_\delta(x_0)\;\forall v\in a_{\partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}F(x)}(g),\quad \langle\ell,v\rangle\geq\varepsilon\lVert g\rVert.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke Chain Rule for a Scalar Outer Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized-gradient chain rule for a locally Lipschitz scalar composition, including the strict-differentiability equality case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m be Lipschitz near x, let g:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R} be Lipschitz near F(x), and set f=g\circ F. Then f is Lipschitz near x and
\[
\partial f(x)\subset\operatorname{co}\{\eta A:\eta\in\partial g(F(x)),\ A\in\partial F(x)\}.
\]
If g is strictly differentiable at F(x), then equality holds and convexification is unnecessary:
\[
\partial f(x)=\nabla g(F(x))\,\partial F(x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The generalized gradient of a Lipschitz scalar composition is contained in the convex hull of products of outer generalized gradients and inner generalized Jacobians. Strict differentiability of the outer function gives equality without convexification.
assumptions_latex: g\text{ is strictly differentiable at }F(x)\quad\text{for the equality case}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is Lipschitz near }x,\quad \partial f(x)\subset\operatorname{co}\{\partial g(F(x))\partial F(x)\};\qquad g\text{ strictly differentiable at }F(x)\Rightarrow\partial f(x)=\nabla g(F(x))\partial F(x)
