knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke Generalized-Jacobian Local Surjectivity Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative local solvability for square locally Lipschitz mappings under pointwise nonsingularity of the Clarke generalized Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n be Lipschitz near x, and suppose that every A\in\partial F(x) is nonsingular. Then there exist a constant m and neighborhoods Y of x and Q of 0 such that, for every q\in Q, there exists y\in Y satisfying F(y)=F(x)-q and \lvert y-x\rvert\le m\lvert q\rvert.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a square mapping is locally Lipschitz and every matrix in its Clarke generalized Jacobian at x is nonsingular, then every sufficiently small output perturbation has a nearby preimage, with displacement bounded linearly by the perturbation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists m,\ \exists Y\ni x,\ \exists Q\ni0,\ \forall q\in Q,\ \exists y\in Y:\ F(y)=F(x)-q\ \wedge\ \lvert y-x\rvert\le m\lvert q\rvert.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic Properties of the Clarke Generalized Jacobian
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued regularity, boundedness, and componentwise properties of the generalized Jacobian of a locally Lipschitz mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F=(f^1,\ldots,f^m):\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m be locally Lipschitz near x. Then: (a) \partial F(x) is a nonempty compact convex subset of \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}; (b) its graph is closed at x: if x_i\to x, Z_i\in\partial F(x_i), and Z_i\to Z, then Z\in\partial F(x); (c) it is upper semicontinuous at x: for every \varepsilon>0 there exists \delta>0 such that y\in x+\delta B implies \partial F(y)\subset\partial F(x)+\varepsilon B_{m\times n}; (d) if f^i has local Lipschitz rank K_i at x and K=\|(K_1,\ldots,K_m)\|_2, then F has rank K and \partial F(x)\subset K\overline B_{m\times n}; and (e) \partial F(x)\subset\partial f^1(x)\times\cdots\times\partial f^m(x), with equality \partial F(x)=\partial f^1(x) when m=1.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke generalized Jacobian is nonempty, compact, convex, graph-closed, and upper semicontinuous. Component Lipschitz bounds give a matrix-norm bound; every row lies in the corresponding component generalized gradient, and for a scalar-valued map the generalized Jacobian equals the generalized gradient.
assumptions_latex: K_i\text{ is a local Lipschitz rank of }f^i\text{ at }x\quad\text{for part (d)}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial F(x)\neq\varnothing\text{ is compact and convex, is graph-closed and upper semicontinuous at }x,\quad \partial F(x)\subset K\overline B_{m\times n},\quad \partial F(x)\subset\prod_{i=1}^m\partial f^i(x),\quad m=1\Rightarrow\partial F(x)=\partial f^1(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized Jacobian and Newton approximation of the Fischer–Burmeister KKT residual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The Fischer–Burmeister residual associated with a KKT formulation of a variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For $(x,\mu,\lambda)\in\mathbb R^{n+\ell+m}$, \(\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(x,\mu,\lambda)\subseteq\mathcal A(x,\mu,\lambda)\), where \(\mathcal A(x,\mu,\lambda)\) comprises the block matrices
\[\begin{bmatrix}J_x\mathbf L(x,\mu,\lambda)&Jh(x)^T&Jg(x)^T\\-Jh(x)&0&0\\-D_g(x,\lambda)Jg(x)&0&D_\lambda(x,\lambda)\end{bmatrix}.\]
Here \(D_\lambda=\operatorname{diag}(a_1,\ldots,a_m)\), \(D_g=\operatorname{diag}(b_1,\ldots,b_m)\), and
\[(a_i,b_i)=\frac{(\lambda_i,-g_i(x))}{\sqrt{g_i(x)^2+\lambda_i^2}}-(1,1)\quad\text{if }(g_i(x),\lambda_i)\ne(0,0),\]
while \((a_i,b_i)\in\operatorname{cl}\mathbb B(0,1)-(1,1)\) when \((g_i(x),\lambda_i)=(0,0)\). Moreover, \(\mathcal A\) is a linear Newton approximation of \(\Phi_{\mathrm{FB}}\) at the triple, and it is strong if \(JF\), every \(\nabla^2g_i\), and every \(\nabla^2h_j\) are locally Lipschitz continuous at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The generalized Jacobian of the Fischer–Burmeister KKT residual is contained in an explicit block-matrix family. This family is a linear Newton approximation and is strong under the stated local Lipschitz conditions on the relevant derivatives.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial\Phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(x,\mu,\lambda)\subseteq\mathcal A(x,\mu,\lambda),\quad \mathcal A\text{ is a linear Newton approximation and is strong under the stated local Lipschitz assumptions.}

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal J_{\mathrm{PS}}F(\bar x)\) is the family of Jacobians of the active smooth selections; under the stated derivative-realizability conditions, it equals \(\partial_BF(\bar x)\), and its convex hull equals \(\partial_CF(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional continuous piecewise-\(C^1\) selection model; the generalized-Jacobian identities require explicit realization by classical derivatives.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
I(\bar x):=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,p\}:F(\bar x)=F_i(\bar x)\},\qquad
\mathcal J_{\mathrm{PS}}F(\bar x):=\{\nabla F_i(\bar x):i\in I(\bar x)\}.
\]
This is the piecewise-smooth Jacobian model at \(\bar x\). Suppose additionally that, at every differentiability point \(z\) of \(F\) sufficiently near \(\bar x\), one has \(DF(z)=\nabla F_i(z)\) for some \(i\in I(z)\), and that for every \(i\in I(\bar x)\) there are differentiability points \(z_k\to\bar x\) satisfying \(DF(z_k)=\nabla F_i(z_k)\). Then
\[
\partial_BF(\bar x)=\mathcal J_{\mathrm{PS}}F(\bar x),
\qquad
\partial_CF(\bar x)=\operatorname{co}\mathcal J_{\mathrm{PS}}F(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The piecewise-smooth Jacobian model collects the Jacobians of active smooth selections. If classical derivatives near the base point come from active selections and every active-selection Jacobian is realized by such derivatives, the model is the Bouligand Jacobian and its convex hull is the Clarke Jacobian.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Active Pieces Need Not Be Realized
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of equality with the Bouligand Jacobian when an incident smooth piece is never selected nearby.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x)\equiv0\), \(F_1(x)\equiv0\), and \(F_2(x)=x\). Then \(F(x)\in\{F_1(x),F_2(x)\}\) and
\[
I(0)=\{1,2\},\qquad \mathcal J_{\mathrm{PS}}F(0)=\{0,1\},
\]
but
\[
\partial_BF(0)=\{0\}.
\]
Thus an active-selection family can strictly overestimate the Bouligand Jacobian unless active derivatives are realized along differentiability points of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth piece that merely meets the selected mapping at the reference point can add a spurious active Jacobian if that piece is never selected nearby.
assumptions_latex: \(F,F_1,F_2:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) are defined by \(F=F_1=0\) and \(F_2(x)=x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial_BF(0)=\{0\}\subsetneq\{0,1\}=\mathcal J_{\mathrm{PS}}F(0)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Active Pieces Need Not Be Realized

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Stability of Active Selections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite continuous selections from finitely many continuous smooth pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
With \(I(x):=\{i:F(x)=F_i(x)\}\), for every \(\bar x\) there is a neighborhood \(V\) such that
\[
I(x)\subseteq I(\bar x)\qquad(x\in V).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Only pieces active at the reference point can remain active arbitrarily nearby.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I(x)\subseteq I(\bar x)\) for all \(x\) sufficiently near \(\bar x\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is semismooth at \(\bar x\) if it is directionally differentiable there and
\[
\lim_{\substack{h\to0\\h\ne0}}\ \sup_{V\in\partial_C F(\bar x+h)}
\frac{\|F(\bar x+h)-F(\bar x)-Vh\|}{\|h\|}=0.
\]
Equivalently, for every sequence \(h_k\to0\) with \(h_k\ne0\) and every choice \(V_k\in\partial_C F(\bar x+h_k)\), one has \(F(\bar x+h_k)-F(\bar x)-V_kh_k=o(\|h_k\|)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Lipschitz, directionally differentiable mapping is semismooth when every nearby Clarke-Jacobian linearization has error smaller than first order.

children.title: Strong Semismoothness
children.top_down_role: Strengthened semismooth approximation behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generalized-Jacobian linearization error is \(O(\|h\|^2)\).

source_refs.locator: 7.2.1 Piecewise smooth functions p. 656

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is strongly semismooth at \(\bar x\) if it is directionally differentiable there and there exist \(c\ge0\) and \(\delta>0\) such that, for every \(h\) with \(0<\|h\|<\delta\) and every \(V\in\partial_C F(\bar x+h)\),
\[
\|F(\bar x+h)-F(\bar x)-Vh\|\le c\|h\|^2.
\]
Thus strong semismoothness implies semismoothness at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong semismoothness requires all nearby generalized-Jacobian linearizations to have uniformly quadratic error, and therefore implies ordinary semismoothness.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Semismoothness

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mapping \(F\) is strongly semismooth at \(\bar x\); in particular, every continuous piecewise-affine mapping is strongly semismooth.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If locally \(F(x)\in\{F_1(x),\ldots,F_N(x)\}\) for finitely many \(C^1\) selections with locally Lipschitz Jacobians, then \(F\) is strongly semismooth at \(\bar x\). Continuous piecewise-affine mappings form a special case.

children.title: Semismoothness Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Mapping irregularities that invalidate semismooth local models.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is defined by \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(t)=t^2\sin(1/t)\) for \(t\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mapping \(f\) is locally Lipschitz and directionally differentiable at \(0\), but is not semismooth there.

notation.meaning: Clarke generalized Jacobian of the scalar mapping

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar counterexample showing that local Lipschitz continuity and directional differentiability do not imply semismoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(t)=t^2\sin(1/t)\) when \(t\ne0\), one has \(f'(0;d)=0\) for every \(d\), but the residuals \(f(t)-f(0)-Vt\), with \(V\in\partial_Cf(t)\), are not \(o(|t|)\) uniformly as \(t\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The function t squared times sin(1/t) is locally Lipschitz and directionally differentiable at zero, yet its nearby generalized-Jacobian models retain a first-order oscillatory error.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional Differentiability Is Not Sufficient
knowledge_statements.title: Directional Differentiability Is Not Sufficient

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Lipschitz Continuity Does Not Ensure Directional Differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A distinct oscillatory failure mechanism in which a locally Lipschitz scalar mapping lacks the directional derivative required for semismoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(h(0)=0\) and, for \(t\ne0\),
\[
h(t)=\int_0^t \sin\!\left(\log\frac1{|s|}\right)\,ds.
\]
Then \(h\) is locally Lipschitz, while the quotient \(h(t)/t\) has no limit as \(t\downarrow0\). Consequently \(h'(0;1)\) does not exist and \(h\) is not semismooth at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integral of a bounded logarithmically oscillating function is locally Lipschitz but has no directional derivative at zero, so it cannot be semismooth there.
assumptions_latex: \(h:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is defined by \(h(0)=0\) and \(h(t)=\int_0^t\sin(\log(1/|s|))\,ds\) for \(t\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h\) is locally Lipschitz at \(0\), but \(h'(0;1)\) does not exist; hence \(h\) is not semismooth at \(0\).

notation.meaning: One-sided directional derivative of h at zero in direction one

knowledge_statements.title: Local Lipschitz Continuity Does Not Ensure Directional Differentiability

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is defined by \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(t)=t\sin(\log|t|)\) for \(t\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local Lipschitz continuity alone does not ensure semismoothness.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by persistent directional oscillation at the base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is locally Lipschitz at \(0\): away from \(0\), its derivative is \(f'(t)=\sin(\log|t|)+\cos(\log|t|)\), which is bounded. Nevertheless,
\[
\frac{f(t)-f(0)}{t}=\sin(\log|t|)
\]
has no limit as \(t\downarrow0\). Hence the directional derivative \(f'(0;1)\) does not exist, so \(f\) is not semismooth at \(0\). This identifies directional differentiability as a genuine boundary not supplied by local Lipschitz continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The locally Lipschitz function t sin(log|t|) oscillates too strongly to possess a directional derivative at zero and hence is not semismooth there.
knowledge_statements.title: Semismoothness Failure Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact coderivative pullback under a surjective derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact regular, normal, and mixed coderivative formulas, together with regularity equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g:X\to Y\), \(F:Y\rightrightarrows Z\), and \(\bar z\in(F\circ g)(\bar x)\). If \(g\) is strictly differentiable at \(\bar x\) and \(\nabla g(\bar x)\) is surjective, then
\[
\widehat D^{*}(F\circ g)(\bar x,\bar z)=\nabla g(\bar x)^{*}\widehat D^{*}F(g(\bar x),\bar z),
\]
and, for \(D^{*}\in\{D_N^{*},D_M^{*}\}\),
\[
D^{*}(F\circ g)(\bar x,\bar z)=\nabla g(\bar x)^{*}D^{*}F(g(\bar x),\bar z).
\]
Moreover, \(F\circ g\) is \(N\)-regular, respectively \(M\)-regular, at \((\bar x,\bar z)\) if and only if \(F\) has the corresponding property at \((g(\bar x),\bar z)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly differentiable inner mapping with a surjective derivative yields exact pullback formulas for regular, normal, and mixed coderivatives. Normal or mixed regularity of the composition is equivalent to the corresponding regularity of the outer multifunction at the image point.
assumptions_latex: g:X\to Y,\quad F:Y\rightrightarrows Z,\quad \bar z\in(F\circ g)(\bar x)
g\text{ is strictly differentiable at }\bar x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat D^{*}(F\circ g)=\nabla g(\bar x)^{*}\widehat D^{*}F,\quad D^{*}(F\circ g)=\nabla g(\bar x)^{*}D^{*}F\text{ for }D^{*}\in\{D_N^{*},D_M^{*}\},\quad (F\circ g)\text{ is }N/M\text{-regular}\iff F\text{ is correspondingly regular.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has locally closed graph near \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)\) is obtained by slicing the regular normal cone to \(\operatorname{gph}F\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(y^*\in Y\), the regular coderivative of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is the set-valued mapping
\[
\widehat D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*):=\{x^*\in X:(x^*,-y^*)\in\widehat N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\}.
\]
The minus sign in the output-dual component is part of the coderivative convention. If \((\bar x,\bar y)\notin\operatorname{gph}F\), the regular coderivative is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regular coderivative consists of input covectors whose pairing with the negative output covector is a regular normal to the mapping's graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Regular Coderivative

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact coderivative sum rules under a smooth perturbation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality formulas for regular, normal, and mixed coderivatives, with invariance of N- and M-regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f:X\to Y$ be Fréchet differentiable at $\bar x$, let $F:X\rightrightarrows Y$, and suppose $\bar y-f(\bar x)\in F(\bar x)$. Then for every $y^*\in Y^*$, $$\widehat D^*(f+F)(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)=\nabla f(\bar x)^*y^*+\widehat D^*F(\bar x,\bar y-f(\bar x))(y^*).$$ If $f$ is strictly differentiable at $\bar x$, then for $D^*$ equal to either the normal or mixed coderivative, $$D^*(f+F)(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)=\nabla f(\bar x)^*y^*+D^*F(\bar x,\bar y-f(\bar x))(y^*)$$ for every $y^*\in Y^*$. Moreover, $f+F$ is $N$-regular, respectively $M$-regular, at $(\bar x,\bar y)$ if and only if $F$ has the corresponding regularity at $(\bar x,\bar y-f(\bar x))$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a Fréchet-smooth single-valued mapping to a multifunction shifts its regular coderivative exactly by the adjoint derivative. Under strict differentiability the same equality holds for normal and mixed coderivatives, and N- or M-regularity is preserved in both directions.
assumptions_latex: f:X\to Y\text{ is Fréchet differentiable at }\bar x
\text{For the normal and mixed formulas, }f\text{ is strictly differentiable at }\bar x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat D^*(f+F)=\nabla f(\bar x)^*+\widehat D^*F;\quad D^*(f+F)=\nabla f(\bar x)^*+D^*F\text{ for normal or mixed }D^*;\quad N\text{- and }M\text{-regularity are preserved equivalently}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(y^*\in Y\), the limiting coderivative of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is
\[
D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*):=\{x^*\in X:(x^*,-y^*)\in N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\}.
\]
Here \(N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\) is the outer limit of regular graph normals at nearby graph points. Consequently, \(\widehat D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\subset D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The limiting coderivative slices the limiting normal cone to the graph and contains the corresponding regular coderivative values.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Limiting Coderivative and Smooth Single-Valued Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limiting coderivative defined by normal geometry of a locally closed graph, with its positive homogeneity and smooth reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\), let \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\), and suppose \(\operatorname{gph}F\) is locally closed around \((\bar x,\bar y)\). Define
\[D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(w):=\left\{v\in\mathbb R^n:(v,-w)\in N\big((\bar x,\bar y);\operatorname{gph}F\big)\right\},\qquad w\in\mathbb R^m.\]
This is a positively homogeneous mapping from \(\mathbb R^m\) to subsets of \(\mathbb R^n\). If \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is smooth around \(\bar x\) and \(\bar y=F(\bar x)\), then
\[D^*F(\bar x)(w)=\{\nabla F(\bar x)^*w\}\qquad\forall w\in\mathbb R^m.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The limiting coderivative is obtained by taking signed slices of the limiting normal cone to a mapping's graph. It is positively homogeneous and reduces to the adjoint Jacobian for a smooth single-valued mapping.
assumptions_latex: \operatorname{gph}F\text{ is locally closed around }(\bar x,\bar y)
F\text{ is single-valued and smooth around }\bar x\text{ for the Jacobian reduction}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(w)=\{v:(v,-w)\in N((\bar x,\bar y);\operatorname{gph}F)\},\qquad D^*F(\bar x)(w)=\{\nabla F(\bar x)^*w\}\text{ in the smooth single-valued case}

children.top_down_role: Convexified coderivative regime.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has locally closed graph near \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_C^*F(\bar x,\bar y)\) uses the closed convex hull of limiting graph normals.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convexified-normal coderivative.

source_refs.locator: B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the Clarke normal cone by
\[
N_C^C(\bar x,\bar y):=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}N_C(\bar x,\bar y),
\]
where \(C:=\operatorname{gph}F\). For \(y^*\in Y\), the Clarke coderivative is
\[
D_C^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*):=\{x^*\in X:(x^*,-y^*)\in N_{
\operatorname{gph}F}^C(\bar x,\bar y)\}.
\]
Thus it convexifies graph-normal directions before taking the coderivative slice; it need not equal the pointwise convex hull of \(D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke coderivative slices the closed convex hull of limiting normals to the graph; convexification occurs before fixing the output covector.
knowledge_statements.title: Clarke Coderivative

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Graphical N-Regularity and M-Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the normal-regularity equivalence, the implication between the two notions, and its failure to reverse generally.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F:X\rightrightarrows Y and (\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F. The mapping F is N\text{-regular at }(\bar x,\bar y) iff D_N^*F(\bar x,\bar y)=\widehat D^*F(\bar x,\bar y), and it is M\text{-regular there} iff D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)=\widehat D^*F(\bar x,\bar y). N\text{-regularity is equivalent to normal regularity of }\operatorname{gph}F\text{ at }(\bar x,\bar y), and N\text{-regularity}\Rightarrow M\text{-regularity}; the converse need not hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifunction is graphically N-regular when its normal and Fréchet coderivatives agree, and graphically M-regular when its mixed and Fréchet coderivatives agree. N-regularity is exactly normal regularity of the graph and always implies M-regularity, but M-regularity alone need not imply N-regularity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is N-regular}\iff D_N^*F=\widehat D^*F;\qquad F\text{ is M-regular}\iff D_M^*F=\widehat D^*F;\qquad N\text{-regular}\Rightarrow M\text{-regular}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coderivative Representation for Convex-Graph Multifunctions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex graph structure yields graphical N-regularity and a global supporting-functional representation of the normal and mixed coderivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F:X\rightrightarrows Y have a convex graph. For every (\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F and y^*\in Y^*, F is N\text{-regular at }(\bar x,\bar y), and D_N^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)=D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)=\left\{x^*\in X^*\mid \langle x^*,\bar x\rangle-\langle y^*,\bar y\rangle=\max_{(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F}\left[\langle x^*,x\rangle-\langle y^*,y\rangle\right]\right\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifunction with a convex graph is graphically N-regular at every graph point. Its normal and mixed coderivatives coincide and consist exactly of the input covectors whose associated linear functional is maximized over the graph at the reference point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is N-regular at }(\bar x,\bar y),\quad D_N^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)=D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)=\left\{x^*\in X^*\mid \langle x^*,\bar x\rangle-\langle y^*,\bar y\rangle=\max_{(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F}[\langle x^*,x\rangle-\langle y^*,y\rangle]\right\}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection inclusion and regularity inheritance for a multifunction with one parameter fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\times Y\rightrightarrows Z\) have locally closed graph around \((\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)\in\operatorname{gph}F\). Suppose that \(F\) is PSNC there and \[(0,y^*)\in D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)(0)\Longrightarrow y^*=0.\] These assumptions hold automatically when \(F\) is Lipschitz-like around the reference point. Then, for every \(z^*\in Z^*\) and \(D^*\in\{D_N^*,D_M^*\}\), \[D_x^*F(\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)(z^*)\subset\operatorname{proj}_xD^*F(\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)(z^*).\] Equality holds when \(F\) is respectively \(N\)-regular or \(M\)-regular, and then \(F(\cdot,\bar y)\) inherits the corresponding regularity at \((\bar x,\bar z)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under PSNC and a zero-coderivative qualification, the partial normal or mixed coderivative in the first variable is contained in the first-coordinate projection of the full coderivative. Corresponding regularity gives equality and passes to the partial multifunction.
assumptions_latex: \operatorname{gph}F\text{ is locally closed around }(\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)
F\text{ is PSNC at }(\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D_x^*F(\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)(z^*)\subset\operatorname{proj}_xD^*F(\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)(z^*)\quad(\forall z^*\in Z^*,\ D^*\in\{D_N^*,D_M^*\}),\text{ with equality and inherited corresponding regularity under }N\text{- or }M\text{-regularity of }F.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The coderivative values are independent of the chosen output covector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \varnothing\ne\Omega\subset X and define \Delta(x;\Omega)=\{0\}\subset Y for x\in\Omega and \Delta(x;\Omega)=\varnothing for x\notin\Omega. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regular, Normal, and Mixed Coderivatives of a Set-Valued Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the off-graph empty-value convention and the weak-star versus norm convergence distinction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F:X\rightrightarrows Y with \operatorname{dom}F\ne\varnothing. For (x,y)\in X\times Y, \varepsilon\ge0, and y^*\in Y^*, define \widehat D^*_{\varepsilon}F(x,y)(y^*):=\{x^*\in X^*:(x^*,-y^*)\in\widehat N_{\varepsilon}((x,y);\operatorname{gph}F)\}; \widehat D^*F:=\widehat D^*_0F. At (\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F, \bar x^*\in D_N^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(\bar y^*) iff there exist \varepsilon_k\downarrow0, (x_k,y_k)\to(\bar x,\bar y), and (x_k^*,y_k^*)\overset{w^*}{\to}(\bar x^*,\bar y^*) with x_k^*\in\widehat D^*_{\varepsilon_k}F(x_k,y_k)(y_k^*). Likewise, \bar x^*\in D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(\bar y^*) iff the same holds with (x_k,y_k,y_k^*)\to(\bar x,\bar y,\bar y^*) in norm and x_k^*\overset{w^*}{\to}\bar x^*. Moreover, D_N^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)=\{x^*:(x^*,-y^*)\in N((\bar x,\bar y);\operatorname{gph}F)\}. All these coderivative values are empty when the base point is outside \operatorname{gph}F.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epsilon-coderivative is defined by epsilon-normal vectors to the graph, and the Fréchet coderivative is its zero-epsilon case. Normal and mixed coderivatives are sequential outer limits: the normal construction uses weak-star convergence for both dual sequences, whereas the mixed construction uses norm convergence for the output dual sequence and weak-star convergence for the input dual sequence. The normal coderivative is equivalently determined by the basic normal cone to the graph. At points outside the graph, every coderivative value is empty.
assumptions_latex: (\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\text{ for the limiting constructions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat D^*_{\varepsilon}F(x,y)(y^*)=\{x^*:(x^*,-y^*)\in\widehat N_{\varepsilon}((x,y);\operatorname{gph}F)\},\quad D_N^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)=\{x^*:(x^*,-y^*)\in N((\bar x,\bar y);\operatorname{gph}F)\},

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normal and mixed coderivative sum rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local and union-form coderivative estimates for a multifunction sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F_i:X\rightrightarrows Y\) for \(i=1,2\), let \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}(F_1+F_2)\), and set
\[
S(x,y):=\{(y_1,y_2):y_i\in F_i(x),\ y_1+y_2=y\}.
\]
For \(D^*\in\{D_N^*,D_M^*\}\) and every \(y^*\in Y^*\): (i) if \((\bar y_1,\bar y_2)\in S(\bar x,\bar y)\), \(S\) is inner semicontinuous there, both graphs are locally closed at their corresponding points, at least one \(F_i\) is PSNC there, and
\[
D_M^*F_1(\bar x,\bar y_1)(0)\cap[-D_M^*F_2(\bar x,\bar y_2)(0)]=\{0\},
\]
then
\[
D^*(F_1+F_2)(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\subset D^*F_1(\bar x,\bar y_1)(y^*)+D^*F_2(\bar x,\bar y_2)(y^*).
\]
(ii) If \(S\) is inner semicompact at \((\bar x,\bar y)\), the mappings have closed graphs locally near \(\bar x\), and the same qualification and PSNC alternative hold for every \((\bar y_1,\bar y_2)\in S(\bar x,\bar y)\), then
\[
D^*(F_1+F_2)(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\subset\bigcup_{(\bar y_1,\bar y_2)\in S(\bar x,\bar y)}\left[D^*F_1(\bar x,\bar y_1)(y^*)+D^*F_2(\bar x,\bar y_2)(y^*)\right].
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For either the normal or mixed coderivative, a stable local decomposition of a sum, local graph closedness, a PSNC alternative, and a mixed-coderivative qualification yield a componentwise coderivative upper estimate. With inner semicompactness and pointwise conditions over every decomposition, the estimate is the union of those componentwise sums.
assumptions_latex: \text{Case (i): }(\bar y_1,\bar y_2)\in S(\bar x,\bar y),\ S\text{ is inner semicontinuous at }(\bar x,\bar y,\bar y_1,\bar y_2)
\operatorname{gph}F_i\text{ is locally closed at }(\bar x,\bar y_i),\quad F_1\text{ or }F_2\text{ is PSNC at its corresponding point}
\text{Case (ii): }S\text{ is inner semicompact at }(\bar x,\bar y),\ F_1,F_2\text{ have locally closed graphs near }\bar x
\forall(\bar y_1,\bar y_2)\in S(\bar x,\bar y):\text{ the qualification holds and at least one corresponding mapping is PSNC}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D^*(F_1+F_2)(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\subset\bigcup_{(\bar y_1,\bar y_2)\in S(\bar x,\bar y)}\left[D^*F_1(\bar x,\bar y_1)(y^*)+D^*F_2(\bar x,\bar y_2)(y^*)\right],\quad D^*\in\{D_N^*,D_M^*\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coderivatives of Differentiable Mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes the Fréchet-differentiable conclusion from the stronger strictly differentiable conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:X\to Y. If f is Fr\acute{e}chet differentiable at \bar x, then for every y^*\in Y^*, \widehat D^*f(\bar x)(y^*)=\{\nabla f(\bar x)^*y^*\}. If f is strictly differentiable at \bar x, then for every y^*\in Y^*, D_N^*f(\bar x)(y^*)=D_M^*f(\bar x)(y^*)=\{\nabla f(\bar x)^*y^*\}, and f is N\text{-regular at }\bar x.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a Fréchet-differentiable single-valued mapping, the Fréchet coderivative is the singleton obtained by applying the adjoint derivative. Under strict differentiability, the normal and mixed coderivatives have the same singleton formula, so the mapping is graphically N-regular.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In finite-dimensional dual spaces, weak-star convergence and norm convergence coincide. Therefore the defining convergence requirements for the mixed and normal coderivatives are identical, and for every \(y^*\in Y^*\),
\[
D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)=D_N^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*).
\]
The equality concerns the entire set-valued coderivative mappings, not merely their values at \(y^*=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, weak-star and norm convergence agree, so mixed and normal coderivatives coincide at every output covector.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential Output-Dual Compactness Coincidence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coincidence under norm precompactness of output-dual sequences admissible in the normal-coderivative construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(y^*\in Y^*\). Suppose every sequence \((y_k^*)\) occurring in a defining normal-coderivative sequence with \(y_k^*\overset{w^*}{\longrightarrow}y^*\) has a subsequence converging to \(y^*\) in norm. Then
\[
D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)=D_N^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*).
\]
If this condition holds for every \(y^*\), the two coderivative mappings coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mixed and normal coderivatives coincide whenever the admissible weak-star-convergent output covectors are sequentially norm precompact; finite dimensionality is a special case.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are Asplund spaces and the sequential mixed and normal coderivatives use the conventions of the sibling definition leaves.
Every admissible output-dual sequence weak-star converging to the selected \(y^*\) has a norm-convergent subsequence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)=D_N^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\).

children.top_down_role: Infinite-dimensional settings where weak-star and strong behavior separate the variants.

assumptions_latex: Mixed and normal coderivatives are defined by the stated sequential convergence modes.

source_refs.locator: 4.2.1 Lipschitzian Properties via Normal and Mixed Coderivatives p. 385

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Norm convergence of \(y_k^*\) implies weak-star convergence, so for every \(y^*\in Y^*\),
\[
D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\subset D_N^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*).
\]
In infinite-dimensional spaces the converse can fail because a weak-star convergent sequence of output covectors need not converge in norm. A normal-coderivative element represented only by such a sequence may therefore be excluded from the mixed coderivative. Finite dimensionality removes this gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The mixed coderivative is contained in the normal coderivative; infinite-dimensional weak-star convergence without norm convergence can make the containment strict.
knowledge_statements.title: Convergence-Mode Gap

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Explicit Weak-Star versus Norm Counterexample
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit infinite-dimensional strict inclusion generated by a weakly null but non-norm-null orthonormal sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The resulting mapping \(f:\mathbb R\to\ell^2\) is locally Lipschitz and satisfies
\[
1\in D_N^*f(0,0)(0),\qquad D_M^*f(0,0)(0)=\{0\}.
\]
Thus the inclusion \(D_M^*f(0,0)(0)\subset D_N^*f(0,0)(0)\) is strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Lipschitz mapping into ell-two converts weakly null orthonormal directions into a nonzero normal-coderivative value at zero, while its mixed coderivative at zero remains trivial.

Define \(f(t)=a_n\phi((t-x_n)/a_n)e_n\) on the \(n\)-th interval and \(f(t)=0\) elsewhere.

D_\diamond^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Valued Mapping Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional limiting-coderivative reduction, including the exact strictly differentiable case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(y^*\in Y\), regard the single-valued mapping as \(x\mapsto\{f(x)\}\). Its limiting coderivative is
\[
D^*f(\bar x)(y^*)=\big\{x^*\in X:(x^*,-y^*)\in N_{\operatorname{gph}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\big\}.
\]
If \(f\) is strictly differentiable at \(\bar x\), then
\[
D^*f(\bar x)(y^*)=\{\nabla f(\bar x)^T y^*\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single-valued coderivative is obtained from normals to the mapping's graph; strict differentiability reduces it to the transpose derivative applied to the dual argument.
assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\), \(Y=\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(f:X\to Y\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
The coderivative and normal cone are the limiting Mordukhovich constructions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D^*f(\bar x)(y^*)=\{x^*:(x^*,-y^*)\in N_{\operatorname{gph}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\}\), with \(D^*f(\bar x)(y^*)=\{\nabla f(\bar x)^T y^*\}\) when \(f\) is strictly differentiable at \(\bar x\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz Coderivative Norm Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional norm bound for a locally Lipschitz single-valued mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) with constant \(L\). Then, for every \(y^*\in\mathbb{R}^m\) and every \(x^*\in D^*f(\bar x)(y^*)\),
\[
\|x^*\|\le L\|y^*\|.
\]
Consequently, \(D^*f(\bar x)(0)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local Lipschitz constant bounds every coderivative output by that constant times the dual argument norm; in particular, the coderivative at the zero dual argument is zero.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is single-valued and Lipschitz on a neighborhood of \(\bar x\) with constant \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\in D^*f(\bar x)(y^*)\Longrightarrow \|x^*\|\le L\|y^*\|,\qquad D^*f(\bar x)(0)=\{0\}.

notation.meaning: A local Lipschitz constant for f

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Piecewise-Smooth Branch Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional coderivative upper representation for a finite piecewise-C1 mapping, retaining normals to branch domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose that near \(\bar x\),
\[
\operatorname{gph}f=\bigcup_{i=1}^r\{(x,f_i(x)):x\in\Omega_i\},
\]
where each \(\Omega_i\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is locally closed, each \(f_i\) is \(C^1\) near \(\bar x\), and \(f=f_i\) on \(\Omega_i\). With \(I(\bar x):=\{i:\bar x\in\Omega_i\}\), for every \(y^*\in\mathbb{R}^m\),
\[
D^*f(\bar x)(y^*)
\subset
\bigcup_{i\in I(\bar x)}
\left(\nabla f_i(\bar x)^Ty^*+N_{\Omega_i}(\bar x)\right).
\]
The branch-domain normal terms cannot generally be omitted at junctions or boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every coderivative value of a finite piecewise-smooth mapping lies in an active branch Jacobian-transpose value plus a normal to that branch domain; the domain normals retain junction effects.
assumptions_latex: The displayed finite graph decomposition holds locally at \((\bar x,f(\bar x))\).
Each \(\Omega_i\) is locally closed, and each \(f_i\) is continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
Coderivatives and branch-domain normals are limiting constructions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D^*f(\bar x)(y^*)\subset\bigcup_{i\in I(\bar x)}\left(\nabla f_i(\bar x)^Ty^*+N_{\Omega_i}(\bar x)\right).

knowledge_statements.title: Inverse-Mapping Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-transposition identity for limiting coderivatives in finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\). Since \(\operatorname{gph}F^{-1}\) is obtained from \(\operatorname{gph}F\) by interchanging coordinates, for every \(x^*\in X\) and \(y^*\in Y\),
\[
y^*\in D^*F^{-1}(\bar y,\bar x)(x^*)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
-x^*\in D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(-y^*).
\]
Equivalently, \((y^*,-x^*)\) is normal to \(\operatorname{gph}F^{-1}\) exactly when \((-x^*,y^*)\) is normal to \(\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Swapping a mapping's graph coordinates swaps the dual coordinates and signs, yielding an exact coderivative identity between the mapping and its inverse.
assumptions_latex: \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\), and the graph is locally closed at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
Coderivatives use the same limiting normal-cone convention for \(F\) and \(F^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y^*\in D^*F^{-1}(\bar y,\bar x)(x^*)\iff -x^*\in D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(-y^*)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(y^*\in\mathbb{R}^m\), define the scalar function \(\varphi_{y^*}:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) by \(\varphi_{y^*}(x)=\langle y^*,f(x)\rangle\). Then
\[
D^*f(\bar x)(y^*)

=\{\nabla f(\bar x)^Ty^*\}.
\]
Thus scalar differentiation and graph-normal coderivation give the same covector, with no convexification or closure required.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f:X\to Y\) is strictly Lipschitzian at \(\bar x\), then for every \(y^*\in Y^*\) its limiting coderivative is recovered by the limiting subdifferential of the scalarization:
\[
D^*f(\bar x)(y^*)
=\partial\big(x\mapsto\langle y^*,f(x)\rangle\big)(\bar x).
\]
The equality uses the limiting coderivative and limiting subdifferential associated with the same normal-cone construction.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \bar x be a local solution of (5.12) in Asplund spaces X,Y, and let F=f:X\to Y be single-valued and strictly Lipschitz at \bar x. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coderivative chain rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition of outer-semicontinuous multifunctions, with a nonconvex inclusion and graph-convex equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let S=S_2\circ S_1, where S_1:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^p and S_2:\mathbb R^p\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m are outer semicontinuous, and let \bar u\in S(\bar x). Put W(\bar x,\bar u)=S_1(\bar x)\cap S_2^{-1}(\bar u). If (x,u)\mapsto S_1(x)\cap S_2^{-1}(u) is locally bounded at (\bar x,\bar u), and D^*S_2(\bar w\mid\bar u)(0)\cap[D^*S_1(\bar x\mid\bar w)]^{-1}(0)=\{0\} for every \bar w\in W(\bar x,\bar u), then \operatorname{gph}S is locally closed at (\bar x,\bar u) and
D^*S(\bar x\mid\bar u)\subset\bigcup_{\bar w\in W(\bar x,\bar u)}D^*S_1(\bar x\mid\bar w)\circ D^*S_2(\bar w\mid\bar u).
Local boundedness holds in particular if S_1 is locally bounded at \bar x or S_2^{-1} is locally bounded at \bar u. The qualification holds in particular under the stated strict-continuity alternatives. If S_1 and S_2 are graph-convex, then S is graph-convex and, for every \bar w\in W(\bar x,\bar u),
D^*S(\bar x\mid\bar u)=D^*S_1(\bar x\mid\bar w)\circ D^*S_2(\bar w\mid\bar u).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a composition of outer-semicontinuous multifunctions, local boundedness of the intermediate-point mapping and a coderivative qualification imply local closedness of the composite graph and an upper coderivative chain rule. The boundedness and qualification admit the stated local-boundedness and strict-continuity sufficient conditions. For graph-convex mappings, the inclusion is an equality for every feasible intermediate point.
assumptions_latex: S=S_2\circ S_1,\quad S_1:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^p,\quad S_2:\mathbb R^p\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\text{ are outer semicontinuous}
(x,u)\mapsto S_1(x)\cap S_2^{-1}(u)\text{ is locally bounded at }(\bar x,\bar u)
D^*S_2(\bar w\mid\bar u)(0)\cap[D^*S_1(\bar x\mid\bar w)]^{-1}(0)=\{0\}\quad\forall\bar w\in S_1(\bar x)\cap S_2^{-1}(\bar u)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{gph}S\text{ is locally closed at }(\bar x,\bar u),\quad D^*S(\bar x\mid\bar u)\subset\bigcup_{\bar w\in S_1(\bar x)\cap S_2^{-1}(\bar u)}D^*S_1(\bar x\mid\bar w)\circ D^*S_2(\bar w\mid\bar u),\text{ with equality for graph-convex }S_1,S_2.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regularity Preserved by Epi-Addition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict continuity with a local Lipschitz bound, plus preservation of upper-C1 and upper-C2 regularity under a local-boundedness hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let f=g\#h, where g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}} is proper and lsc and h:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}. Suppose that for every \alpha\in\mathbb{R}, the multifunction
\[
x\mapsto\{w\mid g(w)+h(x-w)\le\alpha\}
\]
is locally bounded. Define
\[
P(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{w\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{g(w)+h(x-w)\}.
\]
If h is strictly continuous, then f is strictly continuous and
\[
\operatorname{lip}f(x)\le\max_{w\in P(x)}\operatorname{lip}h(x-w).
\]
If h is upper-\mathcal C^1, respectively upper-\mathcal C^2, then f is upper-\mathcal C^1, respectively upper-\mathcal C^2.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under local boundedness of every epi-addition sublevel solution mapping, infimal convolution with a strictly continuous function is strictly continuous, with its local Lipschitz modulus bounded by the largest modulus of the translated second term over minimizers. Upper-C1 and upper-C2 regularity of that term are also preserved.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h\text{ strictly continuous}\Rightarrow f\text{ strictly continuous and }\operatorname{lip}f(x)\le\max_{w\in P(x)}\operatorname{lip}h(x-w);\quad h\text{ upper-}\mathcal C^k\Rightarrow f\text{ upper-}\mathcal C^k\ (k=1,2).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential of a Finite Maximum of Strictly Continuous Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limiting-subdifferential inclusion, with equality and regularity under strict differentiability of all active functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x), where every f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}} is strictly continuous, and let I(\bar x)=\{i\mid f_i(\bar x)=f(\bar x)\}. Then
\[
\partial f(\bar x)\subseteq\left\{\sum_{i\in I(\bar x)}\lambda_i v_i\ \middle|\ v_i\in\partial f_i(\bar x),\ \lambda_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i\in I(\bar x)}\lambda_i=1\right\}.
\]
If every active f_i is strictly differentiable at \bar x, the inclusion is equality and f is regular at \bar x.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite maximum of strictly continuous functions, every limiting subgradient at a point is a convex combination of subgradients of the active functions. If all active functions are strictly differentiable there, equality holds and the maximum function is regular there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f(\bar x)\subseteq\left\{\sum_{i\in I(\bar x)}\lambda_i v_i\mid v_i\in\partial f_i(\bar x),\ \lambda_i\ge0,\ \sum_i\lambda_i=1\right\},\text{ with equality and regularity if all active }f_i\text{ are strictly differentiable at }\bar x.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inner composition with a single-valued mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regular and limiting coderivative rules plus stability and graphical-derivative consequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let F:X\to Y be single-valued and strictly continuous at \bar x, let S_0:Y\rightrightarrows Z be outer semicontinuous, set S=S_0\circ F, and take \bar u\in S(\bar x). Then
\widehat D^*S(\bar x\mid\bar u)\supset\widehat D^*F(\bar x)\circ\widehat D^*S_0(F(\bar x)\mid\bar u).
If no nonzero z\in D^*S_0(F(\bar x)\mid\bar u)(0) satisfies 0\in\partial(zF)(\bar x), then
D^*S(\bar x\mid\bar u)\subset D^*F(\bar x)\circ D^*S_0(F(\bar x)\mid\bar u).
This qualification holds when S_0 has the Aubin property at (F(\bar x),\bar u); then S has the Aubin property and
\operatorname{lip}S(\bar x\mid\bar u)\leq\operatorname{lip}F(\bar x)\operatorname{lip}S_0(F(\bar x)\mid\bar u).
If additionally F is semidifferentiable at \bar x, then
DS(\bar x\mid\bar u)=DS_0(F(\bar x)\mid\bar u)\circ DF(\bar x),
and semidifferentiability of S_0 at (F(\bar x),\bar u) implies that of S. Under the qualification, if S_0 is graphically regular at (F(\bar x),\bar u) and zF is regular at \bar x for every z\in\operatorname{rge}D^*S_0(F(\bar x)\mid\bar u), then S is graphically regular and the limiting coderivative inclusion is an equality; these regularity assumptions hold in particular when F is strictly differentiable at \bar x.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an outer-semicontinuous multifunction composed with a strictly continuous single-valued inner map, the regular coderivative satisfies a reverse inclusion. A no-abnormal-multiplier condition gives the limiting-coderivative chain-rule inclusion. The Aubin property supplies that qualification and yields a product modulus bound; semidifferentiability gives an exact graphical-derivative chain rule. Additional graphical regularity makes the limiting coderivative rule exact.
assumptions_latex: S=S_0\circ F,\quad F\text{ is single-valued and strictly continuous at }\bar x,\quad S_0\text{ is outer semicontinuous}
\nexists z\neq0:\ z\in D^*S_0(F(\bar x)\mid\bar u)(0),\ 0\in\partial(zF)(\bar x)\quad\text{for the limiting rule}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat D^*S\supset\widehat D^*F\circ\widehat D^*S_0,\quad D^*S\subset D^*F\circ D^*S_0\text{ under qualification, together with the stated Aubin, graphical-derivative, semidifferentiability, and graphical-regularity consequences.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: MFCQ multiplier characterization of linear suboptimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional decision space with an Asplund objective space and smooth functional constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to Z\) be strictly differentiable at \(\bar x\), where \(\dim X<\infty\) and \(Z\) is Asplund. Let \(\bar z=f(\bar x)\in\Theta\), with \(\Theta\) normally regular and SNC at \(\bar z\), and let \(\Omega=\{x\mid \varphi_i(x)\le0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ \varphi_i(x)=0\ (i=m+1,\ldots,m+r)\}\), where every \(\varphi_i\) is strictly differentiable at \(\bar x\). If MFCQ holds at \(\bar x\), then \(\bar x\) is linearly suboptimal for \((f,\Omega,\Theta)\) if and only if there exist \(z^*\in N(\bar z;\Theta)\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\lambda\in\mathbb R^{m+r}\) such that \(\nabla f(\bar x)^*z^*+\sum_{i=1}^{m+r}\lambda_i\nabla\varphi_i(\bar x)=0\), while \(\lambda_i\ge0\) and \(\lambda_i\varphi_i(\bar x)=0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under normal regularity, sequential normal compactness, and MFCQ, linear suboptimality is equivalent to a nonzero ordering-set normal multiplier and constraint multipliers satisfying stationarity, nonnegativity, and complementary slackness.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ and every }\varphi_i\text{ are strictly differentiable at }\bar x
\Theta\text{ is normally regular and SNC at }\bar z=f(\bar x)
\exists u\in X:\ \langle\nabla\varphi_i(\bar x),u\rangle<0\ \forall i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\cap I(\bar x),\quad \langle\nabla\varphi_i(\bar x),u\rangle=0\ \forall i=m+1,\ldots,m+r
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar x\text{ is linearly suboptimal}\iff\exists z^*\in N(\bar z;\Theta)\setminus\{0\},\ \lambda\in\mathbb R^{m+r}:\ \nabla f(\bar x)^*z^*+\sum_{i=1}^{m+r}\lambda_i\nabla\varphi_i(\bar x)=0,\ \lambda_i\ge0,\ \lambda_i\varphi_i(\bar x)=0\ (i\le m).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Abnormal conditions for strictly Lipschitz constraints

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \bar x be a local solution of (5.12), where X,Y are Asplund, \Omega,\Theta are closed, and F=f is single-valued and strictly Lipschitz at \bar x. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong minimality characterized by all positive functionals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An equivalence for a closed ordering cone in a locally convex linear space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let S be a nonempty subset of a locally convex linear space X ordered by a closed cone \(C_X\). Then \(\bar x\in S\) is strongly minimal if and only if every \(l\in C_{X^*}\) satisfies \(l(\bar x)\le l(x)\) for all \(x\in S\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=|x|\) and scalarize with \(y^*=-1\). The limiting graph normals arising from the two smooth branches give
\[
D^*f(0)(-1)=\{-1,1\}.
\]
By contrast, Clarke scalarization convexifies the branch information:
\[
\partial_C\langle-1,f\rangle(0)=\partial_C(-|\cdot|)(0)=[-1,1].
\]
Hence a convexified scalar subdifferential can strictly overestimate the limiting coderivative and cannot generally serve as an exact replacement for it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the absolute-value mapping, Clarke scalarization fills the interval between two limiting coderivative values and therefore loses exact nonconvex information.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Derivatives and coderivatives of single-valued mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derivative and coderivative boundedness, norm formulas, and scalarization identities for a single-valued mapping at an interior point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F:D\to\mathbb{R}^m, where D\subset\mathbb{R}^n, and let \bar x\in\operatorname{int}D. If F is calm at \bar x, then DF(\bar x) is nonempty-valued, outer semicontinuous, and locally bounded, and |DF(\bar x)|^+=\limsup_{x\to\bar x,\,x\ne\bar x}\frac{|F(x)-F(\bar x)|}{|x-\bar x|}\le\operatorname{lip}F(\bar x). If F is strictly continuous at \bar x, then D^*F(\bar x) is nonempty-valued, outer semicontinuous, and locally bounded, with D^*F(\bar x)(y)=\partial\langle y,F\rangle(\bar x) for every y and |D^*F(\bar x)|^+=\operatorname{lip}F(\bar x); moreover, \widehat D^*F(\bar x)(y)=\widehat\partial\langle y,F\rangle(\bar x) for every y.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an interior point, calmness of a single-valued mapping makes its derivative mapping nonempty, outer semicontinuous, and locally bounded, with outer norm equal to the radial difference-quotient limsup and no larger than the local Lipschitz modulus. Under strict continuity, the limiting coderivative has the same regularity, is represented by subdifferentials of scalarizations, and has outer norm equal to the Lipschitz modulus; the regular coderivative is represented by regular subdifferentials.
assumptions_latex: F\text{ is calm at }\bar x\quad\text{for the derivative assertions}
F\text{ is strictly continuous at }\bar x\quad\text{for the coderivative assertions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |DF(\bar x)|^+=\limsup_{x\to\bar x,\,x\ne\bar x}\frac{|F(x)-F(\bar x)|}{|x-\bar x|}\le\operatorname{lip}F(\bar x),\quad D^*F(\bar x)(y)=\partial\langle y,F\rangle(\bar x),\quad |D^*F(\bar x)|^+=\operatorname{lip}F(\bar x),\quad \widehat D^*F(\bar x)(y)=\widehat\partial\langle y,F\rangle(\bar x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic properties and polarity of graphical derivatives and coderivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneity, regular-to-limiting inclusions, and primal-dual polarity at a graph point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let S:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m, \bar x\in\operatorname{dom}S, and \bar u\in S(\bar x). Then DS(\bar x\mid\bar u),\widehat DS(\bar x\mid\bar u),D^*S(\bar x\mid\bar u), and \widehat D^*S(\bar x\mid\bar u) are outer semicontinuous and positively homogeneous. The regular mappings are graph-convex, hence sublinear, and
\widehat DS(\bar x\mid\bar u)(w)\subset DS(\bar x\mid\bar u)(w),\qquad \widehat D^*S(\bar x\mid\bar u)(y)\subset D^*S(\bar x\mid\bar u)(y).
If \operatorname{gph}S is locally closed at (\bar x,\bar u), then
v\in\widehat D^*S(\bar x\mid\bar u)(y)\iff \langle v,w\rangle\leq\langle y,z\rangle\ \text{for every }w\text{ and every }z\in DS(\bar x\mid\bar u)(w),
and
z\in\widehat DS(\bar x\mid\bar u)(w)\iff \langle v,w\rangle\leq\langle y,z\rangle\ \text{for every }y\text{ and every }v\in D^*S(\bar x\mid\bar u)(y).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All four graphical derivative and coderivative mappings are outer semicontinuous and positively homogeneous. The regular variants are graph-convex and lie inside their limiting counterparts. When the graph is locally closed at the reference point, membership in each regular object is equivalent to the stated dual pairing inequality against every element of the opposite limiting object.
assumptions_latex: \operatorname{gph}S\text{ is locally closed at }(\bar x,\bar u)\text{ for the polarity equivalences}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: DS,\widehat DS,D^*S,\widehat D^*S\text{ are outer semicontinuous and positively homogeneous};\quad \widehat DS\subset DS,\ \widehat D^*S\subset D^*S;\quad \text{under local closedness, the two stated polarity equivalences hold.}

knowledge_statements.title: Graphical Derivative–Coderivative Polarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact tangent-normal polarity for a locally convex graph in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Local convexity gives the tangent-normal polarity
\[
N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)
=T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)^\circ.
\]
Since \(v\in DF(\bar x,\bar y)(u)\) exactly when \((u,v)\in T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\), for every \(x^*\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(y^*\in\mathbb{R}^m\),
\[
x^*\in D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\langle x^*,u\rangle-\langle y^*,v\rangle\le 0
\quad\text{for every }u\in\mathbb{R}^n\text{ and every }v\in DF(\bar x,\bar y)(u).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a locally convex graph, coderivative membership is equivalent to the polar inequality for every direction pair belonging to the graphical derivative.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\), \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\), and the graph is locally closed and convex near \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
The graphical derivative uses the contingent tangent cone, and the coderivative uses the limiting normal cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\iff \langle x^*,u\rangle-\langle y^*,v\rangle\le 0\) for every \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and every \(v\in DF(\bar x,\bar y)(u)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regular-Coderivative Polarity and Graphical-Regularity Upgrade
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universal finite-dimensional polarity for the regular coderivative, promoted to the limiting coderivative under normal regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the regular coderivative by
\[
\widehat D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)
:=\{x^*:(x^*,-y^*)\in\widehat N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\}.
\]
Then
\[
x^*\in\widehat D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)
\Longleftrightarrow
\langle x^*,u\rangle-\langle y^*,v\rangle\le0
\quad\text{for every }u\in\mathbb{R}^n\text{ and every }v\in DF(\bar x,\bar y)(u).
\]
If the graph is normally regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\), so that \(\widehat N_{\operatorname{gph}F}=N_{\operatorname{gph}F}\) there, the same equivalence holds with \(D^*F\) in place of \(\widehat D^*F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polarizing the graphical derivative always recovers the regular coderivative; it also recovers the limiting coderivative when the graph is normally regular.
assumptions_latex: The graph is locally closed at the reference point.
The upgrade to the limiting coderivative assumes normal regularity of the graph at that point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat D^*F\text{ is the signed polar of }DF;\qquad \widehat N_{\operatorname{gph}F}=N_{\operatorname{gph}F}\Longrightarrow D^*F=\widehat D^*F\text{ in the polarity formula}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f\) is strictly differentiable at \(\bar x\) with derivative \(A\), then its primal generalized derivative agrees with the classical derivative:
\[
Df(\bar x)(u)=\{Au\}\quad\text{for every }u\in X.
\]
Its dual generalized derivative agrees with the classical adjoint:
\[
D^*f(\bar x)(y^*)=\{A^*y^*\}
\quad\text{for every }y^*\in Y.
\]
For a linear mapping, these identities hold at every base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a strictly differentiable mapping, the graphical derivative is the classical derivative and the coderivative is its adjoint.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Adjoint of a bounded linear operator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical adjoints between dual normed spaces and the adjoint representation of the scalar-valued chain rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be normed spaces and \(T\in L_C(X,Y)\). There is a unique operator \(T^*\in L_C(Y^*,X^*)\) such that \(\langle T^*y^*,x\rangle=\langle y^*,Tx\rangle\) for every \(x\in X\) and \(y^*\in Y^*\); it is called the adjoint of \(T\). If \(F:X\to Y\) is differentiable at \(x\) and \(\theta:Y\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable at \(F(x)\), then \((\theta\circ F)'(x)=F'(x)^*\theta'(F(x))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded linear operator has a unique adjoint obtained by transposing the dual pairing. This lets the scalar-valued chain rule be written by applying the adjoint derivative of the inner map to the derivative of the outer function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \langle T^*y^*,x\rangle=\langle y^*,Tx\rangle\quad\forall x\in X,\ y^*\in Y^*,\qquad (\theta\circ F)'(x)=F'(x)^*\theta'(F(x))

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Adjoint of a surjective bounded linear operator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A quantitative adjoint consequence of surjectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:X\to Y\) be a continuous linear surjection between Banach spaces. Then, for every \(y^*\in Y^*\), \[\|A^*y^*\|\ge \kappa\|y^*\|,\qquad \kappa:=\inf_{\|z^*\|=1}\|A^*z^*\|\in(0,\infty).\] Consequently, \(A^*:Y^*\to X^*\) is injective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The adjoint of a surjective continuous linear operator is bounded below by a positive constant and is therefore injective.
assumptions_latex: A:X\to Y\text{ is linear, continuous, and surjective}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall y^*\in Y^*,\quad \|A^*y^*\|\ge\kappa\|y^*\|\text{ for some }\kappa>0;\quad A^*\text{ is injective.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hilbert-space adjoint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inner-product characterization for an adjoint between real Hilbert spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) and \(V\) be real Hilbert spaces and let \(A\in\mathcal L(U,V)\). An operator \(A^\star:V\to U\) is a Hilbert-space adjoint of \(A\) if \[(v,Au)_V=(A^\star v,u)_U\qquad\forall u\in U,\ \forall v\in V.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(x)=|x|\), the graphical derivative satisfies \(Df(0)(u)=\{|u|\}\). If limiting coderivatives were determined by polarizing this graphical derivative, then for \(y^*=-1\) one would require

\[
D^*f(0)(-1)=\{-1,1\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Separation and set-system extremality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives separation as a sufficient condition for extremality and a convex-interiority regime in which the converse holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let n\ge2 and let \Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_n\subset X have a common point. If the sets are separated, then \{\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_n,\bar x\} is extremal for every \bar x\in\bigcap_{i=1}^n\Omega_i. Conversely, if all \Omega_i are convex and \operatorname{int}\Omega_i\ne\varnothing for i=1,\ldots,n-1, then extremality of the system at a common point implies that the sets are separated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separated sets form an extremal system at every common point. For convex sets whose first n−1 members have nonempty interiors, extremality also implies separation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{separated}(\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_n)\Rightarrow\operatorname{extremal}(\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_n,\bar x)\ \forall\bar x\in\bigcap_i\Omega_i;\quad [\forall i\ \Omega_i\text{ convex},\ \operatorname{int}\Omega_i\ne\varnothing\ (i<n)]\Rightarrow(\operatorname{extremal}\Rightarrow\operatorname{separated})

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Locally Extremal Point of a Finite Set System
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for finitely many locally closed subsets of Euclidean space sharing a common point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let s\ge 2, and let \Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_s\subset\mathbb{R}^n be nonempty sets that are locally closed around a common point \bar{x}. The point \bar{x} is locally extremal for \{\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_s\} if there exist a neighborhood U of \bar{x} and vectors a_{ik}\in\mathbb{R}^n such that a_{ik}\to 0 as k\to\infty for every i=1,\ldots,s, and \bigcap_{i=1}^s(\Omega_i-a_{ik})\cap U=\varnothing for every k=1,2,\ldots.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common point of a finite system of locally closed Euclidean sets is locally extremal if vanishing translations of the sets eliminate their common intersection within one fixed neighborhood for every term of the translation sequences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists U\ni\bar{x},\ \exists a_{ik}\in\mathbb{R}^n:\ \left(\forall i,\ a_{ik}\to0\right)\ \land\ \left(\forall k\ge1,\ \bigcap_{i=1}^s(\Omega_i-a_{ik})\cap U=\varnothing\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local extremality of a finite set system
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines local extremality through vanishing translations that locally destroy the common intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let n\ge 2, let \Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_n\subset X be nonempty, and let \bar x\in\bigcap_{i=1}^n\Omega_i. The point \bar x is locally extremal for \{\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_n\} if there exist a neighborhood U of \bar x and sequences a_{ik}\to0 such that \bigcap_{i=1}^n(\Omega_i-a_{ik})\cap U=\varnothing for all sufficiently large k. The tuple \{\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_n,\bar x\} is then an extremal system. For n=2 this is equivalent to the existence of a neighborhood U of \bar x such that, for every \varepsilon>0, some a\in\varepsilon B satisfies (\Omega_1+a)\cap\Omega_2\cap U=\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common point is locally extremal when vanishing translations of the sets eventually eliminate their intersection in a fixed neighborhood. For two sets, every positive translation scale equivalently admits a translation of one set that locally separates the pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar x\text{ is locally extremal}\iff\exists U,\exists a_{ik}\to0:\ \bigcap_{i=1}^n(\Omega_i-a_{ik})\cap U=\varnothing\text{ eventually}

knowledge_statements.title: Localization of Global Extremality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient localization rule obtained by globally extremal truncations around the reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Set \(\widehat\Omega_i=\Omega_i\cap\overline B_r(\bar x)\). If, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), the sets \(\widehat\Omega_i\) admit translations \(a_i\) with \(\max_i\|a_i\|<\varepsilon\) and
\[
\bigcap_{i=1}^s(\widehat\Omega_i-a_i)=\varnothing,
\]
then \(\{\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_s\}\) is locally extremal at \(\bar x\). In particular, translations restricted by \(\max_i\|a_i\|<r/4\) separate the original sets inside \(B_{r/2}(\bar x)\), because every corresponding untranslated point remains in \(\overline B_r(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global extremality of fixed-radius truncations implies local extremality of the original sets, since sufficiently small translations keep nearby source points inside the truncation.
assumptions_latex: The truncated system \(\{\Omega_i\cap\overline B_r(\bar x)\}_{i=1}^s\) is globally extremal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The original system \(\{\Omega_i\}_{i=1}^s\) is locally extremal at \(\bar x\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global Extremality Implies Local Extremality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universal implication between the sibling extremality regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If arbitrarily small translations satisfy \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m(\Omega_i-a_i)=\varnothing\), then they also satisfy \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m(\Omega_i-a_i)\cap U=\varnothing\) for every neighborhood \(U\) of every common point \(\bar x\). Thus global extremality implies local extremality at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global separation by arbitrarily small translations implies local separation at every common reference point.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed linear space and \(\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_m\subset X\).
The system is globally extremal under arbitrarily small translations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{\Omega_i\}_{i=1}^m\text{ is locally extremal at }\bar x.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Global Extremality Implies Local Extremality

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial Local–Global Separation Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit polynomial-graph witness that local extremality is strictly weaker than global extremality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega_1=\mathbb R\times\{0\}\) and \(\Omega_2=\{(x,x^2(x+1)):x\in\mathbb R\}\). Since \(x^2(x+1)\ge0\) near \(0\), an arbitrarily small upward translation of \(\Omega_2\) separates the sets in a fixed neighborhood of \((0,0)\). Nevertheless, \(x\mapsto x^2(x+1)\) is a surjective cubic, so after arbitrary translations of both sets their intersection condition is \(x^2(x+1)=c\) for some \(c\in\mathbb R\), which always has a solution. Thus the pair is locally extremal at \((0,0)\) but not globally extremal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The graph of the surjective cubic x²(x+1) lies on one side of the horizontal axis near the origin, permitting local separation, while its full range prevents separation after any global translations.
assumptions_latex: Local and global extremality use arbitrarily small translations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{\Omega_1,\Omega_2\}\text{ is locally extremal at }(0,0)\text{ but is not globally extremal}.\)

notation.meaning: Surjective cubic having a local minimum at the origin

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose a continuous surjection \(g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(g(x)=x^2\) for \(|x|\le 1\). Near \((0,0)\), translating \(\Omega_2\) upward by \((0,t)\), with \(t>0\), separates it from \(\Omega_1\); hence the pair is locally extremal. For arbitrary translations \(a_1,a_2\in\mathbb{R}^2\), intersection of \(\Omega_1-a_1\) and \(\Omega_2-a_2\) reduces to an equation

for some \(c\in\mathbb{R}\). Surjectivity of \(g\) supplies a solution, so no translations separate the sets globally.

children.title: Rated Extremality
children.top_down_role: Extremal behavior calibrated by a prescribed localization rate.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space and \(\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_m\subset X\) share \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The system is rated extremal at \(\bar x\) with rate \(R\).

notation.meaning: closed ball centered at the reference point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rate-function formulation; the source-specific admissibility convention for \(R\) remains to be checked.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_m\subset X\) contain \(\bar x\), and let \(R:(0,\delta)\to(0,\infty)\). The system is rated extremal at \(\bar x\) with rate \(R\) if there exist perturbations \(a_{ik}\in X\) such that \(r_k:=\max_{1\le i\le m}\|a_{ik}\|>0\), \(r_k\downarrow0\), and, for all sufficiently large \(k\), \[\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^{m}(\Omega_i-a_{ik})\right)\cap B(\bar x,R(r_k))=\varnothing.\] Any additional growth requirement imposed on \(R\) is part of the chosen rated-extremality regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rated extremality means vanishing translations separate all sets inside a neighborhood whose radius is prescribed as a function of the translation size.
knowledge_statements.title: Rated Extremality

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition depends on a source-specific orientation and admissibility convention for the rate function R. With no citation, it is unclear whether R denotes the observation radius itself, whether additional asymptotic conditions are required, and whether the displayed formulation matches the named rated-extremality regime.

children.title: Linear Extremality
children.top_down_role: Extremal behavior governed by a linear localization scale.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space and \(\bar x\in\bigcap_{i=1}^m\Omega_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The translated sets are locally disjoint in balls whose radii are proportional to the translation magnitude.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear localization radius proportional to perturbation size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A collection \(\{\Omega_1,ldots,Omega_m\}\) is linearly extremal at \(\bar x\) if there exist \(\gamma>0\) and translations \(a_{ik}\in X\) with \(r_k:=\max_i\|a_{ik}\|>0\) and \(r_k\downarrow0\) such that, eventually, \[\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^{m}(\Omega_i-a_{ik})\right)\cap B(\bar x,\gamma r_k)=\varnothing.\] Thus separation is required only on a neighborhood whose radius has the same order as the largest perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear extremality requires vanishing translations to separate the sets within a ball proportional to the largest translation.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Extremality

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports this particular definition of linear extremality, and the mathematical convention is not reliable until the parent rated-extremality convention is fixed. The expression intended as \(\{\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_m\}\) also contains malformed LaTeX.

children.title: Linear-Rate Specialization
children.top_down_role: Position of linear extremality within the broader rated family.

assumptions_latex: Rated extremality is parameterized by the power rate \(R_\alpha(r)=\gamma r^\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_1(r)=\gamma r\), so the rated separation condition becomes linear extremality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Endpoint specialization of a power-rate convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the power-rate convention \(R_\alpha(r):=\gamma r^\alpha\), setting \(\alpha=1\) gives \(R_1(r)=\gamma r\). Consequently, the rated-extremality condition specializes to \[\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^{m}(\Omega_i-a_{ik})\right)\cap B(\bar x,\gamma r_k)=\varnothing,\qquad r_k:=\max_i\|a_{ik}\|\downarrow0,\] which is precisely the linear-rate separation condition. Whether the endpoint \(\alpha=1\) is included in the source definition or treated separately must be fixed by convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a power rate, choosing exponent one makes the localization radius proportional to perturbation size and yields linear extremality.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Rate Specialization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algebraic substitution \(\alpha=1\) is correct, and property is an appropriate content kind for this leaf. However, calling it precisely the linear-extremality specialization depends on the unsupported definitions in the two prerequisite records and on whether the cited theory includes the endpoint.

children.title: Sublinear Rate Boundary
children.top_down_role: Rate regimes where linear extremality no longer captures the local separation behavior.

assumptions_latex: The power localization rate is \(R_\alpha(r)=\gamma r^\alpha\) with \(\gamma>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(0\le\alpha<1\), \(R_\alpha(r)/r\to\infty\); at \(\alpha=1\), the ratio equals \(\gamma\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between neighborhoods asymptotically larger than perturbations and neighborhoods of comparable size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(R_\alpha(r):=\gamma r^\alpha\), one has \[\frac{R_\alpha(r)}{r}=\gamma r^{\alpha-1}.\] Hence \(R_\alpha(r)/r\to\infty\) as \(r\downarrow0\) exactly when \(0\le\alpha<1\), whereas \(R_1(r)/r=\gamma\). Thus \(\alpha=1\) is the boundary between sublinear-power localization, whose observation radius dominates the perturbation magnitude, and linear localization, whose two scales remain comparable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Power exponents below one give neighborhoods asymptotically larger than the perturbations; exponent one is the linear boundary.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact-normal certificate for linear subextremality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact limiting-normal necessity under Asplund, local-closedness, and SNC assumptions, together with the finite-dimensional equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \Omega_1,\Omega_2\subset X and \bar x\in\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2. Suppose \{\Omega_1,\Omega_2\} is linearly subextremal around \bar x, X is Asplund, both sets are locally closed around \bar x, and at least one set is sequentially normally compact at \bar x. Then there exists x^*\in X^* such that
\[
0\neq x^*\in N(\bar x;\Omega_1)\cap\big(-N(\bar x;\Omega_2)\big).
\]
If \dim X<\infty, this nonzero opposite-normal condition is necessary and sufficient for linear subextremality of the two-set system around \bar x.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated Asplund, local-closedness, and sequential-normal-compactness assumptions, a linearly subextremal pair has a nonzero limiting normal to one set whose negative is a limiting normal to the other. In finite dimensions, this exact opposite-normal certificate is equivalent to linear subextremality.
assumptions_latex: \Omega_1\text{ and }\Omega_2\text{ are locally closed around }\bar x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x^*\neq0:\ x^*\in N(\bar x;\Omega_1)\cap[-N(\bar x;\Omega_2)];\qquad \dim X<\infty\Rightarrow\big(\text{linear subextremality}\iff\exists x^*\neq0\text{ satisfying this condition}\big).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximate-normal characterization of linear subextremality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-way certificate in Banach spaces, its locally closed Asplund-space converse, and the resulting characterization of Asplund spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \Omega_1,\Omega_2\subset X, where X is a Banach space, and let \bar x\in\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2. If for every \varepsilon>0 there exist \widehat x_i\in\Omega_i\cap(\bar x+\varepsilon\mathbb B) and x_i^*\in\widehat N_\varepsilon(\widehat x_i;\Omega_i), i=1,2, such that
\[
\|x_1^*+x_2^*\|\leq\varepsilon,
\qquad \|x_1^*\|+\|x_2^*\|=1,
\]
then \{\Omega_1,\Omega_2\} is linearly subextremal around \bar x. Conversely, if \Omega_1 and \Omega_2 are locally closed, the system is linearly subextremal around \bar x, and X is Asplund, then for every \varepsilon>0 there exist \widehat x_i\in\Omega_i\cap(\bar x+\varepsilon\mathbb B) and x_i^*\in\widehat N(\widehat x_i;\Omega_i) satisfying the same two inequalities. If this converse property holds for every linearly subextremal two-set system in X, then X is Asplund.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arbitrarily accurate normalized approximate-normal certificates imply linear subextremality. For locally closed sets in an Asplund space, linear subextremality yields normalized Fréchet-normal certificates at nearby points. If that converse is valid for every linearly subextremal pair in a Banach space, the space must be Asplund.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the converse: }\Omega_1,\Omega_2\text{ are locally closed, }\{\Omega_1,\Omega_2\}\text{ is linearly subextremal around }\bar x,\text{ and }X\text{ is Asplund}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \big[\forall\varepsilon>0\text{, the stated normalized }\widehat N_\varepsilon\text{-certificates exist}\big]\Rightarrow\text{linear subextremality};\quad \text{under local closedness and the Asplund hypothesis, linear subextremality yields the stated }\widehat N\text{-certificates}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear subextremality of a two-set system
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for two subsets of a Banach space using the first-order decay of their local overlap measure under translations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \Omega_1,\Omega_2\subset X and \bar x\in\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2. Define
\[
\vartheta_{\mathrm{lin}}(\Omega_1,\Omega_2,\bar x):=\liminf_{\substack{x_i\to\bar x,\ x_i\in\Omega_i\ (i=1,2)\\ r\downarrow0}}\frac{\vartheta\big(([\Omega_1-x_1]\cap r\mathbb B),([\Omega_2-x_2]\cap r\mathbb B)\big)}{r}.
\]
The system \{\Omega_1,\Omega_2\} is linearly subextremal around \bar x precisely when \vartheta_{\mathrm{lin}}(\Omega_1,\Omega_2,\bar x)=0, where \vartheta is the overlap measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two sets containing x̄ form a linearly subextremal system around x̄ when the liminf, over points of the respective sets approaching x̄ and radii decreasing to zero, of their translated local overlap measure divided by the radius is zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{\Omega_1,\Omega_2\}\text{ is linearly subextremal around }\bar x\iff\vartheta_{\mathrm{lin}}(\Omega_1,\Omega_2,\bar x)=0.

Let \(\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_m\subset\mathbb R^n\) be locally closed near a common point \(\bar x\), and suppose that the collection is locally extremal at \(\bar x\).
