knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H:=G\circ F\) and \(K(x,z):=F(x)\cap G^{-1}(z)\). Suppose every tangent to \(\operatorname{gph}H\) at \((\bar x,\bar z)\) lifts through some \(\bar y\in K(\bar x,\bar z)\), and every compatible pair \((u,v)\in T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\), \((v,w)\in T_{\operatorname{gph}G}(\bar y,\bar z)\) is realizable by synchronized graph arcs of the composition. Then
\[
DH(\bar x,\bar z)(u)=\bigcup_{\bar y\in K(\bar x,\bar z)}\ \bigcup_{v\in DF(\bar x,\bar y)(u)}DG(\bar y,\bar z)(v).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When composition tangents lift and component tangent arcs can be synchronized, graphical derivatives propagate directions successively through the two mappings.
assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) and \(G:Y\rightrightarrows Z\) act between finite-dimensional spaces.
The stated two-sided tangent-lifting and synchronization property holds at \((\bar x,\bar z)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(DH(\bar x,\bar z)(u)=\bigcup_{\bar y\in K(\bar x,\bar z)}\bigcup_{v\in DF(\bar x,\bar y)(u)}DG(\bar y,\bar z)(v)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Graphical-Derivative Composition Rule

children.title: Calculus Qualification Architectures
children.top_down_role: Geometric, singular, metric, and compactness regimes controlling calculus validity and exactness.

children.title: Singular-Subgradient Qualifications
children.top_down_role: Qualification regimes expressed through exclusion of horizontal degeneracy.

assumptions_latex: \(f_1,f_2:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\), with \(f_1(\bar x)\) and \(f_2(\bar x)\) finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\partial^\infty f_1(\bar x)\cap(-\partial^\infty f_2(\bar x))=\{0\}\), then \(\partial(f_1+f_2)(\bar x)\subset\partial f_1(\bar x)+\partial f_2(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-function finite-dimensional qualification excluding cancellation of horizontal epigraph normals.

source_refs.locator: 3.2.1 Calculus Rules for Basic and Singular Subgradients p. 296
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The singular-subgradient qualification for addition is
\[
\partial^\infty f_1(\bar x)\cap\bigl(-\partial^\infty f_2(\bar x)\bigr)=\{0\}.
\]
Equivalently, if \(x_1^*\in\partial^\infty f_1(\bar x)\), \(x_2^*\in\partial^\infty f_2(\bar x)\), and \(x_1^*+x_2^*=0\), then \(x_1^*=x_2^*=0\). Under this qualification,
\[
\partial(f_1+f_2)(\bar x)
\subset
\partial f_1(\bar x)+\partial f_2(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Opposing nonzero singular subgradients are excluded; for lower-semicontinuous functions in finite dimensions, this yields the limiting-subdifferential sum inclusion.
knowledge_statements.title: Singular-Subgradient Qualifications

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2.1 Calculus Rules for Basic and Singular Subgradients p. 296
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Sum Singular Qualification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-family extension of the limiting-subdifferential sum qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\) and finite at \(\bar x\), with \(X\) finite-dimensional. If \[x_i^*\in\partial^\infty f_i(\bar x)\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m x_i^*=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x_1^*=\cdots=x_m^*=0,\] then \[\partial\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\right)(\bar x)\subseteq\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(\bar x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite sum, exclusion of every nontrivial balanced tuple of singular subgradients yields the limiting-subdifferential sum inclusion.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) is lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\) and finite at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(\sum_{i=1}^m f_i)(\bar x)\subseteq\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(\bar x).\)
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Sum Singular Qualification

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Lipschitz Sufficient Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Automatic finite-sum singular qualification when all but at most one summand are locally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz around \(\bar x\), then \[\partial^\infty f(\bar x)=\{0\}.\] Consequently, the finite-sum singular no-balancing qualification holds automatically whenever all but at most one summand are locally Lipschitz around \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local Lipschitzness annihilates the singular subdifferential, so a finite sum is automatically singularly qualified when at most one summand is non-Lipschitz.
assumptions_latex: All but at most one of \(f_1,\ldots,f_m\) are locally Lipschitz around \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^\infty f_i(\bar x)=\{0\}\) for every locally Lipschitz summand, and the finite-sum singular qualification holds automatically.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Lipschitz Sufficient Regime

children.title: Normal-Cone Transversality
children.top_down_role: Geometric opposition conditions for intersections and inverse images.

assumptions_latex: \(\Omega_1,\Omega_2\) are locally closed subsets of a finite-dimensional normed space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Transversality yields the limiting-normal intersection inclusion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional normal-cone opposition condition for intersections; inverse-image qualifications follow by applying it to lifted graph sets.

source_refs.locator: 3.1.1 Calculus of Normal Cones p. 262
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The sets \(\Omega_1\) and \(\Omega_2\) are normally transversal at \(\bar x\) when
\[
N_{\Omega_1}(\bar x)\cap\bigl(-N_{\Omega_2}(\bar x)\bigr)=\{0\}.
\]
Under this condition, the limiting normal cone to their intersection satisfies
\[
N_{\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2}(\bar x)
\subset
N_{\Omega_1}(\bar x)+N_{\Omega_2}(\bar x).
\]
The same condition applied to graph and constraint sets supplies the geometric qualification for inverse-image and generalized-equation calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two sets are transversal when their limiting normals cannot oppose nontrivially; then intersection normals decompose into normals to the individual sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Transversality

source_witnesses.locator: 3.1.1 Calculus of Normal Cones p. 262
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Family Normal Transversality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-family extension of the two-set normal-cone qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_m\) be locally closed subsets of a finite-dimensional normed space and let \(\bar x\in\bigcap_{i=1}^m\Omega_i\). If \[x_i^*\in N_{\Omega_i}(\bar x)\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m x_i^*=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x_1^*=\cdots=x_m^*=0,\] then \[N_{\cap_{i=1}^m\Omega_i}(\bar x)\subseteq\sum_{i=1}^mN_{\Omega_i}(\bar x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite set family is normally transversal when no nontrivial selection of limiting normals balances to zero; then intersection normals decompose into component normals.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_m\) are locally closed in a finite-dimensional normed space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\cap_i\Omega_i}(\bar x)\subseteq\sum_iN_{\Omega_i}(\bar x)\) under the no-balancing condition.

notation.meaning: limiting normal cone to the ith set

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Family Normal Transversality

children.title: Metric-Compactness Qualification Coupling
children.top_down_role: Metric regularity and normal-compactness regimes supporting calculus.

children.title: Metric-Regularity Qualifications
children.top_down_role: Metric stability regimes supporting generalized differential calculus.

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has locally closed graph near \((\bar x,\bar y)\) in finite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed coderivative-kernel condition is equivalent to metric regularity around \((\bar x,\bar y)\).

notation.meaning: distance from a point to a set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Mordukhovich coderivative criterion for metric regularity.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is metrically regular around \((\bar x,\bar y)\) precisely when there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\), \(V\) of \(\bar y\), and \(\kappa>0\) such that
\[
d(x,F^{-1}(y))\leq\kappa d(y,F(x))
\quad\text{for all }(x,y)\in U\times V,
\]
and this is equivalent to the coderivative qualification
\[
0\in D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)
\Longrightarrow y^*=0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric regularity is equivalent, in finite dimensions, to the absence of nonzero dual vectors mapped to zero by the coderivative.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Regularity Qualifications

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

children.title: Normal-Compactness Qualifications
children.top_down_role: Sequential compactness regimes controlling limiting normal behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is an Asplund space and \(\Omega\subset X\) is locally closed at \(\bar x\).
Normals in the sequential test are Fréchet normals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed implication defines sequential normal compactness at \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: weak-star convergence in the dual space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential normal compactness for sets in Asplund spaces; it is automatic in finite dimensions.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.4 Sequential Normal Compactness of Sets p. 27
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The set \(\Omega\) is sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\in\Omega\) if every pair of sequences satisfying
\[
x_k\xrightarrow{\Omega}\bar x,
\qquad x_k^*\in\widehat N_\Omega(x_k),
\qquad x_k^*\xrightarrow{w^*}0
\]
also satisfies
\[
\|x_k^*\|\to0.
\]
Thus weak-star disappearance of nearby Fréchet normals cannot occur while their norms remain bounded away from zero. In finite-dimensional spaces, weak-star and norm convergence coincide, so this property holds automatically.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential normal compactness requires weak-star vanishing nearby Fréchet normals to vanish in norm; finite-dimensional sets satisfy it automatically.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Compactness Qualifications

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.4 Sequential Normal Compactness of Sets p. 27
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

children.title: Metric–Compactness Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Interactions between metric stability and normal compactness assumptions.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is Asplund, and \(\Omega_1,\Omega_2\subset X\) are locally closed at \(\bar x\in\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2\).
At least one set is sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\).
The limiting-normal transversality condition holds at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The intersection is sequentially normally compact and obeys the limiting-normal sum inclusion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility of normal transversality and sequential compactness in Asplund-space intersection calculus.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Sequential Normal Compactness of Set Intersections and Inverse Images p. 341
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose
\[
N_{\Omega_1}(\bar x)\cap\bigl(-N_{\Omega_2}(\bar x)\bigr)=\{0\},
\]
and at least one of \(\Omega_1\) and \(\Omega_2\) is sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\). Then \(\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2\) is sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\), and
\[
N_{\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2}(\bar x)
\subset
N_{\Omega_1}(\bar x)+N_{\Omega_2}(\bar x).
\]
Transversality removes abnormal cancellation, while normal compactness prevents nonvanishing multiplier mass from disappearing only in the weak-star topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normal transversality and sequential normal compactness together preserve compactness and yield the limiting-normal intersection rule.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric–Compactness Compatibility

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.1 Sequential Normal Compactness of Set Intersections and Inverse Images p. 341
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transversality as Metric Regularity of the Intersection Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional metric interpretation of the normal qualification used in compactness-supported intersection calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega_1,\Omega_2\subset X\) be locally closed near \(\bar x\in\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2\), where \(X\) is finite-dimensional, and define \[\Phi(x):=(\Omega_1-x)\times(\Omega_2-x).\] Then \(\Phi\) is metrically regular around \((\bar x,(0,0))\) if and only if \[N_{\Omega_1}(\bar x)\cap\bigl(-N_{\Omega_2}(\bar x)\bigr)=\{0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two locally closed finite-dimensional sets, normal transversality is equivalent to metric regularity of the lifted mapping encoding their intersection.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega_1\) and \(\Omega_2\) are locally closed near \(\bar x\in\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi\text{ is metrically regular around }(\bar x,(0,0))\iff N_{\Omega_1}(\bar x)\cap[-N_{\Omega_2}(\bar x)]=\{0\}.\)

notation.meaning: lifted multifunction encoding simultaneous membership in both sets

knowledge_statements.title: Transversality as Metric Regularity of the Intersection Mapping

children.title: Qualification Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Calculus losses caused by failure of metric or compactness support.

assumptions_latex: \(f,g:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper and lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\cap[-\partial^\infty g(\bar x)]\ne\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: Mordukhovich singular subdifferential of f at x

review_flags: Failure of the qualification does not itself assert failure of every calculus conclusion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the standard singular-subgradient qualification for a limiting sum rule.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.4 Subdifferential Calculus in Banach Spaces p. 112
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The singular-subgradient qualification for the limiting sum rule fails at \(\bar x\) precisely when
\[\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\cap[-\partial^\infty g(\bar x)]\ne\{0\}.\]
Equivalently, there is a nonzero \(v\) with \(v\in\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\) and \(-v\in\partial^\infty g(\bar x)\). In this regime the usual qualification-based derivation of \(\partial(f+g)(\bar x)\subset\partial f(\bar x)+\partial g(\bar x)\) is unavailable; the condition alone does not imply that the inclusion is false.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Qualification fails when the summands possess nonzero opposite singular subgradients. The standard sum-rule theorem then becomes inapplicable, although its conclusion may still hold accidentally.
knowledge_statements.title: Qualification Failure Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3.4 Subdifferential Calculus in Banach Spaces p. 112
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential Normal-Compactness Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact sequential failure boundary for the compactness component of the parent qualification architecture.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A locally closed set \(\Omega\subset X\) fails to be sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\in\Omega\) exactly when there exist sequences \[x_k\xrightarrow{\Omega}\bar x,\qquad x_k^*\in\widehat N_\Omega(x_k),\qquad x_k^*\xrightarrow{w^*}0,\] for which \(\|x_k^*\|\not\to0\). After passage to a subsequence and positive normalization, the witness can be chosen with \(\|x_k^*\|=1\) for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: SNC fails precisely when nearby Fréchet normals vanish weak-star without vanishing in norm; unit-norm witnesses can be used.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset X\) is locally closed at \(\bar x\in\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Omega\text{ is not SNC at }\bar x\iff\exists x_k\to_\Omega\bar x,\ x_k^*\in\widehat N_\Omega(x_k),\ x_k^*\xrightarrow{w^*}0,\ \|x_k^*\|\not\to0.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Normal-Compactness Failure

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric-Regularity Qualification Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional failure boundary for the metric component of the parent qualification architecture.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) have locally closed graph near \((\bar x,\bar y)\) in finite-dimensional spaces. The metric-regularity qualification fails exactly when \[\ker D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)\ne\{0\},\] equivalently, when some \(y^*\ne0\) satisfies \[0\in D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, the metric qualification fails exactly when a nonzero output covector is mapped to zero by the coderivative.
assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has locally closed graph near \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is not metrically regular around }(\bar x,\bar y)\iff\ker D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)\ne\{0\}.\)

notation.meaning: output covectors whose coderivative image contains zero

knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Regularity Qualification Failure

children.title: Calculus Sharpness Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Failures of equality, sharpness, or informative inclusion when qualifications break down.

children.title: One-Sided Calculus Inclusions
children.top_down_role: Calculus outcomes limited to a single containment direction.

assumptions_latex: \(f,g:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper and lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\), and \(f\) is locally Lipschitz there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(f+g)(\bar x)\subseteq\partial f(\bar x)+\partial g(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Minkowski sum of subsets of the dual space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional limiting-subdifferential sum rule with a Lipschitz summand.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.4 Subdifferential Calculus in Banach Spaces p. 112
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the Mordukhovich limiting subdifferential, local Lipschitz continuity of one summand removes its nonzero singular subgradients and yields the one-sided estimate
\[\partial(f+g)(\bar x)\subseteq\partial f(\bar x)+\partial g(\bar x).\]
This statement is only an upper calculus inclusion: it does not assert that every vector formed by adding a member of \(\partial f(\bar x)\) to a member of \(\partial g(\bar x)\) belongs to \(\partial(f+g)(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With one summand locally Lipschitz, every limiting subgradient of the sum decomposes into subgradients of the summands; the reverse inclusion need not hold.
knowledge_statements.title: One-Sided Calculus Inclusions

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3.4 Subdifferential Calculus in Banach Spaces p. 112
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

children.title: Equality Recovery Regimes
children.top_down_role: Additional structure restoring equality from one-sided estimates.

assumptions_latex: \(f,g:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(f+g)(x)=\partial f(x)+\partial g(x)\) for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex exact sum rule under relative-interior qualification.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.4 Subdifferential Calculus in Banach Spaces p. 112
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If the relative interiors of the effective domains meet, then for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\) the convex subdifferential satisfies the exact sum rule
\[\partial(f+g)(x)=\partial f(x)+\partial g(x).\]
Thus both the upper calculus inclusion and its reverse hold. In finite dimensions the convex and Mordukhovich limiting subdifferentials coincide for proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions, so the equality also supplies an equality-recovery regime for limiting calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For proper closed convex functions whose domain relative interiors intersect, the subdifferential of their sum equals the Minkowski sum of their subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.title: Equality Recovery Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3.4 Subdifferential Calculus in Banach Spaces p. 112
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

children.title: Sharpness Loss
children.top_down_role: Regimes where valid calculus estimates substantially overapproximate the target object.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(f+g)(0)=\{0\}\subsetneq[-2,2]=\partial f(0)+\partial g(0)\).
review_flags: The cited section supports limiting-subdifferential calculus; the displayed example requires direct source confirmation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete strictness example for the limiting-subdifferential sum inclusion.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.4 Subdifferential Calculus in Banach Spaces p. 112
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At the origin, \(f+g\equiv0\), while
\[\partial f(0)=[-1,1],\qquad \partial g(0)=\{-1,1\}.\]
Consequently,
\[\partial(f+g)(0)=\{0\}\subsetneq[-2,2]=\partial f(0)+\partial g(0).\]
Both functions are locally Lipschitz, so the applicable one-sided sum estimate can be strictly larger than the true limiting subdifferential even when its qualification is satisfied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The functions absolute value and minus absolute value sum to zero, but the sum of their limiting subdifferentials strictly overestimates the exact subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness Loss

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3.4 Subdifferential Calculus in Banach Spaces p. 112
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

children.title: Vacuous Estimate Regimes
children.top_down_role: Failures yielding formally valid but structurally uninformative inclusions.

assumptions_latex: A calculus rule produces an upper estimate \(\partial F(\bar x)\subseteq E(\bar x)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The estimate is vacuous at \(\bar x\) exactly when \(E(\bar x)=\mathbb{R}^n\).
review_flags: Terminological definition synthesized from the information content of a calculus inclusion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vacuity is defined relative to an ambient finite-dimensional dual space.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.4 Subdifferential Calculus in Banach Spaces p. 112
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An upper calculus estimate \(\partial F(\bar x)\subseteq E(\bar x)\) is vacuous at \(\bar x\) when
\[E(\bar x)=\mathbb{R}^n.\]
The displayed inclusion then reduces to the ambient fact \(\partial F(\bar x)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and excludes no candidate subgradient. More generally, vacuity relative to a prescribed admissible set \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) means \(E(\bar x)\supseteq A\), so the estimate supplies no restriction beyond prior admissibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A calculus upper bound is vacuous when it equals the entire ambient dual space, and therefore rules out no possible subgradient.
knowledge_statements.title: Vacuous Estimate Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3.4 Subdifferential Calculus in Banach Spaces p. 112
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vacuous Lower Calculus Estimates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute vacuity for a one-sided lower estimate in a finite-dimensional dual space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A lower calculus estimate \(L(\bar x)\subseteq\partial F(\bar x)\) is vacuous at \(\bar x\) when \[L(\bar x)=\varnothing.\] It then certifies no subgradient of \(F\) at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower subdifferential estimate is vacuous when it is empty and therefore certifies no subgradient.
assumptions_latex: A calculus rule produces a lower estimate \(L(\bar x)\subseteq\partial F(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L(\bar x)=\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.title: Vacuous Lower Calculus Estimates

children.title: Second Directional Derivatives
children.top_down_role: Directional second-order growth constructions.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), \(\bar x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and the finite directional derivative \(f'(\bar x;h)\) exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f''(\bar x;h)=\displaystyle\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(\bar x+th)-f(\bar x)-t f'(\bar x;h)}{\tfrac12t^2}\), when this limit exists finitely.

notation.meaning: first directional derivative at x along h
second directional derivative at x along h

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ray-based second directional derivative normalized by one-half squared step length.

source_refs.locator: 4.2 Second-Order Directional Derivatives p. 162

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The second directional derivative of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) in direction \(h\) is the finite limit
\[f''(\bar x;h):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(\bar x+th)-f(\bar x)-t f'(\bar x;h)}{\tfrac12t^2},\]
provided this one-sided limit exists. With this normalization, if \(f\) is twice Fréchet differentiable at \(\bar x\), then \(f''(\bar x;h)=\langle h,\nabla^2f(\bar x)h\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The second directional derivative is the quadratic-order remainder along a fixed ray after subtracting the first directional term.
knowledge_statements.title: Second Directional Derivatives

source_witnesses.locator: 4.2 Second-Order Directional Derivatives p. 162

assumptions_latex: \(\bar x\) is a local minimizer of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f''(\bar x;h)\ge0.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Raywise second-order necessary condition after the first-order term vanishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\bar x\) is a local minimizer, \(f'(\bar x;h)=0\), and the finite second directional derivative exists, then \[f''(\bar x;h)\ge0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a local minimizer, every direction with zero first-order growth has nonnegative existing second directional curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second Directional Necessary Condition
knowledge_statements.title: Second Directional Necessary Condition

assumptions_latex: The finite first and second one-sided directional derivatives exist in direction \(h\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f''(\bar x;\lambda h)=\lambda^2f''(\bar x;h).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling property of the fixed-ray second directional derivative.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-subderivative tests for local optimality and second-order growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary nonnegativity, finite-dimensional strict-positivity characterization, and reduction of strict testing to critical directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let x_0 be feasible for (P). If x_0 is a local minimizer, then d^2f(x_0\mid0)(h)\ge0 for every h\in X. If X is finite dimensional, the second-order growth condition at x_0 holds if and only if d^2f(x_0\mid0)(h)>0 for every h\in X\setminus\{0\}. Furthermore, f_-^{\downarrow}(x_0,h)>0 implies d^2f(x_0\mid0)(h)=+\infty. Hence, if f_-^{\downarrow}(x_0,\cdot)\ge0, strict second-order conditions need only be checked on C(x_0)\setminus\{0\}, where C(x_0)=\{h\in X:f_-^{\downarrow}(x_0,h)=0\}; this cone need not be convex when f is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local minimizer has a nonnegative second subderivative in every direction. In finite dimensions, strict positivity in every nonzero direction characterizes second-order growth. Directions of positive first-order growth have infinite second subderivative, so under the first-order condition it suffices to test nonzero critical directions; the critical cone may be nonconvex for a nonconvex function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_0\text{ locally optimal}\Rightarrow d^2f(x_0\mid0)(h)\ge0\ \forall h;\quad \dim X<\infty\Rightarrow[\text{second-order growth}\Longleftrightarrow d^2f(x_0\mid0)(h)>0\ \forall h\ne0];\quad f_-^{\downarrow}(x_0,h)>0\Rightarrow d^2f(x_0\mid0)(h)=+\infty

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-Order Growth from Upper Approximation Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite-dimensional sufficient condition using direction-dependent generalized multipliers and upper second-order approximation sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(X\) is finite dimensional. Let \(x_0\) be feasible for \((P)\), with \(\Lambda^g(x_0)\ne\varnothing\). For every \(h\in C(x_0)\), let \(\mathcal A(h)=\mathcal A_{K,M}(y_0,d)\), where \(y_0=G(x_0)\), \(d=DG(x_0)h\), and \(M=DG(x_0)\), be an upper second-order approximation set. If, for every \(0\ne h\in C(x_0)\), there exists \((\alpha,\lambda)\in\Lambda^g(x_0)\) such that \[D_{xx}^2L^g(x_0,\alpha,\lambda)(h,h)-\sigma(\lambda,\mathcal A(h))>0,\] then the second-order growth condition holds at \(x_0\); consequently, \(x_0\) is a strict local solution of \((P)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, if every nonzero critical direction admits a generalized multiplier for which the generalized Lagrangian curvature strictly exceeds the support term of an associated upper second-order approximation of the constraint set, then second-order growth holds and the feasible point is a strict local minimizer.
assumptions_latex: \forall h\in C(x_0),\ \mathcal A(h)=\mathcal A_{K,DG(x_0)}(G(x_0),DG(x_0)h)\text{ is an upper second-order approximation set}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Second-order growth holds at }x_0\ \Longrightarrow\ x_0\text{ is a strict local solution of }(P)

Let \(C=\operatorname{epi}f\) and \(\alpha=df(\bar x)(w)\). Under parabolic epi-differentiability, the second-order tangent geometry of the epigraph agrees with parabolic growth:
\[T^2_C((\bar x,f(\bar x));(w,\alpha))=\left\{(z,\beta)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}:\beta\ge d^2_{\mathrm p}f(\bar x)(w\mid z)\right\}.\]
Equivalently, this second-order tangent set is the epigraph of the acceleration-indexed parabolic subderivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under parabolic epi-differentiability, the epigraph of the parabolic subderivative is exactly the epigraph’s second-order tangent set in the matching direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Parabolic–Tangential Compatibility

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The regular coderivative uses the Fréchet normal at the reference graph point. The mixed coderivative permits graph-point approximation, requires \(u_k\to u\) in norm, and permits \(x_k^{*}\overset{w^{*}}{\longrightarrow}x^{*}\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection–Zero-Slice Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar smooth example separating projection of the full response from a zero-parameter-covector restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x,p)=xp\), one has \(S(x,p)=\partial_xf(x,p)=\{p\}\) and \[D^*S((0,0),0)(u)=\{(0,u)\}.\] Hence the decision-coordinate projection is \(\{0\}\) for every \(u\), whereas \(\{w:(w,0)\in D^*S((0,0),0)(u)\}\) is empty whenever \(u\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even for a smooth coupled function, projecting the full coderivative output differs from requiring the parameter component to vanish.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(u\ne0\), \(\operatorname{proj}_X D^*S((0,0),0)(u)=\{0\}\) but \(\{w:(w,0)\in D^*S((0,0),0)(u)\}=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Projection–Zero-Slice Separation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Full Coderivative Response of a Partial Subgradient Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Treats the coderivative's full product-space output as primary; coordinate projections and zero-coordinate slices are distinct derived constructions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S(x,p):=\partial_x f(x,p)\). For \(u\in X\), define the full partial second-order response by \[\mathcal H_x f((\bar x,\bar p),\bar v)(u):=D^*S((\bar x,\bar p),\bar v)(u)\subset X\times P.\] Its decision and parameter responses are the coordinate projections of this set. Requiring an output of the form \((w,0)\) is a separate zero-parameter-covector slice and is not generally equivalent to projecting onto the decision coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The coderivative of the partial subgradient mapping has a full product-space output; coordinate projections must not be confused with imposing a zero value in another coordinate.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\times P\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D^*(\partial_x f)((\bar x,\bar p),\bar v)(u)\subset X\times P\), with projections and zero-coordinate slices constituting distinct derived objects.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz bound and vanishing asymptotic subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local Lipschitz continuity bounds limiting subgradients and eliminates nonzero asymptotic subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^k\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\} be lower semicontinuous. If f is Lipschitz continuous with constant K on a neighborhood of \bar x\in\mathbb{R}^k, then \partial f(\bar x)\subseteq K\mathbb{B} and \partial^\infty f(\bar x)=\{0\}, where \mathbb{B} is the closed unit ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a lower-semicontinuous function is locally Lipschitz near a point with constant K, every limiting subgradient there has norm at most K, and its asymptotic limiting subdifferential contains only zero.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is Lipschitz continuous with constant }K\text{ on a neighborhood of }\bar x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f(\bar x)\subseteq K\mathbb{B}\quad\text{and}\quad\partial^\infty f(\bar x)=\{0\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Representations of Geometric and Analytic Epsilon-Subgradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coderivative and local-minimum characterizations at a finite-valued point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varphi:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be finite at \(\bar x\) and let \(\varepsilon\ge0\). Then \(\widehat\partial_{g\varepsilon}\varphi(\bar x)=\widehat D^*_{\varepsilon}E_\varphi(\bar x,\varphi(\bar x))(1)\). Moreover, \(x^*\in\widehat\partial_{a\varepsilon}\varphi(\bar x)\) if and only if, for every \(\gamma>0\), the function \(\psi(x):=\varphi(x)-\varphi(\bar x)-\langle x^*,x-\bar x\rangle+(\varepsilon+\gamma)\|x-\bar x\|\) has a local minimum at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a point where the function is finite, the geometric epsilon-subdifferential is the epsilon-coderivative of the epigraphical multifunction applied to one. A covector is an analytic epsilon-subgradient exactly when every positive enlargement of the epsilon norm penalty makes the associated affine-tilted auxiliary function attain a local minimum at the base point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\partial_{g\varepsilon}\varphi(\bar x)=\widehat D^*_{\varepsilon}E_\varphi(\bar x,\varphi(\bar x))(1)\), and \(x^*\in\widehat\partial_{a\varepsilon}\varphi(\bar x)\iff\forall\gamma>0,\ \bar x\text{ locally minimizes }\psi\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Partial limiting-subgradient inclusions under a horizon qualification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates partial limiting and horizon subgradients in the first variable block to projections of the corresponding full subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be lower semicontinuous and let \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{dom}f\). If \((0,\eta)\in\partial^\infty f(\bar x,\bar y)\Rightarrow\eta=0\), then
\[
\partial_x f(\bar x,\bar y)\subseteq\{\xi:\exists\eta\text{ with }(\xi,\eta)\in\partial f(\bar x,\bar y)\},
\]
and
\[
\partial_x^\infty f(\bar x,\bar y)\subseteq\{\xi:\exists\eta\text{ with }(\xi,\eta)\in\partial^\infty f(\bar x,\bar y)\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a lower semicontinuous extended-real-valued function at a point in its domain, assume that every horizon subgradient whose first component is zero also has zero second component. Then every partial limiting subgradient in the first variable block extends to a full limiting subgradient, and every partial horizon subgradient extends to a full horizon subgradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial_x f(\bar x,\bar y)\subseteq\{\xi:\exists\eta,\ (\xi,\eta)\in\partial f(\bar x,\bar y)\},\qquad \partial_x^\infty f(\bar x,\bar y)\subseteq\{\xi:\exists\eta,\ (\xi,\eta)\in\partial^\infty f(\bar x,\bar y)\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower Dini directional derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for extended-real functions using the lower joint limit over directions and positive step sizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}_\infty\), \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\). The lower Dini directional derivative of \(f\) at \(x\) in direction \(v\) is \[df(x;v)=\liminf_{\substack{w\to v\\ t\downarrow0}}\frac{f(x+tw)-f(x)}{t}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower Dini directional derivative at x in direction v is the lower limit of the forward difference quotient as positive step sizes tend to zero while the perturbed directions tend to v.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: df(x;v)=\liminf_{\substack{w\to v\\ t\downarrow0}}\frac{f(x+tw)-f(x)}{t}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coincidence with the convex subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For lower-semicontinuous convex functions, the proximal, strict, and limiting constructions all reduce to the global supporting-hyperplane subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^k\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\} be lower semicontinuous and convex, and let \bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f. Then \partial^P f(\bar x)=\widehat\partial f(\bar x)=\partial f(\bar x)=\{\xi\in\mathbb{R}^k:\xi\cdot(x-\bar x)\le f(x)-f(\bar x)\ \text{for every }x\in\mathbb{R}^k\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a lower-semicontinuous convex function, the proximal, strict, and limiting subdifferentials coincide, and they equal the usual convex subdifferential defined by the global supporting inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial^P f(\bar x)=\widehat\partial f(\bar x)=\partial f(\bar x)=\{\xi:\xi\cdot(x-\bar x)\le f(x)-f(\bar x)\ \forall x\in\mathbb{R}^k\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asymptotic proximal, strict, and limiting subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Horizontal epigraph-normal definitions of the three asymptotic subdifferential variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^k\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\} be lower semicontinuous and x\in\operatorname{dom}f. Define \partial_P^\infty f(x)=\{\xi:(\xi,0)\in N^P_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x))\}, \widehat\partial^{\infty}f(x)=\{\xi:(\xi,0)\in\widehat N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x))\}, and \partial^{\infty}f(x)=\{\xi:(\xi,0)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x))\}. Their elements are respectively asymptotic proximal, asymptotic strict, and asymptotic limiting subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a lower-semicontinuous extended-real-valued function, the asymptotic proximal, strict, and limiting subdifferentials consist of vectors whose pairing with zero is the corresponding epigraph normal at the graph point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact smooth-plus-nonsmooth second-order sum rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality rule for both normal and mixed second-order subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \( ar y\in\partial(\varphi_1+\varphi_2)( ar x)\). Suppose \(\varphi_1\in\mathcal C^1\) around \( ar x\), \(
abla\varphi_1\) is strictly differentiable at \( ar x\), \(\varphi_2:X	o\overline{\mathbb R}\) is finite at \( ar x\), and \( ar y_2:= ar y-
abla\varphi_1( ar x)\in\partial\varphi_2( ar x)\). Then, for every \(u\in X^{**}\), \[\partial^2(\varphi_1+\varphi_2)( ar x, ar y)(u)=
abla^2\varphi_1( ar x)^*u+\partial^2\varphi_2( ar x, ar y_2)(u),\] both when \(\partial^2=\partial_N^2\) and when \(\partial^2=\partial_M^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a sum of a smooth term with strictly differentiable gradient and a nonsmooth term finite at the reference point, both the normal and mixed second-order subdifferentials equal the adjoint Hessian contribution plus the corresponding second-order subdifferential of the nonsmooth term at the shifted subgradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial^2(\varphi_1+\varphi_2)(\bar x,\bar y)(u)=\nabla^2\varphi_1(\bar x)^*u+\partial^2\varphi_2(\bar x,\bar y_2)(u),\quad \partial^2\in\{\partial_N^2,\partial_M^2\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonsmooth chain rule for limiting and horizon subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composite of a locally Lipschitz vector mapping with a lower-semicontinuous extended-real-valued function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be locally Lipschitz, let \(g:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be lower semicontinuous, and let \(G(\bar u)\in\operatorname{dom}g\). Set \(f=g\circ G\). If \(\eta\in\partial^\infty g(G(\bar u))\) and \(0\in\partial(\eta\cdot G)(\bar u)\) imply \(\eta=0\), then
\[\partial f(\bar u)\subseteq\{\xi:\exists\eta\in\partial g(G(\bar u)),\ \xi\in\partial(\eta\cdot G)(\bar u)\},\]
and
\[\partial^\infty f(\bar u)\subseteq\{\xi:\exists\eta\in\partial^\infty g(G(\bar u)),\ \xi\in\partial(\eta\cdot G)(\bar u)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a locally Lipschitz mapping G and a lower-semicontinuous outer function g, the stated singular qualification ensures that every limiting subgradient of g composed with G is a subgradient of a scalarization eta·G for some limiting subgradient eta of g. The analogous inclusion holds for horizon subgradients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f(\bar u)\subseteq\bigcup_{\eta\in\partial g(G(\bar u))}\partial(\eta\cdot G)(\bar u),\qquad \partial^\infty f(\bar u)\subseteq\bigcup_{\eta\in\partial^\infty g(G(\bar u))}\partial(\eta\cdot G)(\bar u)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Limiting-subdifferential chain rule for Lipschitz compositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lipschitz scalar outer function composed with a Lipschitz vector-valued inner mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let G:\mathbb{R}^k\to\mathbb{R}^m and g:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R} be Lipschitz continuous, and let \bar x\in\mathbb{R}^k. Then
\[
\partial(g\circ G)(\bar x)\subseteq\bigcup_{\gamma\in\partial g(G(\bar x))}\partial\bigl(\gamma\cdot G\bigr)(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every limiting subgradient of the Lipschitz composition g composed with G is a limiting subgradient at the reference point of a scalarization gamma dot G for some limiting subgradient gamma of g at G of the reference point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial(g\circ G)(\bar x)\subseteq\bigcup_{\gamma\in\partial g(G(\bar x))}\partial(\gamma\cdot G)(\bar x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Limiting subdifferential and its basic structural properties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential definition from proximal subgradients, including closedness, inclusion, and boundary properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}_\infty\) and \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), \[\partial_L f(x)=\left\{\zeta:\exists x_i\to x,\ f(x_i)\to f(x),\ \zeta_i\to\zeta,\ \zeta_i\in\partial_P f(x_i)\right\}.\] If \(f\) is continuous at \(x\), the condition \(f(x_i)\to f(x)\) is automatic. Moreover, \(\partial_P f(x)\subseteq\partial_L f(x)\), and \(x_i\to x\), \(\zeta_i\to\zeta\), \(\zeta_i\in\partial_L f(x_i)\) imply \(\zeta\in\partial_L f(x)\). In general, \(\partial_L(-f)(x)\ne-\partial_L f(x)\), and points in measure-zero sets cannot in general be discarded when computing \(\partial_L f(x)\) through proximal-subgradient limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The limiting subdifferential consists of limits of proximal subgradients at points converging to x with matching function values. It contains the proximal subdifferential and has a closed graph. Continuity at x makes the function-value condition redundant; negation does not generally commute with it, and null sets cannot generally be ignored.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial_L f(x)=\{\lim_i\zeta_i:\zeta_i\in\partial_Pf(x_i),\ x_i\to x,\ f(x_i)\to f(x)\},\quad \partial_Pf(x)\subseteq\partial_Lf(x),\quad \operatorname{gph}\partial_L\text{ is closed}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closedness and sequential stability of limiting subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-set and closed-cone properties, with sequential closedness under function-value convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^k\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\} be lower semicontinuous and x\in\operatorname{dom}f. The set \partial f(x) is closed, and \partial^\infty f(x) is a closed cone. If x_i\xrightarrow{f}x, meaning x_i\to x and f(x_i)\to f(x), and \xi_i\to\xi, then \xi_i\in\partial f(x_i)\ \forall i implies \xi\in\partial f(x); likewise, \xi_i\in\partial^\infty f(x_i)\ \forall i implies \xi\in\partial^\infty f(x).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The limiting subdifferential is closed and the asymptotic limiting subdifferential is a closed cone. Both mappings have sequentially closed graphs along sequences whose points and function values converge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f(x)\text{ is closed},\quad\partial^\infty f(x)\text{ is a closed cone};\quad \xi_i\in\partial f(x_i)\Rightarrow\xi\in\partial f(x),\quad \xi_i\in\partial^\infty f(x_i)\Rightarrow\xi\in\partial^\infty f(x)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A nonsmooth mean-value inequality along a line segment.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normal and mixed second-order subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions through coderivatives of the first-order subdifferential, including coincidence regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varphi:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be finite at \(\bar x\) and let \(\bar y\in\partial\varphi(\bar x)\). For every \(u\in X^{**}\), define \(\partial_N^2\varphi(\bar x,\bar y)(u):=(D_N^*\partial\varphi)(\bar x,\bar y)(u)\) and \(\partial_M^2\varphi(\bar x,\bar y)(u):=(D_M^*\partial\varphi)(\bar x,\bar y)(u)\). These are respectively the normal and mixed second-order subdifferentials. They agree whenever the corresponding coderivatives agree, in particular in finite dimensions or when \(\partial\varphi\) is \(N\)-regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\); the common mapping is then denoted \(\partial^2\varphi(\bar x,\bar y)\). For \(\mathcal C^2\) functions its values are singletons given by the adjoint classical second derivative. Analogous upper constructions for \(\bar y\in\partial^+\varphi(\bar x)\) reduce to lower second-order subdifferentials of \(-\varphi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a function finite at the reference point and a chosen subgradient, the normal and mixed second-order subdifferentials are the normal and mixed coderivatives of its subgradient mapping. They coincide when those coderivatives coincide, including finite-dimensional and N-regular regimes; for twice continuously differentiable functions they are singleton images of the adjoint second derivative. Upper versions correspond to lower second-order subdifferentials of the negative function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial_N^2\varphi(\bar x,\bar y)(u)=(D_N^*\partial\varphi)(\bar x,\bar y)(u),\qquad \partial_M^2\varphi(\bar x,\bar y)(u)=(D_M^*\partial\varphi)(\bar x,\bar y)(u).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Upper, singular upper, and symmetric subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions at finite values, empty-set convention at infinite values, and negation identities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\varphi:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and \(|\varphi(\bar x)|<\infty\), define \[\partial^+\varphi(\bar x):=\{x^*\in X^*:(-x^*,1)\in N((\bar x,\varphi(\bar x));\operatorname{hypo}\varphi)\},\] \[\partial^{\infty,+}\varphi(\bar x):=\{x^*\in X^*:(-x^*,0)\in N((\bar x,\varphi(\bar x));\operatorname{hypo}\varphi)\}.\] Set both to \(\varnothing\) if \(|\varphi(\bar x)|=\infty\). Moreover, \(\partial^+\varphi=-\partial(-\varphi)\), \(\partial^{\infty,+}\varphi=-\partial^\infty(-\varphi)\), and \[\partial^0\varphi:=\partial\varphi\cup\partial^+\varphi,\qquad \partial^{\infty,0}\varphi:=\partial^\infty\varphi\cup\partial^{\infty,+}\varphi,\] with \(\partial^0(-\varphi)=-\partial^0\varphi\) and \(\partial^{\infty,0}(-\varphi)=-\partial^{\infty,0}\varphi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Upper subdifferentials are defined by normals to the hypograph and equal the negatives of the corresponding lower subdifferentials of the negated function. Symmetric subdifferentials are the unions of the lower and upper constructions and are equivariant under sign reversal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial^+\varphi(\bar x)=-\partial(-\varphi)(\bar x),\quad \partial^{\infty,+}\varphi(\bar x)=-\partial^\infty(-\varphi)(\bar x),\quad \partial^0\varphi=\partial\varphi\cup\partial^+\varphi,\quad \partial^{\infty,0}\varphi=\partial^\infty\varphi\cup\partial^{\infty,+}\varphi

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Limiting-subdifferential product rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite products of locally Lipschitz real-valued functions, including the nonnegative two-factor specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), be locally Lipschitz, and set \(f(x)=\prod_{i=1}^m f_i(x)\). Then
\[\partial f(\bar x)\subseteq\partial\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\left(\prod_{j\ne i}f_j(\bar x)\right)f_i\right)(\bar x).\]
For \(m=2\), if \(f_1(\bar x)\ge0\) and \(f_2(\bar x)\ge0\), then
\[\partial(f_1f_2)(\bar x)\subseteq f_1(\bar x)\partial f_2(\bar x)+f_2(\bar x)\partial f_1(\bar x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The limiting subdifferential of a finite product is contained in the subdifferential of the linear combination obtained by freezing every complementary product at the reference point. For two factors that are both nonnegative there, this yields the usual weighted Minkowski-sum inclusion.
assumptions_latex: m=2,\ f_1(\bar x)\ge0,\ f_2(\bar x)\ge0\quad\text{for the final specialization}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f(\bar x)\subseteq\partial\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\left(\prod_{j\ne i}f_j(\bar x)\right)f_i\right)(\bar x);\quad m=2,\ f_1(\bar x),f_2(\bar x)\ge0\Rightarrow\partial(f_1f_2)(\bar x)\subseteq f_1(\bar x)\partial f_2(\bar x)+f_2(\bar x)\partial f_1(\bar x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Limiting subdifferential under Lipschitz, smooth, and convex regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of the limiting subdifferential with Clarke, classical, and convex subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be Lipschitz near \(x\). Then \[\varnothing\ne\partial_L f(x)\subseteq\partial_C f(x).\] Under the standing local Lipschitz hypothesis, if \(f\) is \(C^1\) near \(x\), then \(\partial_L f(x)=\{f'(x)\}\); if \(f\) is convex, then \(\partial_L f(x)=\partial f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a function locally Lipschitz near x, the limiting subdifferential is nonempty and contained in the Clarke subdifferential. It reduces to the ordinary derivative in the continuously differentiable case and to the convex subdifferential in the convex case.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proximal, strict, and limiting subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph-normal definitions and their inclusion hierarchy for a lower-semicontinuous extended-real-valued function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^k\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\} be lower semicontinuous and x\in\operatorname{dom}f. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epigraph-normal representation by limiting and asymptotic subgradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decomposition of the limiting normal cone at an epigraph boundary point, including the nonemptiness alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^k\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\} be lower semicontinuous and x\in\operatorname{dom}f. Then N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x))=\{(\lambda\xi,-\lambda):\lambda>0,\ \xi\in\partial f(x)\}\cup\bigl(\partial^\infty f(x)\times\{0\}\bigr). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proximal and limiting subdifferential sum rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An approximate proximal sum decomposition and a Lipschitz-qualified limiting sum inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_1,f_2:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}_\infty\) be lower semicontinuous, let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f_1\cap\operatorname{dom}f_2\), and let \(\zeta\in\partial_P(f_1+f_2)(x)\). For every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist \(x_i\in B(x,\varepsilon)\) satisfying \(|f_i(x_i)-f_i(x)|<\varepsilon\) for \(i=1,2\), such that \[\zeta\in\partial_Pf_1(x_1)+\partial_Pf_2(x_2)+B(0,\varepsilon).\] If at least one of \(f_1,f_2\) is Lipschitz near \(x\), then \[\partial_L(f_1+f_2)(x)\subseteq\partial_Lf_1(x)+\partial_Lf_2(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every proximal subgradient of a sum can, to arbitrary positional, value, and subgradient accuracy, be decomposed into proximal subgradients of the summands at nearby points. If one summand is locally Lipschitz, the limiting subdifferential of the sum is contained in the sum of the limiting subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists x_1,x_2\in B(x,\varepsilon):\ |f_i(x_i)-f_i(x)|<\varepsilon,\ \zeta\in\partial_Pf_1(x_1)+\partial_Pf_2(x_2)+B(0,\varepsilon);\quad (f_1\text{ or }f_2\text{ Lipschitz near }x)\Rightarrow\partial_L(f_1+f_2)(x)\subseteq\partial_Lf_1(x)+\partial_Lf_2(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Comparison of Analytic and Geometric Epsilon-Subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided inclusion for all nonnegative epsilon and a converse with an enlarged tolerance when epsilon is below one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varphi:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) satisfy \(|\varphi(\bar x)|<\infty\). For every \(\varepsilon\ge0\), \(\widehat\partial_{a\varepsilon}\varphi(\bar x)\subset\widehat\partial_{g\varepsilon}\varphi(\bar x)\). Conversely, if \(x^*\in\widehat\partial_{g\varepsilon}\varphi(\bar x)\) for some \(0\le\varepsilon<1\), then \(x^*\in\widehat\partial_{a\widetilde\varepsilon}\varphi(\bar x)\), where \(\widetilde\varepsilon=\varepsilon(1+\|x^*\|)/(1-\varepsilon)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a finite-valued point, every analytic epsilon-subgradient is a geometric epsilon-subgradient. Conversely, a geometric epsilon-subgradient with epsilon below one is an analytic subgradient at the enlarged tolerance epsilon times one plus its norm, divided by one minus epsilon.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke subdifferential as the convex hull of limiting subgradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order generalized differentiation for locally Lipschitz functions, with equality under regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be Lipschitz near \(x\). Then \(\partial_C f(x)=\operatorname{co}\partial_L f(x)\). If, additionally, \(f\) is regular at \(x\), then \(\partial_C f(x)=\partial_L f(x)\). In particular, the latter equality holds when \(f\) is convex or continuously differentiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a function that is Lipschitz near a point, its Clarke subdifferential is the convex hull of its limiting subdifferential. If the function is also regular there—including the convex and continuously differentiable cases—the Clarke and limiting subdifferentials coincide.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential and directional criteria for convex differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collects all differentiability and exposed-face assertions in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} be convex and x\in\mathbb{R}^n. Then f is G\hat{a}teaux differentiable at x iff \partial f(x)=\{s\}; in that case f is Fr\acute{e}chet differentiable and \nabla f(x)=s. If \{d_1,\ldots,d_k\} spans \mathbb{R}^n and f'(x;d_i)=-f'(x;-d_i) for every i, then f is differentiable at x. In particular, existence of all two-sided coordinate partial derivatives implies differentiability. Furthermore, for every d\in\mathbb{R}^n, \partial[f'(x;\cdot)](d) is the exposed face F_{\partial f(x)}(d).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite convex function is differentiable exactly when its subdifferential is a singleton. Directional symmetry along a spanning set—and hence existence of all two-sided coordinate partial derivatives—is sufficient. Exposed faces of the subdifferential are subdifferentials of the directional-derivative function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ differentiable at }x\iff\partial f(x)=\{\nabla f(x)\};\quad [\operatorname{span}\{d_i\}=\mathbb{R}^n\ \land\ f'(x;d_i)=-f'(x;-d_i)\ \forall i]\Rightarrow f\text{ differentiable at }x

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ordinary and Proper Twice Epi-Differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates existence of an epi-limit from the additional requirement that the limit be proper.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(t>0\), set \[\Delta_t^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w):=\frac{f(\bar x+tw)-f(\bar x)-t\langle\bar v,w\rangle}{\tfrac12t^2}.\] The function is twice epi-differentiable at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\) when \(\Delta_t^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)\) epi-converges as \(t\downarrow0\); its epi-limit is \(d_e^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)\). It is properly twice epi-differentiable when this epi-limit is additionally a proper extended-real function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Twice epi-differentiability requires an epi-limit of normalized second-order quotients; proper twice epi-differentiability additionally requires that limit to be proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ordinary twice epi-differentiability asserts epi-convergence; proper twice epi-differentiability adds properness of \(d_e^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Ordinary and Proper Twice Epi-Differentiability

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Proto-Derivative Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex correspondence under the one-half squared-step normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper lower semicontinuous convex function, proper twice epi-differentiability of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\) is equivalent to proto-differentiability of \(\partial f\) at \((\bar x,\bar v)\). In that case, \[D(\partial f)(\bar x,\bar v)(w)=\partial\!\left(\tfrac12d_e^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)\right)(w)\qquad(w\in X).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex function, proper twice epi-differentiability is equivalent to proto-differentiability of the subgradient mapping, with the proto-derivative represented by the subdifferential of half the second epi-derivative.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D(\partial f)(\bar x,\bar v)=\partial(\tfrac12d_e^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v))\) whenever the equivalent proper twice-epi/proto-differentiability conditions hold.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Proto-Derivative Correspondence

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous, with \(\bar v\in\partial f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is twice epi-differentiable at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\) exactly when \(\Delta_t^{2}f(\bar x\mid\bar v)\) epi-converges as \(t\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the normalization with denominator one-half times the squared step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(t>0\), define the second-order difference quotient by \[\Delta_t^{2}f(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w):=\frac{f(\bar x+tw)-f(\bar x)-t\langle\bar v,w\rangle}{\tfrac12 t^{2}}.\] The function \(f\) is twice epi-differentiable at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\) if these functions epi-converge as \(t\downarrow0\). The resulting proper extended-real function, when it exists, is \[d_e^{2}f(\bar x\mid\bar v):=\operatorname{e-lim}_{t\downarrow0}\Delta_t^{2}f(\bar x\mid\bar v).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Twice epi-differentiability means that normalized second-order difference quotients have a well-defined epigraphical limit.
knowledge_statements.title: Twice Epi-Differentiability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normalization and epi-convergence formulation are recognizable standard definitions, but the record has no citation. Moreover, calling the resulting epi-limit proper may require the stronger notion of proper twice epi-differentiability rather than twice epi-differentiability alone. An authoritative definition with an exact locator is required before choosing the correct formulation.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let O\subset\mathbb{R}^n be open. children.title: Second-Order Convex Duality
children.top_down_role: Dual correspondence among second-order convex constructions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second Epi-Derivative Conjugacy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex duality under the half-quadratic normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(q_f=d_e^2f(x\mid v)\) and \(q_{f^*}=d_e^2f^*(v\mid x)\), where the second-order difference quotients use denominator \(\tfrac12t^2\). Then
\[
\frac12q_{f^*}=\left(\frac12q_f\right)^{\star},
\]
where \(\star\) on the right denotes Fenchel conjugation. Consequently,
\[
\partial\!\left(\frac12q_{f^*}\right)=\left[\partial\!\left(\frac12q_f\right)\right]^{-1}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At conjugate graph points, the half-scaled convex second epi-derivatives are Fenchel conjugates, so their subdifferentials are inverse relations.
assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb R^n\) and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
The second epi-derivatives of \(f\) at \((x,v)\) and \(f^*\) at \((v,x)\) exist as proper closed convex functions under the denominator \(\tfrac12t^2\) convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tfrac12d_e^2f^*(v\mid x)=\bigl(\tfrac12d_e^2f(x\mid v)\bigr)^{\star}\).

notation.meaning: second epi-derivative at a primal-dual graph point

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(q=d_e^2f(x\mid v)\) and \(q^*=d_e^2f^*(v\mid x)\) through epi-limits of the second-order difference quotients with denominator \(\tfrac12t^2\). Then the primal and conjugate second epi-derivatives satisfy
\[
\frac12 q^*(z)=\sup_{w\in X}\left\{\langle z,w\rangle-\frac12q(w)\right\}
\quad\text{for every }z\in X.
\]
Consequently, \(\partial(\tfrac12q)\) and \(\partial(\tfrac12q^*)\) are inverse relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At conjugate primal-dual points, the half-scaled second epi-derivatives are Fenchel conjugates, and their subdifferential relations are inverses.

notation.meaning: second-order difference quotient in direction one

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete oscillatory failure when second-order directional regularity is absent.

source_refs.locator: 4.2 Second-Order Directional Derivatives p. 162

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Although \(f\) is differentiable at \(0\) with \(f'(0)=0\), its second-order quotient in direction \(1\) is
\[
Q_t=\frac{f(t)-f(0)-t f'(0)}{\tfrac12t^2}=2\sin(1/t).
\]
Thus \(Q_t\) has no limit as \(t\downarrow0\). Removing second-order directional regularity therefore destroys the ordinary second directional derivative at the reference point; identities or chain rules requiring that derivative, twice epi-differentiability, or a compatible second-order limit are not applicable without additional hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An oscillating quadratic perturbation is differentiable at zero but has no second directional derivative there, blocking calculus that requires a stable second-order limit.
knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Calculus Failure Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is prox-regular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\) if there exist \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(r\ge0\) such that
\[
f(x')\ge f(x)+\langle v,x'-x\rangle-\frac r2\lVert x'-x\rVert^2
\]
whenever \(\lVert x-\bar x\rVert<\varepsilon\), \(\lvert f(x)-f(\bar x)\rvert<\varepsilon\), \(v\in\partial f(x)\), \(\lVert v-\bar v\rVert<\varepsilon\), and \(\lVert x'-\bar x\rVert<\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prox-regularity requires nearby subgradients to support the function locally up to one uniform negative quadratic error.
knowledge_statements.title: Prox-Regularity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Localized Proximal Resolvent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local resolvent consequence; no global uniqueness of the proximal mapping is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(T\) is an attentive localization with hypomonotonicity modulus \(r\), then for \(0<\lambda<1/r\) the inverse of \(I+\lambda T\) has a single-valued Lipschitz localization near \((\bar x+\lambda\bar v,\bar x)\). This localization is the local proximal branch and has Lipschitz modulus at most \((1-\lambda r)^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a sufficiently small proximal parameter, prox-regularity yields a locally single-valued Lipschitz proximal branch.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is prox-regular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\), with attentive hypomonotonicity modulus \(r\).
The subgradient mapping and resolvent are localized at the specified graph points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((I+\lambda T)^{-1}\) has a single-valued Lipschitz localization taking \(\bar x+\lambda\bar v\) to \(\bar x\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Localized Hypomonotonicity Characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional subgradient-attentive characterization at a selected graph point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is prox-regular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\) if and only if an \(f\)-attentive localization \(T\) of \(\partial f\) at \((\bar x,\bar v)\) and \(r\ge0\) exist such that
\[
\langle v_1-v_2,x_1-x_2\rangle\ge-r\|x_1-x_2\|^2
\]
for all \((x_i,v_i)\in\operatorname{gph}T\). Equivalently, \(T+rI\) is monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prox-regularity at a selected subgradient is equivalent to hypomonotonicity of an attentive localization of the subgradient mapping.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
The localization restricts base points, function values, and subgradients near \((\bar x,f(\bar x),\bar v)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is prox-regular at }(\bar x,\bar v)\iff T\text{ is locally hypomonotone}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential characterization of prox-regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes pointwise prox-regularity of an extended-real-valued function through localized hypomonotonicity of its subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be finite and locally lower semicontinuous at \(\bar x\), and let \(\bar v\in\partial f(\bar x)\) be a proximal subgradient. Then \(f\) is prox-regular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\) if and only if \(\partial f\) admits an \(f\)-attentive localization \(T\) around \((\bar x,\bar v)\) such that \(T+\rho I\) is monotone for some \(\rho\in\mathbb{R}_+\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a function finite and locally lower semicontinuous at the reference point and a proximal subgradient there, prox-regularity at that point for that subgradient is equivalent to the existence of an attentive localization of the subdifferential that becomes monotone after adding a nonnegative multiple of the identity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tilt-Stable Local Minimizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional localized-argmin definition under linear perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\gamma>0\), define
\[
M_\gamma(v)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{\|x-\bar x\|\le\gamma}\{f(x)-\langle v,x\rangle\}.
\]
The point \(\bar x\) is a tilt-stable local minimizer if, for some \(\gamma>0\), \(M_\gamma\) has a single-valued Lipschitz localization near \(v=0\) and \(M_\gamma(0)=\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tilt stability means that the localized minimizer under a small linear tilt is unique and Lipschitz in the tilt.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\(\bar x\) is a local minimizer with \(f(\bar x)<+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_\gamma\) is locally single-valued and Lipschitz at \((0,\bar x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform Generalized-Hessian Characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional prox-regular characterization using nearby attentive graph points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The point \(\bar x\) is a tilt-stable local minimizer if and only if there are \(\eta>0\) and \(c>0\) such that
\[
\langle w,u\rangle\ge c\|u\|^2

For sufficiently small \(\gamma>0\), define

M_\gamma(v)=\mathop{\operatorname{argmin}}_{\lVert x-\bar x\rVert\le\gamma}\{f(x)-\langle v,x\rangle\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform continuity bounds from strict-continuity moduli
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strictly continuous mappings on open sets, with uniform conclusions on convex subsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(S:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\) is strictly continuous on an open set \(O\subset\mathbb{R}^n\). For every \(\rho\ge0\), \(\operatorname{lip}_\rho S\) is finite and upper semicontinuous on \(O\), and \(\operatorname{lip}_\rho S\le\operatorname{lip}_\infty S\). If \(X\subset O\) is convex and \(\operatorname{lip}_\rho S\) is bounded above on \(X\) for every \(\rho\ge0\)—in particular, if \(X\) is compact—then \(S\) is sub-Lipschitz continuous on \(X\), with \(\kappa_\rho=\sup_{x\in X}\operatorname{lip}_\rho S(x)\). If the constants \(\kappa_\rho\) have a common upper bound \(\kappa\), then \(S\) is Lipschitz continuous on \(X\) with constant \(\kappa\). In particular, this holds when \(\operatorname{lip}_\infty S\) is bounded above on \(X\), with \(\kappa=\sup_{x\in X}\operatorname{lip}_\infty S(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a strictly continuous mapping on an open set, every truncated local Lipschitz modulus is finite, upper semicontinuous, and bounded by the full modulus. Uniform bounds on these moduli over a convex set yield sub-Lipschitz continuity; a common bound yields full Lipschitz continuity. Compact convex subsets automatically provide the separate truncated bounds.
assumptions_latex: X\subset O\text{ is convex for the uniform continuity conclusions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall\rho\ge0:\ \operatorname{lip}_\rho S\text{ is finite and usc on }O,\ \operatorname{lip}_\rho S\le\operatorname{lip}_\infty S;\quad \sup_X\operatorname{lip}_\rho S<\infty\ \forall\rho\Rightarrow S\text{ is sub-Lipschitz on }X;\quad \sup_{\rho}\sup_X\operatorname{lip}_\rho S\le\kappa\Rightarrow S\text{ is Lipschitz on }X

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict continuity and local Lipschitz moduli of a set-valued mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes continuity relative to a set, the unrestricted interior-domain version, and strict continuity at every point of a set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\), \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(\bar x\in X\). The mapping \(S\) is strictly continuous at \(\bar x\) relative to \(X\) if it is nonempty-closed-valued on a relative neighborhood of \(\bar x\) and, for every \(\rho\ge0\), \[\operatorname{lip}_{X,\rho}S(\bar x):=\limsup_{\substack{x,x'\to\bar x,\ x,x'\in X\\x\ne x'}}\frac{d_\rho(S(x'),S(x))}{\lVert x'-x\rVert}<\infty.\] Without relativization, one requires \(\bar x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}S)\), closed values around \(\bar x\), and finiteness of \(\operatorname{lip}_\rho S(\bar x)\) for every \(\rho\ge0\). The cases \(\rho=\infty\) define the corresponding full Lipschitz moduli. The mapping is strictly continuous relative to \(X\) if this property holds at every \(\bar x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict continuity at a point means that nearby pairs of arguments have truncated set values whose distance grows at a finite local linear rate, for every truncation radius. The definition may be relative to a set; strict continuity relative to X means the pointwise property holds everywhere on X.
assumptions_latex: S\text{ is nonempty-closed-valued on a neighborhood of }\bar x\text{ relative to }X
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is strictly continuous at }\bar x\text{ relative to }X\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \forall\rho\ge0:\ \operatorname{lip}_{X,\rho}S(\bar x)<\infty

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Graphically hemi-Lipschitzian, graphically Lipschitzian, graphically hemismooth, and graphically smooth mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local graph-representation classes for multifunctions between Banach spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\). The mapping \(F\) is graphically hemi-Lipschitzian around \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if there exist a Banach space \(Z=X_1\times Y_1\), a mapping \(g:X\times Y\to Z\) strictly differentiable at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with surjective derivative, neighborhoods \(O\) of \((\bar x,\bar y)\) and \(O_1\) of \(\bar z=g(\bar x,\bar y)\), and a locally Lipschitz mapping \(f:X_1\to Y_1\) such that \((\operatorname{gph}F)\cap O=g^{-1}((\operatorname{gph}f)\cap O_1)\). It is graphically Lipschitzian if, additionally, \(\nabla g(\bar x,\bar y)\) is invertible. It is graphically hemismooth at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if it is graphically hemi-Lipschitzian there and \(f\) can be chosen strictly differentiable at \(\bar u\in X_1\) with \((\bar u,f(\bar u))=\bar z\). It is graphically smooth if, additionally, \(\nabla g(\bar x,\bar y)\) is invertible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: These four classes describe graphs that locally become graphs of single-valued Lipschitz or strictly differentiable mappings under a strictly differentiable transformation. Surjectivity gives the hemi-classes, while invertibility gives the corresponding graphical Lipschitz or smooth classes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ belongs to the respective graphical class exactly under the stated representation, differentiability, and derivative conditions.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: The classes \(\mathcal C^{k+}\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smoothness classes strengthened by strict continuity of the highest-order partial derivatives on an open finite-dimensional domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(O\subset\mathbb R^n\) be open. A mapping \(F:O\to\mathbb R^m\) is of class \(\mathcal C^{k+}\) if \(F\) is of class \(\mathcal C^k\) and all its \(k\)-th partial derivatives are strictly continuous on \(O\). Thus a continuous mapping is regarded as \(\mathcal C^0\), a strictly continuous mapping as \(\mathcal C^{0+}\), and a \(\mathcal C^1\) scalar function whose gradient is strictly continuous is called \(\mathcal C^{1+}\); such a function need not be \(\mathcal C^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mapping is of class C-k-plus when it is C-k and its partial derivatives of order k are strictly continuous. In particular, C-zero-plus means strict continuity, and a C-one-plus scalar function has a strictly continuous gradient without necessarily being twice continuously differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\in\mathcal C^{k+}(O)\iff F\in\mathcal C^k(O)\text{ and every }k\text{-th partial derivative of }F\text{ is strictly continuous on }O.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential characterization of strict continuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes strict continuity of a locally lower-semicontinuous extended-real-valued function at a finite point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}} be locally lower semicontinuous at \bar x, with f(\bar x) finite. The following are equivalent: (a) f is strictly continuous at \bar x; (b) \partial^\infty f(\bar x)=\{0\}; (c) x\mapsto\widehat\partial f(x) is locally bounded at \bar x; (d) x\mapsto\partial f(x) is locally bounded at \bar x; (e) \widehat d f(\bar x)(w) is finite for every w\in\mathbb{R}^n; (f) f is finite around \bar x and, for every w\in\mathbb{R}^n, x\mapsto d f(x)(w) is bounded above on some neighborhood of \bar x. When these conditions hold, \partial f(\bar x) is nonempty and compact, and \operatorname{lip}f(\bar x)=\max_{\lVert w\rVert=1}\widehat d f(\bar x)(w)=\max_{v\in\partial f(\bar x)}\lVert v\rVert.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a function locally lower semicontinuous at a point where it is finite, strict continuity is equivalent to a trivial horizon subdifferential, local boundedness of either the regular or limiting subdifferential mapping, finiteness of the regular directional derivative in every direction, and the stated local boundedness of directional derivatives. Under these conditions the limiting subdifferential is nonempty and compact, and the exact Lipschitz modulus equals both the largest regular directional derivative over unit directions and the largest subgradient norm.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is locally lsc at }\bar x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (a)\Longleftrightarrow(b)\Longleftrightarrow(c)\Longleftrightarrow(d)\Longleftrightarrow(e)\Longleftrightarrow(f),\quad \partial f(\bar x)\ne\varnothing\text{ is compact},\quad \operatorname{lip}f(\bar x)=\max_{\lVert w\rVert=1}\widehat d f(\bar x)(w)=\max_{v\in\partial f(\bar x)}\lVert v\rVert.
