knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-dimensional mixed-convergence analogue; the precise variant is source-sensitive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mixed-coderivative nondegeneracy condition at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is \[D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(0)=\{0\}.\] Here membership \(x^*\in D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\) is obtained from nearby Fréchet normals \((x_k^*,-y_k^*)\) to \(\operatorname{gph}F\), with primal graph points converging in norm, \(y_k^*\to y^*\) in norm, and \(x_k^*\overset{w^*}{\longrightarrow}x^*\). Under the additional compactness or qualification hypotheses appropriate to the chosen mixed coderivative, this kernel condition yields the corresponding Lipschitz-like stability criterion.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^*\) solve \(\operatorname{VI}(K(\mathbf p^*),F(\cdot,\mathbf p^*))\) and satisfy MFCQ, CRCQ, and SCOC. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes SCOC by uniform nonzero determinant orientation and states the resulting positivity of the relevant Schur-complement determinants.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz-like stability of irregular canonical perturbations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient coderivative qualification for canonical systems whose base mapping admits a strong approximation rather than classical differentiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\bar y\in\Sigma(\bar x,\bar q)\), \(\bar s:=\bar q-f(\bar x,\bar y)\), and let \(X,Y,Z\) be Asplund spaces. Suppose that \(f\) admits a strong approximation in \(y\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\), is continuous near this point, is locally Lipschitz in \(x\) uniformly in \(y\), and \(f(\bar x,\cdot)\) is PSNC at \(\bar y\). Suppose also that \(Q\) has closed graph around \((\bar x,\bar y,\bar s)\) and is SNC there. If \[\big[y^*\in D_y^*f(\bar x,\bar y)(z^*),\ (x^*,-y^*)\in D^*Q(\bar x,\bar y,\bar s)(z^*)\big]\Longrightarrow x^*=y^*=z^*=0,\] then \(\Sigma\) is Lipschitz-like around \((\bar x,\bar q,\bar y)\). If \(f(\bar x,\cdot)\) is strictly Lipschitz at \(\bar y\), this qualification is equivalently expressible as \[\big[y^*\in\partial_y\langle z^*,f\rangle(\bar x,\bar y),\ (x^*,-y^*)\in D^*Q(\bar x,\bar y,\bar s)(z^*)\big]\Longrightarrow x^*=z^*=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong approximation, continuity, uniform parameter Lipschitzness, PSNC, closed-graph, and SNC assumptions, together with a trivial coderivative interaction, imply the Aubin property of the canonical solution map. Strict Lipschitzness of the state mapping gives the stated equivalent scalarized-subdifferential qualification.
assumptions_latex: \bar y\in\Sigma(\bar x,\bar q),\qquad \bar s=\bar q-f(\bar x,\bar y)
f\text{ admits a strong approximation in }y\text{ at }(\bar x,\bar y)
f\text{ is continuous and locally Lipschitz in }x\text{ uniformly in }y
f(\bar x,\cdot)\text{ is PSNC at }\bar y
Q\text{ has closed graph around and is SNC at }(\bar x,\bar y,\bar s)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Sigma\text{ is Lipschitz-like around }(\bar x,\bar q,\bar y).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coderivative characterizations of the Aubin property for canonically perturbed variational-system solution maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\bar y\in\Sigma(\bar x,\bar q)\), where \(X,Y,Z\) are Asplund spaces, \(f:X\times Y\to Z\) is strictly differentiable in \(y\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) and locally Lipschitz in \(x\) uniformly in \(y\), and \(Q:X\times Y\rightrightarrows Z\) has closed graph and is SNC at \((\bar x,\bar y,\bar s)\), with \(\bar s:=\bar q-f(\bar x,\bar y)\). children.title: Subdifferential Duality
children.top_down_role: Dual relationships among directional growth, support constructions, epigraph normals, and subgradients.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subderivative–subgradient duality for regular functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order duality at a subdifferentially regular point, with an unconditional horizon-domain polar relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be subdifferentially regular at \(\bar x\). Then \[\partial f(\bar x)\neq\varnothing\iff df(\bar x)(0)\neq-\infty.\] Under these equivalent conditions, \(f\) is properly epi-differentiable at \(\bar x\), with epi-derivative \(df(\bar x)\), and for every \(w\in\mathbb R^n\), \[df(\bar x)(w)=\sigma_{\partial f(\bar x)}(w)=\sup_{v\in\partial f(\bar x)}\langle v,w\rangle,\] \[\partial f(\bar x)=\{v:\langle v,w\rangle\leq df(\bar x)(w)\ \forall w\}.\] Moreover, \(\partial f(\bar x)\) is closed and convex and \(df(\bar x)\) is lsc and sublinear. Without requiring the equivalent nonemptiness conditions, \[\partial^\infty f(\bar x)=[\operatorname{dom}df(\bar x)]^*,\qquad [\partial^\infty f(\bar x)]^*=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{dom}df(\bar x)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a subdifferentially regular point, the subdifferential is nonempty exactly when the subderivative at zero is not minus infinity. In that regime the subderivative is the support function of the closed convex subdifferential, and each object recovers the other; proper epi-differentiability also follows. Independently of that nonemptiness condition, the horizon subdifferential and the domain of the subderivative satisfy the stated polar identities.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every direction \(d\in\mathbb R^n\), the convex directional derivative \[f'(x;d):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+td)-f(x)}{t}\] equals the support function of the convex subgradient set at \(x\): \[f'(x;d)=\sigma_{\partial f(x)}(d)=\sup_{v\in\partial f(x)}\langle v,d\rangle.\] Thus the directional first-order data of \(f\) are precisely the support values generated by \(\partial f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper closed convex function, its directional derivative is the support function of its subdifferential.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Boundary Failure of the Forward Support Identity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the directional-derivative support identity at a convex domain boundary where no finite subgradient exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(f:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by
\[
f(t)=\begin{cases}-\sqrt t,&t\geq0,\\+\infty,&t<0.\end{cases}
\]
Then \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, but \(\partial f(0)=\varnothing\). Moreover,
\[
f'(0;d)=\begin{cases}-\infty,&d>0,\\0,&d=0,\\+\infty,&d<0,
\end{cases}
\]
whereas, under the convention \(\sup\varnothing=-\infty\), \(\sigma_{\partial f(0)}\equiv-\infty\). Hence the forward identity \(f'(0;\cdot)=\sigma_{\partial f(0)}\) can fail at a convex boundary point outside the relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex function can have an empty subdifferential at a domain boundary, causing its directional derivative to differ from the support function of that empty set.
assumptions_latex: The support function of the empty set uses \(\sup\varnothing=-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(0)=\varnothing\) and \(f'(0;\cdot)\neq\sigma_{\partial f(0)}\).

notation.meaning: support function of the empty set, identically minus infinity under the stated convention

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Boundary Failure of the Forward Support Identity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sublinearity of the Directional Support Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural consequence of representing convex directional derivatives as support functions of subgradient sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the convex support representation at \(x\), the map
\[
d\mapsto f'(x;d)=\sigma_{\partial f(x)}(d)
\]
is lower semicontinuous, positively homogeneous, and subadditive as an extended-real-valued function. In particular,
\[
f'(x;\lambda d)=\lambda f'(x;d)\quad(\lambda\geq0),
\qquad
f'(x;d_1+d_2)\leq f'(x;d_1)+f'(x;d_2).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Because it is a support function, the convex directional derivative is a lower-semicontinuous sublinear function of direction.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d\mapsto f'(x;d)=\sigma_{\partial f(x)}(d)\) is lower semicontinuous and sublinear.

notation.meaning: one-sided convex directional derivative as a function of direction

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H_S(\zeta)=\sup_{x\in S}\langle\zeta,x\rangle\quad(\zeta\in X^*).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The subdifferential is recovered from the directional derivative by intersecting its supporting half-spaces: \[\partial f(x)=\bigcap_{d\in\mathbb R^n}\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\langle v,d\rangle\leq f'(x;d)\}.\] Indeed, the directional derivative is the support function of the nonempty closed convex set \(\partial f(x)\), and a closed convex set is uniquely determined by its support function. The formula therefore recovers every subgradient using only directional first-order data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All convex subgradients are recovered as the vectors whose pairing with every direction does not exceed the directional derivative.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary-Point Recovery Without Subdifferentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp finite-dimensional convex recovery formula at arbitrary domain points, including points with an empty subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex and let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). With the one-sided directional derivative interpreted in the extended-real sense,
\[
\partial f(x)=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\langle v,d\rangle\leq f'(x;d)\ \text{for every }d\in\mathbb R^n\}.
\]
No relative-interior or nonemptiness assumption on \(\partial f(x)\) is required; at a boundary point the displayed intersection may be empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper convex function, universal directional inequalities recover the convex subdifferential at every domain point, even when that subdifferential is empty.
assumptions_latex: \(f'(x;d)\) is interpreted as an extended-real one-sided directional derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)=\{v:\langle v,d\rangle\leq f'(x;d)\ \forall d\in\mathbb R^n\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The support function of a dual set \(C\subset X^*\) is evaluated on primal directions and is defined by \[\sigma_C(d):=\sup_{x^*\in C}\langle x^*,d\rangle\quad(d\in X),\] with the canonical pairing \(\langle x^*,d\rangle:=x^*(d)\). In a Hilbert space identified with its dual by the Riesz map, this pairing may be written as an inner product. Without such an identification, primal directions and dual subgradients remain distinct types.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Support functions pair dual subgradients with primal directions; only a Hilbert-space identification turns this pairing into an inner product.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Pairing Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak-Star Closed Convex Hull Determined by Pairings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological precision for the object identified by primal-direction support values in a Banach dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a real Banach space and let \(C\subset X^*\) be nonempty. Then
\[
\sigma_C=\sigma_{\operatorname{cl}^{w^*}\operatorname{co}C},
\qquad
\operatorname{cl}^{w^*}\operatorname{co}C=\{x^*\in X^*: \langle x^*,d\rangle\leq\sigma_C(d)\ \forall d\in X\}.
\]
Thus canonical pairings with primal directions determine exactly the weak-star closed convex hull of a dual set, not its nonconvex or non-weak-star-closed structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Support values on primal directions determine precisely the weak-star closed convex hull of a subset of the Banach dual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_C=\sigma_{\operatorname{cl}^{w^*}\operatorname{co}C}\) and \(\operatorname{cl}^{w^*}\operatorname{co}C=\{x^*: \langle x^*,d\rangle\leq\sigma_C(d)\ \forall d\in X\}\).

support function evaluated through the canonical dual pairing

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the nonconvex function \(f(x)=-|x|\), the limiting subdifferential at the origin is \(\partial f(0)=\{-1,1\}\). Its support function is \[\sigma_{\partial f(0)}(d)=\max\{-d,d\}=|d|.\] However, the directional derivative is \[f'(0;d)=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{-|td|}{t}=-|d|.\] Therefore \(f'(0;d)\neq\sigma_{\partial f(0)}(d)\) whenever \(d\neq0\), demonstrating that the convex support representation does not extend to general nonconvex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the concave cusp of minus absolute value, the limiting-subgradient support is positive absolute value while the directional derivative is negative absolute value.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support Data Lose Nonconvex Subgradient Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General information-loss boundary behind support-based recovery of nonconvex limiting-subgradient sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every nonempty set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\),
\[
\sigma_C=\sigma_{\overline{\operatorname{co}}C}.
\]
Hence support data cannot distinguish a nonconvex limiting-subgradient set from its closed convex hull. In particular, \(C=\{-1,1\}\) and \(\overline{\operatorname{co}}C=[-1,1]\) both have support function \(d\mapsto|d|\), although the sets differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Support scalarization retains only the closed convex hull, so it cannot recover the nonconvex structure of a limiting-subgradient set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_C=\sigma_{\overline{\operatorname{co}}C}\); therefore support data do not uniquely determine a nonconvex set.
knowledge_statements.title: Support Data Lose Nonconvex Subgradient Structure

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At the boundary point \((x,f(x))\) of the epigraph, limiting normals encode two subgradient slices. The ordinary limiting subdifferential is \[\partial f(x):=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:(v,-1)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x))\},\] while the horizontal slice gives the singular subdifferential \[\partial^\infty f(x):=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:(v,0)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x))\}.\] Thus vertical component \(-1\) represents ordinary first-order slopes, whereas vertical component \(0\) records horizontal epigraph-normal contributions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordinary and singular subgradients are respectively the vertical minus-one and horizontal slices of the epigraph's limiting normal cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stratification of the Epigraph Normal Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reconstruction of the full limiting epigraph normal cone from its negative-vertical and horizontal strata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous and let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). Then
\[
N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x))=\{\lambda(v,-1):\lambda>0,\ v\in\partial f(x)\}\cup\{(v,0):v\in\partial^\infty f(x)\}.
\]
Thus every negative-vertical normal is a positive multiple of a normalized subgradient normal, while the zero-height stratum consists of singular normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The full limiting epigraph normal cone consists of positive multiples of normalized ordinary-subgradient normals together with horizontal singular normals.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
Limiting normals, limiting subgradients, and horizon subgradients are used.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be an Asplund space, let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and write \(\bar r=f(\bar x)\). The limiting subdifferential is the normalized nonhorizontal slice of the limiting normal cone to the epigraph:
\[
\partial f(\bar x)=\bigl\{x^*\in X^*\mid (x^*,-1)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,\bar r)\bigr\}.
\]
Thus every limiting subgradient corresponds to an epigraph normal whose scalar component equals \(-1\), and conversely every normal in that slice determines a limiting subgradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The limiting subdifferential is exactly the slice of the epigraph’s limiting normal cone whose vertical component equals minus one.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be an Asplund space and let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). The horizontal slice of the limiting epigraph normal cone is
\[

\]
These zero-vertical-component normals record singular first-order behavior. In particular, they cannot generally be recovered by rescaling normals with a strictly negative vertical component to the normalized level \(-1\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conic Structure of Horizontal Contributions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic algebraic and topological structure of the horizontal limiting-normal slice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous and let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). Then
\[
\partial^\infty f(x)=\{v:(v,0)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x))\}
\]
is a closed cone containing the origin. Hence \(v\in\partial^\infty f(x)\) and \(\lambda\geq0\) imply \(\lambda v\in\partial^\infty f(x)\). Convexity need not hold in the nonconvex setting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The horizon subdifferential is a closed cone containing zero, but it need not be convex for a nonconvex function.

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraphical Representation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the normalization argument underlying epigraph-normal representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be an Asplund space, let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and let \((x^*,\alpha)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\). Epigraph geometry gives \(\alpha\leq 0\). If \(\alpha<0\), positive homogeneity permits normalization and yields \(x^*/(-\alpha)\in\partial f(\bar x)\). If \(\alpha=0\), normalization to vertical level \(-1\) is impossible, and \(x^*\in\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\). If \(\bar x\notin\operatorname{dom}f\), there is no finite boundary point \((\bar x,f(\bar x))\) at which either slice representation can be formed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative vertical epigraph normals can be normalized into ordinary subgradients, whereas horizontal normals cannot and instead represent singular subgradients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha<0\Rightarrow x^*/(-\alpha)\in\partial f(\bar x)\), whereas \(\alpha=0\Rightarrow x^*\in\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Convexity–Smooth Conjugate Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space conjugacy between quadratic strong convexity and Lipschitz smoothness of the Fenchel conjugate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f:H	o(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and let \(\mu>0\). Then \(f- rac{\mu}{2}\|\cdot\|^2\) is convex if and only if \(f^*\) is finite and Fréchet differentiable on \(H\) with \[
abla f^*=(\partial f)^{-1},\qquad \|
abla f^*(p)-
abla f^*(q)\|\le  rac1\mu\|p-q\|\quad(p,q\in H).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex function is strongly convex exactly when its conjugate is globally smooth with the reciprocal Lipschitz modulus.
assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex if and only if \(f^*\) is Fréchet differentiable on \(H\) and \(\nabla f^*\) is \(1/\mu\)-Lipschitz.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fenchel–Young Equality and Subgradient Inversion in Hilbert Space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topology-unambiguous Hilbert-space form of conjugate-subgradient duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. For \(x,p\in H\), \[p\in\partial f(x)\iff f(x)+f^*(p)=\langle p,x\rangle\iff x\in\partial f^*(p).\] Equivalently, \(\partial f^*=(\partial f)^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fenchel–Young equality holds exactly for primal-dual subgradient pairs, so the subgradient relations of a closed convex function and its conjugate are inverse.
assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\in\partial f(x)\iff f(x)+f^*(p)=\langle p,x\rangle\iff x\in\partial f^*(p)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel–Young equality and inversion of convex subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a locally convex space paired with \(X^*\), and let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. For every \(x\in X\) and \(x^*\in X^*\),
\[
x^*\in\partial f(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
f(x)+f^*(x^*)=\langle x^*,x\rangle
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x\in\partial f^*(x^*).
\]
Equivalently, the subgradient relations of a closed convex function and its conjugate are inverse relations: \(\partial f^*=(\partial f)^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector is a subgradient exactly when Fenchel–Young equality holds, equivalently when the primal point subdifferentiates the conjugate.
knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate-Subgradient Interface

notation.meaning: projection onto parameter and value coordinates

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex perturbation model viewed through projection of its epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(U\) be locally convex spaces and define \(v(u)=\inf_{x\in X}\Phi(x,u)\) for a proper convex function \(\Phi:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\). Then
\[
\pi_{U\times\mathbb R}(\operatorname{epi}\Phi)
\subseteq \operatorname{epi}v
\subseteq \operatorname{cl}\pi_{U\times\mathbb R}(\operatorname{epi}\Phi).
\]
The first inclusion becomes equality when the infimum is attained whenever \(v(u)\le r\); closure of the projected epigraph guarantees lower semicontinuity of \(v\). Hence normals and subgradients of \(v\) describe supporting geometry of the projected perturbation epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A perturbation value function is governed by the projection of the perturbation epigraph; nonattainment or nonclosed projection creates a geometric gap.
knowledge_statements.title: Perturbation-Function Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projected-epigraph inclusions are plausible, but the attainment and closed-projection consequences require an authoritative source and precise epigraph conventions. The representation kind fits the container.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-Stage Value Function and Differentiable Resource Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of a parameterized second-stage value function and its local sensitivity when differentiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\beta\in\mathbb R^{m_2}\), define
\[
\phi(\beta)=\inf_{y\in\mathcal P_2(\beta)\cap Y} d^2y\in\mathbb R\cup\{\pm\infty\}.
\]
If \(\phi\) is differentiable at \(b\), then its first-order change in direction \(h\) is \(D\phi(b)[h]=\langle\nabla\phi(b),h\rangle\), so the gradient records the marginal change in optimal value under resource perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The value function gives the optimal second-stage value for each resource vector. If it is differentiable at b, its gradient describes the first-order marginal change in that value as resources change.
assumptions_latex: \phi\text{ is differentiable at }b\text{ for the sensitivity interpretation}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \phi(\beta)=\inf_{y\in\mathcal P_2(\beta)\cap Y}d^2y,\qquad D\phi(b)[h]=\langle\nabla\phi(b),h\rangle.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Marginal-Subgradient Lifting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact convex marginal formula under properness and attainment of the infimal projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex on finite-dimensional spaces, define \(v(u)=\inf_x\Phi(x,u)\), and suppose \(v\) is proper and \(S(\bar u)\ne\varnothing\). Then, for every \(\bar x\in S(\bar u)\), \[\partial v(\bar u)=\{u^*:(0,u^*)\in\partial\Phi(\bar x,\bar u)\}.\] Consequently the same set is obtained by taking the union over all \(\bar x\in S(\bar u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex value-function subgradient is exactly a perturbation subgradient with zero decision component at any attained optimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\bar x\in S(\bar u)\), \(\partial v(\bar u)=\{u^*:(0,u^*)\in\partial\Phi(\bar x,\bar u)\}\).

notation.meaning: argmin set of the marginal problem

assumptions_latex: \(\Phi:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
\(v(u):=\inf_x\Phi(x,u)\) is finite at \(\bar u\), with an optimizer \(\bar x\).
A marginal subdifferential qualification holds at \((\bar x,\bar u)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial v(\bar u)=\{u^*:(0,u^*)\in\partial\Phi(\bar x,\bar u)\text{ for some }\bar x\in S(\bar u)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex marginal-function formula under attainment and an applicable projection qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Phi:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and let \(v(u)=\inf_x\Phi(x,u)\). Suppose \(S(\bar u)\neq\varnothing\) and a qualification ensuring exact marginal subdifferential calculus holds. Then
\[
\partial v(\bar u)=igl\{u^*\in U^*\mid \text{for some }\bar x\in S(\bar u),\ (0,u^*)\in\partial\Phi(\bar x,\bar u)\bigr\}.
\]
The zero component expresses stationarity in the eliminated decision variable, while \(u^*\) is the first-order sensitivity with respect to the parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A value-function subgradient is the parameter component of a perturbation subgradient whose decision-variable component vanishes at an optimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Value-Function Subgradients

children.title: Multiplier Representations
children.top_down_role: Dual-variable representations of value-function sensitivity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Right-Hand-Side Multipliers Represent Value Subgradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex inequality system under Slater's condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[v(u)=\inf\{f(x):g(x)\le u\},\] where \(f\) and every component of \(g\) are proper convex functions on \(\mathbb R^n\). Suppose \(v(\bar u)\) is finite and attained and there is \(x^0\in\operatorname{dom}f\) with \(g(x^0)<\bar u\). For the Lagrangian \(L(x,\lambda;u)=f(x)+\langle\lambda,g(x)-u\rangle\), let \(\Lambda(\bar u)\) be the set of optimal multipliers. Then \[\partial v(\bar u)=\{-\lambda:\lambda\in\Lambda(\bar u)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under finite-dimensional convex Slater regularity, subgradients of a right-hand-side value function are exactly the negatives of its optimal inequality multipliers.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and the components of \(g\) are proper convex functions on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial v(\bar u)=\{-\lambda:\lambda\in\Lambda(\bar u)\}\).

notation.meaning: set of optimal nonnegative Lagrange multipliers

knowledge_statements.title: Right-Hand-Side Multipliers Represent Value Subgradients

assumptions_latex: \(v(u)=\inf\{f(x):g(x)\le u\}\) is a convex program with attained optimum at \(\bar u\).
Strong duality and multiplier attainment hold at \(\bar u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial v(\bar u)=\{-\lambda:\lambda\in\Lambda(\bar u)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Right-hand-side sensitivity for a finite-dimensional convex inequality-constrained problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
v(u)=\inf\bigl\{f(x)\mid g(x)\leq u\bigr\},
\]
where \(f\) and the components of \(g\) are convex, and suppose the optimum, strong duality, and dual attainment hold at \(\bar u\). With Lagrangian \(L(x,\lambda;u)=f(x)+\langle\lambda,g(x)-u\rangle\), let \(\Lambda(\bar u)\) be the set of optimal multipliers \(\lambda\geq0\). Under the exact sensitivity qualification,
\[
\partial v(\bar u)=\{-\lambda\mid\lambda\in\Lambda(\bar u)\}.
\]
The sign is determined by parameterizing the constraints as \(g(x)\leq u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For right-hand-side perturbations, value-function subgradients are the negatives of optimal inequality multipliers, provided exact convex duality and sensitivity qualifications hold.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier Representations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The multiplier sign is consistent with constraints parameterized as g(x)≤u, and representation is the correct kind. However, strong duality and multiplier attainment alone do not transparently establish the full subdifferential equality; the exact sensitivity qualification and an authoritative locator are required.

children.title: Solution-Map Contributions
children.top_down_role: Influence of minimizing selections and solution-map geometry on sensitivity estimates.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Single Active Minimizer Does Not Determine Value Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite active-set example isolating the contribution of all minimizing solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\{-1,1\}\), \(\Phi(x,u)=xu\), and \(v(u)=\min_{x\in X}\Phi(x,u)=-|u|\). At \(\bar u=0\), \(S(0)=X\), while \(\Phi'_u(1,0;d)=d\) and \(\Phi'_u(-1,0;d)=-d\). Hence \[v'(0;d)=-|d|=\min_{x\in S(0)}\Phi'_u(x,0;d).\] An arbitrary single active minimizer can therefore give the wrong slope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With two active minimizers of opposite parameter slopes, an arbitrary optimizer need not determine the value derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v'(0;d)=\min_{x\in S(0)}\Phi'_u(x,0;d)=-|d|\), while one arbitrary active minimizer need not yield this value.

notation.meaning: directional derivative of the marginal value

knowledge_statements.title: A Single Active Minimizer Does Not Determine Value Sensitivity

assumptions_latex: \(\Phi(x,\cdot)\) is directionally differentiable near \(\bar u\), uniformly enough for the envelope formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v'(\bar u;d)=\min_{x\in S(\bar u)}\Phi'_u(x,\bar u;d)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional envelope formula showing how multiple optimal solutions contribute to value sensitivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be compact, define \(v(u)=\min_{x\in X}\Phi(x,u)\), and suppose \(S(\bar u)\neq\varnothing\). Assume \(\Phi(x,\cdot)\) is directionally differentiable and the dependence on \(x\) is regular enough to interchange the active minimum and directional limit. Then, for every parameter direction \(d\),
\[
v'(\bar u;d)=\min_{x\in S(\bar u)}\Phi'_u(x,\bar u;d).
\]
Thus all solutions active at \(\bar u\) may affect directional sensitivity; selecting an arbitrary single optimizer is generally invalid when their directional derivatives differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The directional derivative of a minimum value is the minimum of parameter-directional derivatives across all currently optimal solutions, under envelope regularity.
knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Map Contributions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated directional envelope formula is a recognizable Danskin-type result, but 'regular enough' is not a verifiable hypothesis. A source must specialize the continuity, compactness, and directional differentiability conditions supporting the minimum formula.

At \(u=0\), the unique optimizer is \(\bar x=0\), the active constraint gradient vanishes, no \(\lambda\ge0\) satisfies \(0=1+2\lambda\bar x\), and \(\partial v(0)=\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure modes of multiplier-based sensitivity when qualification, strong duality, or dual attainment is absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(v(u)=\inf\{f(x)\mid g(x)\leq u\}\), the representation
\[
\partial v(\bar u)=\{-\lambda\mid\lambda\in\Lambda(\bar u)\}
\]
is not unconditional. If a constraint qualification fails, the dual optimum may not be attained, so \(\Lambda(\bar u)=\varnothing\) even while \(\partial v(\bar u)\neq\varnothing\). A duality gap may also prevent multipliers from supporting the primal value function. Consequently, multiplier vectors provide an exact sensitivity description only after the relevant strong-duality, attainment, and subdifferential-calculus conditions are verified.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\) is convex, but it need not be lower semicontinuous or have a closed epigraph.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic structural property of partial minimization without an attainment or closedness assertion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\Phi:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is convex and \(v(u):=\inf_x\Phi(x,u)\) never equals \(-\infty\), then \(v\) is convex as an extended-real function. Lower semicontinuity and closedness of \(\operatorname{epi}v\) do not follow from convexity alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial minimization preserves convexity but need not preserve lower semicontinuity or closed epigraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity Preservation under Infimal Projection
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Preservation under Infimal Projection

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v(u)=\inf_{x\in X}\Phi(x,u)\).

notation.meaning: infimal projection of the perturbation function onto the parameter space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real infimal projection obtained by eliminating the decision variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given vector spaces \(X\) and \(U\) and an extended-real function \(\Phi:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), its infimal projection onto \(U\) is the function \(v:U\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) defined by
\[
v(u):=\inf_{x\in X}\Phi(x,u).
\]
The projection is proper when it never equals \(-\infty\) and is finite somewhere. Its effective domain is \(\operatorname{dom}v=\{u\in U\mid \exists x\in X,\ \Phi(x,u)<+\infty\}\), provided no projected value equals \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infimal projection eliminates the decision variable by taking the infimum of the joint function over every decision-space fiber.
knowledge_statements.title: Infimal Projections

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition of infimal projection is precise, internally consistent, and correctly classified, but the record supplies no source with a specific locator.

children.title: Conjugate Representations
children.top_down_role: Dual descriptions associated with projected or marginal functions.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(U\) are paired locally convex spaces.

notation.meaning: Fenchel conjugate on the relevant paired space
zero functional on the eliminated space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel conjugate of an infimal projection as a zero-slice of the joint conjugate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(v(u)=\inf_{x\in X}\Phi(x,u)\), where \(\Phi:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and \(v\) is proper. For every \(u^*\in U^*\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
v^*(u^*)&=\sup_{u\in U}\bigl(\langle u^*,u\rangle-v(u)\bigr)\\
&=\sup_{(x,u)\in X\times U}\bigl(\langle u^*,u\rangle-\Phi(x,u)\bigr)\\
&=\Phi^*(0,u^*).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus conjugating after eliminating \(x\) is exactly restriction of the joint conjugate to the zero dual coordinate associated with \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of an infimal projection equals the joint conjugate restricted to zero in the eliminated variable’s dual coordinate.
knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate Representations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The zero-dual-coordinate conjugate identity is mathematically standard and the representation kind fits, but no inspectable citation is supplied.

children.title: Dual Commutation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural settings where projection behavior is compatible with conjugate operations.

assumptions_latex: \(\Phi:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and \(v(u)=\inf_x\Phi(x,u)\) is proper.
For every \(\bar u\in U\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), some neighborhood \(V\) of \(\bar u\) makes \(\{x:\exists u\in V,\ \Phi(x,u)\le\alpha\}\) bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every finite value \(v(u)\) is attained, \(v\) is proper lower semicontinuous convex, and \(v=v^{**}\) with \(v^*(u^*)=\Phi^*(0,u^*)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional no-escape condition ensuring attainment and exact closed-convex recovery of an infimal projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v(u)=\inf_x\Phi(x,u)\), where \(\Phi\) is proper lower semicontinuous convex on finite-dimensional \(X\times U\) and is locally level-bounded in \(x\) uniformly in \(u\). If \(v\) is proper, then every finite marginal value is attained, \(v\) is lower semicontinuous and convex, and \(v=v^{**}\) together with \(v^*(u^*)=\Phi^*(0,u^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform local level-boundedness in the eliminated variable prevents escape of minimizing sequences, making the marginal attained and closed and its Fenchel recovery exact.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Inf-Compactness Commutation Regime
knowledge_statements.title: Local Inf-Compactness Commutation Regime

assumptions_latex: \(\Phi:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\) is proper closed convex and \(v=v^{**}\), with \(v^*(u^*)=\Phi^*(0,u^*)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed-projection regime in which infimal projection and Fenchel closure commute exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(U\) be finite-dimensional and let \(\Phi:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Define \(v(u)=\inf_x\Phi(x,u)\). If \(v\) is proper and \(\pi_{U\times\mathbb R}(\operatorname{epi}\Phi)\) is closed, then \(v\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Consequently,
\[
v=v^{**}
\quad\text{and}\quad
v^*(u^*)=\Phi^*(0,u^*)
\]
for every \(u^*\in U^*\). Thus infimal projection, conjugation, and biconjugate closure commute without an additional closure correction in this regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closedness of the projected epigraph ensures that infimal projection remains closed convex, so conjugation and biconjugation introduce no closure gap.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Commutation Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind is appropriate, and the conclusion is plausible when properness and closedness identify the projected epigraph with epi v. An authoritative source is required to verify that identification and the claimed no-closure-gap regime.

children.title: Closure Gaps
children.top_down_role: Dual discrepancies caused by missing closedness, attainment, or regularity.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
\(F:X\times Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and \(h(x):=\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y)\) is proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h^*(x^*)=F^*(x^*,0)\) for every \(x^*\in X^*\), but \(h\) need not be lower semicontinuous and hence may differ from \(h^{**}=\operatorname{cl\,conv}h\).

notation.meaning: Infimal projection of F onto X

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed-convex inf-projection closure gap; conjugacy at the zero dual fiber remains exact.

source_refs.locator: D. Continuity, Closure and Growth p. 13

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x^*\in X^*\), direct conjugation of the infimal projection gives \[h^*(x^*)=\sup_{x\in X,\,y\in Y}\{\langle x^*,x\rangle-F(x,y)\}=F^*(x^*,0).\] Although \(F\) is lower semicontinuous and convex, its infimal projection \(h\) need not be lower semicontinuous because projection need not preserve closed epigraphs. Since \(h\) is proper and convex, biconjugation yields \[h^{**}=\operatorname{cl\,conv}h\le h,\] and the inequality can be strict. Thus exact recovery \(h=h^{**}\) holds precisely when \(h\) is lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even for a proper closed convex function, infimal projection can lose closedness. Conjugation remains exact at the zero dual fiber, while biconjugation recovers only the lower-semicontinuous convex hull.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure Gaps

source_witnesses.locator: D. Continuity, Closure and Growth p. 13

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h=\delta_{(0,+\infty)}\) is not lower semicontinuous and \(h^{**}=\delta_{[0,+\infty)}\ne h\).

notation.meaning: extended-real indicator of the set C
infimal projection of F onto the u-coordinate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit finite-dimensional example realizing loss of closedness under projection of a closed convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{(x,u)\in\mathbb R^2:u>0,\ x\ge u^{-1}\}\) and \(F=\delta_C\). Then \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, whereas \(h(u):=\inf_xF(x,u)=\delta_{(0,+\infty)}(u)\). Consequently \(h\) is convex but not lower semicontinuous and \(h^{**}=\delta_{[0,+\infty)}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex set can have the open positive half-line as its coordinate projection, so the associated marginal is convex but not closed and differs from its biconjugate.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Convex Inf-Projection with Nonclosed Domain

children.title: Saddle-Stationarity Geometry
children.top_down_role: Primal–dual generalized differential geometry of saddle systems.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(M\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, and \(\Lambda\subset M\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.

For every relevant \(\lambda\in\Lambda\), the slice \(L(\cdot,\lambda)\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex; for every relevant \(x\in X\), the slice \(-L(x,\cdot)\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The saddle inequalities are equivalent to \(0\in\partial(L(\cdot,\bar\lambda))(\bar x)\) and \(0\in\partial(-L(\bar x,\cdot))(\bar\lambda)+N_\Lambda(\bar\lambda)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pair \((\bar x,\bar\lambda)\in X\times\Lambda\) is a saddle point when \[L(\bar x,\lambda)\le L(\bar x,\bar\lambda)\le L(x,\bar\lambda)\qquad\text{for all }(x,\lambda)\in X\times\Lambda.\] Under the stated slice hypotheses, these inequalities are equivalent to \[0\in\partial\bigl(L(\cdot,\bar\lambda)\bigr)(\bar x),\qquad 0\in\partial\bigl(-L(\bar x,\cdot)\bigr)(\bar\lambda)+N_\Lambda(\bar\lambda).\] The first inclusion characterizes minimization of the primal slice, and the second characterizes maximization of the multiplier slice over \(\Lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex-concave saddle point is characterized by stationarity of the convex primal slice and constrained stationarity of the negative multiplier slice.

children.title: Nonconvex Duality Gaps
children.top_down_role: Discrepancies between primal and dual values in nonconvex settings.

assumptions_latex: The primal problem is minimization subject to \(g(x)\le0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d\le p\), and the extended-real difference \(p-d\) is the Lagrangian duality gap whenever the values are defined without an indeterminate form.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General inequality-constrained minimization without convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[p:=\inf\{f(x):g(x)\le0\},\qquad q(\lambda):=\inf_x\bigl(f(x)+\langle\lambda,g(x)\rangle\bigr),\qquad d:=\sup_{\lambda\ge0}q(\lambda),\] weak duality gives \(d\le p\). When the extended-real difference is well-defined, \(p-d\) is the Lagrangian duality gap; the gap is strict when \(d<p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Lagrangian dual supplies a lower bound, and the difference between primal and dual values is the duality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lagrangian Duality Gap and Weak Duality
knowledge_statements.title: Lagrangian Duality Gap and Weak Duality

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The problem is nonconvex but its primal and Lagrangian dual values both equal \(1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonconvexity permits but does not imply a positive Lagrangian duality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R}x^2\quad\text{subject to}\quad(x^2-1)^2\le0,\] the feasible set is \(\{-1,1\}\), hence the problem is nonconvex. Nevertheless, its primal value and Lagrangian dual value are both \(1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A genuinely constrained nonconvex problem can still have zero Lagrangian duality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonconvexity Does Not Force a Positive Gap
knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvexity Does Not Force a Positive Gap

assumptions_latex: \(v(u):=\inf\{f(x):g(x)\le u\}\) is a proper extended-real perturbation value function.
The Lagrangian uses multipliers \(\lambda\ge0\), so the dual variables for conjugacy are \(-\lambda\).

notation.meaning: Lower-semicontinuous convex biconjugate of the perturbation value

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lagrangian duality represented by the closed convex envelope of the perturbation value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[v(u):=\inf\{f(x):g(x)\le u\},\qquad p=v(0).\] For the standard nonnegative-multiplier Lagrangian, the dual value satisfies \[d=v^{**}(0).\] Hence \[p-d=v(0)-v^{**}(0).\] In particular, equality \(v(0)=v^{**}(0)\) eliminates the gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Lagrangian gap is the loss from replacing the perturbation value by its closed convex envelope at the reference perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Perturbation-Function Characterization of the Gap
knowledge_statements.title: Perturbation-Function Characterization of the Gap

assumptions_latex: The primal problem is \(\inf\{f(x):x\in X,\ g(x)\le0\}\), with multipliers \(\lambda\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p=1\), \(d=\sup_{\lambda\ge0}\inf_{x\in X}(f(x)+\lambda g(x))=\tfrac12\), and \(p-d=\tfrac12\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite nonconvex problem with a strict Lagrangian duality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sole feasible point is \(x=0\), so the primal value is \(p=f(0)=1\). The Lagrangian dual function is \[q(\lambda)=\inf_{x\in\{0,1\}}\{f(x)+\lambda g(x)\}=\min\{1-\lambda,\lambda\},\qquad \lambda\ge0.\] Its maximum occurs at \(\lambda=\tfrac12\), giving \[d=\sup_{\lambda\ge0}q(\lambda)=\tfrac12<1=p.\] Hence weak duality holds, but nonconvexity permits the strict gap \(p-d=\tfrac12\); the dual value cannot certify the primal optimum exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-point nonconvex problem has primal value one and Lagrangian dual value one-half, producing a strict duality gap.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Duality Gaps

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Shapley–Folkman theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexification of a finite Minkowski sum requires at most the ambient dimension many genuinely convexified summands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_i\subseteq\mathbb R^{r+1}\) be nonempty for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), let \(m>r+1\), and set \(S=S_1+\cdots+S_m\). For every \(s\in\operatorname{conv}(S)\), there exist \(s_i\in\operatorname{conv}(S_i)\) such that \[s=\sum_{i=1}^m s_i,\qquad \#\{i:s_i\notin S_i\}\leq r+1.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point in the convex hull of a Minkowski sum in R^(r+1) can be represented using points from the individual convex hulls, with at most r+1 summands outside their original sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall s\in\operatorname{conv}(S)\;\exists s_i\in\operatorname{conv}(S_i):\ s=\sum_{i=1}^m s_i,\quad\#\{i:s_i\notin S_i\}\leq r+1

children.title: Saddle Certificate Failures
children.top_down_role: Regimes where differential information does not support a saddle interpretation.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{\lambda\in\Lambda}L(x,\lambda)=\sup_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,\lambda)=0\), but no \((\bar x,\bar\lambda)\) is a saddle point because the common value is not attained in \(\Lambda\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-gap convex-concave example showing that dual attainment is independently necessary for a saddle certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X=\{0\}\), \(\Lambda=[0,+\infty)\), and \(L(0,\lambda)=-e^{-\lambda}\), both minimax values equal \(0\). The multiplier slice is continuous and concave but has no maximizer on \(\Lambda\), so no saddle pair exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex-concave problem can have zero minimax gap but no saddle certificate because the dual supremum is not attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero-Gap Saddle Failure through Nonattainment
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Gap Saddle Failure through Nonattainment

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No \((\bar x,\bar\lambda)\in X\times\Lambda\) satisfies \(L(\bar x,\lambda)\le L(\bar x,\bar\lambda)\le L(x,\bar\lambda)\) for all \((x,\lambda)\in X\times\Lambda\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict duality gap prevents existence of a primal-dual saddle certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x=0\), one has \(L(0,\lambda)=1-\lambda\), whose maximum over \(\lambda\ge0\) occurs at \(\lambda=0\); however, \(x=0\) does not minimize \(L(\cdot,0)\). For \(x=1\), one has \(L(1,\lambda)=\lambda\), which has no maximum on \(\Lambda\). Therefore neither primal point can participate in a saddle pair. Equivalently, the strict gap \(\sup_{\lambda\ge0}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,\lambda)=\tfrac12<1\) rules out any saddle certificate attaining the primal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the finite gap example, neither primal point can form a saddle pair, so no saddle certificate recovers the primal optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Saddle Certificate Failures

children.title: Multiplier Certificate Failures
children.top_down_role: Regimes where multipliers fail to provide exact or informative certificates.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\bar x,\bar\lambda)=(0,0)\) satisfies KKT, but \(\bar x\) is a strict local maximum and is not a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of KKT sufficiency despite a valid multiplier tuple.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R}-x^2\quad\text{subject to}\quad x^2-1\le0,\] the pair \((\bar x,\bar\lambda)=(0,0)\) satisfies primal feasibility, dual feasibility, complementarity, and stationarity. Nevertheless, \(\bar x=0\) is a strict local maximum and is not a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconvex problem can have a valid KKT multiplier at a strict local maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: KKT Multipliers Need Not Certify Optimality in Nonconvex Problems
knowledge_statements.title: KKT Multipliers Need Not Certify Optimality in Nonconvex Problems

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible optimizer is unique, while the multiplier set \(\{(\mu_1,\mu_2):1+\mu_1+2\mu_2=0\}\) is infinite.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonuniqueness of equality multipliers under linearly dependent constraint gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min_x x\) subject to \(x=0\) and \(2x=0\), the unique feasible point is \(\bar x=0\), but its equality-multiplier set is \[\{(\mu_1,\mu_2):1+\mu_1+2\mu_2=0\},\] which is infinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Redundant constraints can leave a unique optimizer with infinitely many multiplier certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Redundancy Destroys Multiplier Identifiability
knowledge_statements.title: Redundancy Destroys Multiplier Identifiability

assumptions_latex: A classical multiplier certificate requires \(\lambda\ge0\), stationarity, feasibility, and complementarity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unique feasible optimizer is \(\bar x=0\), but no \(\lambda\ge0\) satisfies \(1+2\lambda\bar x=0\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of multiplier existence when the active constraint has zero derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The constraint \(x^2\le0\) forces \(x=0\), so \(\bar x=0\) is the unique global minimizer. A KKT multiplier would have to satisfy \[0=f'(\bar x)+\lambda g'(\bar x)=1+2\lambda\bar x,\qquad \lambda\ge0,\qquad \lambda g(\bar x)=0.\] At \(\bar x=0\), stationarity reduces to \(0=1\), independently of \(\lambda\). Thus no multiplier certificate exists. The failure is caused by degeneracy of the active constraint, since \(g'(0)=0\), and illustrates why a constraint qualification is needed for multiplier necessity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degenerate active constraint yields a unique optimizer but no KKT multiplier, demonstrating failure of multiplier certification without constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier Certificate Failures

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(\bar\lambda\ge0\) such that \((\bar x,\bar\lambda)\) is a saddle point, satisfies KKT conditions, and yields zero duality gap.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the program \(\min_x f(x)\) subject to \(g_i(x)\le0\), Slater's condition and primal attainment imply the existence of \(\bar\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\) such that \[0\in\partial f(\bar x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\bar\lambda_i\partial g_i(\bar x),\qquad g_i(\bar x)\le0,\qquad \bar\lambda_i g_i(\bar x)=0.\] Moreover, \((\bar x,\bar\lambda)\) satisfies \[L(\bar x,\lambda)\le L(\bar x,\bar\lambda)\le L(x,\bar\lambda)\] for all \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\). Consequently, the dual optimum is attained and equals the primal optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an attained convex program satisfying Slater's condition, KKT multipliers exist, a saddle certificate holds, and the duality gap vanishes.
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Recovery Regimes
